# EUDI Wallet: Relying Party Integration Flows

**DR-0002** · Published · Last updated 2026-07-26 · ~42,000 lines

> Exhaustive investigation of the EU Digital Identity Wallet ecosystem from the Relying Party (RP) perspective. Covers every RP-facing flow at protocol depth: registration with Member State Registrars (CIR 2025/848, TS2/TS5/TS6 registration baseline, ETSI TS 119 475 certificate-facing mappings), trust infrastructure (Access Certificates, Registration Certificates, Trusted Lists, issuer-side WIA/KA assurance, Certificate Transparency, the ETSI TR 119 411-9 CT ecosystem/governance layer, and ETSI TS 119 615 trusted-list interpretation for qualified-status conclusions), remote presentation (same-device and secure local cross-device mediation through the W3C Digital Credentials API where supported, plus controlled redirects/QR compatibility paths, with SD-JWT VC and mdoc verification sharpened by the ETSI TS 119 472-2 presentation profile and ETSI TS 119 472-1 semantic baseline), proximity presentation (supervised and unsupervised via ISO/IEC 18013-5), wallet-to-wallet interactions (TS9), SCA for electronic payments (TS12, PSD2 Dynamic Linking, OID4VCI SCA attestation issuance, and the adjacent bank/PSP certificate-profile layer for PSD2/open-banking `QWAC` / `QSealC` semantics via ETSI TS 119 495), pseudonym-based authentication (Use Cases A–D, WebAuthn credential binding, progressive assurance), combined presentations via DCQL (multi-attestation identity matching), data deletion requests (TS7), DPA reporting (TS8), the intermediary architecture, and document signing with remote Qualified Electronic Signatures (QES through the CIR 2026/1731-selected ETSI TS 119 432 V1.3.1 profile, three signing flow patterns — QTSP Web Portal / Wallet-Channelled / RP-Channelled, document retrieval protocol, and PAdES/XAdES/CAdES/JAdES signature formats). Extends beyond protocol flows into production engineering: a cryptographic verification pipeline deep-dive (signature, revocation, device binding, user binding, issuer trust), RP verification architecture patterns (policy engine tiers, webhook delegation, callback integration, session management, policy-as-code), a 16-vendor evaluation matrix with unified capability scoring, ecosystem readiness assessment (W3C DC API browser support, Member State wallet implementations, interoperability testing), WSCD architecture taxonomy (local, remote, external, hybrid), cross-border presentation scenarios (LoTE discovery, language handling, attribute compatibility), a §31 security threat model plus Appendix D 45-threat card catalogue (STRIDE classification, CIR 2024/2981 Annex I risk register traceability, MITRE CWE mapping, Mermaid attack sequence diagrams, step-by-step walkthroughs, concrete protocol payloads, and audit telemetry), a consolidated risk assessment matrix, a named Verification Signal Intelligence (VSI) taxonomy with three-layer classification and SIEM integration schema, and operational readiness guidance (monitoring metrics, alert triggers, structured audit trail with per-credential verification result objects). Includes exact protocol payloads (SD-JWT VC, mdoc DeviceResponse, JWE envelopes, DC API parameters), annotated Mermaid sequence diagrams with step-by-step walkthroughs, a Status List verification deep-dive appendix, regulatory compliance mapping (eIDAS 2.0, PSD2/PSR, GDPR, DORA, AML/KYC), a persona-based reading guide, and a 43-step implementation checklist. Applicable to banks, financial institutions, public sector bodies, and any entity integrating with the EUDI Wallet as a Relying Party.

## Reader Orientation

This document is easiest to read if the EUDI Wallet is treated first as a natural-person presentation system, and only then as a platform for regulated, sector-specific, legal-person, payment, intermediary, and signing extensions. The baseline RP question is simple but strict: what did the Wallet User disclose, from which Wallet Unit, under which RP request, and what verifier evidence survives before the RP makes a service decision?

The later chapters deliberately expand that baseline. A bank adds AML/KYC, PSD2 SCA, DORA, and payment certificate concerns. A public-sector RP adds public-task and authentic-source constraints. A retail RP may need only an age predicate or a small PID subset. A B2B flow adds LPID and mandates. A QES flow adds signing-application and QTSP boundaries. Those cases are important, but they are extensions of the ordinary Wallet User -> Wallet Unit -> RP presentation path.

---

> **Note**: Read the document by integration track, not by assuming the richest bank path is the universal case.

### Executive Decision Summary

This research formalizes every RP-facing integration flow in the EUDI Wallet ecosystem, but the decision surface starts with the natural-person baseline: a registered RP asks a Wallet User for PID or a narrow attestation, the Wallet authenticates the RP before disclosure, the User approves or rejects the request, and the RP verifier converts the response into decision-grade evidence. Remote, proximity, W2W, SCA, EBW/LPID, intermediary, and QES flows all reuse or extend that baseline rather than replacing it.

:::important[EUDI Wallet acceptance is a regulated integration program, not a narrow feature add-on]
The critical path is not just a presentation-layer UX project. Registration, trust infrastructure, request construction, verifier architecture, minimisation policy, sector-specific compliance, deletion/reporting obligations, and operating-model decisions all have to line up before the RP can rely on Wallet-presented evidence in production.
:::

#### Top Integration Decisions

**Universal RP Baseline**

1. **Start from the Wallet User/PID disclosure loop, not from the bank or EBW special case** — every RP needs to understand the baseline natural-person path before adding payment SCA, LPID/mandates, QES, or intermediary operation. The verifier result is the RP's evidence artifact; the Wallet response itself is not the business decision.
2. **Register with the national Registrar before building production request flows** — registration is the prerequisite for Wallet-facing RP authentication material, public RP metadata, use-case/purpose visibility, and the Access Certificate path. Delays here compress every later implementation workstream.
3. **Make data minimisation executable in the request layer** — PID can carry broad identity data, but the RP should request only the attributes needed for the service. Age, pseudonym, address-dependent, and AML/KYC flows should produce different DCQL and policy bundles rather than one universal identity request.
4. **Treat verification as a decision-grade pipeline, not a boolean library call** — issuer signature, credential status, holder binding, request satisfaction, policy outcome, and audit evidence are separate facts. The verifier should preserve per-check evidence for compliance, monitoring, and incident reconstruction.

**High-Assurance and Sector Extensions**

5. **Support both SD-JWT VC and mdoc where your use cases require both credential families** — the two stacks have different selective-disclosure, holder-binding, device-authentication, and trust-anchor mechanics. A high-assurance RP cannot collapse them into one parser abstraction without losing evidence.
6. **Implement HAIP/OpenID4VP and DCQL as the remote-presentation baseline, then tighten with ETSI presentation-profile requirements where applicable** — request construction has to bind purpose, audience, nonce/state, response encryption, credential query, and RP authentication material before the Wallet response arrives.
7. **For banks and PSPs, separate Wallet RP trust from PSD2/open-banking institution trust** — WRPAC/WRPRC and Wallet SCA solve Wallet-facing presentation and RP authentication; QWAC/QSealC, QCStatements, and NCA/EBA register-backed roles solve open-banking institution authorization. They may coexist, but they are not interchangeable.
8. **Choose Direct RP, Intermediary, or Hybrid operation early** — the Direct RP model gives the RP direct control over request construction and verifier evidence; intermediary models delegate interaction but introduce Art. 5b(10), data-forwarding, tenant isolation, audit, and third-party-risk constraints.

**Operations, Readiness, and Forward-Compatible Tracks**

9. **Build status-list, trusted-list, Wallet-assurance, and CT-readiness handling as operational dependencies** — LoTE endpoints, national trusted lists where qualified status matters, status services, certification/breach evidence, issuer-side WIA/KA dependencies for dual-role organisations, and Access Certificate validity create hard failure modes that should be monitored like production infrastructure.
10. **Implement deletion, DPA-reporting, audit, and monitoring infrastructure alongside presentation flows** — post-presentation obligations are not a late compliance appendix. They depend on the same request snapshot, registered contacts, purpose text, verifier result, and transaction-log evidence that the runtime flow produces.
11. **Keep pseudonym, age, combined-presentation, LPID/mandate, and QES support modular** — these tracks have different maturity and binding assumptions. The RP should design extension points for future ZKP profiles and combined-presentation proof formats without forcing all users through full PID disclosure.
12. **Maintain separate evidence registers for certification, conformance, accessibility, readiness, and legal compliance** — wallet certification, CAB scope, OIDF conformance, sandbox evidence, vendor accessibility evidence, and RP compliance approvals answer different questions. Do not substitute one for another in go-live gates.

#### RP Integration Model Selector

Your EUDI integration architecture is shaped by three dimensions: the **baseline evidence loop** every RP must own, the **engineering model** used to operate that loop, and the **sector/legal extension** that changes the request or verification policy. The quadrant chart below still captures the build/buy and corporate-structure decision, but it should be read after the baseline Wallet/RP evidence loop is understood.

```mermaid

    title Where Does Your RP Sit?
    x-axis "Standalone Entity" --> "Cross-border Group"
    y-axis "Limited Capacity" --> "Strong Capacity"
    quadrant-1 "Self-Hosted / Hybrid"
    quadrant-2 "Vendor Connector"
    quadrant-3 "SaaS Intermediary"
    quadrant-4 "Vendor + Group IT"

    "Insurance": [0.60, 0.58]
```

Each quadrant implies a deployment model: **bottom-left** -> SaaS Intermediary; **bottom-right** -> Vendor Connector plus Group IT intermediary registration; **top-left** -> Direct RP plus vendor verifier components; **top-right** -> Self-Hosted / Hybrid with full request, verifier, policy, and audit control. Corporate groups add the Group Intermediary registration pattern: one group IT entity may operate as an intermediary RP, while each subsidiary remains accountable for its end-RP registration, purposes, and evidence obligations. Cross-border groups additionally require per-Member-State registration through the applicable home Member State path; passporting does not remove RP registration obligations.

| Sector | Typical zone | Baseline credential pattern | Extension pressure | Key regulation |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Bank / PSP | Strong × group/cross-border | PID + SCA + selected PuB-EAA | AML/KYC, PSD2 SCA, DORA, open-banking certificate coexistence | eIDAS, PSD2/PSR, AMLD, DORA |
| Public sector | Moderate × standalone | PID + PuB-EAA | public-task basis, authentic-source attributes, accessibility, cross-border language handling | eIDAS, GDPR Art. 6(1)(e), sector law |
| Healthcare | Limited-moderate × standalone | PID + health-sector attestations | special-category data, professional credentials, consent boundaries | GDPR Art. 9, sector EAAs |
| VLOP / telecom | Strong × cross-border | PID subset, age attestation, pseudonym | mandatory wallet acceptance, age assurance, anti-linkability | eIDAS Art. 5f(2), DSA, EECC |
| Insurance | Moderate × group | PID + address + vehicle/professional attestations | cross-border entities, DORA, claim-specific evidence | Solvency II, DORA, GDPR |
| eCommerce / retail | Limited-moderate × standalone | age predicate, birth-date fallback, narrow PID | minimisation, return flows, deletion/reporting contacts | eIDAS Art. 5b, GDPR |
| B2B / corporate service | Moderate-strong × group | PID + LPID + mandate | representative-vs-organisation binding, EBW maturity | eIDAS 2.0, company/register law |

#### Top Open Risks

1. **Combined-presentation cryptographic binding is still a maturity risk** — the current high-level requirements identify the need, but deployed proof formats remain unsettled. Until standardised, RPs must distinguish presentation-level, attribute-level, and policy-level binding rather than assuming multi-credential identity matching is cryptographically solved.
2. **EU-governed Certificate Transparency for WRPACs is not a settled deployment baseline** — access-certificate CT logging and SCT handling are important for Wallet-side RP authentication, but log admission, lifecycle, governance, and Member State operational practice remain architecture risks.
3. **W2W verifier authentication is a category exception** — in Wallet-to-Wallet flows, the verifier may be another Wallet User without WRPAC or registration-certificate material. Most ordinary RP trust infrastructure does not apply.
4. **ZKP-based selective disclosure remains forward-compatible architecture, not a universal production baseline** — RPs should keep proof-type interfaces pluggable, but ordinary PID, age-attestation, and predicate fallbacks still have to work without assuming broadly deployed ZKP profiles.
5. **Data deletion is contact/process based rather than one standard machine API** — TS7-style deletion surfaces span browser, email, and phone channels. The RP must register usable contacts and build an auditable process rather than waiting for one universal deletion endpoint.
6. **SCA attestation identification is profile- and rulebook-driven** — RPs must dispatch by requested attestation type, category, profile, and Rulebook semantics instead of hard-coding one VCT or one bank-only interpretation.
7. **Device binding is evidence, not a universal policy knob** — RPs must handle both device-bound and non-device-bound attestations. High-assurance services can prefer or require stronger evidence only where the credential profile and legal basis support that requirement.
8. **QES architecture has additional actor and certificate-model boundaries beyond the Wallet presentation baseline** — CSC, QTSP, signing application, WSCD/remote QSCD, document retrieval, and signature format choices should be treated as a separate advanced track, not as the ordinary identity-presentation model.

#### How to Use This Document

Start with the baseline mental model below unless you already understand the Wallet User, Wallet Unit, PID/attestation, request, verifier, and audit boundaries. Then follow the track that matches your integration pressure: trust/registration, presentation mechanics, regulated high assurance, sector blueprint, vendor/intermediary architecture, security/operations, or QES. The bank/PSP path remains the richest worked example, but it is no longer the only entry point into the document.

---

## Context and Scope

The **European Digital Identity Wallet (EUDI Wallet)** is the centrepiece of the revised eIDAS Regulation ([Regulation (EU) 2024/1183](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32024R1183)), commonly known as **eIDAS 2.0**. By **24 December 2026**, every EU Member State must provide at least one EUDI Wallet to its citizens. By **24 December 2027**, regulated private-sector entities — including banks, payment service providers, telecom operators, healthcare providers, and very large online platforms — **must accept** the EUDI Wallet for user identification, authentication, and, where applicable, Strong Customer Authentication.

This investigation examines the EUDI Wallet ecosystem **exclusively from the Relying Party (RP) perspective** — the entity that requests, verifies, minimises, stores, rejects, or relies on credentials presented by Wallet Users. The document is for all RPs, not only banks. The bank/PSP remains the richest recurring worked example because it combines mandatory wallet acceptance, AML/KYC onboarding, PSD2 SCA, DORA resilience, high-assurance audit, certificate-profile coexistence, and cross-border operating complexity in one integration programme.

The scope is therefore layered. The ordinary natural-person presentation path is the baseline; each later use case changes the request policy, evidence boundary, legal basis, or operational duty on top of that path.

### First-Wave Baseline vs Extension Tracks

| Track | Reader question | Covered by |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Universal natural-person baseline** | How does an RP request and verify PID or a narrow attestation from a Wallet User? | Core Wallet and RP Mental Model; RP Registration; DCQL; Remote Presentation; Verification; RP Obligations |
| **Regulated high-assurance baseline** | What extra evidence is needed for AML/KYC, LoA, status, audit, and cross-border reliance? | PID/minimisation; trust infrastructure; cryptographic verification pipeline; regulatory compliance |
| **Sector extension** | What changes for banks, PSPs, healthcare, public sector, telecom, VLOPs, insurance, or eCommerce? | Sector blueprints; compliance mapping; monitoring and operational readiness |
| **Legal-person extension** | What changes when the subject is an organisation or a representative acting for one? | EBW, LPID, mandate credentials, representative binding, combined presentations |
| **Advanced product extension** | What changes for payment SCA, pseudonyms, age predicates, intermediary models, QES, or vendor delegation? | Specialized flows, advanced identity/query patterns, QES signing, intermediary and vendor architecture |

---

### Why Now?

1. **Regulatory deadline pressure** — The 24 December 2027 mandate for private-sector acceptance is about 20 months away. Banks and financial institutions must begin integration planning now to meet the timeline.
2. **Specification maturity** — The RP-critical Technical Specifications are concrete enough to implement against, but they no longer sit at one version/maturity level: TS2 is V1.0.1, TS5 V1.3, TS6 V1.0.1, TS7/TS8 V0.11, TS9 V1.1, TS10 V1.2, TS11 V1.0.1, TS12 V1.0, and TS1 V1.2. Published ETSI baselines include TS 119 475, TS 119 478, EN 319 401, TS 119 472-1/-2, TS 119 615, and TS 119 495. The EN 319 482 series, EN 319 486, EN 319 487, TS 119 476-2, and TS 119 476-3 remain draft/work-programme source-watch items. OpenID4VP 1.0 achieved Final status in July 2025; HAIP 1.0 was approved in December 2025. The document's July 2026 evidence baseline uses the locally cloned ARF v3.0.0 release and reflects 27+ adopted CIRs.
3. **Pilot programme insights** — The EU Large-Scale Pilots (POTENTIAL, EWC, DC4EU, NOBID) have generated real-world implementation experience that informs the flows documented here. Their evidence informs architecture and readiness choices, but it does not create RP requirements unless the ARF, Annex 2, a Technical Specification, a Rulebook, or binding law carries the requirement forward.
4. **SCA integration** — TS12 (SCA Implementation with Wallet, v1.0 December 2025) defines the complete payment authentication flow using EUDI Wallet, creating an urgent integration requirement for banks under PSD2.
5. **Trust infrastructure deployment** — Member States are establishing Registrars, Access Certificate Authorities, and national registries per CIR 2025/848, creating the operational infrastructure that RPs must integrate with.

---

### Scope

#### In Scope

- Identifier and trust model analysis: X.509 vs. DIDs, platform wallet landscape, and RP DID requirements
- Complete RP registration flow with Member State Registrar (CIR 2025/848, TS2/TS5/TS6 registration baseline, ETSI TS 119 475 mappings)
- Trust infrastructure: Access Certificates (WRPAC), Registration Certificates (WRPRC), Trusted Lists, issuer-mediated Wallet trust with issuance-only WIA/KA, Certificate Transparency with the ETSI TR 119 411-9 ecosystem/governance layer, and ETSI TS 119 615-based trusted-list interpretation for qualified-status conclusions
- Credential format internals: SD-JWT VC (selective disclosure, Key Binding JWT) and mdoc (MSO, namespaces, device binding)
- Remote presentation: same-device and cross-device flows via OpenID4VP (HAIP 1.0, DCQL, ETSI TS 119 472-2 presentation profile)
- Proximity presentation: supervised and unsupervised flows via ISO/IEC 18013-5
- Wallet-to-wallet interactions (TS9) — where the RP is another Wallet User acting as Verifier
- SCA for electronic payments: issuer-requested and third-party-requested flows (TS12, PSD2)
- Bank/PSP certificate-profile cross-links: PSD2/open-banking `QWAC` / `QSealC`, `QCStatement` semantics, and NCA/EBA register-backed role interpretation (ETSI TS 119 495)
- Document signing: RP integration with qualified electronic signature flows (wallet-channelled, RP-channelled, QTSP web portal), the CIR 2026/1731-selected ETSI TS 119 432 V1.3.1 clauses, companion CSC API behavior, Document Retrieval protocol, and PAdES signature formats
- Pseudonym-based authentication (Use Cases A–D, WebAuthn integration)
- Combined presentations via DCQL (multi-attestation requests)
- RP obligations: data deletion (TS7), DPA reporting (TS8), embedded disclosure policy evaluation
- Intermediary model and trust flows
- Regulatory compliance: eIDAS 2.0 obligations, PSD2/PSR SCA bridge, GDPR, AML/KYC, DORA
- W3C Digital Credentials API implications for RP integration

#### Out of Scope

- Wallet Provider implementation internals, except where WSCA/WSCD architecture, key-management, WUA/WIA, certification, or lifecycle evidence changes RP-visible assurance, UX, or verification policy
- PID Provider and Attestation Provider issuance internals (covered only where they intersect RP flows)
- Wallet Solution certification by CABs (covered at a high level for RP trust assessment)
- National-level implementation variations (each Member State's specific registration procedures)
- Cross-surface consistency monitoring (read-replica lag, cache invalidation, webhook/API timing discrepancies between downstream surfaces — these are infrastructure/observability concerns, not verifier-engine defects; the verifier writes one canonical result and downstream disagreement is detected externally)

---

## Core Wallet and RP Mental Model

This group establishes the baseline path that the rest of the document extends: a natural-person Wallet User controls a Wallet Unit, the RP requests PID or another attestation for a defined purpose, the Wallet authenticates the RP before disclosure, the User approves or rejects the request, and the RP verifier turns the response into decision-grade evidence before any business process relies on it.

---

### 1. Baseline: Wallet User, Wallet Unit, PID, and Attestations

The simplest EUDI Wallet relying-party integration is not a legal-person mandate, a payment SCA ceremony, a QES signing flow, or an intermediary topology. It is a natural person presenting a PID or narrowly scoped attestation from a Wallet Unit to a registered RP, with the Wallet authenticating the RP before disclosure, the User approving the request, and the RP validating the returned evidence before any business decision relies on it.

That baseline matters because every later extension composes with it. A bank onboarding flow adds AML/KYC policy and recordkeeping. An age-verification flow removes most identity attributes and prefers a predicate or age attestation. A B2B flow adds LPID and mandate binding. A QES flow adds signing-application and trust-service boundaries. None of those extensions makes sense unless the reader first understands the ordinary natural-person presentation path.

:::important[The Wallet helps the RP obtain evidence; it does not make the RP's business decision]
The Wallet authenticates the RP to the User, helps the User disclose selected credentials, and returns signed evidence. The RP still owns credential validation, request-policy satisfaction, data minimisation, audit evidence, and the final service decision. A presentation response is therefore an input to the RP's verifier and policy engine, not an automatic login, onboarding, payment, or entitlement result.
:::

#### 1.1 Baseline Runtime Model

The baseline flow has three actors on the runtime path and several trust actors behind them. The User controls a Wallet Unit. The RP requests attributes for a service. Issuers and trust infrastructure provide the evidence that the RP and Wallet consume.

```mermaid
---
config:
  flowchart:
    nodeSpacing: 45
    rankSpacing: 55
---
flowchart LR
    User(("`**Wallet User**
    Natural person
    approves disclosure`"))
    WU["`**Wallet Unit**
    Stores PID and attestations
    presents selected attributes`"]
    RP["`**Relying Party**
    Requests attributes
    verifies evidence
    makes service decision`"]
    SVC["`**RP Service**
    Service ID and intended use
    scopes request and certificates`"]

    REG["`**Registrar / Certificate CAs**
    RP registration
    Service-scoped WRPAC / WRPRC`"]
    PIDP["`**PID Provider**
    Issues natural-person PID`"]
    AP["`**Attestation Provider**
    Issues QEAA / PuB-EAA / EAA`"]
    TRUST["`**Trusted Lists / LoTE / Status**
    Issuer trust, Wallet trust,
    revocation and suspension evidence`"]

    User -->|"controls / activates"| WU
    RP -->|"operates"| SVC
    SVC -->|"signed request for PID / attributes"| WU
    WU -->|"RP identity and purpose shown to User"| User
    User -->|"approves or rejects disclosure"| WU
    WU -->|"presentation response"| RP

    REG -. "RP and Service authentication material" .-> SVC
    PIDP -. "PID issuance" .-> WU
    AP -. "attestation issuance" .-> WU
    TRUST -. "trust and status evidence" .-> RP
    TRUST -. "RP trust evidence" .-> WU
```

The diagram deliberately separates the runtime path from the trust path. Runtime presentation is a Wallet-to-RP interaction mediated by User consent. Trust establishment is broader: the Wallet needs to authenticate the RP before disclosure, and the RP needs to authenticate issuers, credential status, Wallet assurance signals, and holder-binding evidence before relying on the returned data.

| Runtime question | Actor that answers it | Evidence consumed by the RP |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Who is asking the User for data? | Wallet authenticates the RP and current Service using the carried registration and access material | One applicable WRPRC by value, the matching WRPAC, their authorized LoTE/status chains, and request-signature evidence |
| What did the User approve? | Wallet shows request details and collects consent | Request object, purpose text, DCQL query, Wallet transaction log context |
| Is the presented credential genuine? | RP verifier validates credential cryptography and issuer trust | SD-JWT VC issuer signature, mdoc MSO, issuer certificate or trusted-list evidence |
| Is the credential current? | RP verifier checks validity and status according to format and Rulebook | `exp`, `nbf`, MSO validity, Status List / revocation result |
| Is the presenter bound to the credential for this session? | RP verifier checks holder binding | KB-JWT, `cnf`, mdoc DeviceAuth, nonce, audience, SessionTranscript |
| Does the evidence satisfy the service policy? | RP policy engine evaluates business and legal purpose | DCQL result, attribute set, LoA, minimisation policy, sector policy |
| What survives for audit? | RP emits canonical result and redacted evidence | verification result id, policy id, check results, VSI signals, audit correlation id |

#### 1.2 Core Terms

The early document uses these terms consistently before introducing EBW, SCA, QES, or sector-specific variants.

| Term | Baseline meaning | RP implementation consequence |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Wallet User** | The natural person controlling the Wallet Unit and deciding whether to disclose attributes | Treat consent and credential subject as related but distinct concepts; the User approves disclosure, but each credential's subject model still comes from the Rulebook |
| **Wallet Unit** | The User-controlled wallet instance that stores and presents PID and attestations | Do not assume one physical person has exactly one Wallet Unit; multi-wallet and migration cases create different keys and pseudonyms |
| **PID** | Person Identification Data for a natural person, issued by a PID Provider | Treat as the first-wave identity baseline; request only the attributes needed for the service |
| **Attestation** | A signed attribute credential other than PID, such as QEAA, PuB-EAA, or EAA | Verify the Rulebook-defined subject model before treating the attributes as identifying the Wallet User |
| **Relying Party** | The service provider requesting attributes from the Wallet Unit | Register intended use, authenticate to the Wallet, verify returned evidence, and enforce minimisation |
| **RP Instance** | A specific software/hardware system the RP uses to interact with Wallet Units | Bind WRPACs, callbacks, request snapshots, tenants, and audit evidence to the correct instance |
| **Verifier** | The RP-side component that turns a presentation response into a decision-grade result | Preserve per-check evidence; do not collapse verification to a library boolean |

#### 1.3 PID Is the Natural-Person Baseline

PID is the natural-person identity credential that most first-wave RP flows start from. It is not the only credential in the ecosystem, but it is the reader's baseline for understanding Wallet presentation. The RP should understand PID before it tries to reason about LPID, mandates, SCA attestations, age attestations, education credentials, or document-signing flows.

| PID element group | Typical identifiers | Baseline RP use | Minimisation warning |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Core identity | `family_name`, `given_name`, `birthdate` / `birth_date`, `place_of_birth`, `nationalities` / `nationality` | KYC, legal contract identity, public-service eligibility, high-assurance account recovery | Do not request full core identity when a predicate or single attribute is enough |
| Residence | `address.*` in SD-JWT VC; `resident_*` in mdoc | delivery, jurisdiction, billing, regulated onboarding where address is required | Optional attributes vary by Member State; design graceful fallback |
| Administrative identifier | `personal_administrative_number` | national identity matching where law and national scheme permit use | High sensitivity; do not treat as universal cross-border key |
| Contact attributes | `email`, `phone_number` / `email_address`, `mobile_phone_number` | contactability when a rule or service requires it | Contact channels may be better collected directly from the User under RP policy |
| Portrait / visual evidence | `picture` / `portrait` | supervised or high-risk visual comparison where legally justified | Biometric and special-category constraints may apply outside ordinary verification |
| Validity / issuer metadata | `exp`, `nbf`, `date_of_expiry`, `issuing_authority`, `issuing_country` | proof validation, trust routing, audit | Usually consumed by the verifier; do not request metadata as application claims unless needed |

:::note[Mandatory in PID is not mandatory to request]
The PID Rulebook can define mandatory attributes inside the credential, but the RP's request still has to satisfy purpose limitation and data minimisation. An RP proving age should not request full name and address merely because those fields may exist in PID. A bank performing customer due diligence may need a wider set. A retail age gate should prefer an age attestation, predicate, or minimal birth-date fallback.
:::

#### 1.4 PID, QEAA, PuB-EAA, and EAA

The RP should treat "credential presented by this Wallet Unit" as a presentation fact first. The credential's subject and legal meaning come from its category and Rulebook.

| Credential class | What it usually proves | Example RP use | Verification consequence |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **PID** | Natural-person identity attributes issued by a PID Provider | account opening, public-service access, high-assurance identity proofing | Verify issuer trust, status, validity, holder binding, and requested claims |
| **QEAA** | Qualified electronic attestation of attributes under qualified trust-service rules | regulated qualification or attribute proof where qualified status matters | Verify qualified trust status and Rulebook-specific attribute semantics |
| **PuB-EAA** | Public-sector body attestation or authentic-source-backed public attribute | education, professional status, vehicle or public-register attributes | Verify public-sector issuer trust, status, and subject relationship |
| **EAA** | Non-qualified electronic attestation of attributes | loyalty, membership, non-qualified claims, private-sector attributes | Verify issuer trust according to applicable scheme and RP risk policy |
| **Pseudonym / authentication credential** | Repeated or unlinkability-conscious authentication handle | returning-user sign-in where legal identity is not required | Do not force PID where Art. 5b(9) requires pseudonym acceptance |
| **Age attestation / predicate** | Age threshold without full identity | retail, gambling, social media, adult-content gating | Prefer minimal disclosure; full PID fallback should be exceptional and justified |

Subject models matter because not every credential presented from the same Wallet Unit names the same kind of subject:

| Subject model | RP interpretation |
|:--|:--|
| Natural-person subject | The credential can identify the Wallet User only after issuer trust, status, holder binding, and any Rulebook-required checks pass |
| Object or asset subject | The credential proves something about an object; the RP still needs the Rulebook-defined relationship between User and object |
| Representation or mandate subject | The credential connects a representative to another natural or legal person; do not collapse representative and represented party |
| Bearer-style / no-subject credential | Valid possession may be the relevant fact unless the Rulebook adds User binding or PID co-verification |

ETSI TR 119 479-1 adds useful vocabulary for this boundary. An RP should not infer role identity from the delivery channel: the entity that requested issuance, the entity described by the attributes, the entity that received the EAA, the Wallet or vault holder, and the final relying party can be different actors.

| EAA role | RP interpretation |
|:--|:--|
| **Subscriber** | Entity entitled to request issuance or subscribe to the EAA service. It may be the subject, but it can also request an EAA about another person, legal person, object, or entitlement. |
| **Attribute Subject** | Person, legal person, object, or relationship the attributes describe. This is the first question the RP must answer before using the claims. |
| **EAA Recipient** | Entity that receives the issued EAA. The recipient can be the Wallet User, a business wallet, a vault holder, or another authorized recipient. |
| **Wallet / Vault Holder** | Storage and presentation controller. Wallet possession can supply holder-binding evidence; vault delivery usually cannot prove third-party presentation control by itself. |
| **Authorized Party** | Entity allowed by the applicable EAA Policy to request revocation or lifecycle change. This is not automatically the same as the RP. |
| **Relying Party / Intermediary** | Entity that consumes the EAA or a verified result. It must verify the subject model, recipient/presenter relationship, and binding evidence before relying on the attributes. |

#### 1.5 Minimal Request Patterns

The RP's business purpose should drive the DCQL request. These examples are intentionally compact; the full DCQL chapter later defines format negotiation, credential sets, fallback behavior, and profile-specific request details.

##### 1.5.1 Age Threshold Fallback Using PID

An RP that cannot use a dedicated age attestation or ZKP proof may request only the birth-date claim and compute the threshold locally.

```json
{
  "credentials": [
    {
      "id": "pid_age_fallback",
      "format": "dc+sd-jwt",
      "meta": { "vct_values": ["urn:eudi:pid:1"] },
      "claims": [
        { "path": ["birthdate"] }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "credential_sets": [
    {
      "purpose": "Verify age eligibility without collecting full identity",
      "options": [["pid_age_fallback"]]
    }
  ]
}
```

The verifier still checks issuer trust, status, validity, holder binding, and request satisfaction. The business layer then computes the threshold and stores only the minimum evidence required by policy.

##### 1.5.2 Retail Identity Check

A retail or ecommerce RP that needs identity for a regulated transaction may request name and birth date without automatically requesting address, administrative number, portrait, or contact fields.

```json
{
  "credentials": [
    {
      "id": "pid_identity",
      "format": "dc+sd-jwt",
      "meta": { "vct_values": ["urn:eudi:pid:1"] },
      "claims": [
        { "path": ["given_name"] },
        { "path": ["family_name"] },
        { "path": ["birthdate"] }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "credential_sets": [
    {
      "purpose": "Verify customer identity for regulated purchase",
      "options": [["pid_identity"]]
    }
  ]
}
```

##### 1.5.3 Address-Dependent Flow

When address is required, the RP should request address attributes explicitly and treat absence as a policy outcome rather than a verifier defect, because optional PID attributes vary by Member State.

```json
{
  "credentials": [
    {
      "id": "pid_address",
      "format": "dc+sd-jwt",
      "meta": { "vct_values": ["urn:eudi:pid:1"] },
      "claims": [
        { "path": ["given_name"] },
        { "path": ["family_name"] },
        { "path": ["address", "formatted"] },
        { "path": ["address", "country"] }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "credential_sets": [
    {
      "purpose": "Verify customer identity and residence for service eligibility",
      "options": [["pid_address"]]
    }
  ]
}
```

#### 1.6 Normal Presentation Walkthrough

The sequence below shows the baseline remote-presentation ceremony before any sector extension changes the request. Its main point is boundary discipline: transport receipt, RP authentication to the Wallet, User approval, credential verification, policy evaluation, and audit evidence are related but not interchangeable facts.

```mermaid
---
config:
  themeVariables:
    noteBkgColor: "transparent"
    noteBorderColor: "transparent"
  sequence:
    messageAlign: left
    noteAlign: left
    actorMargin: 250
---
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant User as Wallet User
    participant RP as Relying Party
    participant Wallet as Wallet Unit
    participant Registrar as RP Certificate Trust
    participant Trust as Issuer Trust and Status
    participant Verifier as RP Verifier
    participant Policy as RP Policy / Audit

    RP->>RP: Create request snapshot and DCQL query
    RP->>Wallet: Send signed presentation request
    Wallet->>Registrar: Validate carried WRPAC / WRPRC<br/>chain, status, identifiers, scope
    Registrar-->>Wallet: Return certificate trust<br/>and status outcome
    Wallet->>User: Show RP, purpose, and requested attributes
    User-->>Wallet: Approve selected disclosure
    Wallet-->>RP: Return presentation response
    RP->>Verifier: Submit response and immutable request snapshot
    Verifier->>Trust: Resolve issuer trust and status
    Trust-->>Verifier: Return trust and status evidence
    Verifier->>Verifier: Verify crypto, holder binding, and request satisfaction
    Verifier->>Policy: Emit canonical verification result
    Policy-->>RP: Return business decision and audit record
    Note right of Policy: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
```

<details><summary><strong>1. Relying Party creates the request snapshot and DCQL query</strong></summary>

The RP translates a service purpose into a minimal attribute request. The request snapshot captures `state`, nonce, response mode, DCQL query ids, accepted formats, policy version, tenant/RP context, expiry, and response-encryption material. Later verification compares the Wallet response against this immutable snapshot rather than reconstructing request state from mutable application data.

**Artifact Produced:** immutable request snapshot, signed request object, DCQL query, policy id.

</details>

<details><summary><strong>2. Relying Party sends the signed presentation request to the Wallet Unit</strong></summary>

The RP delivers the request through the selected channel: same-device browser or app mediation, cross-device QR handoff, proximity transport, or another supported presentation surface. The Wallet sees a signed request, not a business decision; the request still has to pass RP authentication and User disclosure checks.

</details>

<details><summary><strong>3. Wallet Unit verifies RP identity and registered purpose</strong></summary>

Before the Wallet asks the User to disclose attributes, it checks whether the requesting RP can be authenticated and whether the request aligns with registered RP information. This protects the User from judging arbitrary names, domains, or app labels without trust evidence.

**Evidence Consumed by Wallet:** the matching WRPAC and one applicable WRPRC carried by value, the authorized LoTE/status chains for those certificates, the request signature, and the Service/intended-use scope.

</details>

<details><summary><strong>4. RP certificate trust path returns validation evidence</strong></summary>

The Wallet resolves the carried certificates through their authorized LoTE and status sources; it does not perform a live Registrar repair lookup. The result supplies the authenticated RP, Service, intended-use, and registered-attribute context. An access-certificate authentication failure stops disclosure, while an absent or invalid registration certificate follows the explicit warning and Wallet Provider policy path.

</details>

<details><summary><strong>5. Wallet Unit shows the RP, purpose, and requested attributes to the User</strong></summary>

The disclosure screen is where the technical request becomes a User-facing decision. The Wallet should show who is asking, why the attributes are requested, and which attributes will be disclosed. This step is not a substitute for the RP's downstream GDPR, deletion, or audit obligations.

</details>

<details><summary><strong>6. Wallet User approves selected disclosure</strong></summary>

The User approves or rejects disclosure through the Wallet UX. Approval permits the Wallet to return selected evidence for this request; it does not prove the RP may retain every disclosed attribute indefinitely, nor does it prove the returned credential satisfies the RP's service policy.

**Boundary:** User consent to disclosure is not the same as RP policy satisfaction or long-term retention permission.

</details>

<details><summary><strong>7. Wallet Unit returns the presentation response to the RP</strong></summary>

The response carries the selected credential evidence and holder-binding material according to the chosen format and response mode. At this point the RP has received a payload, not yet a verified identity or entitlement decision.

</details>

<details><summary><strong>8. Relying Party submits the response and immutable request snapshot to the verifier</strong></summary>

The RP verifier receives both the Wallet response and the original request snapshot. That pairing prevents the verifier from accepting a valid credential for the wrong session, tenant, audience, nonce, policy bundle, or response channel.

</details>

<details><summary><strong>9. RP Verifier resolves issuer trust and status</strong></summary>

The verifier routes each credential by format, issuer, Rulebook, and query id, then resolves the trust and status material needed for the credential class. PID, QEAA, PuB-EAA, EAA, mdoc, and SD-JWT VC evidence can require different trust and freshness checks.

</details>

<details><summary><strong>10. Trust and status sources return evidence to the verifier</strong></summary>

Trusted lists, LoTE material, certificate chains, status services, and Wallet-assurance evidence return the inputs needed to finish validation. A status-fetch failure is not the same as a revoked credential, and a trusted issuer does not by itself prove request-policy satisfaction.

</details>

<details><summary><strong>11. RP Verifier checks cryptography, holder binding, and request satisfaction</strong></summary>

The verifier validates issuer signatures, disclosure hashes, mdoc MSO or SD-JWT VC structure, holder-binding proof, nonce/audience binding, status, freshness, and DCQL satisfaction. A valid signature is only one gate in the chain.

</details>

<details><summary><strong>12. RP Verifier emits the canonical verification result</strong></summary>

The verifier records the terminal result and per-check evidence in a canonical result object. Downstream systems should consume this object rather than reinterpreting raw Wallet payloads or treating transport success as credential validity.

**Artifact Produced:** canonical `verification_result` with per-check evidence, terminal state, policy id, redaction decisions, and audit correlation id.

</details>

<details><summary><strong>13. RP policy layer returns the business decision and audit record</strong></summary>

The RP's business layer may approve access, ask for additional attributes, fall back to another route, reject the transaction, or trigger manual review. Audit and monitoring systems consume the same result lineage rather than separate ad hoc interpretations of the Wallet response.

**Operational consequence:** downstream systems should depend on the verifier's terminal result, not on raw Wallet payloads or transport-success labels.

</details>

#### 1.7 Evidence Boundaries

The baseline evidence boundaries below are reused throughout the rest of the document. Later chapters add sector-specific rules, but they should not collapse these layers.

| Boundary | What is proven | What is not proven |
|:--|:--|:--|
| RP authentication to Wallet | The Wallet can identify the RP or RP Instance and registered request context | That the RP's business purpose is legally sufficient in every downstream context |
| User consent | The User approved disclosure through the Wallet UX | That every disclosed attribute may be stored indefinitely |
| Issuer signature | The credential was signed by a key accepted under the relevant trust model | That the credential satisfies this RP's request or business policy |
| Credential status | The credential is usable under its class-, format-, and Rulebook-specific lifecycle: for PID/QEAA/PuB-EAA, not revoked; for another profile, any additional permitted state was evaluated | That all external source systems are currently accurate |
| Holder binding | The presenter proved possession of the bound key for this session | That the same natural person will use the same Wallet Unit in future sessions |
| DCQL satisfaction | The response matched the requested credential/claim structure | That the RP should approve the service transaction |
| Canonical result | The RP can reconstruct the verifier decision later | That raw PII or cryptographic tracking handles should be retained by default |

#### 1.8 Handoff to Later Chapters

This baseline chapter is intentionally a starting point, not a replacement for the rest of the document. Each later chapter answers a more specific integration question:

| Reader question after this chapter | Destination in the document |
|:--|:--|
| How does the RP register and obtain Wallet-facing trust material? | RP Registration, Data Model, and Registrar API; Trust Infrastructure: Certificates, Attestations, and Trusted Lists |
| Which PID attributes exist and which should I request? | Natural-Person PID and Attribute Minimisation (§8); Credential Formats: SD-JWT VC, mdoc, and Format Selection |
| How do I encode the request? | DCQL Query Language and Request Construction (§9) |
| How does same-device or cross-device presentation work? | Same-Device Remote Presentation; Cross-Device Remote Presentation |
| How does the verifier decide what is proven? | RP Authentication and Presentation Verification; Cryptographic Verification Pipeline Deep-Dive |
| What if I only need age or a pseudonym? | Pseudonym-Based Authentication and WebAuthn; Age Verification Attestation Pipelines |
| What if the presenter represents a company? | Legal-Person Extension: EBW, LPID, and Mandates (§20); Combined Presentations and Binding Models (§19) |
| What obligations follow after presentation? | RP Obligations; Regulatory Compliance |

---

## Regulatory and Trust Foundations

This group establishes the legal and infrastructural prerequisites for Relying Party participation in the EUDI ecosystem. It details the eIDAS 2.0 regulatory framework, the mandatory registration process with Member State Registrars, the credential formats (SD-JWT VC, mdoc), and the trust infrastructure (WRPACs, Trusted Lists, and the trusted-list interpretation layer for qualified-status determination) required to perform cryptographic verification.

---

### 2. Regulatory Foundation: eIDAS 2.0, CIRs, ARF, and Technical Specifications

:::important[Legal force and implementation force are not the same, but RPs must track both]
For RP integration, the binding baseline comes from the Regulation and the Commission Implementing Regulations. The ARF and Technical Specifications often carry less formal legal weight, but they still shape the concrete interoperability and certification expectations the ecosystem will enforce in practice, so implementation planning has to treat both layers seriously.
:::

#### 2.1 eIDAS 2.0 and the EUDI Wallet Regulation

The revised eIDAS Regulation ([Regulation (EU) 2024/1183](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32024R1183)), adopted on 11 April 2024 and entering into force on 20 May 2024, amends the original eIDAS Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 to establish the legal framework for the European Digital Identity Wallet. For Relying Parties, the key articles are:

| Article | Requirement | RP Impact |
|:--------|:------------|:----------|
| **Art. 5a** | Member States shall provide at least one EUDI Wallet by 24 Dec 2026 | Creates the ecosystem RPs must integrate with |
| **Art. 5b** | RP obligations: registration, data minimisation, transparency, non-discrimination | Core compliance requirements for all RPs |
| **Art. 5b(2)** | RPs shall not request more attributes than necessary for the service | Data minimisation — enforceable obligation |
| **Art. 5b(3)** | RPs shall inform Users of the identity and contact details they can verify | Transparency — RP must expose registration data |
| **Art. 5b(4)** | RPs shall ensure data presented is not shared with third parties without consent | Data protection — restricts downstream sharing |
| **Art. 5f(2)** | Specific private-sector entities shall accept the EUDI Wallet by 24 Dec 2027 | **Mandatory acceptance** for banks, telecom, VLOPs |
| **Art. 5b(9)** | RPs shall not refuse pseudonyms where identification not required by law | Pseudonym acceptance — mandatory |
| **Art. 5b(10)** | Intermediaries deemed RPs; shall not store transaction content data | Intermediary obligations |
| **Art. 5f(2)** | EUDI Wallet shall support Strong User Authentication for electronic payments | SCA integration requirement for PSPs |

##### 2.1.1 Mandatory Acceptance by Private Sector (Art. 5f(2))

Article 5f(2) specifies that the following categories of private-sector entities **must accept** the EUDI Wallet when strong user authentication for online identification is required by Union or national law, or by contractual obligation:

- **Transport service providers** (airlines, railways, etc.)
- **Energy sector operators**
- **Financial services** (banks, PSPs, insurers, investment firms) — under PSD2, MiFID II, Solvency II, AMLD
- **Social security institutions**
- **Healthcare providers and institutions**
- **Drinking water supply and waste treatment services**
- **Postal services**
- **Digital infrastructure and services** — including Very Large Online Platforms (Art. 33 DSA)
- **Education and training institutions** — for educational credentials
- **Telecom operators** — under EECC

The acceptance deadline is **24 December 2027** (36 months after the first wallet core/certification implementing acts entered into force on 24 December 2024).

##### 2.1.2 Key Timelines for RPs

```mermaid
gantt
    title eIDAS 2.0 Implementation Timeline for RPs
    dateFormat YYYY-MM-DD
    axisFormat %Y-%m
    tickInterval 3month

    section Legal & Regulatory
    eIDAS 2.0 enters into force                 :milestone, 2024-05-20, 0d
    Batch adoption of CIRs                      :2024-11-01, 2025-12-31
    First wallet core IAs enter into force      :milestone, 2024-12-24, 0d

    section Technical Specs
    OpenID4VP 1.0 Final status                  :milestone, 2025-07-01, 0d
    TS1–TS14 reach v1.0                         :2025-01-01, 2025-12-31
    HAIP 1.0 Final Specification                :milestone, 2025-12-01, 0d

    section Rollout & Mandates
    CIR 2025/1569 Arts. 6-9 apply              :milestone, 2026-08-19, 0d
    CIR 2025/848 applies (RP registration infra)  :milestone, 2026-12-24, 0d
    MS provide at least 1 EUDI Wallet           :milestone, 2026-12-24, 0d
    Authentic-source amendment applies          :milestone, 2027-01-01, 0d
    CIR 2025/1566 applies (QEAA ID verification):milestone, 2027-08-19, 0d
    Mandatory private-sector acceptance         :crit, milestone, 2027-12-24, 0d
    RPRC Wallet validation transition            :milestone, 2028-08-11, 0d
```

The dates in this timeline do not all represent the same legal event. The July 2026 amending acts enter into force on **11 August 2026**, but the amended registration framework in CIR 2025/848 applies from **24 December 2026**. CIR 2025/1569 Articles 6–9 apply from **19 August 2026**, while CIR 2026/1735's replacement authentic-source verification mechanism applies from **1 January 2027**. CIR 2026/1731 separately delays the Wallet-side registration-certificate validation obligation until **11 August 2028**. Publication, entry into force, base-act application, and provision-specific transitions must therefore remain separate in implementation plans.

#### 2.2 Commission Implementing Regulations (CIRs)

The Commission has adopted a comprehensive set of Implementing Regulations that operationalise the eIDAS 2.0 framework. The following CIRs are directly relevant to Relying Parties:

| CIR | Subject | RP Relevance |
|:----|:--------|:-------------|
| [CIR 2024/2977](https://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2024/2977/oj) | PID and EAA | Defines credential attributes RPs can request |
| [CIR 2024/2979](https://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2024/2979/oj) | Integrity and core functionalities | Specifies Wallet capabilities RPs can rely on |
| [CIR 2024/2980](https://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2024/2980/oj) | Ecosystem notifications | Notification infrastructure for trust events |
| [CIR 2024/2981](https://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2024/2981/oj) | Certification of Wallet Solutions | Basis for RP trust in Wallet Unit authenticity |
| **[CIR 2024/2982](https://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2024/2982/oj)** | **Protocols and interfaces** | **Core protocol requirements for RP interaction** |
| [CIR 2025/846](https://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2025/846/oj) | Cross-border identity matching | Relevant for RPs accepting cross-border PIDs |
| [CIR 2025/847](https://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2025/847/oj) | Security breaches and reactions | RP breach notification, wallet solution suspension/withdrawal handling (§23.7) |
| **[CIR 2025/848](https://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2025/848/oj)** | **Registration of Wallet-Relying Parties** | **Primary registration framework for RPs** |
| [CIR 2025/849](https://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2025/849/oj) | List of certified EUDI Wallets | RPs can verify Wallet Solution certification status |
| [CIR 2025/1566](http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2025/1566/oj) | Verification of QC/QEAA holder identity | Relevant for RPs verifying qualified attestations |
| [CIR 2025/1569](https://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2025/1569/oj) | QEAAs and PuB-EAAs | QEAA/PuB-EAA revocation status available to RPs (Art. 4(5)); catalogue of attributes (§13.13) |
| **[CIR 2026/1730](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202601730)** | **Amendment of RP registration rules** | **Amends CIR 2025/848: Service-aware registration, registration-field provenance, automated registration-certificate issuance, and current WRPAC/WRPRC profiles** |
| **[CIR 2026/1731](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202601731)** | **Amendments to PID, Wallet, notification, and presentation rules** | **Registration-certificate validation and carriage, overasking, portrait safeguards, remote-channel rules, Trust Mark lifecycle, credential status, and QES profile changes** |
| [CIR 2026/1735](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202601735) | Amendment of QEAA/PuB-EAA rules | Updates provider standards and establishes signed/sealed authentic-source verification under ETSI TS 119 478 |

**CIR 2024/2982**, as amended by CIR 2026/1731, remains the central protocols-and-interfaces act for RPs. The amendment deletes former Article 3(8), so an ordinary RP no longer requests a Wallet Unit Attestation as presentation evidence; issuance-side WIA/KA and conditional Wallet-to-Wallet proof remain separate mechanisms. The amended act specifies:

- The use of OpenID4VP for remote presentation requests (Art. 3)
- The use of ISO/IEC 18013-5 for proximity presentation (Art. 4)
- Requirements for RP authentication towards Wallet Units (Art. 5)
- Data deletion request support (Art. 6)
- DPA reporting support (Art. 7)
- Pseudonym support requirements (Art. 14)
- Transaction data support for SCA (implicit in Art. 3, detailed in TS12)

**CIR 2025/848**, as amended by CIR 2026/1730, is the operational foundation for RP onboarding. The amended registration obligations apply from **24 December 2026**. They specify:

- National register establishment and maintenance (Art. 3)
- Common registration policies (Art. 4)
- Public API for querying RP registration information (Art. 3(5)–(6))
- Access Certificate issuance (Art. 7) — the WRPAC
- At least one authorised Registration Certificate CA per Member State and automated issuance without undue delay
- A separate registration certificate for each `(Relying Party Service, intended use)` combination
- Registrar verification of Annex I points 1–6 and 11–16, while points 7–10 are collected automatically for transparency without a preauthorisation process
- ETSI TS 119 411-8 V1.1.1 for WRPACs and ETSI TS 119 475 V1.2.1 for registration certificates

The amended acts use layered dates. CIRs 2026/1730, 2026/1731, and 2026/1735 enter into force on **11 August 2026**, but that date does not override a base act's application clause or a later provision-specific transition. In particular, CIR 2025/848 applies from **24 December 2026**; CIR 2025/1569 Articles 6–9 apply from **19 August 2026**; CIR 2026/1735 Article 1(3) applies from **1 January 2027**; and CIR 2026/1731's Wallet-side registration-certificate validation obligation applies from **11 August 2028**. The document uses the amended text as the target architecture while attaching legal deadlines only to the provisions they govern.

#### 2.3 Architecture and Reference Framework (ARF)

The current baseline is [ARF v3.0.0](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-architecture-and-reference-framework/releases/tag/v3.0.0), dated **21 July 2026** on the official documentation site and published as a GitHub release on **23 July 2026**. The ARF is the Commission-maintained technical reference that interprets the Regulation and CIRs into an implementable architecture. It remains **informative**, not binding law, but supplies the ecosystem's current architecture and high-level requirements (HLRs).

The migration path matters because v3 is not merely a relabelled v2.8 baseline:

| Release | Date | RP-facing consequence |
|:--|:--|:--|
| [v2.8.0](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-architecture-and-reference-framework/releases/tag/v2.8.0) | 2 February 2026 | Baseline used by the earlier article audit; consolidated Wallet maintenance, payment SCA, pseudonym, and user-to-device authentication work |
| [v2.9.0](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-architecture-and-reference-framework/releases/tag/v2.9.0) | 21 May 2026 | Intervening release that advanced RP registration, Wallet lifecycle, issuer assurance, and related Topic refinements |
| [v3.0.0](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-architecture-and-reference-framework/releases/tag/v3.0.0) | 21/23 July 2026 | Current target: first-class RP Services, mandatory registration-certificate request material, revised intermediary/UI semantics, current remote-channel matrix, FCAF, W2W proof behavior, and expanded trust/status/lifecycle controls |

Older ARF notes, figures, and discussion papers remain useful provenance, but they are background unless the tagged v3 main text, Annex 2, Technical Specifications, Rulebooks, or binding law still carry the claim.

Key ARF surfaces relevant to RPs:

| ARF surface | Content |
|:------------|:--------|
| ARF §2.6 | Use-case framing: online identification, mDL, SCA for payments, representation, and future examples such as health, education, DTC, CBDC, and social security |
| ARF §3.11 and §3.17–§3.19 | Relying Parties, RP Services, RP Instances, intermediaries, Registrars, Access CAs, and Registration Certificate Providers |
| ARF §4.3–§4.6 | Wallet Unit components, Wallet Unit interfaces, remote/proximity presentation flows, WSCD architecture types, and lifecycle state diagrams |
| ARF §2.5 | Pseudonym use cases and relation to WebAuthn/passkeys and future mechanisms |
| ARF §5.1–§5.7 | Attestation elements, categories, formats, Rulebooks, catalogues, OpenID4VP presentation, ISO 18013-5 proximity presentation, and transactional data |
| ARF §6.2–§6.6 | Trust throughout Wallet Provider, PID/Attestation Provider, RP, Wallet Unit, and PID/attestation lifecycles |
| ARF §6.6.3–§6.6.5 | Presentation to RPs, presentation to another Wallet Unit, and presentation through intermediaries |
| ARF §7.2–§7.5 and §8 | Wallet Solution certification, risk management, FCAF functional conformance, and accessibility scope |
| Annex 2 Topics 1, 6, 10, 19, 27, 31, 40, 43, 44, 48, 52, 55, 56 | RP-facing HLRs for online access, RP authentication, issuance assurance, logging, registration, notification/publication, user authentication, disclosure policies, registration certificates, Wallet-to-Wallet proof, intermediaries, Certificate Transparency, and Wallet Provider support/maintenance |

This map is intentionally RP-biased. ARF use cases such as CBDC are included as watchlist context only; they do not create a separate RP integration workstream in this document until a concrete Rulebook, protocol profile, or payment-sector requirement exists.

#### 2.5 Source Precedence Used in This Document

This document uses semi-official, standards, pilot, and discussion sources together, but not with equal authority. When sources conflict, the integration guidance follows this order:

| Source family | How this document treats it |
|:--------------|:----------------------------|
| **Binding law and implementing acts** | Highest authority for RP legal obligations, including eIDAS 2.0, the CIR stack, GDPR, PSD2/PSR, DORA, NIS2, AMLD, and sector law. |
| **Current ARF main text and Annex 2 HLRs** | Authoritative architecture and current high-level requirement baseline for this research pass, while still informative rather than binding law. |
| **Technical Specifications and profiled standards** | Implementation authority for protocol, data model, interface, and conformance details when they are current and within scope. |
| **European Standards and certificate-profile common structures** | Normative or profiled substrate for interpreting X.509 certificate fields. For example, ETSI EN 319 412-1 explains how `serialNumber`, `organizationIdentifier`, semantics identifiers, and validity-assured short-term certificate extensions should be interpreted; Draft ETSI EN 319 412-2 V2.5.0 adds the current draft natural-person certificate profile for subject naming, key usage, and revocation-pointer handling. These sources do not define wallet credential claim semantics or RP request authorization scope. Draft ENAP material is treated as source-watch until finalized. |
| **Rulebooks and attestation schemes** | Attribute, format, trust-anchor, revocation, and verification authority for the specific attestation type. Rulebook-specific claims override generic examples. |
| **Informative ETSI Technical Reports and conceptual reports** | Architecture vocabulary, standards-gap signals, and implementation framing. They sharpen interpretation but do not create binding RP requirements unless a law, ARF requirement, Technical Specification, or Rulebook incorporates the same rule. |
| **Annex 4 blueprints and Annex 5 design guides** | Useful design and service-flow guidance, but not standalone legal or protocol authority. They become implementation requirements only where current ARF, Annex 2, TS, Rulebook, or law says so. |
| **Large-Scale Pilots, reference implementations, launchpads, and sandboxes** | Evidence about feasibility, interoperability, and operational readiness. They inform risk and adoption planning but do not define obligations by themselves. |
| **Historic discussion papers** | Background and source-provenance material. Once integrated, they stop being updated; the latest Annex 2 and current ARF text control HLR claims. |

For that reason, later sections may cite a discussion paper, blueprint, pilot, or implementation report to explain why a design exists, but the actual RP requirement should always be traced back to binding law, the current ARF/Annex 2, a Technical Specification, or a Rulebook.

### 3. Ecosystem Roles from RP Perspective

#### 3.1 Relying Party Definition

A **Relying Party (RP)** is a service provider that requests attributes contained within a PID, QEAA, PuB-EAA, or EAA from a Wallet Unit, subject to User approval and within the limits of applicable legislation and rules.

> **Important distinction**: The term "Relying Party" in the ARF refers **exclusively** to service providers requesting attributes — not to Attestation Providers (QEAA Providers, PuB-EAA Providers, EAA Providers), even though the Regulation technically classifies Attestation Providers as Relying Parties too.

An RP may rely on the Wallet Unit for different reasons:

- **Legal requirement** — Art. 5f(2) mandates acceptance by specific sectors
- **Contractual agreement** — business decision to accept EUDI Wallet credentials
- **Own decision** — voluntary adoption for competitive advantage

#### 3.2 RP Services and RP Instances

ARF v3 inserts a **Relying Party Service** between the registered RP legal entity and its technical RP Instances. The Service is the registration, certificate-selection, and data-separation boundary for one business-facing service of the RP:

- Every RP registers **at least one Service**.
- The RP chooses a **Service identifier** that is unique within that RP. An existing OAuth `client_id` may be reused; for a one-Service RP, a Registrar may permit an empty or placeholder value.
- Each Service maps to one or more **intended uses**. The Registrar, not the RP, creates the intended-use identifiers.
- The Registration Certificate CA issues a separate WRPRC for every registered `(Service, intended use)` pair.

An **RP Instance** is the software-and-hardware system that interacts with Wallet Units on behalf of a Service. It maintains the presentation interface, protects the request-signing private key, and uses the access and registration certificates applicable to the current Service and intended use. One RP can operate multiple Instances, and one Instance can serve multiple Services, but the Instance needs a **separate WRPAC for each Service** it serves. Each WRPAC binds the RP identifier, Service identifier, Service trade name, and Instance public key; the RP must distribute only matching WRPRCs to that Instance and select exactly one applicable WRPRC for each presentation request.

#### 3.3 Intermediaries

An **intermediary** is a special class of RP defined in Art. 5b(10):

> *"Intermediaries acting on behalf of relying parties shall be deemed to be relying parties and shall not store data about the content of the transaction."*

An intermediary:

- Offers services to other RPs (called "intermediated RPs") to connect to Wallet Units on their behalf
- Registers as an RP with intermediary intent and obtains association-specific WRPACs
- Uses the single end-RP WRPRC selected by the end RP for the current Service and intended use; the WRPAC and WRPRC carry reciprocal RP/Service associations
- Performs the agreed credential-verification tasks assigned under Topic 52
- **Must not store** the content of the transaction data (User attributes)
- Forwards attributes only to the named end RP after every agreed verification succeeds, and to no entity when a verification fails
- Is suppressed from the Wallet approval display, which shows the end RP and end-RP Service, while remaining recorded with its Service in the Wallet transaction log

#### 3.4 Supporting Ecosystem Entities

From the RP perspective, the following ecosystem entities are critical:

| Entity | Role for RP |
|:-------|:------------|
| **Wallet User** | Controls the Wallet Unit and approves disclosure. For PID, the User is the subject; for other attestations, subject binding is Rulebook-specific. |
| **Registrar** | Registers the RP, records intended attributes and purposes, issues registration data |
| **Access Certificate Authority** | Issues WRPACs that bind an RP Instance public key to one registered RP Service; an Instance serving multiple Services receives a separate WRPAC for each |
| **Provider of Registration Certificates / Registration Certificate CA** | Issues a separate WRPRC automatically and without undue delay for each registered `(Service, intended use)` pair |
| **Trusted List / LoTE Provider** | Publishes trust anchors that Wallet Units use to verify RP certificates |
| **Wallet Provider** | Builds the Wallet Solution that Users interact with; RP has no direct interface |
| **PID Provider** | Issues PIDs that RPs request and verify |
| **Attestation Provider** | Issues QEAAs, PuB-EAAs, EAAs that RPs request and verify |
| **Attestation Scheme Provider** | Defines Attestation Rulebooks and machine-readable schemes for QEAAs, PuB-EAAs, and EAAs |
| **Conformity Assessment Body (CAB)** | Certifies Wallet Solutions and audits relevant trust-service providers — RP relies on certification through Wallet/issuer trust signals |
| **National Accreditation Body (NAB)** | Accredits CABs as competent, independent certification bodies under the Member State's authority |
| **Supervisory Body** | Oversees RP compliance with eIDAS 2.0 obligations |
| **Device Manufacturers and Related Subsystem Providers** | Provide hardware, OS, secure cryptographic subsystems, libraries, and app-store surfaces used by Wallet Units |

A single legal entity may combine several ecosystem roles only when it satisfies the legal and technical requirements for each role. RP systems should therefore keep the role labels separate in policy, logging, and trust-chain handling even when the same commercial counterparty appears in multiple places.

Do not infer that every non-PID attestation directly identifies the Wallet User. The ARF explicitly allows attestations about objects owned or used by the User, and attestations with no subject at all, such as bearer-style vouchers. For those credentials, the RP must rely on the Rulebook, attestation scheme, PID co-verification rule, and binding evidence to decide whether the presented attribute identifies the User, an object, a represented party, or only possession of a valid bearer credential.

The ARF role model is easier to reason about as a relationship map rather than a flat list. For RP architects, the important split is between the runtime path (Wallet Unit presenting to the RP), the issuer path (PID/attestation providers issuing into the Wallet Unit), and the registration/trust-publication path that lets Wallet Units verify the RP before any disclosure occurs.

For RP architecture, Figure 1 is useful because it separates the integration surface into three dependency planes:

| Plane | RP-facing dependency | Engineering consequence |
|:------|:---------------------|:------------------------|
| **Registration and access** | Registrar, Access CA, and Registration Certificate CA | Own the RP identifier, Service/intended-use registry mappings, Service-bound WRPAC lifecycle, and per-`(Service, intended use)` WRPRC lifecycle. Failures here stop the Wallet from accepting new RP requests. |
| **Issuer and trust discovery** | PID/QEAA/PuB-EAA/EAA Providers, Authentic Sources, Trusted Lists, and LoTEs | Own issuer trust anchors, attestation status information, schema/rulebook discovery, and qualified/non-qualified trust-framework branching. Failures here affect RP acceptance of presented credentials. |
| **Wallet and device assurance** | Wallet Provider, Wallet Solution, Wallet Unit, WSCA/WSCD, device manufacturers, CABs, and supervisory bodies | Mostly indirect for RPs. Issuers consume WIA/KA; ordinary verifiers consume issuer-mediated credential trust/status, holder binding, Wallet Solution certification, and breach/suspension notifications rather than direct device inspection. |

The practical result is that an RP should not build a single "EUDI trust cache." It needs separate cache and monitoring domains for RP authentication material, issuer trust and status, and wallet/provider assurance signals, because each plane fails differently and has a different fallback path.

### 4. RP Registration, Data Model, and Registrar API

:::important[Registration state reaches runtime through Service-bound certificates]
Registration is not one-time onboarding paperwork. It creates the RP, Service, and intended-use identifiers that drive certificate issuance, suspension, user-facing transparency, and request-scope checks. In the ARF v3 target model, however, a normal presentation carries the applicable registration certificate by value; the Registrar API remains the authoritative publication and lifecycle surface, not a synchronous fallback hop in every Wallet interaction.
:::

#### 4.1 Registration Obligation

To rely on Wallet Units for providing a service, an RP **must register** with a Registrar in the Member State where it is established (Art. 5b(1), CIR 2025/848 Art. 3, as amended). Registration establishes:

1. An EU-wide unique **RP identifier** assigned by the Registrar
2. At least one **Service**, with an RP-chosen Service identifier and trade name
3. One or more Registrar-created **intended-use identifiers** mapped to each Service
4. One or more **WRPACs**, each binding an RP Instance key to one RP Service
5. A separate **WRPRC** for every registered `(Service, intended use)` pair, issued automatically and without undue delay
6. A public **national-register** record for transparency, administration, certificate issuance, and lifecycle evidence

From an RP integration perspective, the result is a two-certificate trust model plus an authoritative register:

| Artifact | Target availability | Primary role in RP integration |
|:---------|:--------------------|:-------------------------------|
| **WRPAC** | Required for each wallet-facing Instance/Service binding | Authenticates the live RP Instance or intermediary and binds its signing key to the registered RP and Service |
| **WRPRC** | Required for each registered `(Service, intended use)` pair | Carries the applicable registered scope, purpose, policy, and transparency data; one matching certificate is included by value in each presentation request |
| **National register / Registrar API** | Mandatory publication and lifecycle surface | Supplies authoritative registration data to certificate issuers, the RP, supervisors, auditors, and public transparency consumers; it is not the normal live-presentation fallback |

In practical terms, the WRPAC answers **who and which Service is interacting with the Wallet**, while the WRPRC answers **which intended use and attribute scope applies to this request**. CIR 2026/1730 makes the registration-certificate infrastructure and automated issuance part of the amended CIR 2025/848 model applying from 24 December 2026. CIR 2026/1731 separately phases the Wallet-side registration-certificate validation requirement to 11 August 2028; deployments should therefore distinguish target request construction from the later legal validation gate.

Supporting instruments remain secondary to this model:

- **Electronic Attestations of Attributes (EAAs)** may supplement RP attribute information, but they do **not** replace mandatory WRPACs where regulation requires access certificates.
- **Identity and role attributes** carried in WRP certificates may be used as inputs to embedded disclosure-policy decisions in the Wallet ecosystem, but the disclosure-policy mechanism itself is defined elsewhere and is outside the scope of this document.

Beyond initial registration, CIR 2025/848 Art. 5(2)–(3) imposes ongoing obligations: the RP must ensure that all information provided is **accurate at the time of registration** (Art. 5(2)) and must **update any previously registered information without undue delay** (Art. 5(3)). Failure to maintain accurate registration data — for instance, not updating contact information, changed service scope, or revised intended attributes — constitutes a ground for registrar-initiated suspension under Art. 9(2)(a). Additionally, Art. 6(7) requires that when an RP **no longer intends to rely upon wallet units** for a specific registration, it must notify the registrar without undue delay and request cancellation of that registration.

##### 4.1.1 Institutional Architecture for Registration and Certification

ETSI TS 119 475 clause `4.6.1`, read together with amended CIR 2025/848 Article 8, describes the institutional architecture behind every RP registration and certificate-issuance flow. At a minimum, each Member State maintains at least one national register of wallet-relying parties, exposes that register through both a website and an API, designates at least one Registrar to manage it, authorizes at least one provider of WRPACs, and authorizes at least one Registration Certificate CA.

This matters because the diagram below is **not** a detailed request sequence. It is the governance and operating topology that explains who maintains the authoritative register, who issues each certificate type, and why both wallets and certificate issuers ultimately depend on the same Member State registration information.

