```mermaid
    WI->>TA: Fetch Entity Configuration
    TA-->>WI: Trust Anchor Entity<br/>Configuration JWT
    WI->>TA: Fetch Subordinate Statement<br/>about Intermediate
    TA-->>WI: Subordinate Statement JWT<br/>(Intermediate keys)
    Note right of TA: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(46, 204, 113, 0.14)
    Note right of WI: Phase 3: Chain Validation & Policy Application
    WI->>WI: Validate full trust chain<br/>(signatures, iat/exp,<br/>issuer-subject binding)
    WI->>WI: Apply metadata policies<br/>(cascade from TA downward)
    WI->>WI: Derive RP final metadata<br/>(VP formats, scopes,<br/>client authentication)
    WI->>WI: Validate Trust Marks<br/>(optional)
    Note right of TA: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end
```

<details>
<summary><strong>1. Relying Party sends signed presentation request to Wallet Instance</strong></summary>

The Relying Party initiates the flow by sending a credential presentation request to the Wallet Instance. In the OID-FED trust model, the Relying Party's `client_id` uses the `openid_federation` scheme (rather than `x509_hash` used in the WRPAC model). The request is signed with the Relying Party's federation entity key. The Wallet Instance does not yet trust this Relying Party — it must resolve the trust chain before processing the request.

**Artifact Produced:** Inbound Presentation Request (OAuth 2.0).

**Audit Telemetry:** The Wallet Instance logs an `INBOUND_PRESENTATION_REQUEST_RECEIVED` event.

```http
GET /authorize?client_id=https%3A%2F%2Frp.example.org
    &request_uri=urn%3Aietf%3Aparams%3Aoauth%3Arequest_uri%3Afoo
    &response_type=vp_token
    &response_mode=direct_post HTTP/1.1
Host: wallet.example.eu
```

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>2. Wallet Instance fetches Relying Party's Entity Configuration</strong></summary>

The Wallet Instance sends an HTTP GET to the Relying Party's `/.well-known/openid-federation` endpoint. This is the standard OID-FED discovery mechanism — every entity in the federation publishes its Entity Configuration at this well-known path. The request uses the `Accept: application/entity-statement+jwt` media type.

**Audit Telemetry:** The Wallet Instance logs an `RP_ENTITY_CONFIGURATION_FETCH_INITIATED` event to track trust discovery.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>3. Relying Party returns Entity Configuration JWT</strong></summary>

The Relying Party responds with its self-signed Entity Configuration — a JWT containing: `metadata` (the Relying Party's declared capabilities, including `openid_credential_verifier` with VP formats and requested scopes), `jwks` (the Relying Party's public keys), `authority_hints` (URLs of superior entities in the federation hierarchy), and `trust_marks` (optional attestations of Relying Party authorisation). The Wallet Instance uses `authority_hints` in the next step to walk upward through the trust hierarchy.

**Artifact Produced:** Relying Party Entity Configuration (JWT).

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>4. Wallet Instance verifies Relying Party Entity Configuration self-signature</strong></summary>

The Wallet Instance verifies that the Entity Configuration JWT was signed by one of the keys declared in its own `jwks` field. This is a self-consistency check — it proves the JWT was not tampered with in transit, but does not yet establish trust. Trust is established only after the full chain (steps 5–14) is validated.

**Failure Path:** If the self-signature fails, the Wallet Instance immediately terminates the flow as the Entity Configuration is corrupt or forged.

**Audit Telemetry:** The Wallet Instance logs an `RP_ENTITY_CONFIGURATION_SIGNATURE_VERIFIED` event or failure alert.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>5. Wallet Instance extracts authority_hints from Relying Party Entity Configuration</strong></summary>

The Wallet Instance parses the `authority_hints` array from the Relying Party's Entity Configuration. Each entry is the URL of a superior entity (Intermediate or Trust Anchor) that has issued a Subordinate Statement about the Relying Party. In a single-level federation, this points directly to the Trust Anchor. In the Italian model, it typically points to an Intermediate (e.g., a sector-specific registrar).

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>6. Wallet Instance fetches Intermediate Entity Configuration</strong></summary>

The Wallet Instance sends an HTTP GET to the Intermediate's `/.well-known/openid-federation` endpoint. This retrieves the Intermediate's own Entity Configuration, which contains its public keys (needed to verify its Subordinate Statements) and its own `authority_hints` (pointing to the Trust Anchor).

**Audit Telemetry:** The Wallet Instance logs an `INTERMEDIATE_ENTITY_CONFIGURATION_FETCH_INITIATED` event.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>7. Intermediate returns its Entity Configuration JWT</strong></summary>

The Intermediate responds with its self-signed Entity Configuration. The Wallet Instance extracts the Intermediate's `jwks` (for verifying the Subordinate Statement about the Relying Party) and `authority_hints` (for continuing the chain walk upward to the Trust Anchor).

**Artifact Produced:** Intermediate Entity Configuration (JWT).

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>8. Wallet Instance fetches Subordinate Statement about Relying Party from Intermediate</strong></summary>

The Wallet Instance queries the Intermediate's Fetch endpoint (`/fetch?sub=https://rp.example.org`) to obtain the Subordinate Statement — the signed JWT that attests the Relying Party is a registered member of the federation under this Intermediate. This is the critical attestation that links the Relying Party to the federation hierarchy.

**Audit Telemetry:** The Wallet Instance logs an `INTERMEDIATE_SUBORDINATE_STATEMENT_FETCH_INITIATED` event.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>9. Intermediate returns Subordinate Statement about Relying Party</strong></summary>

The Intermediate responds with a signed Subordinate Statement JWT. This contains: the Relying Party's public keys (which must match the keys in the Relying Party's Entity Configuration from step 3), optional `metadata_policy` rules (constraints on the Relying Party's metadata, such as allowed VP formats or scope restrictions), and optional Trust Marks. The Wallet Instance verifies this JWT using the Intermediate's keys from step 7.

**Artifact Produced:** Relying Party Subordinate Statement (JWT).

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>10. Wallet Instance fetches Trust Anchor Entity Configuration</strong></summary>

Continuing upward, the Wallet Instance fetches the Trust Anchor's Entity Configuration from `/.well-known/openid-federation`. The Wallet Instance typically has the Trust Anchor's public keys pre-configured (distributed out-of-band by the Member State). This is the final HTTP fetch in the chain walk.

**Audit Telemetry:** The Wallet Instance logs a `TRUST_ANCHOR_ENTITY_CONFIGURATION_FETCH_INITIATED` event.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>11. Trust Anchor returns its Entity Configuration JWT</strong></summary>

The Trust Anchor responds with its Entity Configuration. The Wallet Instance verifies this JWT using its pre-configured Trust Anchor public keys — this is the **root of trust** anchoring the entire chain.

**Failure Path:** If the signature does not match the pre-configured keys, the Wallet Instance immediately rejects the chain.

**Audit Telemetry:** The Wallet Instance logs a `TRUST_ANCHOR_SIGNATURE_VERIFIED` event or failure alert.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>12. Wallet Instance fetches Subordinate Statement about Intermediate from Trust Anchor</strong></summary>

The Wallet Instance queries the Trust Anchor's Fetch endpoint to obtain the Subordinate Statement attesting the Intermediate's membership in the federation. This completes the chain: Relying Party → Intermediate → Trust Anchor.

**Audit Telemetry:** The Wallet Instance logs a `TA_SUBORDINATE_STATEMENT_FETCH_INITIATED` event.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>13. Trust Anchor returns Subordinate Statement about Intermediate</strong></summary>

The Trust Anchor responds with a signed Subordinate Statement about the Intermediate, containing the Intermediate's public keys. The Wallet Instance verifies this using the Trust Anchor's keys from step 11.

**Artifact Produced:** Intermediate Subordinate Statement (JWT).

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>14. Wallet Instance validates the complete trust chain</strong></summary>

With all chain components assembled — [Relying Party Entity Configuration, Subordinate Statement from Intermediate, Intermediate Entity Configuration, Subordinate Statement from Trust Anchor, Trust Anchor Entity Configuration] — the Wallet Instance performs comprehensive validation: (a) signature integrity at each level, (b) temporal validity (`iat`/`exp`) for every JWT, (c) issuer-subject binding (each `iss` must match the expected superior, each `sub` must match the expected subordinate), (d) key consistency (the Relying Party's keys in the Subordinate Statement must match those in its Entity Configuration).

**Failure Path:** If any aspect of the chain validation fails (e.g., expired timestamp or inconsistent keys), the Wallet Instance aborts the presentation immediately.

**Audit Telemetry:** The Wallet Instance logs a `TRUST_CHAIN_VALIDATION_COMPLETED` event.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>15. Wallet Instance applies metadata policies from Trust Anchor downward</strong></summary>

Metadata policies from each Subordinate Statement are applied in cascade — from Trust Anchor downward through Intermediates to the Relying Party. Operators like `subset_of`, `one_of`, `add`, and `default` constrain the Relying Party's declared metadata. For example, the Trust Anchor might enforce `vp_formats` to include only `dc+sd-jwt` with `ES256`/`ES384`, overriding any broader format declarations by the Relying Party.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>16. Wallet Instance derives Relying Party's final metadata</strong></summary>

After policy application, the Wallet Instance has the Relying Party's **final metadata** — the effective set of capabilities the Relying Party is authorised to use within the federation. This includes: which VP formats the Relying Party may accept, which attribute scopes it may request, which client authentication methods it supports, and its organisation information (name, logo, contacts). The Wallet Instance uses this metadata to evaluate the presentation request from step 1.

**Audit Telemetry:** The Wallet Instance logs a `RP_FINAL_METADATA_DERIVED` event.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>17. Wallet Instance validates Trust Marks (optional)</strong></summary>

If the Relying Party's Entity Configuration or Subordinate Statements contain Trust Marks, the Wallet Instance may optionally validate them by querying the Trust Mark Status endpoint (`/status`). Trust Marks provide fine-grained authorisation signals — e.g., "this Relying Party is certified for LoA High interactions" or "this Relying Party may interact with minors". Trust Mark validation is optional because federation membership (established in steps 14–16) already provides baseline trust.

</details>
<br/>

> **Comparison with WRPAC-based RP verification**: In the standard EU-wide model (§5.2, §13.1), the Wallet verifies the RP using its **WRPAC** — an X.509 certificate containing the RP's registration data. This is a single certificate chain verification against a pre-cached Access CA trust anchor. The OID-FED model replaces this with the multi-hop trust chain resolution described above. The key trade-off: OID-FED provides richer metadata discovery and policy enforcement but requires more HTTP fetches and online connectivity (unless the RP includes a pre-built `trust_chain` in its presentation request).

##### 5.5.11 When OpenID Federation Applies: Credential Type Trust Framework Map

OID-FED and ETSI Trusted Lists are complementary, not competing, trust frameworks in the EUDI ecosystem. Their applicability depends on the credential type and the use case. The following tables clarify when each applies.

##### 5.5.12 Structural Comparison: OID-FED Trust Chains vs ETSI Trusted Lists

| Dimension | OID-FED Trust Chain | ETSI Trusted Lists |
|:----------|:--------------------|:-------------------|
| **Data format** | JWT (Entity Statement) | XML (TS 119 612) or JSON (TS 119 602 Annex H) |
| **Trust model** | Hierarchical (Trust Anchor → Intermediates → Leaves) | Flat published list (LoTE Provider publishes all entities) |
| **Discovery** | Automatic: walk `authority_hints` upward | Manual: fetch list URL from Common Trust Infrastructure |
| **Metadata delivery** | Embedded in Entity Configuration | Separate from trust anchor; RP metadata not in Trusted Lists |
| **Policy enforcement** | Metadata policies cascade through Subordinate Statements | No metadata policy mechanism |
| **Revocation** | Subordinate Statement expiry or unavailability | Trusted List status field (`ServiceStatus`) |
| **Offline support** | Trust Chain can be embedded in JWT `trust_chain` header | LoTE can be cached and verified offline |
| **Key rotation** | Entity updates its Entity Configuration; superior re-issues Subordinate Statement | LoTE Provider re-publishes the list |
| **Scalability** | O(depth) HTTP fetches per trust chain resolution | O(1) list download per jurisdiction |
| **Signing** | JWS (JWT) — ES256, RS256 | XAdES or JAdES (depending on format) |

##### 5.5.13 Credential Type Applicability

| Use Case | Trust Framework | Rationale |
|:---------|:----------------|:----------|
| PID Provider trust | ETSI TS 119 602 PID Provider LoTE (mandatory) | Carries the notified PID credential-signing and applicable revocation-list anchor classes |
| QEAA Provider trust | ETSI TS 119 612 Trusted List (mandatory) | Qualified status requires the Article 22 qualified-service path |
| PuB-EAA Provider trust | ETSI TS 119 602 PuB-EAA Provider LoTE (mandatory) | Carries the notified PuB-EAA credential-signing and applicable revocation-list anchor classes |
| Non-qualified EAA Provider trust | OID-FED (permitted) or ETSI TS 119 602 LoTE | TS11 allows OID-FED for non-qualified only |
| RP trust (EU-wide) | X.509 WRPAC | ARF mandates access certificates |
| RP trust (Italian model) | OID-FED trust chain resolution | SPID/CIE legacy + IT-Wallet design (§5.5.14) |
| Wallet Provider trust | ETSI TS 119 602 Wallet Provider LoTE (mandatory for actors consuming WIA/KA assurance) | Carries distinct WIA/KA-signing and status-list anchor classes |

> **TS11 constraint**: The `trustedAuthorities` field in TS11 attestation schemas supports X.509 Authority Key Identifier, ETSI list references, and OpenID Federation, while restricting OID-FED to non-qualified EAA types. Treat the catalogue entry as routing metadata: PID and PuB-EAA provider trust resolves through their TS 119 602 LoTE profiles, QEAA qualification through TS 119 612, and a revocable Rulebook additionally identifies the status/revocation-list URL and applicable separately authorized signer class.

##### 5.5.14 National Precedent: Italian IT-Wallet and Full OID-FED Trust Infrastructure

Italy's IT-Wallet implementation is the **only EUDI Large Scale Pilot that uses OpenID Federation as its complete trust infrastructure** — not merely as a data format (as all other Member States do for LoTEs), but as the full protocol for RP onboarding, trust establishment, and metadata discovery. This makes it the most significant real-world reference for OID-FED in the EUDI ecosystem.

##### 5.5.15 Key Architectural Facts

1. **All entities** (Trust Anchor, Intermediates, Wallet Providers, Credential Issuers, Relying Parties) are required to publish an Entity Configuration at `/.well-known/openid-federation`.
2. **RP onboarding** is federation-based: the RP publishes its Entity Configuration (signed with its Federation Entity Private Key), and the Trust Anchor (or an Intermediate) issues a Subordinate Statement attesting the RP's membership. Metadata policies in the Subordinate Statement constrain allowed VP formats (e.g., `dc+sd-jwt` with `ES256`/`ES384`).
3. **Wallet Instance RP verification** uses the OID-FED trust chain resolution process described in §5.5.6.
4. **Trust Marks** provide fine-grained RP authorisation — including public/private RP classification and whether an RP may interact with minors.

##### 5.5.16 Dual Trust Path: OID-FED and ETSI Coexistence

Italy operates **both** trust models simultaneously:

| Entity Type | Trust Framework |
|:------------|:----------------|
| QTSPs (QEAA Providers) | ETSI TS 119 612 XML Trusted Lists |
| Non-qualified EAA Providers | ETSI TS 119 602 Annex H LoTE (JSON) |
| RPs, Wallet Providers, Credential Issuers | OID-FED federation |

Entities listed in national Trusted Lists are **also** registered in the national Federation Registry. Key validation can occur through both mechanisms — verification against the Trusted List and verification through federation endpoints. This dual-path approach provides redundancy and enables gradual migration without abandoning the established ETSI model.

##### 5.5.17 Cross-Border Interoperability: Dual `client_id` Scheme

When an Italian Wallet User interacts with an RP from a Member State that uses the standard WRPAC/X.509 model (e.g., Germany), a **trust model mismatch** occurs — the Italian Wallet expects OID-FED trust chains, but the foreign RP presents an X.509 WRPAC. The Italian specification resolves this through the OpenID4VP `client_id` scheme mechanism:

- **`client_id` scheme = `openid_federation`** → Wallet performs OID-FED trust chain resolution (§5.5.10)
- **`client_id` scheme = `x509_hash`** → Wallet performs X.509 WRPAC verification, with RP metadata conveyed in `client_metadata` instead of via Entity Configuration

This dual-scheme approach ensures cross-border interoperability, but adds implementation complexity for both RPs and Wallet Providers that must support both trust models.

##### 5.5.18 RP Entity Configuration Example (Italian Model)

An RP participating in the Italian OID-FED federation publishes the following Entity Configuration (decoded JWT payload):

```json
{
    "iss": "https://rp.example.org",
    "sub": "https://rp.example.org",
    "iat": 1649417862,
    "exp": 1649590602,
    "jwks": { "keys": [{ "kty": "EC", "crv": "P-256", "..." }] },
    "metadata": {
        "openid_credential_verifier": {
            "application_type": "web",
            "client_id": "https://rp.example.org/",
            "client_registration_types": ["automatic"],
            "vp_formats": {
                "dc+sd-jwt": {
                    "sd-jwt_alg_values": ["ES256", "ES384"],
                    "kb-jwt_alg_values": ["ES256", "ES384"]
                }
            }
        },
        "federation_entity": {
            "organization_name": "Example RP",
            "homepage_uri": "https://rp.example.it",
            "logo_uri": "https://rp.example.it/static/logo.svg",
            "contacts": ["tech@example.it"]
        }
    },
    "trust_marks": [{ "id": "...", "trust_mark": "..." }],
    "authority_hints": ["https://intermediate.eidas.example.org"]
}
```

> **Forward-looking note**: If other Member States adopt OID-FED for RP trust establishment (following the Italian model), the EU could establish a **cross-federation Trust Anchor** where the European Commission's `/.well-known/openid-federation` serves as the root, with Member State Trust Anchors as Intermediates. This would parallel the Italian model at EU scale but requires political agreement on EU-wide OID-FED adoption, harmonisation of metadata types, and consensus on metadata policy cascading rules.

##### 5.5.19 Non-Qualified EAA Issuer Trust: Three Verification Paths

When an RP receives a **non-qualified EAA** — e.g., a gym membership attestation, a loyalty card credential, or an employer attestation — the trust path differs from PID/QEAA verification. TS11's `trustedAuthorities` framework permits three trust mechanisms for non-qualified EAA Providers:

| Trust Path | Mechanism | RP Verification |
|:-----------|:----------|:----------------|
| **OID-FED** | RP resolves the EAA Provider's Trust Chain via `/.well-known/openid-federation` → Subordinate Statements → Trust Anchor (§5.5.10) | RP must trust the Trust Anchor governing the non-qualified EAA Provider; full OID-FED trust chain resolution required |
| **ETSI TS 119 602 LoTE** | RP verifies the EAA Provider's public key against the national EAA Provider LoTE (Annex H format) | Same as PID Provider verification (§5.5.10) — LoTE-based trust anchor lookup |
| **Self-signed** | No `trustedAuthorities` field; the EAA Provider's key is not anchored to an external trust framework | RP must make its own trust decision — no external trust anchor; highest risk |

> **Engineering implication**: RPs accepting non-qualified EAAs add as many as three credential-specific resolution paths (OID-FED, TS 119 602 LoTE, or RP-local trust for self-signed material) on top of the mandatory TS 119 602/TS 119 612 management capability. The verification logic must branch on the attestation legal category, Rulebook, and `trustedAuthorities` type rather than treating the catalogue field alone as acceptance authority.

#### 5.6 Credential Rotation and Re-Issuance

RPs must handle credential lifecycle events as follows:

| Event | RP Impact | Recommended Handling |
|:------|:----------|:---------------------|
| **PID re-issuance** (new `cnf` key) | The `cnf.jwk` in the new PID differs from the old PID. Any RP-side binding to the old key (e.g., cached device key) becomes invalid. | RP should match users by its verified account identity profile and current PID attribute policy, not by `cnf` key alone. Update stored device key on each successful presentation. |
| **Attestation expiry** | Expired attestation is rejected by RP verification pipeline | RP should inform the User with a clear message (e.g., "Your credential has expired — please re-issue it from your Wallet Provider"). Do not silently fail. |
| **Wallet Unit migration** (device change) | **Device-bound** credentials (PIDs, most QEAAs) are re-issued with new `cnf` keys. **Non-device-bound** attestations may be copied from the encrypted Migration Object without re-issuance — the same attestation instance where User choice and provider policy permit (TS10 V1.2, `nonDeviceBoundCredentials`). | RP-side pseudonym bindings (WebAuthn, §18) may be lost if not backed up. RP should support account recovery via alternative verification (§5.6.1). For a copied non-device-bound attestation, no credential-level change may be visible. |
| **PID Provider rotation** (new signing key) | New PIDs are signed with a new key from the same or different Provider | RP should rely on LoTE-based trust anchor validation (§5.5), not on cached specific signing keys. |

:::important[Do Not Treat `cnf.jwk` as a Stable User Identifier]
The `cnf.jwk` device-bound key changes when credentials are re-issued or the user migrates to a new device. Use PID attributes or pseudonym credentials for persistent user identification.
:::

Topic 10 makes that churn intentional. Issuers and Wallet Units can use several privacy-preserving reuse strategies, advertised through the ETSI TS 119 472-3 §4.2.4 `credential_reuse_policy` rather than inferred by the RP. `ISSU_40a` makes that clause—not a look-alike private metadata field—the common implementation contract for Methods A–D:

| Topic 10 method | Wallet behaviour | RP interpretation |
|:----------------|:-----------------|:------------------|
| **Method A — once-only attestations** | Wallet requests batches, presents each PID/attestation only once, and replenishes before the unused count is exhausted. | Expect frequent new signatures, salts, status indices, and holder keys; do not treat churn as fraud by itself. |
| **Method B — limited-time attestations** | Wallet presents the same credential until near expiry, then requests re-issuance. | Expiry-driven refresh is normal; temporal validity checks still belong to the RP. |
| **Method C — rotating batches** | Wallet presents each credential in a batch once in random order, then resets the batch. | Presentation order is not a stable signal and should not feed identity continuity. |
| **Method D — per-RP attestations** | Wallet can reuse the same credential for the same RP while using different credentials for different RPs. | Same-RP continuity may exist, but cross-RP correlation should remain unavailable. |
| **Re-issuance failure** | Wallet handles refusal or outage gracefully, for example by retrying after delay. | RPs should surface clear retry/fallback UX rather than interpreting every absence as fraud. |

##### 5.6.1 Wallet Migration: Consolidated RP Handling Guide

Wallet migration — when a User changes device or Wallet Provider — is a credential lifecycle event that the RP must handle transparently. The RP has **no direct interaction** with the underlying Migration Object (ARF Topic 34, EC TS10 V1.2); migration is inferred from observable cryptographic changes in subsequent presentations. `ETSI EN 319 482-6 V0.0.2` was an early draft when checked on 2026-07-23.

TS10 encrypts migration and transaction-log export objects as JWE using a password-derived key and authenticated encryption. That protects the Wallet-to-Wallet export/import path, but it creates no RP-visible proof that migration occurred. RPs continue to validate the next presented credential normally and apply their own account-recovery policy.

Topic 34 puts strict boundaries around that Migration Object:

| Topic 34 requirement | RP-facing consequence |
|:---------------------|:----------------------|
| The object contains the Wallet transaction log plus a list of PIDs and attestations, but excludes WIA, KA, and private keys. | Issuance-assurance evidence is established again for the new Wallet Unit; it is neither portable nor verifier evidence. |
| For PIDs and device-bound attestations, the object contains only data needed to request issuance again; it does not contain attribute identifiers, attribute values, or private keys. | A migrated PID or device-bound attestation is a new issuance event with new holder-binding material. |
| For non-device-bound attestations, the User can choose whether the object stores only re-issuance data or full transfer data including attribute identifiers and values. | Some non-device-bound attestations may be restored without RP-visible churn, depending on the Wallet/provider policy and User choice. |
| If the User deletes a PID or attestation, the Wallet Unit deletes the corresponding Migration Object entry. | Data portability does not override User deletion inside the Wallet. |
| Restore is User-selected; if a PID is selected, it is restored first, and log restoration is optional. | RP account recovery must tolerate partial restoration and should not assume a fixed credential set after migration. |
| Restoring a PID or device-bound attestation means requesting a new credential of the same type through the normal Topic 10 issuance process. | The provider's Service registration certificate, WIA and where applicable KA, desired security levels, holder-key binding, issuer policy, and status-list obligations all apply again. |

**Device-bound vs non-device-bound: two migration paths.** The RP's handling differs based on whether the presented attestation was device-bound:

| Aspect | Device-Bound Attestations | Non-Device-Bound Attestations |
|:-------|:--------------------------|:------------------------------|
| **In Migration Object** | Listed in `ListOfCredentials` (metadata only) | Included in full as `nonDeviceBoundCredentials` |
| **Restoration method** | New same-type issuance via OID4VCI from the original Provider | Directly copied to new Wallet Unit |
| **New issuance needed** | ✅ Yes — normally a new WSCA key pair and new `cnf.jwk` | ❌ No — same attestation instance |
| **RP observable change** | Yes — different `cnf.jwk`, different `status.idx` | No — identical attestation presented |
| **User involvement** | User authenticates to each Provider | Transparent — automatic restoration |
| **PID handling** | A new PID of the same type is always issued first (Mig_07) | PID is always device-bound — N/A |

**RP migration detection and decision tree.** The following flowchart captures the RP's decision logic when a returning user's passkey authentication fails — the primary signal that migration (or device loss) may have occurred:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["`**User arrives at RP**`"]
    B{"`Passkey
    authentication
    succeeds?`"}
    C["`**Normal session**
    No migration handling needed`"]
    D{"`User has
    EUDI Wallet?`"}
    E["`**Fallback auth**
    Email / SMS / Manual`"]
    F["`**Request PID via DCQL**
    account-matching
    attributes`"]
    G{"`PID attribute bundle
    matches existing
    account?`"}
    H{"`Current holder key
    matches last observed
    key?`"}
    I["`**New user**
    Create account or reject`"]
    J["`**Known key observed**
    Continue recovery
    ceremony`"]
    K["`**Key change observed**
    Rotation or migration
    may have occurred`"]
    L["`**Record current holder-key
    evidence**`"]

    Mark old credential_id
    as superseded`"]

    Based on cached KYC/age

    A --> B
    B -- "✅ Yes" --> C

    style P text-align:left
```

Key decision points:

1. **Passkey succeeds → No action needed.** Migration is invisible if the user has a synced passkey (`BE=1, BS=1`) or never migrated. See §18.11.1 for synced vs device-bound passkey characteristics.
2. **Passkey fails + PID attribute bundle matches an existing account → Migration handling.** The RP updates the device key, re-registers a passkey, and restores assurance level. See §18.11.2 for the full account recovery sequence diagram.
3. **Passkey fails + no PID match → New user.** Standard new-account or rejection flow applies.
4. **Passkey fails + no Wallet → Fallback.** Standard non-EUDI recovery methods (email, SMS OTP) apply.

**Progressive assurance restoration after migration.** After re-binding a pseudonym via PID step-up (§18.11.2), the RP should restore the account's effective assurance level to at least **Substantial**, since PID verification just occurred during recovery. If the RP stored previous verification results (e.g., `identity_verified: true`, `verification_method: qeaa_presentation`) against the account's verified identity profile rather than the wallet-bound device key, those results can be carried forward — restoring the account to **High** assurance without requiring the user to re-present the QEAA. See §18.13 for the progressive assurance lifecycle.

**Transaction log continuity.** The Migration Object includes the User's transaction log (TS10 V1.2), and the User can choose whether to restore it on the new Wallet Unit. This means the User may retain the ability to exercise data deletion rights (TS07) for presentations made prior to migration. RPs must be prepared to receive deletion requests referencing transactions from a previous Wallet Unit.

**Wallet-local deletion is not provider revocation.** Topic 51 gives the User a Wallet-side deletion right for any PID or attestation, but the deletion stays local to the Wallet Unit:

| Topic 51 deletion rule | RP-facing consequence |
|:-----------------------|:----------------------|
| The User can delete any PID or attestation at any time. | A later presentation may simply omit a credential that was previously present; this is not proof of provider revocation. |
| If the selected logical PID or attestation has multiple physical copies, the Wallet deletes every copy in that **same Credential Dataset**: same type, same Provider, and same attribute values. | Once-only or batch-issued copies can disappear as a set, while another same-type credential from the same Provider survives when its Dataset differs. |
| The Wallet does not notify the PID/Attestation Provider when the User deletes locally. | Provider status lists do not necessarily reveal local deletion. |
| For PIDs and device-bound attestations, associated WSCA/WSCD or keystore assets must be securely destroyed, with User authentication where required. | Old holder-binding keys should not reappear after a correct deletion; if they do, treat it as a wallet/security anomaly. |
| If the Wallet supports DC API and had disclosed credential availability, `PAD_05` requires it to disclose that the credential is no longer stored. | Browser/platform credential availability can shrink without any RP-side status-list event. |

**Solved deletion-scope example.** A university Provider has issued two logical diploma attestations to one Wallet: a bachelor's diploma with physical copies `B1` and `B2`, and a master's diploma `M1`. All three share the same attestation type and Provider, but the bachelor's and master's attribute values form different Credential Datasets. If the User selects the bachelor's diploma for deletion, `PAD_02` requires deletion of `B1` and `B2`; deleting `M1` would be an over-broad scope error. The Wallet then destroys the bachelor's related key assets where device binding applies and emits the Digital Credentials API “no longer stored” notification only if it previously disclosed that bachelor's credential as available.

| Event | What is deleted or changed | What it does **not** establish |
|:------|:---------------------------|:-------------------------------|
| **User deletes a logical PID/attestation** | All physical copies in the selected Credential Dataset and related device-bound key assets; the Provider is not notified. | Provider revocation, RP-side erasure, factory reset, or removal of another same-type Dataset. |
| **Factory reset** | Wallet-local contents, settings, logs, and reachable related key assets, subject to the external/remote-key limitation above. | Guaranteed erasure of disconnected or remote keys, issuer revocation, or RP-side GDPR erasure. |
| **App uninstallation** | The application is removed through the operating system. | Secure destruction of Wallet keys or data in external/remote components. |
| **Issuer revocation** | The issuer changes authoritative credential status; the credential instance becomes permanently revoked where the profile so requires. | Proof that every Wallet-local copy was physically deleted. |
| **RP-side GDPR erasure** | The RP evaluates and fulfils a data-subject request against data in its own systems. | Deletion of the credential from the Wallet or revocation by its Provider. |

> **Cross-references**: §13.5 (re-issued PID handling), §13.9 (credential churn by design), §18.11.1 (synced vs device-bound passkeys), §18.11.2 (account recovery flow), §18.13 (progressive assurance lifecycle), §18.13.3 (edge cases including wallet migration).
