### 6. Credential Formats: SD-JWT VC, mdoc, and Format Selection

:::important[This chapter is about dual-format operational reality, not format preference]
For RPs, SD-JWT VC and mdoc are not competing options where one can be cleanly standardized away. The ecosystem requires both, and the real engineering challenge is building verification, query construction, transport handling, and trust resolution that can branch cleanly by format without fragmenting the rest of the RP stack.
:::

Before format selection, treat each PID or attestation as the ARF's five-part object:

| Element | What the RP should understand |
|:--------|:------------------------------|
| **Attributes** | The data values the RP requests and relies on, such as names, dates, entitlements, or sector-specific facts. |
| **Metadata** | Attestation type, provider, validity, status, trust-anchor, legal-category, and device-binding metadata about the attestation itself. |
| **Proof** | The issuer proof and selective-disclosure mechanism the RP verifies: SD-JWT VC issuer signature and disclosures, or mdoc MSO/IssuerAuth and value digests. |
| **Attestation scheme** | The logical model for the attestation type: mandatory/optional attributes, identifiers, syntax, allowed values, namespaces, `vct`, `docType`, and metadata. |
| **Proof mechanism** | The standardised cryptographic method that protects authenticity, integrity, holder binding, and selective disclosure for the selected format. |

The practical consequence is that `vct`, `docType`, namespace, claim names, metadata, and proof processing are separate checks. A verifier that only validates the signature but ignores the Rulebook's scheme semantics is not Rulebook-complete.

#### 6.1 SD-JWT VC Overview

**SD-JWT VC** (Selective Disclosure JSON Web Token Verifiable Credential) is one of two mandatory credential formats in the EUDI Wallet ecosystem (alongside mdoc). It is the primary format for remote (over-the-internet) presentation flows.

An SD-JWT VC consists of three parts, serialised as a single string separated by tildes (`~`):

```
&lt;Issuer-signed JWT>~&lt;Disclosure 1>~&lt;Disclosure 2>~...~&lt;Key Binding JWT>
```

| Component | Purpose |
|:----------|:--------|
| **Issuer-signed JWT** | Contains the credential metadata and hashed attribute references; signed by the PID/Attestation Provider |
| **Disclosures** | Base64url-encoded `[salt, claim_name, claim_value]` arrays — one per selectively-disclosed attribute |
| **Key Binding JWT** | Proves the presenter (Wallet Unit) possesses the private key bound to the credential; signed by the Wallet Unit |

> **Specification layering — SD-JWT vs. SD-JWT VC**: SD-JWT VC is an application profile built on top of the base SD-JWT specification ([RFC 9901](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9901), finalised November 2025). RFC 9901 defines the general-purpose selective disclosure primitive — the `_sd` hash mechanism, Disclosures, and optional Key Binding JWT. SD-JWT VC ([draft-ietf-oauth-sd-jwt-vc-15](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-sd-jwt-vc/15/)) layers credential-specific semantics on top: the mandatory `vct` claim (credential type identifier), the `dc+sd-jwt` media type, the `status` claim for revocation, and Issuer Metadata / Type Metadata discovery. Key Binding is optional in RFC 9901 but effectively required in the EUDI context (device binding via WSCA). In the EUDI ecosystem, all credentials use the SD-JWT VC profile — bare SD-JWTs (without `vct` and `dc+sd-jwt` typing) are not valid credential presentations. RPs should validate the `vct` presence and `typ` header as part of their verification pipeline (§13.3).

#### 6.2 SD-JWT VC Structure: Decoded Issuer JWT

The decoded payload of the Issuer-signed JWT for a PID:

```json
{
  "iss": "https://pid-provider.example.de",
  "iat": 1719504000,
  "exp": 1751040000,
  "vct": "urn:eudi:pid:1",
  "cnf": {
    "jwk": {
      "kty": "EC",
      "crv": "P-256",
      "x": "oB3MnEqRFGT7vbq-hLsTIwoFUx7GnzLkc5xw2Ef44Gk",
      "y": "9e3K4L-hPmv0kZNG3v6j2iP5U38roAqhfVjhUb4Q8DA"
    }
  },
  "status": {
    "status_list": {
      "idx": 4321,
      "uri": "https://pid-provider.example.de/statuslist/1"
    }
  },
  "_sd": [
    "09vKrJMOGniTguCgaSferQ3JnE-qHcslWfuVxjKl_kY",
    "2FK0leQ_7mlJPG0VGNSBqj-nA36-tVac3K5vGqhlBPo",
    "Cmz3HYpvJPl9C_x4EQk6gSsqakzGVhGP3aeNOmTi8DI"
  ],
  "_sd_alg": "sha-256"
}
```

Key fields:

- `vct` — Verifiable Credential Type: `urn:eudi:pid:1` for the EU-wide SD-JWT VC PID type, or a domestic `urn:eudi:pid:*` type extending it
- `cnf.jwk` — Confirmation key: the public key of the Wallet Unit (device binding)
- `status` — Status List reference for revocation checking
- `_sd` — Array of hashes of the selectable disclosures
- `_sd_alg` — Hash algorithm used (`sha-256`)

#### 6.3 SD-JWT VC Selective Disclosure in Practice

When the RP requests only `family_name` and `birthdate`, the Wallet Unit:

1. Includes only the corresponding Disclosures (not all of them)
2. The RP can verify these Disclosures by hashing them and comparing with the `_sd` array in the Issuer JWT
3. Attributes NOT included in the Disclosures remain hidden — the RP sees only their hashes

Example Disclosures included:

```
WyJfMjZCY1R0ckJNR0RpaVl3UmRhZ0xBIiwiZmFtaWx5X25hbWUiLCJNw7xsbGVyIl0
~
WyJlbHVWNU9nM2dTTklJOEVZbnN4QV9BIiwiYmlydGhkYXRlIiwiMTk5MC0wMy0xNSJd
```

Decoded: `["_26BcTrkBMGDiiYwRdagLA", "family_name", "Müller"]` and `["eluV5Og3gSNII8EYnsxA_A", "birthdate", "1990-03-15"]`

> **Age-verification note**: PID Rulebook v1.5 does not define PID attributes such as `age_over_18`, `age_over_NN`, `age_in_years`, or `age_birth_year`. If the RP relies on the PID itself for age checks, it must request `birthdate` or an equivalent valid PID date claim and compute the threshold locally. For privacy-preserving age checks without date-of-birth disclosure, use a dedicated age-verification attestation or the ZKP-based age-verification profile discussed in §21.

#### 6.4 SD-JWT VC Key Binding JWT

The Key Binding JWT proves the presenter controls the private key referenced in `cnf.jwk`. Its payload:

```json
{
  "aud": "https://verifier.example-bank.de",
  "nonce": "dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk",
  "iat": 1709769600,
  "sd_hash": "fUMUMhki0LFWse...base64url_of_sha256_of_sd_jwt"
}
```

- `aud` — The RP's identifier (prevents replay to a different RP)
- `nonce` — The nonce from the presentation request (prevents replay)
- `sd_hash` — Hash of the entire SD-JWT (binds the KB-JWT to the specific presentation)

#### 6.5 mdoc Overview

**mdoc** (mobile document) is the credential format defined by ISO/IEC 18013-5, originally for mobile driving licences (mDL). In the EUDI Wallet ecosystem, it is the mandatory format for **proximity** presentation flows and is also supported for remote flows via ISO/IEC 18013-7.

mdoc uses CBOR (Concise Binary Object Representation) encoding, which is more compact than JSON and optimised for constrained environments (NFC, BLE).

#### 6.6 mdoc Structure

An mdoc consists of two main structures:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph MSO["MobileSecurityObject - MSO"]
        M0["`**Signed by Issuer**
        (PID/Attestation Provider)`"]
        M1["`Version`"]
        M2["`Digest algorithm (SHA-256)`"]
        M3["`Value digests
        (hash of each data element, per namespace)`"]
        M4["`Device key info
        (public key bound to Wallet Unit)`"]
        M5["`DocType
        e.g. eu.europa.ec.eudi.pid.1`"]
        M6["`Validity info
        (signed, validFrom, validUntil)`"]
        M0 --- M1
        M0 --- M2
        M0 --- M3
        M0 --- M4
        M0 --- M5
        M0 --- M6
    end

    subgraph ISI["IssuerSignedItem[]"]
        I1["`Per-namespace arrays of data elements`"]
        I2["`Each item: digestID, random,
        elementIdentifier, elementValue`"]
        I3["`Selective disclosure by omission
        (omit items not to disclose)`"]
        I1 --- I2 --- I3
    end

    MSO ~~~ ISI
    style M0 text-align:left
    style M3 text-align:left
    style M4 text-align:left
    style M5 text-align:left
    style M6 text-align:left
    style I2 text-align:left
    style I3 text-align:left
```

#### 6.7 MSO in CBOR Diagnostic Notation

```json
{
  "version": "1.0",
  "digestAlgorithm": "SHA-256",
  "valueDigests": {
    "eu.europa.ec.eudi.pid.1": {
      0: h'75167029...',  ; digest of family_name
      1: h'67e539d6...',  ; digest of given_name
      2: h'3394372d...',  ; digest of birth_date
      3: h'2e35ad3c...',  ; digest of nationality
    }
  },
  "deviceKeyInfo": {
    "deviceKey": {
      1: 2,      ; kty: EC2
      -1: 1,     ; crv: P-256
      -2: h'...' ; x-coordinate
      -3: h'...' ; y-coordinate
    }
  },
  "docType": "eu.europa.ec.eudi.pid.1",
  "validityInfo": {
    "signed": "2026-01-15T00:00:00Z",
    "validFrom": "2026-01-15T00:00:00Z",
    "validUntil": "2027-01-15T00:00:00Z"
  }
}
```

#### 6.8 Selective Disclosure in mdoc

Unlike SD-JWT VC (which uses hash-based selective disclosure), mdoc achieves selective disclosure by **omission**:

1. The MSO contains digests (hashes) of ALL data elements
2. The Wallet Unit includes only the `IssuerSignedItem` entries for the attributes the User approves
3. The RP can verify each received item by recomputing its hash and checking against the MSO digest
4. Items NOT included are invisible to the RP — the RP only sees their digest IDs

#### 6.9 Device Authentication (mdoc)

In proximity flows, the Wallet Unit provides a `DeviceAuth` structure:

```
DeviceAuth = {
  "deviceSignature": COSE_Sign1  ; over SessionTranscript
}
```

The `SessionTranscript` binds the response to the specific session, preventing replay. The RP verifies the signature using the `deviceKey` from the MSO.

#### 6.10 Format Selection: SD-JWT VC vs. mdoc

| Aspect | SD-JWT VC | mdoc (ISO 18013-5) |
|:-------|:----------|:-------------------|
| **Encoding** | JSON / JWT (Base64url) | CBOR (binary) |
| **Transport** | HTTP / OpenID4VP | BLE / NFC / Wi-Fi Aware + ISO 18013-5 |
| **Primary use** | Remote flows (internet) | Proximity flows (face-to-face) |
| **Remote support** | Native via OpenID4VP | Via ISO 18013-7 over OpenID4VP |
| **Selective disclosure** | Hash-based (`_sd` array + Disclosures) | Omission-based (exclude IssuerSignedItems) |
| **Device binding** | Key Binding JWT (KB-JWT) | DeviceAuth (COSE_Sign1) |
| **Revocation** | Status List (JWT claim) | Status List or issuer-defined |
| **Size efficiency** | Larger (JSON text + Base64) | Smaller (CBOR binary) |
| **Offline verification** | Conditional — all steps (signature, disclosures, KB-JWT) execute offline if Issuer trust anchor is pre-cached; only revocation check requires connectivity | Native (designed for offline; MSO verification is self-contained) |
| **W2W interactions** | NOT supported (TS9) | Mandatory for W2W |
| **HAIP 1.0 support** | Yes | Yes (via ISO 18013-7) |

> **RP implementation note**: RPs MUST support both formats. For remote flows, the RP typically receives SD-JWT VCs. For proximity flows, the RP receives mdoc. For remote flows, the RP may also receive mdoc via ISO 18013-7 encapsulation in OpenID4VP. The DCQL query language allows the RP to express format preferences.

> **Format-governance note**: The ARF's mandatory interoperability baseline is ISO/IEC 18013-5 / ISO/IEC 23220-2 mdoc plus SD-JWT VC. W3C VCDM is optional and limited to non-qualified EAAs; any W3C VCDM use needs a Rulebook profile that chooses the security mechanism, signature format, and transport, such as VC-JOSE-COSE or VC Data Integrity. QEAA and PuB-EAA Rulebooks choose from mdoc and SD-JWT VC only. If a Rulebook requires offline or proximity presentation, it must specify ISO/IEC 18013-5 mdoc because OpenID4VP / SD-JWT VC depends on internet connectivity.


#### 6.11 Rulebook Architecture

Attestation Rulebooks define the lifecycle and presentation rules for specific attestation types. They are maintained in the [EUDI Attestation Rulebooks Catalog](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-attestation-rulebooks-catalog/tree/36f8adcf914ac06cac18d685add04e0a8a06d685). The catalogue snapshot inspected on 26 July 2026 contains the template's version `1.0` header (24 June 2025), PID Rulebook v1.7, and the mDL working document. The template covers attributes, encoding, usage obligations, trust anchors, revocation, and compliance—see the chapter mapping in §6.12.

**Rulebook inventory** (pinned catalogue commit `36f8adcf`, 20 July 2026):

| Rulebook | Status | Attestation Type | Formats | RP Relevance |
|:---------|:-------|:-----------------|:--------|:-------------|
| **PID** | ✅ Published (v1.7) | mdoc `docType` / namespace: `eu.europa.ec.eudi.pid.1`; SD-JWT VC `vct`: `urn:eudi:pid:1` or domestic `urn:eudi:pid:*` | mdoc + SD-JWT VC | Core identity; v1.7 adds that the PID private key must not sign transactional data |
| **mDL** | ✅ Published working document (no legal value) | `org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL` | mdoc only; SD-JWT VC is not allowed for Wallet mDLs | Driving licence — transport, insurance, rental RPs |
| **LPID** | 📋 EWC RFC005 | `EWC_LPID_Attestation` | SD-JWT VC only | Legal person identity — B2B onboarding, procurement (§20.5) |
| **Healthcare** | ⚪ Not in pinned EC catalogue | Candidate families include ePrescription, HPC, and Patient Summary | Profile-dependent | Pilot/planning evidence only until a governing Rulebook/profile is accepted |
| **Education** | ⚪ Not in pinned EC catalogue | Candidate families include Digital Diploma, Microcredential, and EDCL | Profile-dependent | Existing sector infrastructure does not establish an EUDI Rulebook |
| **Travel / DTC** | ⚪ Not in pinned EC catalogue | Candidate Digital Travel Credential family | Profile-dependent | Separate ICAO/legislative track; no EC-catalogue Rulebook in the snapshot |
| **Social Security** | ⚪ Not in pinned EC catalogue | Candidate PDA1/EHIC families | Profile-dependent | Pilot/planning evidence only |
| **SCA** | ⚪ Scheme/profile-defined, not in pinned EC catalogue | Payment-scheme credential type | Profile-dependent | Payment-specific; use TS12 and the accepted issuer profile (§17) |

> **Catalogue boundary**: Only PID and mDL appear under `rulebooks/` in the pinned EC catalogue. The mDL Rulebook is explicitly a working document with no legal value, but it remains the catalogue source for the mDL-only encoding boundary. LPID originates from EWC RFC005 and is not in that catalogue snapshot. Healthcare, education, travel, and social-security pilots do not themselves create published Rulebooks. RPs should monitor later catalogue revisions and keep the pluggable verification architecture in §6.18, but activate a type only from an accepted, versioned Rulebook/profile rather than a projected publication.

**Rulebook vs. EAA Policy vs. Service Policy.** ETSI TR 119 479-1 adds a useful trust-service distinction that the Rulebook catalogue does not always make explicit. A pan-EU Rulebook can define the interoperability surface for an attestation type. An **EAA Policy** can then define the durable rules for a specific EAA type, Member State, sector, or community. The provider's **EAA Service Policy** or Trust Service Policy describes how a specific EAASP operates its service and conforms to those rules.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Owner["EAA type owner"]
        Requirements["Sector law, legislation, standard,<br/>or community requirements"]
        EAAP["EAA Policy<br/>(attestation-type rules)"]
        Requirements --> EAAP
    end

    subgraph Provider["EAA Service Provider"]
        ServiceBaseline["eIDAS and ETSI service requirements"]
        TSPolicy["EAA Service Policy /<br/>Trust Service Policy"]
        ServiceBaseline --> TSPolicy
    end

    EAA["Issued EAA"]

    EAAP -->|"can be supported by many EAASPs"| TSPolicy
    TSPolicy -->|"can support multiple EAA Policies"| EAAP
    EAA -->|"refers to specific EAA Policy"| EAAP
    EAA -->|"issued under service policy"| TSPolicy
```

| Policy surface | What it answers | RP consequence |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Rulebook** | What the EUDI ecosystem expects for this attestation family: attributes, encoding, usage, trust anchors, revocation, and compliance. | Use it as the human-readable interoperability baseline and compliance source. |
| **EAA Policy** | What this specific EAA type means: source quality, identity proofing, requester authorization, recipient model, binding, dissemination, lifecycle/status, validation, and versioned trust semantics. | Where the credential or scheme exposes an EAA Policy identifier or URI, capture it in the verification result and route obligation evaluation through it. |
| **EAA Service Policy / Trust Service Policy** | How a specific EAASP operates and audits its service under eIDAS, ETSI standards, and the relevant EAA Policy. | Use provider policy evidence for issuer/provider due diligence; do not treat provider identity alone as acceptance of every EAA type it can issue. |
| **Scheme / Catalogue metadata** | How software discovers the attestation type, schema, supported formats, and trust-authority references. | Treat as discovery and routing data, not an automatic acceptance decision. |

#### 6.12 RP-Relevant Rulebook Content

A Rulebook follows the standardised chapter structure in the pinned catalogue template (version-header `1.0`). The table below maps each Rulebook aspect to its machine-readable counterpart in the TS11 Catalogue of Attestations `SchemaMeta` model (§6.16). The `Rulebook Chapter` links point to the corresponding chapter in that pinned template:

| Aspect | Rulebook Chapter | What It Defines | `SchemaMeta` Field | RP Impact |
|:-------|:-----------------|:----------------|:-------------------|:----------|
| **Attribute catalogue** | [Ch. 2 — Attributes](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-attestation-rulebooks-catalog/blob/36f8adcf914ac06cac18d685add04e0a8a06d685/template/attestation-rulebook-template.md#2-attestation-attributes-and-metadata) | Mandatory vs. optional attributes within the attestation | `schemaURIs[].uri` → JSON schema | RP knows which attributes it *can* request |
| **Namespace / DocType** | [Ch. 3 — Encoding](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-attestation-rulebooks-catalog/blob/36f8adcf914ac06cac18d685add04e0a8a06d685/template/attestation-rulebook-template.md#3-attestation-encoding) | DocType and namespace identifiers (for mdoc) | `supportedFormats` | RP must use exact identifiers in DeviceRequest |
| **VCT** | [Ch. 3 — Encoding](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-attestation-rulebooks-catalog/blob/36f8adcf914ac06cac18d685add04e0a8a06d685/template/attestation-rulebook-template.md#3-attestation-encoding) | Verifiable Credential Type URI (for SD-JWT VC) | `schemaURIs[].uri` | RP uses this in DCQL `meta.vct_values` |
| **Attestation type uniqueness** | [Ch. 3 — Encoding](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-attestation-rulebooks-catalog/blob/36f8adcf914ac06cac18d685add04e0a8a06d685/template/attestation-rulebook-template.md#3-attestation-encoding) | Ecosystem-unique attestation type; maps to mdoc `docType`, OpenID4VP Credential Query `meta`, and SD-JWT VC `vct` | `supportedFormats`, `schemaURIs[]` | RP must not conflate mdoc identifiers with SD-JWT VC type values |
| **Issuer trust model** | [Ch. 5 — Trust Anchors](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-attestation-rulebooks-catalog/blob/36f8adcf914ac06cac18d685add04e0a8a06d685/template/attestation-rulebook-template.md#5-trust-anchors) | How the issuer chain is validated | `trustedAuthorities[]` | RP builds verification logic accordingly (§6.16) |
| **Legal category / trust-anchor metadata** | [Ch. 5 — Trust Anchors](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-attestation-rulebooks-catalog/blob/36f8adcf914ac06cac18d685add04e0a8a06d685/template/attestation-rulebook-template.md#5-trust-anchors) and template metadata | `attestation_legal_category`, Annex V/VII issuer data, and trust-anchor lookup location where applicable | `trustedAuthorities[]`, Rulebook text | RP distinguishes PID, QEAA, PuB-EAA, and non-qualified EAA validation paths |
| **Selective disclosability** | [Ch. 3 — Encoding](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-attestation-rulebooks-catalog/blob/36f8adcf914ac06cac18d685add04e0a8a06d685/template/attestation-rulebook-template.md#3-attestation-encoding) | Per-claim selective disclosure policy (ARB_30) | `schemaURIs[].uri` → claim metadata | RP must respect per-claim disclosability rules |
| **Subject / PID co-verification** | [Ch. 4 — Usage](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-attestation-rulebooks-catalog/blob/36f8adcf914ac06cac18d685add04e0a8a06d685/template/attestation-rulebook-template.md#4-attestation-usage) | Whether RP must also verify PID, user-subject binding, or another relationship alongside this attestation | *(indirect — current Rulebook text)* | RP's obligation engine checks the current Rulebook; do not cite `ARB_27`, which is empty in the current Annex Topic 12 |
| **Device binding** | [Ch. 4 — Usage](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-attestation-rulebooks-catalog/blob/36f8adcf914ac06cac18d685add04e0a8a06d685/template/attestation-rulebook-template.md#4-attestation-usage) | Device-bound vs. non-device-bound (ARB_34) | `bindingType` | RP verification pipeline differs based on binding |
| **Cross-attestation binding** | [Ch. 4 — Usage](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-attestation-rulebooks-catalog/blob/36f8adcf914ac06cac18d685add04e0a8a06d685/template/attestation-rulebook-template.md#4-attestation-usage) | `cryptographically_bound_to` field for binding to PID (ARB_28) | *(indirect — Rulebook text)* | RP must verify cryptographic binding when specified |
| **Disclosure policies** | [Ch. 3 — Encoding](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-attestation-rulebooks-catalog/blob/36f8adcf914ac06cac18d685add04e0a8a06d685/template/attestation-rulebook-template.md#3-attestation-encoding) | Default and allowed disclosure policies | *(indirect — Rulebook text)* | RP knows if embedded restrictions may apply |
| **Revocation** | [Ch. 6 — Revocation](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-attestation-rulebooks-catalog/blob/36f8adcf914ac06cac18d685add04e0a8a06d685/template/attestation-rulebook-template.md#6-revocation) | Whether the attestation is revocable, the applicable mechanism, and under `ARB_24a` the status/revocation-list URL | *(indirect — Rulebook text plus profile trust publication)* | RP selects the endpoint and separately authorized status-signer trust class; it does not reuse the credential-signing key by assumption |
| **Validity period** | [Ch. 6 — Revocation](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-attestation-rulebooks-catalog/blob/36f8adcf914ac06cac18d685add04e0a8a06d685/template/attestation-rulebook-template.md#6-revocation) | Maximum credential lifetime | *(indirect — Rulebook text)* | RP can enforce freshness thresholds |
| **Level of Security** | [Ch. 7 — Compliance](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-attestation-rulebooks-catalog/blob/36f8adcf914ac06cac18d685add04e0a8a06d685/template/attestation-rulebook-template.md#7-compliance) | ISO 18045 security evaluation level | `attestationLoS` | RP can apply risk-based acceptance policies |

> **Machine-readable discovery**: The `SchemaMeta` fields above are queryable via the TS11 Catalogue of Attestations REST API — see §6.16 for the discovery mechanism and RP integration flow.

TR 119 479-1 makes the EAA Policy a second policy surface that can sit below a broad Rulebook or, for a narrowly defined attestation type, effectively act as the Rulebook. RPs should therefore keep a place in their verification result model for `eaa_policy_id`, `eaa_policy_uri`, or equivalent profile-specific evidence when it is exposed by the credential, issuer metadata, scheme, or Rulebook.

| EAA Policy dimension | RP use |
|:--|:--|
| Attribute source and source quality | Decide whether the attribute can satisfy the RP's legal or risk threshold, especially when multiple sources can issue the same claim. |
| Subscriber / requester authorization | Check whether the party that requested issuance was allowed to request an EAA about the relevant Attribute Subject. |
| Recipient and delivery model | Distinguish wallet issuance, business-wallet issuance, file delivery, direct delivery, and vault delivery before applying holder-binding assumptions. |
| Binding mode | Route verification through identity binding, wallet/key binding, certificate/signature-context binding, or bearer-style possession as applicable. |
| Status and revocation rules | Set runtime freshness, audit retention, and long-term evidence policies for this attestation type. |
| Embedded disclosure policy | Treat Wallet-enforced disclosure constraints as meaningful only when a capable wallet/intermediary is in the presentation path. |

Rulebooks are also where the RP learns who or what an attestation is about. PID is user-identifying by design, but other attestations can be user-subject, representation-subject, object-subject, or no-subject artifacts. A vehicle registration, professional entitlement, holiday voucher, ticket, or mandate credential can have a different binding model than natural-person PID. The RP should therefore treat "attestation presented by this Wallet Unit" as a presentation fact first, not automatically as "this attribute identifies the Wallet User."

| Attestation subject model | RP interpretation |
|:--------------------------|:------------------|
| **Natural-person subject** | Verify issuer trust, status, device binding, and any Rulebook-required PID co-verification before treating the attributes as identifying the Wallet User. |
| **Object or asset subject** | Treat the credential as evidence about the object and then verify the Rulebook-defined relationship between the User and that object, such as ownership, use, or entitlement. |
| **Representation or mandate subject** | Verify the mandate/representation chain and the represented party separately from the presenter. Do not collapse representative identity and represented-party identity. |
| **No-subject / bearer-style credential** | Treat possession and valid presentation as the relevant evidence unless the Rulebook adds a separate User-binding or PID co-verification rule. |

#### 6.13 PID Rulebook: RP-Relevant Attributes

The natural-person PID attribute groups and RP minimisation patterns are now promoted into Natural-Person PID and Attribute Minimisation (§8). This credential-format chapter keeps only the hook: PID is the baseline natural-person identity credential, but the RP still chooses the smallest lawful claim set for the service before encoding that choice in DCQL (§9).

#### 6.14 Complete PID Attribute Catalogue

The complete PID claim catalogue, SD-JWT VC `claim_path` values, mdoc `elementIdentifier` values, claim-name boundaries, validity notes, metadata-minimisation notes, and Member State variation guidance are now consolidated in Complete PID Attribute Catalogue (§8.3). Keep §6 focused on credential formats; use §8 when deciding which PID claims to request.

#### 6.15 LPID Credential Format (Legal Person)

LPID is a legal-person extension credential rather than part of the natural-person PID baseline. This credential-format chapter keeps the dispatch hook only: RPs should recognise `EWC_LPID_Attestation` (and any future standardised LPID VCT) as a separate credential type, route it through SD-JWT VC verification, and then apply the legal-person attribute, EUID, trust-anchor, and mandate-binding rules in Legal-Person Extension: EBW, LPID, and Mandates (§20).

| RP implementation point | Baseline format decision | Legal-person extension consequence |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `vct` / credential type | Do not hardcode all identity credentials as `urn:eudi:pid:1`. | LPID currently uses `EWC_LPID_Attestation`; future ARF harmonisation may introduce another value. |
| Format | Treat LPID as SD-JWT VC in current EWC material. | The natural-person SD-JWT VC verifier can be reused, but issuer trust, attribute validation, and binding policy differ. |
| mdoc | No standard mdoc LPID profile is currently defined. | Proximity legal-person verification should wait for standardisation or use remote SD-JWT VC presentation. |
| Disclosure | Claims are independently disclosable under SD-JWT. | The RP still usually needs the legal-person identifier, legal-person name, representative PID, and mandate fields to make a B2B decision. |

#### 6.16 Rulebook Discovery via Catalogue of Attestations (TS11/EN 319 482-3)

The ARF defines a **three-layer architecture** for attestation governance:

| Layer | Name | Format | Purpose |
|:------|:-----|:-------|:--------|
| 1 | **Attestation Rulebook** | Human-readable (Markdown) | Governance document — attributes, encoding, usage, trust anchors, revocation, compliance |
| 2 | **Attestation Scheme** | Machine-readable (JSON schema) | Software-consumable version of the Rulebook — data model, namespaces, attribute types |
| 3 | **Catalogue of Attestations** | REST API + catalogue | Discovery service where Wallet Units and RPs find attestation Rulebooks and machine-readable schemas |

Rulebooks are for **humans** (product managers, compliance teams), while schemas are for **software** (the RP's verification pipeline ingests them at runtime). The Catalogue is the **discovery mechanism** that bridges the two. EC TS11 V1.0.1 (January 2026) is the current published precursor. Its ETSI successor, EN 319 482-3 V0.0.2, reached stable draft on 13 July 2026; until that EN is published, implementation claims in this section remain anchored to TS11.

**Catalogue boundary for RPs.** The ARF defines two different catalogues that solve different problems:

| Catalogue | Primary audience | What it gives the RP |
|:----------|:-----------------|:---------------------|
| **Catalogue of attributes** | QTSPs and other authorised issuance-side requesters | Attribute identifiers, semantic/schema metadata, and authentic-source data-service endpoints. ETSI TS 119 478 calls this the DIP/I1 Discover surface: `search` identifies attributes and `retrieve` locates I2 Verify or optional I3 Retrieve services. It is not the ordinary verifier RP's catalogue of accepted claims. |
| **Catalogue of attestations** | RPs, Attestation Providers, Wallet Units, and ecosystem tooling | Discovery of attestation types, machine-readable schemas, supported formats, trust-authority references, and the human-readable Rulebook pointer. This is the RP-facing discovery surface for verifier pipelines. |

Registration in the Catalogue of Attestations is not mandatory for every QEAA, PuB-EAA, or non-qualified EAA, and publication does not force an RP to accept the attestation type or create automatic cross-border recognition. Catalogue metadata is therefore a discovery input; the Rulebook and applicable law still control acceptance policy.

##### 6.16.1 SchemaMeta Data Model

The `SchemaMeta` class is the core data model an RP consumes from the Catalogue of Attestations API:

| Field | Type | RP Use |
|:------|:-----|:-------|
| `id` | UUID | Unique schema identifier — used as cache key |
| `version` | SemVer string | Version tracking — cache invalidation trigger |
| `rulebookURI` | URI (+ optional SRI hash) | Link to the human-readable Rulebook; RP can retrieve for compliance documentation |
| `trustedAuthorities` | Array of `TrustAuthority` | **Critical** — resolves to trust anchors (§6.16.2) |
| `attestationLoS` | String enum | Level of security: `iso_18045_high` / `moderate` / `enhanced-basic` / `basic` |
| `bindingType` | String enum | `claim`, `key`, `biometric`, or `none` — determines KB-JWT verification requirement |
| `supportedFormats` | Array of strings | `dc+sd-jwt`, `mso_mdoc`, `jwt_vc_json`, `jwt_vc_json-ld`, `ldp_vc` |
| `schemaURIs` | Array of `Schema` objects | Persistent URIs for format-specific JSON schemas — used for structural validation |

##### 6.16.2 TrustAuthority Sub-Model

The `TrustAuthority` object within `SchemaMeta.trustedAuthorities[]` determines which trust verification path the RP must follow:

| `frameworkType` | `value` | `isLoTE` | RP Verification Path |
|:----------------|:--------|:---------|:---------------------|
| `aki` | Base64URL-encoded Authority Key Identifier | N/A | Direct X.509 trust — RP matches AKI to cached issuer certificate |
| `etsi_tl` | URI of Trusted List | `false` (ETSI TS 119 612) | Qualified-service path, including QEAA Provider/service interpretation |
| `etsi_tl` | URI of LoTE | `true` (ETSI TS 119 602) | EUDI entity path, including PID and PuB-EAA Provider profiles and non-qualified EAA profiles where applicable |
| `openid_federation` | Entity Identifier URI | N/A | OID-FED — non-qualified EAAs only. Trust chain resolution per §5.5.10 |

> **Cross-reference**: The three trust verification paths correspond to the branching logic described in §5.5.19 (Non-Qualified EAA Issuer Trust). The `frameworkType` value is the machine-readable equivalent of the trust model diagram in §7.2.3.

##### 6.16.3 REST API

The Catalogue of Attestations exposes an OpenAPI 3.1–compatible REST API:

| Method | Endpoint | Purpose |
|:-------|:---------|:--------|
| `GET` | `/schemas` | Parameterised query — filter by `id`, `supportedformat`, `attestationlos`, `bindingtype`, `trustedAuthoritiesFrameworkType`, `schemauri`, `rulebookuri` |
| `GET` | `/schemas/{schemaId}` | Retrieve specific `SchemaMeta` by UUID |

All `GET` endpoints are **publicly accessible** (no authentication needed for read access). Responses are JWS-signed and paginated.

##### 6.16.4 RP Discovery Flow

When an RP receives an attestation type it has not previously verified, the following discovery flow applies:

1. **Extract identifier** — from the VP: `vct` claim (SD-JWT VC) or `docType` (mdoc)
2. **Query Catalogue** — `GET /schemas?supportedformat=dc+sd-jwt` with the VCT or format as filter
3. **Resolve trust authority** — read `trustedAuthorities[].frameworkType` together with the attestation legal category to determine the verification path (X.509 AKI, QEAA/qualified-service Trusted List, PID/PuB-EAA/applicable LoTE, or permitted non-qualified OID-FED); for a revocable Rulebook, also bind the status URL to the separately authorized status-signer anchor class
4. **Validate against schema** — fetch the JSON schema from `schemaURIs[].uri`; validate the VP payload for structural correctness
5. **Apply Rulebook and policy obligations** — retrieve the Rulebook from `rulebookURI`; when an EAA Policy identifier/URI is exposed, load or match that policy too; check subject/PID co-verification, binding, selective-disclosure, device-binding, and revocation requirements

##### 6.16.5 Caching Strategy

The Catalogue API has rate limits. RPs should implement:

- **TTL-based caching**: Cache `SchemaMeta` locally with a configurable TTL (e.g., 24 hours)
- **Version-based invalidation**: When `SchemaMeta.version` changes, invalidate the cached entry and re-fetch
- **Schema pre-fetching**: For known attestation types (PID, mDL), pre-fetch and cache schemas at startup
- **Graceful degradation**: If the API is unreachable, fall back to the most recently cached `SchemaMeta`

> **Source**: TS11 v1.0.1 (January 2026), Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1569.

#### 6.17 Sector-Specific Attestation Profiles

The following profiles are **planning envelopes** derived from Large-Scale Pilot (LSP) outputs and earlier discussion material. The pinned EC catalogue snapshot from 20 July 2026 contains no sector-specific Rulebooks beyond PID and mDL. These tables therefore illustrate likely RP decision surfaces only; an accepted, versioned Rulebook/profile and applicable law control production behavior. Cross-reference: §30.3 (LSP and interoperability testing table).

##### 6.17.1 Healthcare

Healthcare is a **priority use case** validated by the POTENTIAL Large-Scale Pilot (cross-border ePrescription flows).

**Key credentials:**

| Credential | Description | Expected Category | Expected Format |
|:-----------|:------------|:------------------|:----------------|
| **ePrescription** | Electronic prescription for cross-border pharmacy dispensation | QEAA or PuB-EAA | SD-JWT VC + mdoc (offline pharmacy) |
| **Health Professional Card (HPC)** | Proves healthcare professional qualification | PuB-EAA | SD-JWT VC |
| **Patient Summary** | Emergency medical data (allergies, conditions, medications) | QEAA or PuB-EAA | SD-JWT VC + mdoc |

**RP planning questions (not current Rulebook obligations):**

| Obligation | Rationale |
|:-----------|:----------|
| Patient/PID co-verification | Determine from the accepted healthcare Rulebook/profile whether and how patient identity must accompany the health credential; do not cite the empty current `ARB_27` row |
| `cryptographically_bound_to` PID (ARB_28) | Health credentials likely required to be device-bound and bound to PID |
| Proximity/offline support (ARB_02) | Pharmacies, ambulances, and emergency rooms may lack connectivity → mdoc format likely mandatory |
| GDPR Article 9 compliance | Health data is special category — RP needs explicit lawful basis |
| Data minimisation enforcement | Strict selective disclosure — request only the health and identity attributes required for the transaction |

**Trust model**: Category-dependent: a QEAA uses the TS 119 612 qualified-service path, while a PuB-EAA Provider and its separately authorized revocation-list signer use the applicable TS 119 602 LoTE profile. Healthcare credential providers could be national health authorities or QTSPs; MyHealth@EU may add sector routing but does not collapse those trust categories. POTENTIAL completed pilot work, but the pinned catalogue contains no healthcare Rulebook and this article assigns no publication date.

##### 6.17.2 Education

Education has substantial adjacent infrastructure (EDCL, EBSI, Europass), but that infrastructure does not establish an EUDI Rulebook or a publication sequence.

**Key credentials:**

| Credential | Description | Expected Category | Expected Format |
|:-----------|:------------|:------------------|:----------------|
| **Digital Diploma** | University degree certificate | QEAA or non-qualified EAA | SD-JWT VC |
| **Microcredential** | Short learning achievement (course, certificate) | Non-qualified EAA | SD-JWT VC |
| **Europass Digital Credential** | Standardised EU-wide learning credential (EDCL) | QEAA or PuB-EAA | SD-JWT VC |

**RP planning questions (not current Rulebook obligations):**

| Obligation | Rationale |
|:-----------|:----------|
| Holder/PID co-verification | Apply only when the accepted education Rulebook/profile requires a holder relationship; do not invent a `SHOULD` before that source exists |
| Accreditation verification | RP (employer, university) should verify the issuing institution is accredited |
| Revocation checking | Diplomas may have long validity but should be checkable (institution closure, degree revocation) |
| Cross-border recognition | European Qualifications Framework (EQF) level should be verifiable |

**Trust model**: Education is a sector where EBSI/DID may be relevant for specifically profiled non-qualified credentials. DC4EU tested EBSI-backed credentials with `did:ebsi` identifiers (§7.3.2). Keep that optional non-qualified path separate from the mandatory category paths: TS 119 612 for QEAAs and a TS 119 602 PuB-EAA Provider LoTE for PuB-EAAs. DC4EU concluded in July 2025 and EBSI supplied adjacent schema infrastructure, but the pinned EC catalogue contains no education Rulebook and establishes no publication order.

##### 6.17.3 Travel

Travel credentials operate on a **parallel regulatory track** — the DTC has its own regulation (COM/2024/670, COM/2024/671) and follows ICAO/ISO standards rather than the Attestation Rulebook template.

**Key credentials:**

| Credential | Description | Expected Category | Expected Format |
|:-----------|:------------|:------------------|:----------------|
| **Digital Travel Credential (DTC)** | Digital passport / ID card | PuB-EAA | mdoc (ICAO 9303 / ISO 23220-2) |
| **Hotel Check-in** | Age/identity for hotel registration | Non-qualified EAA | SD-JWT VC |
| **Vehicle Rental** | Age/identity + driving qualification | Non-qualified EAA | SD-JWT VC |

**RP planning questions (not current Rulebook obligations):**

| Obligation | Rationale |
|:-----------|:----------|
| Identity co-verification | Apply the final DTC scheme and border-law profile; this planning table does not create a Wallet Rulebook duty |
| Proximity/offline support (ARB_02) | Border gates, hotel lobbies may use NFC/BLE → mdoc likely mandatory for DTC |
| ICAO alignment | DTC must align with ICAO 9303 Machine Readable Travel Document standards |
| Biometric verification | DTC likely includes facial image — live face matching possible |

**Trust model**: The final DTC scheme controls. If issued as a PuB-EAA, provider and revocation-list anchors belong to the applicable TS 119 602 LoTE profile; a QEAA-class service instead uses the TS 119 612 path. DTC follows a separate ICAO/ISO and legislative track. The 2024 proposals and EWC pilot do not create a catalogue Rulebook or justify a publication forecast.

##### 6.17.4 Social Security

Social security credentials are critical for **cross-border worker mobility**, driven by the DC4EU Large-Scale Pilot.

**Key credentials:**

| Credential | Description | Expected Category | Expected Format |
|:-----------|:------------|:------------------|:----------------|
| **PDA1 (Portable Document A1)** | Confirms social security coverage for cross-border workers | PuB-EAA | SD-JWT VC |
| **EHIC** | European Health Insurance Card replacement | PuB-EAA | SD-JWT VC |
| **Social Benefits Attestation** | Entitlement to specific social benefits | PuB-EAA | SD-JWT VC |

**RP planning questions (not current Rulebook obligations):**

| Obligation | Rationale |
|:-----------|:----------|
| PID/user co-verification | Apply the accepted social-security Rulebook/profile; this planning table does not define the binding mechanism or normative level |
| Issuing Member State verification | RP must verify which Member State is responsible for coverage |
| Cross-border portability | PDA1 must be recognised across all Member States |
| No proximity requirement | Administrative processes are predominantly online |

**Trust model**: A PuB-EAA implementation would resolve national social-security institutions and their separately authorized revocation-list signers through the applicable TS 119 602 PuB-EAA Provider LoTE, not a generic QTSP Trusted List. EESSI may provide backend sector integration without replacing the Wallet credential trust path. DC4EU piloted PDA1 digitalisation, but the pinned EC catalogue contains no social-security Rulebook and establishes no publication date.

#### 6.18 Rulebook-Aware Verification Pipeline

##### 6.18.1 The Problem

Most current RP implementations hardcode their verification logic for PID. When sector-specific Rulebooks arrive, this approach fails to scale:

- **Maintenance burden** — each new Rulebook requires code changes to the verification pipeline
- **Trust model fragmentation** — healthcare uses Trusted Lists, education may use EBSI/LoTE, travel uses government TLs
- **Format heterogeneity** — some attestations are mdoc-only (mDL, DTC), some SD-JWT VC-only, some both

The solution is a **Rulebook-driven verification architecture** that dynamically adapts based on the `SchemaMeta` retrieved from the Catalogue of Attestations (§6.16).

##### 6.18.2 Architecture Pattern

```mermaid
---
config:
  flowchart:
    subGraphTitleMargin:
      bottom: 10
---
flowchart TD
    A["`**Incoming VP**`"]
    B["`**1. Extract VCT / DocType**
    SD-JWT VC: vct claim
    mdoc: docType`"]
    C["`**2. Catalogue Lookup**
    GET /schemas?supportedformat=...`"]
    D["`**3. Trust Model Router**`"]
    E["`**4. Schema Validation**
    Fetch JSON schema from
    schemaURIs — validate VP`"]
    F["`**5. Obligation Engine**
    Subject / PID binding?
    Binding verification?
    Selective disclosure policy?
    Revocation check?`"]
    G(["`✅ **VP Verified**`"])

    A --> B --> C --> D --> E --> F --> G

    D1["`X.509 AKI
    verify`"]
    D2["`Trusted List
    resolve`"]
    D3["`LoTE
    resolve`"]
    D4["`OID-FED
    Entity resolve`"]

    D --> D1 & D2 & D3 & D4

    style A text-align:left
    style B text-align:left
    style C text-align:left
    style E text-align:left
    style F text-align:left
```

##### 6.18.3 Design Decisions

| Decision | Options | Recommendation |
|:---------|:--------|:---------------|
| **Schema caching** | Cache `SchemaMeta` locally vs. always query | Cache with TTL (e.g., 24h), invalidate on version change. The Catalogue API has rate limits (§6.16.5). |
| **Trust model plugin** | Hardcode vs. pluggable trust resolvers | Pluggable — implement `TrustResolver` interface with `X509AKIResolver`, `TrustedListResolver`, `LoTEResolver`, `OpenIDFederationResolver` implementations |
| **Format routing** | Separate pipelines vs. unified | Separate: mdoc (§13.4) and SD-JWT VC (§13.3) parsing are fundamentally different. Use a `FormatHandler` abstraction. |
| **Subject / PID binding** | Always verify PID vs. per-Rulebook | Per-Rulebook. Check the current Rulebook's usage chapter for user-subject, object-subject, bearer, PID co-verification, and representation requirements. |
| **Obligation engine** | Static rules vs. Rulebook / EAA Policy-derived | Hybrid: static rules for regulation-mandated obligations, Rulebook-derived rules for ecosystem interoperability, and EAA Policy-derived rules for source quality, requester/recipient authorization, binding, status, and delivery constraints where a policy identifier is exposed. |

##### 6.18.4 New Attestation Type Onboarding Checklist

When a new sector-specific Rulebook is published, an RP should follow this 5-step process:

1. **Register** — query the Catalogue of Attestations (§6.16.3) for the new VCT/DocType to obtain the `SchemaMeta`
2. **Configure trust** — extract `trustedAuthorities[]` from `SchemaMeta`; add the corresponding trust resolver to the pipeline (e.g., add a `LoTEResolver` for education credentials using EBSI/LoTE)
3. **Configure schema** — download the JSON schema from `schemaURIs[].uri`; add format-specific validation rules (SD-JWT VC claims, mdoc namespace/elementIdentifiers)
4. **Configure obligations** — read Rulebook Chapters 3–6 and, when separate, the applicable EAA Policy; set flags for subject/PID co-verification from current Rulebook text, `cryptographically_bound_to` (ARB_28), per-claim SD-JWT VC selective disclosure (ARB_30/ARB_31), device binding type (ARB_34), legal category / trust-anchor metadata, source-quality policy, recipient/delivery model, and revocation mechanism
5. **Test** — validate end-to-end with the LSP/pilot reference implementation (if available) or the EU Reference Wallet (§30)

> **RP planning impact**: Implement the pluggable trust resolution module and format routing abstraction **now**, even while only PID and mDL Rulebooks are published. When sector-specific Rulebooks arrive, onboarding a new attestation type becomes a configuration change rather than a code change.

##### 6.18.5 EAA Project Design Framework: Regulatory Regime First

§6.18.4 addresses the RP's perspective when *consuming* a new attestation type. This section addresses the complementary question: **how should an organisation design an EAA project from scratch** — whether as an issuer, a sector body publishing a Rulebook, or a dual-role RP that both issues and consumes attestations?

The critical first-order decision is not about credential formats or technical architecture — it is about **which regulatory regime** the attestation falls under. Only after the regulatory regime is determined do source verification, issuer governance, wallet issuance, registration, publication, technical modelling, and status/revocation follow.

**Three regulatory regimes**: Within the EUDI ecosystem, four categories of attestations exist (PID, QEAA, PuB-EAA, and non-qualified EAA), but for EAA project design the distinction collapses to three regimes:

| Regime | Who Issues | Legal Basis | Key Obligations |
|:-------|:-----------|:------------|:----------------|
| **Non-qualified EAA** | Any trust service provider | eIDAS Art. 45b–45c | Risk management (CIR 2025/2160); personal data separation (Art. 45b(3)); no qualified legal claim |
| **QEAA** | Qualified Trust Service Provider (QTSP) | eIDAS Art. 45d + Annex V | Full QTSP obligations; identity verification under Art. 24 eIDAS; conformity assessment; CIR 2025/1569 revocation framework |
| **PuB-EAA** | Public sector body responsible for an authentic source (or on its behalf) | eIDAS Art. 45f + Annex VII | Notification to Commission (CIR 2025/1569 Art. 5); Commission-published provider list (Art. 6); conformity assessment equivalent to QTSP |

> **Design rule**: The same attestation content (e.g., a diploma, a professional licence) may fall into a different regulatory regime depending on *who* issues it. A university directly issuing diplomas into wallets operates under the PuB-EAA regime; a commercial credential aggregator issuing the same diploma attestation on the university's behalf would likely need a QTSP designation under the QEAA regime.

**Design considerations** every EAA project must address:

- **Regulatory regime**: Non-qualified EAA, QEAA, or PuB-EAA — without this determination, downstream decisions cannot be made correctly
- **Subject, attributes, and source**: Which person or entity is the subject, which attributes are attested, from which authentic source each attribute is obtained, and how the issuer verifies correctness before issuance (for QEAAs, this is part of the issuance regime per CIR 2025/1569 Art. 9)
- **EUDI Wallet issuance scope**: Whether the attestation must be issued into an EUDI Wallet — if yes, CIR 2024/2977 applies (format, namespace, binding); if the attestation targets a proprietary wallet, the EUDI legal framework does not automatically apply
- **Attestation Rulebook, EAA Policy, and scheme registration**: A human-readable interoperability specification, a policy surface for the specific EAA type where needed, and a machine-readable definition (§6.16), with attestation type and namespace registered in the Catalogue of Attestations (§6.16.3)
- **Trust infrastructure**: How issuing parties, relying parties, trust anchors, and registrations are published and discovered — including RP registration (§4), access certificates (§5.2), and LoTE publication (§5.5)
- **Validity and revocation model**: Short-lived, ASL, ARL, or hybrid — chosen early in the design, not retrofitted (see §B.1 for the binding legal framework)

**Topic 42 authentic-source access for QEAAs**: Annex Topic 42 describes an upstream **QTSP/QEAA issuance** path, not an ordinary verifier-RP lookup right. A verifier RP consumes the resulting QEAA through issuer signature validation, Trusted List qualification/status, Rulebook/schema metadata, holder binding, and revocation status. It should not query civil, business, or sector authentic sources during presentation verification unless a separate sector law and integration profile explicitly creates that path.

| Topic 42 step | Actor | Design implication |
|:--------------|:------|:-------------------|
| Discovery and designation of Authentic Sources or recognised intermediaries (`QTSPAS_01`, `QTSPAS_06`) | Member State | Issuer projects must know which source or intermediary is primary/recognised for each attribute and how QTSPs are allowed to request verification. |
| Requester authentication (`QTSPAS_02`) | Authentic Source / intermediary | The source authenticates the requester as a QTSP issuing QEAAs, for example through Trusted List lookup; this is source-side access control, not RP presentation-time trust resolution. |
| User approval and possible additional User authentication (`QTSPAS_02`, `QTSPAS_08`) | QTSP and, where legally required, Authentic Source | The QTSP obtains User approval before source verification; the source may separately authenticate or approve the User if its legal basis requires it. |
| Attribute verification response (`QTSPAS_02`-`QTSPAS_04`) | Authentic Source / intermediary | Responses are per-attribute verification outcomes. From 1 January 2027, CIR 2026/1735 and ETSI TS 119 478 make the concrete outcome vocabulary `Match`, `MatchWithVariation`, `NoMatch`, and `Unknown`; a deferred or failed exchange is transport/process state, not a fifth comparison outcome. |
| Direct request after discovery (`QTSPAS_05`) | QTSP | The QTSP sends the verification request directly to the nationally recognised source or intermediary after discovery. |
| Current technical baseline | Authentic Source / recognised intermediary | CIR 2026/1735 selects ETSI TS 119 478 clauses 6.1.1 or 6.2.3, with EU adaptations, for the signed-or-sealed verification result. `QTSPAS_07` and `QTSPAS_07a` are empty in ARF v3 and must not be cited as substantive current requirements. |

> **Dual-role RP impact**: If the organisation is only a verifier RP, Topic 42 is consumed as upstream assurance embedded in the QEAA ecosystem. If the organisation also operates as a QTSP/QEAA issuer, Topic 42 becomes an issuer-side integration requirement that must be designed before issuance goes live.

From **1 January 2027**, the source or recognised intermediary identifies the responsible Authentic Source/public body and signs or seals the verification result using at least the advanced-signature/advanced-seal based-on-qualified-certificate level required by CIR 2026/1735. `MatchWithVariation` means the submitted value is not identical but the source can return its authoritative value under the selected TS 119 478 profile; it is not permission for an issuer to silently coerce or overwrite the User's claim. The QTSP records the returned outcome, source identity, signature/seal validation, request correlation, and any policy decision before issuance.

**QEAA identity verification hardening**: For QEAAs, the main identity verification obligation derives from eIDAS Art. 24: before issuing a qualified certificate or QEAA, the QTSP must verify the identity and relevant attributes of the person concerned. CIR 2025/1566 makes this concrete by designating **ETSI TS 119 461 V2.1.1 (2025-02)** as the reference standard, specifically Annex C, clause C.4, with EU-specific adaptations. CIR 2025/1566 entered into force but becomes applicable on **19 August 2027**. Specific hardenings include:

- Identity proofing connected to authoritative evidence must be peer reviewed or certified at assurance level *high* under eIDAS, or comply with ETSI TS 119 461 C3.1–C3.6
- Independent conformity assessment bodies must be accredited; certification must reference eIDAS assurance levels for notified eID means or certified EUDI Wallets
- Fully automated identity proofing requires defined target FAR/FRR values based on risk analysis; values may not be weaker than for comparable hybrid cases
- Physical identity document validation must be tested by an accredited laboratory or national authority by 19 August 2027 and every two years thereafter

> **RP impact**: For RPs that also operate as QEAAs issuers (dual-role organisations), these identity verification hardening requirements directly affect onboarding flows. Where the user already holds a PID in the EUDI Wallet, the QTSP can request and verify PID attributes as a high-assurance identification input under the current ARF v3.0 presentation model, though doing so is not an independent legal exemption from Art. 24.

**Adjacent upstream onboarding act — CIR 2026/798**: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/798 performs a related but distinct function for the Wallet ecosystem: it also designates **ETSI TS 119 461 V2.1.1 (2025-02)** as the conformance baseline, but for **remote onboarding of wallet users** where an eID means at **LoA substantial** is combined with additional remote onboarding procedures that together satisfy **LoA high**. For RPs, this matters mainly as an **upstream trust enabler** rather than a new RP-duty source: it strengthens the legal basis for trusting that PID issuance and wallet-user binding may have been achieved through a harmonised, high-assurance remote proofing process before the RP ever receives a presentation.

**Recommended sequencing**: Since downstream requirements cascade from upstream decisions, the design considerations above should be addressed in roughly this order: (1) determine the regulatory regime, (2) decide EUDI Wallet scope and applicable CIRs, (3) define the attribute model and source verification chain, (4) design the Rulebook, EAA Policy if separate, and attestation scheme registration, (5) select the validity/revocation model, and — for QEAAs specifically — design the issuance flow against Art. 24 + CIR 2025/1566 from the outset rather than treating identity verification as an afterthought.

---

### 7. Identifier and Trust Model: X.509, DIDs, and the Wallet Landscape

:::important[Most RPs should treat DID support as an exception path, not a baseline requirement]
This chapter matters because DID terminology appears frequently around wallets, SSI ecosystems, and vendor materials, which can make the EUDI trust model look more decentralized than it is in practice. For core RP integration, the default path remains X.509-based trust anchored in the ARF and Trusted Lists; DID resolution becomes relevant only for specific non-qualified or adjacent ecosystem scenarios.
:::

#### 7.1 Scope of This Chapter

A common question for RP integration architects is: **does the EUDI Wallet ecosystem use Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs), and does my RP need to support DID resolution?** This is particularly relevant because several non-EU digital identity systems — including the Swiss swiyu wallet and the EBSI infrastructure — use DIDs, and some commercial wallet SDKs advertise DID support as a feature.

This chapter provides a definitive answer by examining:

- The ARF's official position on X.509 vs. DIDs, including the authoritative clarification from the ARF team (see §7.2)
- The DID methods that exist in the European identity landscape and their relevance to the EUDI ecosystem (§7.3)
- The trust model used by every category of wallet an RP may encounter: platform wallets like Apple Wallet and Google Wallet (§7.4), national EUDI wallets (§7.5), and commercial/SSI wallets (§7.6)
- The W3C Digital Credentials API browser mediation layer that connects RPs to wallets (§7.7)
- A practical RP decision matrix answering "do you need DID support?" for each wallet type (§7.8)

**A Decentralized Identifier (DID)** is a globally unique URI (e.g., `did:web:example.com`, `did:ebsi:z123...`) that resolves to a **DID Document** containing public keys, service endpoints, and authentication methods. Unlike X.509 certificates — which derive trust from a hierarchical Certificate Authority chain — DIDs derive trust from the DID method's resolution mechanism (DNS, blockchain, distributed hash table, etc.). The W3C DID Core v1.0 specification achieved Recommendation status in July 2022; the latest published DID Core v1.1 report remains the Candidate Recommendation Snapshot dated 5 March 2026.

> **Relationship to other sections**: This chapter builds on §5 (Trust Infrastructure — certificates, trusted lists, LoTEs) and §6 (Credential Formats — SD-JWT VC, mdoc, Rulebooks). It must be read before §8 (OpenID4VP), which explains the `x509_hash:<base64url-hash>` Client Identifier Prefix required by HAIP for signed requests; OpenID4VP 1.0 does not use a separate `client_id_scheme` parameter for that prefix. For RPs considering non-qualified EAA acceptance or interoperability with Member States that use OpenID Federation for RP trust (notably Italy), see §5.5.10–§5.5.19 for the OID-FED protocol, trust chain resolution, and the dual trust model precedent.

#### 7.2 The ARF Mandate: X.509 for the Core, DIDs Optional for Non-Qualified EAAs

##### 7.2.1 The Core Rule

The ARF Trust Model (ARF §6.1) establishes the foundational rule:

> *"For PIDs, qualified EAAs, PuB-EAAs, access certificates, and registration certificates, interoperability is essential (ARF §4.2.3). Interoperability is achieved by using a PKI following X.509 certificate standards ([RFC5280], [RFC3647]). **Non-qualified EAAs may adopt alternative trust models and verification mechanisms.**"*
> — ARF Main Document, §6.1

This rule is reinforced by the high-level requirement **RPA_02** (ARF Topic 6): Wallet Units and Relying Party Instances must support X.509 certificates for authentication.

##### 7.2.2 Official Clarification: GitHub Issue #278

The question of DID inclusion was formally raised in [GitHub Issue #278](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-architecture-and-reference-framework/issues/278) — "Request for inclusion of Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) in the ARF" — filed on 2024-07-09 by representatives of the Decentralized Identity Foundation (DIF), the Digital Credentials Consortium (DCC), and the Trust over IP Foundation. The issue received 94 reactions (49 👍, 11 🎉, 20 ❤️, 14 🚀) and 26 substantive comments before being closed on 2025-05-15.

The **official ARF team response** (December 2024, from a contributor with the `CONTRIBUTOR` role) stated:

> *"Whether this is possible depends on the legal attestation type. For PIDs, qualified EAAs, and PuB-EAAs, a primary objective is interoperability (see ARF §4.1.3). This means we need a single trust model that is supported by all actors and components in the ecosystem. Therefore, these types of attestations will be implemented using X509 certificates and 'classical' X509-based Certificate Authorities according to [RFC5280] and [RFC3647]. The same is true for non-qualified EAAs complying with ISO/IEC 18013-5, because the use of X.509 certificates is specified in that standard. **However, for non-qualified EAAs complying with [SD-JWT VC], other trust frameworks may be used, including ones that use DIDs.** This will be clarified in §6.1 of the ARF."*

##### 7.2.3 Trust Model Decision Flowchart

The following flowchart shows the decision path an RP follows to determine whether DID resolution is needed for a given attestation:

```mermaid
---
config:
  flowchart:
    subGraphTitleMargin:
      bottom: 10
---
flowchart TD
    A{"`**What is the
    attestation type?**`"} -->|PID| B
    A -->|QEAA| B
    A -->|PuB-EAA| B
    A -->|Non-qualified EAA| C

    B["`**X.509 Mandatory**
    Art. 5a / 45d / 45f
    Trusted Lists / LoTEs`"]
    B --> D

    C{"`**What credential
    format?**`"}
    C -->|ISO/IEC 18013-5| E["`**X.509 per ISO standard**
    IACA certificates`"]

    framework?**`"}
    C -->|W3C VCDM 2.0| G

    E --> D

    F -->|EUDI Rulebook| H["`**X.509 default**
    Standard ARF trust model`"]
    F -->|Custom Rulebook| I

    H --> D

    may specify DID-based trust`"] --> I

    D(["`✅ **Use X.509 path**
    No DID resolution for

```

> **RP planning impact**: The overwhelmingly common case is the left branch — PIDs, QEAAs, PuB-EAAs, and ISO 18013-5 credentials use the X.509 path, so the RP does not invoke DID resolution for those attestations. The amber branch (DID possible) is reached **only** for non-qualified EAAs using SD-JWT VC with a custom Rulebook or W3C VCDM 2.0. The locally pinned Attestation Rulebook catalogue snapshot at commit `36f8adcf914ac06cac18d685add04e0a8a06d685` (20 July 2026) contains only the PID and mDL Rulebooks; neither mandates DID-based trust. A future domain Rulebook could make a DID method relevant, so the RP must decide from the selected attestation's actual Rulebook rather than from wallet marketing.

##### 7.2.4 Classification by Attestation Type

| Attestation Type | Legal Basis | Trust Model | DID Allowed? |
|:---|:---|:---|:---:|
| **PID** (Person Identification Data) | Art. 5a eIDAS 2.0 | X.509 PKI — Trusted Lists / LoTEs | ❌ |
| **QEAA** (Qualified EAA) | Art. 45d eIDAS 2.0 | X.509 PKI — QTSP Trusted Lists | ❌ |
| **PuB-EAA** (Public Body EAA) | Art. 45f eIDAS 2.0 | X.509 PKI — qualified certificate on issuer | ❌ |
| **Non-qualified EAA** (ISO/IEC 18013-5 format) | Art. 45e eIDAS 2.0 | X.509 per the ISO standard | ❌ |
| **Non-qualified EAA** (SD-JWT VC format) | Art. 45e eIDAS 2.0 | **Alternative trust frameworks allowed** | ✅ |
| **Non-qualified EAA** (W3C VCDM 2.0 format) | Art. 45e eIDAS 2.0 | Optional format; Rulebook defines trust | ✅ |

##### 7.2.5 Classification by Credential Format

| Format | Mandatory for Wallet Units? | Trust Model | DID Allowed? |
|:---|:---|:---|:---:|
| **ISO/IEC 18013-5** (CBOR/mdoc) | ✅ Mandatory | X.509 PKI per the ISO standard | ❌ |
| **SD-JWT VC** | ✅ Mandatory | X.509 for qualified; **alternative trust** for non-qualified | ✅ (non-qualified only) |
| **W3C VCDM 2.0** (JSON-LD) | ❌ Optional (non-qualified only) | Rulebook defines | ✅ (implicitly) |

##### 7.2.6 Why the Mandatory Core Uses X.509

The rationale, as documented in ARF §5.2.3 and ARF §6.1, and the GitHub Issue #278 discussion:

1. **Interoperability mandate**: eIDAS 2.0 interoperability requirements, reinforced by ARF §4.2.3, require a *single* trust model for PIDs, QEAAs, and PuB-EAAs that all 30 participating countries (27 EU + 3 EEA/EFTA) can implement uniformly. A single trust model eliminates the combinatorial explosion of method-specific resolution, verification, and key management that would arise from supporting multiple DID methods.

2. **Existing PKI infrastructure**: EU Member States already operate qualified trust service provider (QTSP) PKI infrastructure under eIDAS 1.0. X.509 builds on this existing investment — the trust anchors (Trusted Lists, LoTEs) described in §5.5 are inherently X.509-based.

3. **ETSI standards alignment**: ETSI TS 119 475 defines the RP attribute and certificate-linkage model, while ETSI TS 119 411-8 defines policy and profile requirements for X.509 access certificates. Together they reinforce the X.509-based RP authentication layer used in the EUDI ecosystem, even though WRPRCs themselves are JWT/CWT artifacts. These standards are referenced by the CIRs and cannot be replaced without regulatory action.

4. **ISO/IEC 18013-5 compatibility**: The mobile driving licence standard mandates X.509 reader authentication certificates (IACA — Issuing Authority CA). Using DIDs would break interoperability with deployed mDL infrastructure in 30+ countries.

5. **DID method proliferation risk**: The W3C DID registry lists 100+ registered DID methods, each with different trust assumptions, resolution infrastructure, key management, and security guarantees. Mandating DID support would require selecting specific methods — which itself fragments the ecosystem and creates governance complexity that X.509 PKI avoids.

The core philosophical position is: *identity in the eIDAS model structurally stems from sovereign states* — the EUDI trust model is anchored in government-operated Trusted Lists and LoTEs (§5.5), which inherently use X.509 PKI. DIDs, by contrast, enable self-sovereign or organisationally-sovereign identity — a fundamentally different trust paradigm.

#### 7.3 DID Methods in the European Landscape

While the EUDI mandatory core does not use DIDs, several European identity ecosystems do. RPs should be aware of these methods because: (a) non-qualified EAA Rulebooks may reference them, (b) EBSI pilot credentials use them, and (c) the Swiss swiyu ecosystem uses `did:webvh` for its entire trust infrastructure.

##### 7.3.1 DID Method Reference Table

| Method | Anchoring | Key Rotation | Decentralisation | European Usage | W3C Status |
|:---|:---|:---:|:---:|:---|:---|
| `did:key` | Self-contained — public key encoded in DID | ❌ | Full (no infra) | EBSI Natural Persons | Community spec |
| `did:jwk` | Self-contained — JWK embedded in DID | ❌ | Full (no infra) | — | Community spec |
| `did:web` | DNS / HTTPS endpoint | ✅ | Low (centralised DNS) | Some SSI wallets | W3C CCG spec |
| `did:webvh` | DNS + verifiable history log | ✅ | Medium | **swiyu** (Swiss e-ID) | DIF spec |
| `did:ebsi` | EBSI permissioned blockchain | ✅ | Consortium chain | **EBSI**, DC4EU pilots | EBSI spec |
| `did:ion` | Bitcoin + IPFS (Sidetree) | ✅ | High (Bitcoin) | — | DIF spec |
| `did:ethr` | Ethereum blockchain | ✅ | High (Ethereum) | Talao wallet | Community spec |
| `did:dht` | Distributed Hash Table (Mainline DHT) | ✅ | High (P2P) | Talao wallet | TBD spec |

##### 7.3.2 EBSI: The EU's Own DID Infrastructure

The **European Blockchain Services Infrastructure (EBSI)** — operated by the European Commission — has two DID profiles:

- **Legal Entities**: DID documents stored on EBSI's permissioned ledger (Hyperledger Besu). Supports key rotation. ~40 European public bodies participate.
- **Natural Persons**: DID documents generated and stored *only* in the wallet (not on ledger) — effectively a `did:key` profile to preserve privacy.

The **DC4EU** Large-Scale Pilot (Digital Credentials for Europe — educational credentials, social security) is actively evaluating tools to integrate EBSI capabilities — specifically `did:ebsi` and `did:key` — into the EUDI Wallet Reference Implementation. This evaluation will determine whether EBSI DIDs can coexist with the X.509 trust model in a single wallet.

##### 7.3.3 swiyu: Switzerland's DID-First e-ID System

Switzerland occupies a unique position: an EFTA member but not an EEA member, it develops its own e-ID system under Swiss federal law (not eIDAS 2.0). The **swiyu** wallet uses `did:webvh` (DID Web + Verifiable History) — an enhancement of `did:web` that adds a verifiable audit trail (`did.jsonl` log file) and self-certifying identifiers (SCIDs) without blockchain dependency.

Key technical details:

- **Credential format**: SD-JWT VC — the same format used in the EUDI ecosystem
- **Trust infrastructure**: swiyu Base Registry (public registry of DIDs, public keys, revocation lists) + swiyu Trust Registry (trust statements certifying legitimate issuers/verifiers)
- **Deployment state**: The Public Beta and swiyu app have run since the end of March 2025. On 30 June 2026 the Swiss programme postponed the e-ID launch to add security and privacy work; it now expects the trust infrastructure to enter operation in the first half of 2027 and does not support the former “summer 2026 full launch” claim.
- **Interoperability**: swiyu uses SD-JWT VC and OpenID4VC, matching EUDI at the protocol level — but differs at the trust anchoring level (DID-based Base Registry vs. X.509-based Trusted Lists)

The Switzerland–EU Bilaterals III package was signed on 2 March 2026 and entered the Swiss parliamentary phase, but it does not itself establish eIDAS recognition for swiyu. Separate trust-service recognition work would need to define the legal and technical bridge; the use of `did:webvh` in the Swiss beta does not prove that a future recognition profile will expose those anchors directly to EUDI RPs.

> **RP planning impact**: Swiss cross-border legal interoperability is not yet established. Keep non-EU trust resolution behind a separate adapter and wait for an enacted recognition instrument plus its technical profile before assigning eIDAS effect or requiring `did:webvh` in the EUDI verifier.

#### 7.4 Platform Wallets: Apple Wallet and Google Wallet

Platform wallets represent the wallets with the largest installed base — hundreds of millions of users already have them on their devices. Their trust model directly impacts RP integration requirements because they may be the first wallet type a user presents.

##### 7.4.1 Apple Wallet

**Credential format**: Apple's publicly documented digital-identity presentation path uses the **mdoc** format (ISO/IEC 18013-5/7). Public sources reviewed through 26 July 2026 did not establish an Apple Wallet SD-JWT VC or DID-based digital-identity path; that bounded observation is not a claim about every internal or future Apple capability.

**Current capabilities** (as of iOS 26, Fall 2025):
- Mobile Driver's Licences (mDL) in multiple U.S. states; Japan My Number Card
- "Verify with Wallet on the Web" — uses the **W3C Digital Credentials API** (§7.7) with the `org-iso-mdoc` protocol (ISO/IEC 18013-7 Annex C)
- Passport storage as digital ID derived from mdoc format
- NFC Secure Element opened to third-party developers (iOS 18.1, August 2024)

**EUDI integration status**: Apple has **not announced** providing an EUDI Wallet itself. Apple platform security and third-party document-provider APIs may be inputs to a Wallet implementation, but they do not by themselves prove WSCD suitability, designation, composite certification, or EUDI profile support. Safari 26 shipped W3C Digital Credentials API support for the documented `org-iso-mdoc` path, enabling web-based presentation from Apple Wallet and registered third-party document providers within that protocol boundary.

**DID relevance**: The documented Apple digital-ID path uses the ISO mdoc/X.509 IACA trust model. That gives an RP no reason to add DID resolution for this path; it does not establish a timeless statement about every credential type that Apple platforms or third-party providers could mediate.

##### 7.4.2 Google Wallet

**Credential format**: Google Wallet supports **mdoc** for digital IDs. The Android Credential Manager supports both mdoc and W3C Verifiable Credentials formats, though Google Wallet itself focuses on mdoc.

**Current capabilities** (as of Android 16, 2025):
- Digital IDs (mDL, state IDs) in multiple U.S. states
- Zero-Knowledge Proof work for age verification, with the experimental `longfellow-zk` implementation now available as open source; the pinned source snapshot does not establish a universal Google Wallet product profile, proof size, latency, or certification result
- Native **OpenID4VP** support built into Android (April 2025) — the EUDI-mandated presentation protocol
- Android Credential Manager provides the `DigitalCredential` API for credential presentation
- Chrome 141 (September 2025) shipped stable W3C Digital Credentials API support

**EUDI integration status**: Google has built **native OpenID4VP directly into Android** — this is the exact protocol the EUDI ecosystem mandates for remote attestation presentation.  The Android platform acts as a selector/mediator: any EUDI-compliant wallet app on Android can present credentials via the system credential selector.

**DID relevance**: The documented Google Wallet digital-ID path uses mdoc with X.509 issuer certificates; public sources reviewed through 26 July 2026 did not establish a DID-based Google Wallet digital-ID path. Android's *platform* OpenID4VP mediation is not a trust model: a third-party Wallet could use another trust mechanism only where the requested attestation's actual Rulebook/profile permits it (§7.2.3, amber branch).

##### 7.4.4 Platform Wallet Protocol Summary

| Platform | Proximity Protocol | Remote Protocol | Issuer Auth | RP Auth |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Apple Wallet documented digital-ID path** | ISO 18013-5 (BLE/NFC) | W3C DC API (`org-iso-mdoc`) | X.509 IACA certificate | ISO reader-authentication/profile-specific X.509 evidence |
| **Google Wallet documented digital-ID path** | ISO 18013-5 (BLE/NFC) | mdoc presentation; Android also mediates OpenID4VP for third-party Wallets | X.509 IACA certificate for the documented Google mdoc path | ISO reader authentication for mdoc; HAIP `x509_hash` for a signed EUDI OpenID4VP request |

> **RP planning impact**: The documented Apple and Google Wallet digital-ID paths do not create a DID-resolution requirement for the RP. For mdoc, follow the ISO reader/issuer X.509 profile; for a third-party EUDI Wallet reached through Android OpenID4VP, follow HAIP and the credential's actual Rulebook. Platform mediation does not make those authentication models interchangeable.

##### 7.4.5 WSCD Architecture Types (ARF clause 4.5)

The security of every EUDI Wallet depends on how and where its cryptographic keys are stored and used. The Architecture and Reference Framework (ARF), clause 4.5, defines four **Wallet Secure Cryptographic Device (WSCD)** architecture types. While the RP never directly inspects the WSCD type — trust is established indirectly via Wallet Unit Attestations and Trusted Lists (§5, §13.9) — understanding these architectures is important for ecosystem awareness, availability planning, and user-support scenarios.

The ARF Figure 2 reference architecture separates the Wallet Instance from the secure cryptographic components it uses, and it also separates standardised ecosystem interfaces from provider- or manufacturer-specific internals. The RP-facing implication is that presentation protocols stay stable even when the Wallet Provider chooses a different WSCD placement behind the Wallet Instance.

Use the diagram below as an RP-readable equivalent of ARF Figure 2, not as a claim that the RP can inspect every internal component directly. The RP observes protocol outputs, certificates, attestations, status results, and trust-list evidence. The Wallet Provider, PID Provider, Attestation Provider, CAB, and Member State assurance chain decide whether the hidden Wallet Unit internals are acceptable.

A single User device can host multiple Wallet Instances, possibly from different Wallet Providers. In ARF terms, that means the same physical device can participate in multiple independent Wallet Units, each with separate requirements, issuance WIA/KA, device keys, credential state, and RP-visible trust consequences.

The component boundary is the first RP design point:

| ARF Figure 2 component | Wallet-side meaning | RP interpretation |
|:-----------------------|:--------------------|:------------------|
| **User device** | Hosts the Wallet Instance and the surrounding OS/hardware environment. | Device choice can affect UX, availability, and proximity capability, but the RP normally does not inspect the device directly. |
| **Wallet Instance** | Application instance that implements business logic, consent screens, protocol handling, and interactions with WSCA/WSCD or keystores. | The RP talks to this component only through presentation protocols and wallet-authentication evidence, not through private provider APIs. |
| **WSCA / WSCD** | Secure cryptographic application and device protecting critical assets, including PID keys at LoA High. | RP assurance is indirect: the issuer checks WIA/KA and binds the credential; the RP later verifies issuer trust, credential status, holder binding, certification, and breach evidence. |
| **Keystore** | Hardware-backed storage/service for non-critical cryptographic assets. | Do not assume every key has PID-grade LoA High; check the Rulebook, issuer metadata, and binding profile. |
| **Local QSCD** | Optional local signing device, possibly co-resident with WSCD but separately certified as QSCD when used for qualified signatures/seals. | Treat QES/QSeal flows as a separate signing workstream from attribute presentation. |
| **Wallet Provider backend** | Issues WIA/KA, performs support and maintenance, and manages Wallet Unit lifecycle functions over the Wallet Provider Interface. | Directly relevant to issuer assurance; indirectly relevant to ordinary RPs through certification, credential lifecycle, breach/suspension notifications, and support/maintenance boundaries. |

The interface boundary is the second RP design point:

| Interface or feature | ARF / standards status | RP consequence |
|:---------------------|:-----------------------|:---------------|
