> **LoA semantics**: The `assurance_level` field is an RP-side classification, not an eIDAS certification. The pseudonym itself has no eIDAS LoA because it is not an electronic identification means. See §13.11 for LoA inference procedures and the distinction between PID LoA (inferred from trust chain) and pseudonym assurance semantics. See §18.13 for the full progressive assurance lifecycle.

#### 18.11 Pseudonym Revocation and Recovery

Pseudonym lifecycle events from the RP perspective:

| Event | Mechanism | RP Impact |
|:------|:----------|:----------|
| **User deletes pseudonym** | User removes the passkey from their Wallet Unit | RP account becomes inaccessible; User must re-register |
| **RP revokes pseudonym** | RP invalidates the credential locally | User cannot authenticate; other Wallet functionality unaffected |
| **Wallet Unit revoked** | Wallet Provider revokes the Wallet Unit and its issuer-facing WIA/KA status; PID Provider applies the required PID cascade | Wallet-managed pseudonym keys become unusable with the deactivated Wallet Unit; the RP uses its account-recovery policy rather than requesting WIA/KA |
| **Device loss** | User loses device with Wallet Unit | Verifiable/passkey pseudonyms may be lost unless the passkey is synced or otherwise recoverable; RP account recovery must be available |
| **Wallet migration** | User moves to new device/Wallet Unit | Ordinary passkey/WebAuthn pseudonyms may fragment across Wallet Units; only scope rate-limited pseudonyms have a Topic 11 persistence requirement across Wallet Unit changes (`PA_31`) |

> **Key RP consideration**: Unlike PID credentials (which can be re-issued by the PID Provider), pseudonym credentials are **locally generated**. If a User loses their device and did not back up, the pseudonym is permanently lost. RPs should implement account recovery flows that allow Users to re-bind a new pseudonym to their existing account using alternative verification methods (e.g., email, PID presentation as a one-time step-up).

##### 18.11.1 Synced vs Device-Bound Passkeys

The recoverability of a pseudonym after device loss depends on the passkey type:

| Characteristic | Synced Passkey | Device-Bound Passkey |
|:---------------|:---------------|:---------------------|
| **Storage** | Cloud keychain (iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager) | Hardware keystore (Secure Enclave, StrongBox) only |
| **Survives device loss** | ✅ Yes — restored on new device from cloud backup | ❌ No — permanently lost with device |
| **Cross-device availability** | ✅ Available on all User's devices via sync | ❌ Available only on the registering device |
| **NIST SP 800-63-4 classification** | AAL2 | AAL2 or AAL3 (depending on attestation) |
| **WebAuthn `BE` flag** | `BE=1` (Backup Eligible), `BS=1` (Backup State) in `authenticatorData` | `BE=0` (Not Backup Eligible) |
| **EUDI Wallet implication** | May not meet all Wallet Provider requirements if WSCA-level key protection is expected | Provides stronger hardware assurance but creates recovery burden |

> **RP detection**: RPs can determine whether a credential is synced or device-bound by inspecting the `BE` (Backup Eligible) and `BS` (Backup State) flags in the `authenticatorData` returned during registration (WebAuthn L3 §7.1). RPs should store `backup_eligible` in their pseudonym data model (§18.10) to inform recovery UI and policy decisions.

> **Wallet migration implication**: For users with synced passkeys (`BE=1`), wallet migration is transparent — the passkey is restored from cloud backup (iCloud Keychain or Google Password Manager) and the RP experiences no authentication disruption. The Account Recovery Flow (§18.11.2) only applies when the pseudonym uses a device-bound passkey (`BE=0`). Cross-platform passkey migration (e.g., iPhone → Android) may additionally depend on FIDO CXP/CXF support, which is on the roadmap but not yet universally deployed. See §5.6.1 for the full migration decision tree.

##### 18.11.2 Account Recovery Flow After Device Loss

When a User loses their device and the pseudonym was device-bound (not backed up), the RP must provide an account recovery path. The recommended flow:

```mermaid
---
config:
  themeVariables:
    noteBkgColor: "transparent"
    noteBorderColor: "transparent"
  sequence:
    messageAlign: left
    noteAlign: left
    actorMargin: 250
---
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant User as 👤 User
    participant Wallet as 📱 Wallet Unit
    participant RP as 🏦 RP Server

    rect rgba(231, 76, 60, 0.14)
    Note right of User: Phase 1: Authentication Failure
    User->>RP: User visits RP on new device
    Note right of User: Passkey missing
    RP->>User: Offer<br/>"Recover Account"
    Note right of RP: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(241, 196, 15, 0.14)
    Note right of User: Phase 2: Identity Verification Step-Up
    RP->>Wallet: RP requests identity verification (DCQL)
    Wallet->>RP: Wallet presents PID attributes
    RP->>RP: Validate presentation<br/>Match existing account
    Note right of RP: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(46, 204, 113, 0.14)
    Note right of User: Phase 3: Passkey Re-Binding
    RP->>Wallet: RP initiates new WebAuthn registration
    Wallet->>RP: Return new bound passkey
    RP->>RP: RP invalidates old credential<br/>Store new credential
    Note right of RP: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end
```

<details>
<summary><strong>1. User visits RP on new device</strong></summary>

The User arrives at the Relying Party service from a new device but lacks the device-bound passkey required for standard authentication. The RP detects the failure or absence of a credential and explicitly offers a "Recover account" option.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>2. RP Server offers "Recover Account" option</strong></summary>

The RP detects that the User's session lacks a valid device-bound passkey. Instead of rejecting the authentication attempt outright, the RP presents an explicit "Recover Account" option in the user interface, guiding the User through a re-verification flow using their EUDI Wallet.

**Audit Telemetry:** The RP Server logs an `ACCOUNT_RECOVERY_INITIATED` event.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>3. RP Server requests identity verification via DCQL</strong></summary>

To recover the account safely, the RP launches an OpenID4VP DCQL query requesting the same PID attributes that were used for the original KYC step-up (if the account had a verified identity) or a broader set to ensure identity continuity.

```json
{
  "purpose": "account_recovery_rebinding",
  "credentials": [
    {
      "id": "recovery_pid",
      "format": "dc+sd-jwt",
      "meta": { "vct_values": ["urn:eudi:pid:1"] },
      "claims": [
        { "path": ["family_name"] },
        { "path": ["given_name"] },
        { "path": ["birthdate"] }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "intent_to_retain": false
}
```

The claim set should match the RP's existing recovery policy and original verification evidence. The example shows a conservative identity-continuity query; a lower-risk RP should request fewer attributes or a dedicated recovery attestation where available.

**Audit Telemetry:** The RP Server logs a `RECOVERY_DCQL_REQUEST_DISPATCHED` event.

**Artifact Produced:** `OpenID4VP DCQL Authorization Request` (JSON Payload)

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>4. Wallet Unit presents PID attributes</strong></summary>

The Wallet Unit securely presents the requested PID attributes. The RP evaluates the presentation and cryptographically matches the attributes against the existing account's verification record, assuring it is the same User.

**Artifact Produced:** `SD-JWT VC Presentation`

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>5. RP Server validates presentation and matches existing account</strong></summary>

The RP Server validates the cryptographic presentation (signature, nonce, audience) and then executes an account lookup against its user store, matching the received PID attributes under its identity-matching policy (for SD-JWT VC PID, for example, `birthdate` plus the legally justified identity attributes retained from the original verification record). If a match is found, the RP confirms identity continuity.

**Failure Path:** If identity matching fails, the RP MUST terminate the recovery process and log a `RECOVERY_IDENTITY_MISMATCH` security alert.

**Audit Telemetry:** On success, the RP Server logs a `RECOVERY_IDENTITY_MATCHED` event.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>6. RP Server initiates new WebAuthn registration</strong></summary>

Having proven the User's identity, the RP initiates a fresh WebAuthn registration ceremony. The User creates a completely new device-bound passkey on their new apparatus which is securely bound to the existing account.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>7. Wallet returns new bound passkey</strong></summary>

The User's new device creates a fresh FIDO2 credential using the platform authenticator (Touch ID, Face ID, Android Biometric). The Wallet returns the new `PublicKeyCredential` containing the `credentialId` and public key, bound to the RP's `rp.id` domain.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>8. RP Server invalidates old credential and stores new</strong></summary>

The backend securely revokes the old `credential_id` preventing it from being misused by whoever found the lost device, while permanently committing the new credential for subsequent logins.

**Audit Telemetry:** The RP Server logs an `OLD_CREDENTIAL_REVOKED` followed by a `NEW_RECOVERY_CREDENTIAL_BOUND` event.

**Artifact Produced:** `Updated Account Record` (New Passkey Bound)

</details>
<br/>

> **Privacy trade-off**: Account recovery **temporarily breaks pseudonymity** — the RP sees the User's recovery evidence during the recovery session. RPs should minimise the attributes requested, prefer predicate or dedicated age evidence when enough, and discard raw PID attributes after matching unless another legal basis requires retention. The `intent_to_retain: false` DCQL flag (§9.2.1) should be set for recovery-related attribute requests where the RP does not need retention.

> **Pseudonym fragmentation across Wallet Units.** A user holding multiple Wallet Units (e.g., phone + tablet, or Wallet Provider X + Wallet Provider Y) may generate **separate, unlinked passkeys** at the same RP. When a user authenticates from a second Wallet Unit, the RP sees an unrecognised passkey. The account recovery flow above (§18.11.2) handles this similarly to device loss: the user presents PID or another legally justified verification package, the RP matches the existing account under its identity-matching policy, and the new passkey is registered alongside (or replacing) the old one. RPs that support multi-device users may choose to store **multiple passkeys per account** rather than invalidating the old credential. Scope rate-limited pseudonyms (`PA_31`) are explicitly designed to persist across Wallet Unit changes and are **not** affected by this ordinary passkey fragmentation.


#### 18.12 Security Considerations

| Threat | Mitigation | Standard Reference |
|:-------|:-----------|:-------------------|
| **Pseudonym presented to wrong RP** | WebAuthn scopes credentials to `rp.id`; browser verifies origin | TR26 |
| **Cross-RP linking via attestation** | Prefer `attestation: "none"` for low-risk privacy-first services; require stronger authenticator attestation only with documented need | TR39, TR84; ARF §4.7.2.2.3 |
| **Replay of assertion** | Challenge-response protocol; `signCount` tracking | TR91 |
| **RP impersonation during registration** | Browser verifies RP origin via TLS; Wallet trusts browser (PA_20) | TR102 |
| **MITM during pseudonym flow** | TLS between browser and RP; WebAuthn binding to origin | TR105 |
| **Bypass of user authentication** | Wallet requires biometric/PIN before signing assertion | TR55 |
| **Unjustified pseudonym revocation** | RP can only revoke locally; no mechanism for RP to revoke Wallet Unit | TR1 |

#### 18.13 Progressive Assurance: Register Low, Verify Identity, Authenticate High

This is the most strategically important passkey user journey for Relying Parties. It enables **progressive onboarding** — the User creates a pseudonymous account with zero identity verification, presents additional EUDI Wallet evidence only when a policy decision requires it, and subsequently authenticates with the passkey while the RP applies the assurance state retained for that account. The upgrade is conditional: an age predicate may unlock an age-gated feature, but only identity evidence with adequate issuer proofing, holder binding, freshness, and a verifiable pseudonym-to-User binding can justify `identity_verified: true` or a higher identity-assurance tier.

> **ARF basis**: Topic 11's current HLRs require RP-verifiable same-User binding when pseudonym registration is combined with PID or attestation presentation (`PA_12`). The earlier Topic E discussion paper explains the late-binding pattern, but the current integration rule is stricter: late attribute binding is useful only if the RP can prove that the attribute presentation and pseudonym registration/authentication belong to the same User.

> **LoA semantics**: The pseudonym *itself* has no eIDAS Level of Assurance because it is not an electronic identification means. However, the **RP account** to which the pseudonym is bound can have an *effective* assurance level based on the identity verification that was performed and bound to it. The RP must track this distinction in its data model (§18.13).

##### 18.13.1 Progressive Assurance Sequence Diagram

```mermaid
---
config:
  themeVariables:
    noteBkgColor: "transparent"
    noteBorderColor: "transparent"
  sequence:
    messageAlign: left
    noteAlign: left
    actorMargin: 250
---
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant User as 👤 User
    participant WU as 📱 Wallet Unit
    participant Browser as 🖥️ Browser
    participant RP as 🏦 RP Server

    rect rgba(148, 163, 184, 0.14)
    Note right of User: Phase 1 — Pseudonym Registration (LoA Low)
    User->>Browser: Visit marketplace, choose<br/>"Sign up with Wallet"
    RP->>Browser: PublicKeyCredentialCreationOptions<br/>(rp.id, user.id, challenge_R)
    Browser->>WU: Forward creation request
    WU->>User: Approve + biometric/PIN
    WU->>WU: Generate key pair, scope to rp.id
    WU->>Browser: PublicKeyCredential<br/>(credentialId, publicKey)
    Browser->>RP: Forward credential
    RP->>RP: Store credential<br/>assurance_level: low<br/>identity_verified: false
    Note right of RP: Account created with<br/>pseudonym only — no KYC
    Note right of RP: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(52, 152, 219, 0.14)
    Note right of User: Phase 2 — Pseudonymous Interaction (days later)
    User->>Browser: Return to marketplace, login
    RP->>Browser: PublicKeyCredentialRequestOptions<br/>(rpId, challenge_A1)
    Browser->>WU: Forward assertion request
    WU->>User: Biometric/PIN
    WU->>Browser: Signed assertion
    Browser->>RP: Forward assertion
    RP->>RP: Verify — authenticated<br/>as pseudonym (LoA Low)
    Note right of RP: User browses, buys low-value<br/>items — no identity needed
    Note right of RP: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(241, 196, 15, 0.14)
    Note right of User: Phase 3 — Step-Up Identity Verification
    User->>Browser: Request to sell goods<br/>(requires identity verification)
    RP->>RP: Check: identity_verified == false<br/>→ trigger step-up
    RP->>Browser: Signed DC API request<br/>(minimal policy evidence,<br/>fresh nonce_VP)
    Note right of RP: Correlate the active account<br/>server-side and require profile proof<br/>that both actions involve one User
    Browser->>WU: Present DCQL request
    WU->>User: "Share age evidence with<br/>marketplace.example.com?"
    User->>WU: Consent + biometric
    WU->>Browser: Opaque encrypted response<br/>(credential.data.response)
    Browser->>RP: Forward JWE to first-party<br/>application endpoint
    RP->>RP: Decrypt and verify credential<br/>Verify nonce_VP and session mapping<br/>Evaluate same-User proof
    RP->>RP: Apply evidence-specific result:<br/>entitlement and, only if justified,<br/>identity assurance upgrade
    Note right of RP: Never infer KYC or LoA<br/>from age evidence or<br/>session correlation alone
    Note right of RP: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(46, 204, 113, 0.14)
    Note right of User: Phase 4 — High-Assurance Pseudonymous Login (weeks later)
    User->>Browser: Return to marketplace
    RP->>Browser: PublicKeyCredentialRequestOptions<br/>(rpId, challenge_A2)
    Browser->>WU: Forward assertion request
    WU->>User: Biometric/PIN
    WU->>Browser: Signed assertion
    Browser->>RP: Forward assertion
    RP->>RP: Verify — authenticated<br/>as pseudonym
    RP->>RP: Check: identity_verified == true<br/>→ session LoA: substantial
    Note right of RP: Passkey-only login treated at<br/>LoA Substantial because account<br/>was KYC-verified in Phase 3
    Note right of RP: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end
```

<details>
<summary><strong>1. User visits marketplace and chooses "Sign up with Wallet"</strong></summary>

The User navigates to an online marketplace that offers EUDI Wallet integration. The marketplace's registration page presents multiple sign-up options: email/password, social login, and "Sign up with EUDI Wallet". The Wallet option promises frictionless, pseudonymous account creation — no email required, no personal data collected. The marketplace is classified as a sector where legal identification is **not** required (§18.4), so pseudonym acceptance is mandatory under Art. 5b(9). The RP detects WebAuthn support via `PublicKeyCredential.isUserVerifyingPlatformAuthenticatorAvailable()` before offering the option.


</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>2. RP Server sends WebAuthn registration options to Browser</strong></summary>

The RP initiates a WebAuthn `create()` ceremony by generating `PublicKeyCredentialCreationOptions`. The options include the RP's identifier (`rp.id`), a unique `user.id` (opaque handle), and a fresh `challenge_R` (cryptographic random nonce). This follows the standard WebAuthn registration flow documented in §18.5.1, but with a key difference: the account will be created at **LoA Low** with no identity verification.

**Audit Telemetry:** The RP Server logs a `LOW_ASSURANCE_REGISTRATION_INITIATED` event.

**Artifact Produced:** `PublicKeyCredentialCreationOptions` (Client-Side JSON)

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>3. Browser forwards credential creation request to Wallet Unit</strong></summary>

The browser receives the `PublicKeyCredentialCreationOptions` and forwards the request to the Wallet Unit via the platform's WebAuthn API. On platforms where the Wallet Unit is registered as a platform authenticator, this triggers a direct invocation. The request includes the RP's origin, which the Wallet Unit will verify before proceeding.


</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>4. Wallet Unit prompts User for approval and biometric/PIN</strong></summary>

The Wallet Unit displays a consent prompt: *"Create a passkey for marketplace.example.com?"*. The User approves and authenticates via biometric (Face ID, fingerprint) or device PIN. This user verification step ensures that only the legitimate device owner can create credentials bound to this Wallet Unit.


</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>5. Wallet Unit generates key pair scoped to RP's origin</strong></summary>

The Wallet Unit generates a new asymmetric key pair (typically P-256 ECDSA). The private key is scoped to the RP's `rp.id` — it cannot be used to authenticate to any other RP, preventing cross-RP correlation. The key is stored in the Wallet Unit's secure enclave/TEE, wrapped with the device's hardware-backed keystore. No identity attributes are requested or collected.


</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>6. Wallet Unit returns PublicKeyCredential to Browser</strong></summary>

The Wallet Unit returns a `PublicKeyCredential` object containing the `credentialId` (unique identifier for this credential) and the `publicKey` (COSE-encoded). The private key never leaves the Wallet Unit. The credential also includes an `attestationObject` and `clientDataJSON` that the RP will verify to ensure the credential was genuinely created by this authenticator.

**Artifact Produced:** `PublicKeyCredential` (JSON payload)

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>7. Browser forwards credential to RP Server</strong></summary>

The browser POSTs the `PublicKeyCredential` to the RP's WebAuthn registration endpoint. The payload is JSON-serialized from the browser's `navigator.credentials.create()` response. The RP's origin is verified by the browser before the credential is forwarded, preventing MITM attacks during the registration flow.


</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>8. RP Server stores credential with LoA Low assurance level</strong></summary>

The RP verifies the WebAuthn attestation and stores the credential with the following account metadata:

```json
{
  "credential_id": "dGVzdC1jcmVkZW50aWFsLWlk",
  "user_handle": "YW5vbnltb3VzLXVzZXItaWQ",
  "public_key": "pQECAyYgASFYI...",
  "assurance_level": "low",
  "identity_verified": false,
  "created_at": "2026-03-18T01:00:00Z"
}
```

No identity attributes are requested or presented — the User's account is purely pseudonymous. The RP assigns an opaque `user_handle` and stores the credential's public key, but has **zero** information about the User's real identity.

**Audit Telemetry:** The RP Server logs a `LOW_ASSURANCE_ACCOUNT_CREATED` event.

**Artifact Produced:** `LoA Low Account Record` (`identity_verified: false`, stored in RP DB)

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>9. User returns to marketplace and initiates login (days later)</strong></summary>

The User returns to the marketplace after some days. The marketplace's login page offers "Sign in with passkey" as an option. The User clicks this button, triggering the WebAuthn `get()` ceremony. This is a **pseudonymous authentication** — no email, no password, just the passkey created during Phase 1.


</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>10. RP Server sends WebAuthn assertion request to Browser</strong></summary>

The RP generates `PublicKeyCredentialRequestOptions` containing the RP's `rpId` and a fresh `challenge_A1` (cryptographic random nonce). The RP may include `allowCredentials` if it knows which credentials the User previously registered, or omit it for a "discoverable credential" (passkey) flow where the User selects from credentials stored on the device.

**Artifact Produced:** `PublicKeyCredentialRequestOptions` (Client-Side JSON with challenge_A1)

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>11. Browser forwards assertion request to Wallet Unit</strong></summary>

The browser receives the `PublicKeyCredentialRequestOptions` and forwards the request to the Wallet Unit via the platform's WebAuthn API. The Wallet Unit identifies which stored credentials match the RP's `rpId` and prepares to prompt the User for authentication.


</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>12. Wallet Unit prompts User for biometric/PIN</strong></summary>

The Wallet Unit prompts the User to authenticate via biometric (Face ID, fingerprint) or device PIN. This user verification step proves the User's presence and consent to this authentication. The Wallet Unit ensures the User knows which RP they are authenticating to (marketplace.example.com).


</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>13. Wallet Unit returns signed assertion to Browser</strong></summary>

The Wallet Unit uses the stored private key to sign the challenge (`challenge_A1`), creating an assertion. The assertion includes the `credentialId`, `authenticatorData` (containing the RP's origin hash and flags), and `signature`. The private key never leaves the secure enclave; only the signed output is returned.

**Artifact Produced:** `AuthenticatorAssertionResponse` (ECDSA P-256 Signature)

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>14. Browser forwards assertion to RP Server</strong></summary>

The browser POSTs the `PublicKeyCredential` assertion to the RP's WebAuthn authentication endpoint. The payload includes the signed challenge, allowing the RP to verify that the User controls the private key associated with the stored credential.


</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>15. RP Server verifies assertion and grants LoA Low access</strong></summary>

The RP verifies the signature using the stored public key, validates the `authenticatorData` (origin, `signCount` for clone detection), and checks the `challenge_A1` matches the expected value. Upon successful verification, the RP grants access. Because the account has `identity_verified: false`, the RP treats this session at **LoA Low** — the User can browse, purchase low-value items, leave reviews, and perform any action that does not require identity verification. For the marketplace, this might mean limiting the User to buying (not selling), or capping transaction values.

**Failure Path:** If signature validation fails, the RP MUST terminate the login and log a `WEBAUTHN_ASSERTION_FAILED` alert.

**Audit Telemetry:** On success, the RP Server logs a `LOW_ASSURANCE_SESSION_GRANTED` event.

**Artifact Produced:** `LoA Low Session Token` (Cookie / Bearer Token tied to pseudonymous account)

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>16. User requests higher-privilege action (sell goods)</strong></summary>

The User decides to sell goods on the marketplace, which requires identity verification. This might be age verification (to ensure the seller is over 18) or full KYC depending on the marketplace's policies and local regulations. The User clicks "Become a seller" or similar, triggering a backend check by the RP.


</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>17. RP Server checks identity_verified flag and triggers step-up</strong></summary>

The RP's backend checks the pseudonym account's `identity_verified` flag. Finding it `false`, the RP determines that a **step-up** identity verification is required before the User can access seller functionality. The RP does not reject the User — it initiates a seamless upgrade flow within the current session. The RP prepares an OpenID4VP authorization request to request the necessary identity attributes.

**Audit Telemetry:** The RP Server logs a `STEP_UP_VERIFICATION_TRIGGERED` event.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>18. RP Server sends OpenID4VP Authorization Request to Browser</strong></summary>

The RP initiates a signed OpenID4VP request with a DCQL query for the minimum evidence required by the action. For an age-only decision, it should prefer a dedicated age-verification attestation and store only the predicate result; for an identity-verification decision, it requests only the PID or attestation claims justified by that policy. The RP creates a fresh, single-use `nonce_VP` and stores it under the active authenticated pseudonym session. This correlation does not replace the profile-defined same-User proof required before identity evidence is permanently linked to the pseudonym (§18.7.3). In a same-device browser branch, the handoff uses the DC API:

```javascript
const credential = await navigator.credentials.get({
  digital: {
    requests: [{
      protocol: "openid4vp-v1-signed",
      data: {
        request: "&lt;signed JAR with x509_hash client_id, expected_origins, and nonce_VP>"
      }
    }]
  }
});
```

The signed JAR contains the DCQL query:

```json
{
  "credentials": [{
    "id": "pid",
    "format": "dc+sd-jwt",
    "meta": { "vct_values": ["urn:eudi:pid:1"] },
    "claims": [{ "path": ["birthdate"] }]
  }]
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Signed OpenID4VP Request Object and server-side request snapshot containing `nonce_VP`

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>19. Browser forwards DCQL request to Wallet Unit</strong></summary>

The browser and operating system mediate the signed OpenID4VP request to the selected Wallet Unit through the Digital Credentials API. The Wallet Unit receives the DCQL query, validates the RP request and origin binding, and parses the requested credential and claims. A redirects/custom-scheme handoff is a separately governed fallback, not the default same-device mechanism.


</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>20. Wallet Unit prompts User for consent to share age evidence</strong></summary>

The Wallet Unit displays a consent prompt such as *"marketplace.example.com requests age verification"*. This shows the RP's human-readable name, the specific evidence being requested, and the purpose (if provided by the RP). With a dedicated proof-of-age attestation or ZKP, the Wallet can show that no date of birth will be shared; with PID fallback, it should make clear that `birthdate` is being disclosed for threshold calculation.


</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>21. User consents and authenticates via biometric</strong></summary>

The User reviews the consent prompt and approves the disclosure. The Wallet Unit requires user verification (biometric or PIN) before releasing any credential data. This ensures that even if the device is unlocked, an attacker cannot silently extract the User's identity attributes.

**Failure Path:** If the User explicitly denies consent or authentication fails, the Wallet Unit aborts the presentation and logs a `STEP_UP_CONSENT_DENIED` event.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>22. Wallet Unit returns an encrypted DC API response</strong></summary>

The Wallet Unit constructs the DCQL result, binds the selected presentation to `nonce_VP`, and encrypts the OpenID4VP response for `response_mode: "dc_api.jwt"`. The Browser receives an opaque API result:

```json
{
  "response": "eyJraWQiOiJlcGhlbWVyYWwta2V5LTEiLCJlbmMiOiJBMjU2R0NNIiwiYWxnIjoiRUNESC1FUyJ9..."
}
```

The Browser must not decode, log, or persist the presentation. The `vp_token` map and selectively disclosed claims become visible only after backend decryption and successful envelope validation.

**Artifact Produced:** `credential.data.response` containing an opaque response JWE

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>23. Browser forwards the opaque result to the first-party RP application</strong></summary>

The Browser POSTs `credential.data.response` to a first-party application endpoint while the authenticated pseudonym session remains active. This is not a Wallet submission to an OpenID4VP `response_uri`: the DC API branch has no direct-post callback. The backend authorizes the application request, maps it to the retained request snapshot, and passes the still-opaque JWE into the `dc_api.jwt` intake pipeline.


</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>24. RP Server verifies the presentation, transaction, and same-User evidence</strong></summary>

The RP's backend decrypts the JWE, validates the response mode and DCQL result, and performs the credential-format verification in §16. It then keeps three decisions separate:

1. **Presentation binding** — the KB-JWT or mdoc session transcript contains the expected fresh `nonce_VP`, correct audience/origin evidence, and acceptable holder/device binding.
2. **RP transaction correlation** — the authenticated first-party session selects the expected pseudonym account and request snapshot; the transaction is unexpired and not already consumed. TLS-session continuity is neither required nor a stable application binding primitive.
3. **Same-User binding** — if the selected pseudonym profile supplies a `PA_12`/`PA_13` proof, validate it under that profile. Session correlation, temporal proximity, and two biometric prompts are defence-in-depth controls, not substitutes for this evidence.

**Failure Path:** A failed envelope, nonce, transaction, credential, or supplied same-User proof terminates the request. If the needed binding proof is simply unavailable in the selected profile, the RP records `SAME_USER_BINDING_UNAVAILABLE` and must not make an identity-assurance upgrade that depends on it.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>25. RP Server applies the evidence-specific account decision</strong></summary>

If the RP verified identity evidence and the required same-User proof at the policy's required strength, it may update the pseudonym account's internal assurance state:

```json
{
  "credential_id": "dGVzdC1jcmVkZW50aWFsLWlk",
  "assurance_level": "substantial",
  "identity_verified": true,
  "identity_verified_at": "2026-03-18T02:00:00Z",
  "verification_method": "pid_with_profile_same_user_proof",
  "verification_expiry": "2027-03-18T02:00:00Z",
  "age_verified": true,
  "same_user_binding_profile": "profile-and-version"
}
```

If the evidence proves only an age predicate, the RP instead records `age_verified: true` and the relevant expiry while leaving `identity_verified` and `assurance_level` unchanged. If identity evidence is valid but a required pseudonym-to-User proof is unavailable, the RP may complete the immediate identity-dependent transaction only where its risk and legal policy allow, but it must not persist a stronger assurance state as though `PA_12` had been verified.

> **Data minimisation**: Store the policy result and verification metadata, not the raw PID attributes. If PID `birthdate` was disclosed, compute the threshold and discard the raw date unless another legal basis requires retention. A dedicated age attestation or ZKP path avoids date-of-birth disclosure entirely.

**Audit Telemetry:** The RP Server logs either `ACCOUNT_ASSURANCE_UPGRADED`, `ACCOUNT_ENTITLEMENT_UPDATED`, or `STEP_UP_COMPLETED_WITHOUT_PERSISTED_BINDING`, together with the evidence and same-User-binding decision classes.

**Artifact Produced:** Evidence-specific account update with the assurance and entitlement decisions recorded separately

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>26. User returns to marketplace (weeks later)</strong></summary>

The User returns to the marketplace weeks after completing the step-up identity verification in Phase 3. The User initiates a login by clicking "Sign in with passkey" — the same frictionless authentication experience they had during Phase 2, but now the account is KYC-verified and the session will be treated at a higher assurance level.


</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>27. RP Server sends WebAuthn assertion request to Browser</strong></summary>

The RP generates `PublicKeyCredentialRequestOptions` containing the RP's `rpId` and a fresh `challenge_A2` (a new cryptographic random nonce, distinct from the `challenge_A1` used in Phase 2). This is a standard WebAuthn assertion request, identical to Phase 2 — no special handling is required for the KYC-verified status at this step.

**Artifact Produced:** `PublicKeyCredentialRequestOptions` (Client-Side JSON with challenge_A2)

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>28. Browser forwards assertion request to Wallet Unit</strong></summary>

The browser receives the `PublicKeyCredentialRequestOptions` and forwards the request to the Wallet Unit via the platform's WebAuthn API. The Wallet Unit identifies the stored credential for this RP (the same passkey created in Phase 1) and prepares to prompt the User for authentication.


</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>29. Wallet Unit prompts User for biometric/PIN</strong></summary>

The Wallet Unit prompts the User to authenticate via biometric (Face ID, fingerprint) or device PIN. This is the same user verification step as in Phase 2 — the Wallet Unit does not treat this differently because the underlying account is now KYC-verified. The verification is purely about proving possession of the device and consent to authenticate.


</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>30. Wallet Unit returns signed assertion to Browser</strong></summary>

The Wallet Unit uses the stored private key to sign the challenge (`challenge_A2`), creating an assertion. The assertion includes the `credentialId`, `authenticatorData`, and `signature`. This is cryptographically identical to the Phase 2 authentication — the passkey has not changed, only the RP's internal account metadata has been upgraded.

**Artifact Produced:** `AuthenticatorAssertionResponse` (ECDSA P-256 Signature)

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>31. Browser forwards assertion to RP Server</strong></summary>

The browser POSTs the `PublicKeyCredential` assertion to the RP's WebAuthn authentication endpoint. The payload is identical to Phase 2 — a signed challenge proving possession of the private key associated with the stored credential.


</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>32. RP Server verifies assertion and authenticates pseudonym</strong></summary>

The RP verifies the signature using the stored public key, validates the `authenticatorData`, and checks the `challenge_A2` matches the expected value. Upon successful verification, the RP identifies the User as the holder of this pseudonymous credential. The authentication itself is identical to Phase 2 — it's the subsequent lookup of account metadata that differs.


</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>33. RP Server checks identity_verified flag and grants LoA Substantial access</strong></summary>

After authenticating the pseudonym, the RP checks the account's `identity_verified` and `assurance_level` fields. Finding `identity_verified: true` and `assurance_level: "substantial"`, the RP grants access to seller functionality — even though this session involves only a passkey login and no attribute presentation. The identity verification from Phase 3 "carries forward" through the pseudonym binding. The User can now sell goods, access higher-value transactions, or perform any action requiring LoA Substantial.

> **Re-verification policy**: RPs should define a `verification_expiry` after which the identity verification must be refreshed. For age verification, this might be years (age doesn't reverse). For KYC-sensitive operations, the RP might re-verify annually or upon suspicious activity. If the `verification_expiry` has passed, the RP triggers a new step-up flow (returning to Phase 3).

**Artifact Produced:** `LoA Substantial/High Session Token` (Cookie / Bearer Token tied to KYC-verified account)

</details>

##### 18.13.2 RP Data Model Changes for Progressive Assurance

To support progressive assurance, the RP-side pseudonym storage model (§18.10) must include the following additional fields:

| Field | Type | Description |
|:------|:-----|:------------|
| `assurance_level` | enum(`low`, `substantial`, `high`) | RP-internal assurance tier for this pseudonymous account. Starts at `low`; any upgrade requires an explicit policy mapping from verified evidence, including same-User binding where the identity result is attached to the pseudonym. |
| `identity_verified` | boolean | Whether identity verification has been performed and bound to this pseudonym |
| `identity_verified_at` | timestamp | When the step-up verification occurred |
| `verification_method` | string | Evidence path and profile used, such as `pid_with_profile_same_user_proof`, `age_attestation`, or `qeaa_presentation`; keep authentication-only factors in a separate field |
| `verification_expiry` | timestamp | When the identity verification should be re-confirmed (RP-defined policy) |

> **LoA semantics**: The pseudonym itself has no eIDAS LoA. The `assurance_level` field represents the RP's *effective* trust in the account holder, based on what identity verification was performed. This is an RP-side classification, not an eIDAS certification.

##### 18.13.3 Edge Cases

| Scenario | RP Behaviour |
|:---------|:-------------|
| **PID revoked after KYC binding** | RP should flag the account for re-verification at next login. The pseudonym itself remains valid, but the identity assurance may be stale. |
| **User refuses step-up** | RP denies access to the higher-privilege feature but does not revoke the pseudonym. The User retains LoA Low access. |
| **Multiple step-ups** | RP can add evidence incrementally, but an age predicate is not automatically LoA substantial and a PID-plus-address presentation is not automatically LoA high. Assign an RP assurance tier only from the credential/profile, issuer proofing, binding, freshness, channel, and policy evidence. |
| **Verification expiry** | RP triggers re-verification. The User presents the same (or updated) attribute. The RP updates `identity_verified_at` and extends the expiry. |
| **Wallet migration** | User's device-bound passkey is lost after wallet migration. RP triggers Account Recovery Flow (§18.11.2): request PID or another legally justified verification package, match against the retained verification record under the RP identity-matching policy, and register a new passkey. After successful PID step-up, restore assurance to at least **Substantial**. If stored KYC/QEAA verification results are indexed by the RP's durable identity-matching record rather than by device key, carry them forward to restore **High** assurance without re-presentation. For synced passkeys (`BE=1`), migration is transparent — no recovery needed (§18.11.1). See §5.6.1 for the full decision tree. |

#### 18.14 Cross-Device Pseudonym Flows

The sequence diagrams in §18.6 and §18.13 assume a **same-device** flow where the browser and the Wallet Unit run on the same device (`authenticatorAttachment: "platform"`). Current Topic 11 explicitly requires pseudonym generation/registration and authentication to work whether the RP interaction starts on the same device hosting the Wallet Instance or on another device (`PA_03`).

In the cross-device scenario, the User browses a website on their **laptop** (desktop browser) while the EUDI Wallet runs on their **phone**. The WebAuthn ceremonies use CTAP 2.2 hybrid transport:

| Aspect | Same-Device | Cross-Device |
|:-------|:------------|:-------------|
| `authenticatorAttachment` | `"platform"` | `"cross-platform"` or omitted |
| Transport | Internal (OS API) | CTAP 2.2 hybrid (caBLE): QR code → BLE tunnel → FIDO exchange |
| User experience | Seamless biometric prompt | User scans QR code on laptop with phone → authenticates on phone |
| Binding strength | Strong (single device) | Moderate (two devices, linked by BLE proximity) |
| Session binding (§18.7.3) | Session cookie on same browser | Session cookie on laptop browser; Wallet response tunnelled from phone |

> **RP implementation**: To support cross-device flows, RPs should **not** restrict `authenticatorAttachment` to `"platform"`. Omitting this parameter or setting it to `"cross-platform"` allows both flows. The Wallet Unit on the phone acts as a **roaming authenticator** via CTAP 2.2 — the same protocol used by hardware security keys (YubiKey, etc.), but tunnelled over BLE instead of USB/NFC.

---
### 19. Combined Presentations and Binding Models

:::important
Treat combined presentations as a binding problem, not just a parsing problem. The RP must verify each credential individually and then prove the required same-wallet, same-person, or person-to-entity relationships before any business decision relies on the merged claims.
:::

This chapter covers the generic **same-user** combined-presentation model: one Wallet User presents multiple credentials or attestations in one response, and the RP verifies that the credentials are individually valid and jointly attributable at the assurance level required by the use case. A common public key is only one possible evidence path; distinct keys may be managed by the same WSCA/WSCD or keystore, or may require Rulebook-governed attribute or presentation evidence. Legal-person presentations are intentionally separated because they add a different binding problem: Person A may be authorised to act for Legal Person B. That cross-entity model is covered in Legal-Person Extension: EBW, LPID, and Mandates (§20).

#### 19.1 Identity Matching in Combined Presentations

When the RP receives a combined presentation (multiple attestations in one response), it must verify that all attestations belong to the same User. The ARF (ARF §6.6.3.10) defines three binding methods, in ascending order of assurance:

| Method | Description | Assurance Level | Privacy Impact |
|:-------|:------------|:----------------|:---------------|
| **Presentation-Based Binding** | RP assumes attributes in a single presentation response belong to the same User — trusting the Wallet Unit is not compromised | Low | ✅ None — no extra attributes needed |
| **Attribute-Based Binding** | Attestations share a common identifier (e.g., PID number, name + DOB) used as a cross-reference | Medium | ❌ Requires presenting identifying attributes even when not needed for the use case |
| **Cryptographic Binding** | WSCA/WSCD or keystore generates a proof that it manages the private keys of all involved attestations | Profile-dependent and potentially high; evaluate the storage boundary and proof profile rather than assigning a universal hardware grade | ✅ Minimal — no extra attributes needed; only a cryptographic proof |

> **Current state (ARF v3.0.0)**: Annex 2 Topic 18 defines the cryptographic-binding HLRs as `ACP_01`-`ACP_07`. These HLRs require a scheme that lets a WSCA/WSCD or keystore prove management of two or more private keys, uses only ECCG v2.0 algorithms, should use a Topic 53-compatible ZKP, and works across issuance plus remote/proximity presentation. They do not define a deployed proof format or give every permitted keystore the same assurance. Until a concrete scheme is standardised, RPs should use presentation-based binding only where its lower assurance is acceptable and attribute-based binding where the business decision requires stronger same-User evidence.

#### 19.2 ARF High-Level Requirements for Combined Presentations

The ARF Annex 2, Topic 18 defines a narrow current HLR set for **cryptographic binding of attestations**. Some rows are directly verifier-facing; others are issuance-time obligations for Attestation Providers that matter to RPs only because they determine whether a future binding proof can be trusted.

| HLR | Requirement | RP Impact |
|:----|:------------|:----------|
| **ACP_01** | A binding scheme SHALL enable a WSCA/WSCD or keystore to prove it manages two or more private keys whose public keys may appear in WUAs, PIDs, attestations, or pseudonyms; proof may be transitive through a third managed key. | Defines the future verifier security claim: "these public keys are under one stated key-management boundary." The verifier still evaluates that boundary's assurance. |
| **ACP_02** | The scheme SHALL rely only on ECCG Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms v2.0 algorithms. | RP proof-verification modules must enforce the ecosystem algorithm allowlist rather than accepting arbitrary ZKP/signature schemes. |
| **ACP_03** | The scheme SHOULD use a ZKP mechanism satisfying Topic 53. | RP architecture should be proof-type-pluggable and prepared for ZKP verification, but should not assume a concrete ZKP format exists today. |
| **ACP_04** | The scheme SHALL be compatible with Topic 10 issuance, Topic 1 remote presentation, and Topic 24 proximity presentation. | RPs should expect one future binding model to span issuance and both presentation topologies, not a web-only proof. |
| **ACP_05** | During attestation issuance, an Attestation Provider SHALL be able to request proof that the new attestation's private key is managed by the same WSCA/WSCD or keystore as an existing PID or attestation key. | This is provider-facing; it creates upstream evidence an RP may later consume, but it is not a direct RP request obligation. |
| **ACP_06** | Empty. | Do not cite or assign semantics to this row. |
| **ACP_07** | Before making an `ACP_05` request, the Attestation Provider SHALL verify that the new attestation belongs to the User of the existing PID or attestation. | The RP should treat future binding proofs as relying on an issuance-time User-binding check, not merely on same-device key possession. |

#### 19.3 Security Considerations for Combined Presentations

1. **Strictest policy prevails**: When attestations in a combined presentation carry different embedded disclosure policies, the **most restrictive** policy applies to the entire presentation. If one attestation's policy denies disclosure to the RP, the User is warned — but can override (§22.3).

2. **Validity period**: The combined presentation's validity is determined by the **minimum validity** of all included attestations. If one attestation expires in 5 minutes and another in 24 hours, the RP should treat the combined presentation as valid for 5 minutes.

3. **Privacy risk of combination**: Individual attributes may not be personally identifying on their own, but their **combination across attestations** may create a unique tracking vector. RPs must be mindful of this when designing DCQL queries — request only what is necessary.

4. **Single intended use per request**: Per ARF §6.6.3.5.5, each presentation request can have only **one** intended use. If the RP has multiple purposes for requesting attributes, it must send **multiple presentation requests**, each triggering a separate consent screen.

5. **Sequential presentation UX guidance**: When an RP needs multiple presentation requests within a single user session (e.g., identity verification followed by address proof), the following implementation patterns are recommended:

   | Concern | Recommendation |
   |:--------|:---------------|
   | **Pre-warning** | Before the first request, inform the user: *"This service requires 2 approvals in your Wallet"* — reducing abandonment from unexpected second prompts |
   | **Inter-request delay** | Wait at least 1 second between sequential requests to avoid overwhelming the Wallet's consent UI. Some Wallet implementations may queue overlapping requests unpredictably |
   | **Progressive disclosure** | Present results from the first request before triggering the second — e.g., *"Welcome, Anna. We now need to verify your address"* |
   | **Partial failure** | If the user approves the first request but declines the second, the RP must decide: (a) proceed with partial data, or (b) discard all data received. Design for both outcomes |
   | **Session binding** | Each request uses a fresh `nonce` and ephemeral key, but the `state` parameter should encode sequential ordering (e.g., `state: "onboarding-step-2-of-3"`) for RP-side correlation |
   | **Timeout between steps** | Allow generous timeouts (60–120s) between sequential steps — the user may need time to re-authenticate to their Wallet for each approval |

#### 19.4 Combined Presentation Verification Flow (Agnostic: Applies to Direct RP and Intermediary)

```mermaid
---
config:
  themeVariables:
    noteBkgColor: "transparent"
    noteBorderColor: "transparent"
  sequence:
    messageAlign: left
    noteAlign: left
    actorMargin: 250
---
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant RP as 🏦 RP Instance
    participant SL as 📋 Format-Specific Status Evidence

    rect rgba(148, 163, 184, 0.14)
    Note right of RP: Phase 1: Response Decryption
    RP->>RP: Decrypt JWE, extract vp_token
    RP->>RP: Parse multiple attestations<br/>from vp_token
    Note right of SL: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(52, 152, 219, 0.14)
    Note right of RP: Phase 2: Per-Credential Verification
    loop For each attestation
        RP->>RP: Verify issuer signature<br/>(trust anchor from LoTE)
        RP->>RP: Validate claims (exp, iat, vct)
        RP->>RP: Verify selective disclosures
        RP->>RP: Verify device binding<br/>(KB-JWT / DeviceAuth)
        RP->>SL: Check selected status mechanism
        SL-->>RP: Profile-scoped status result
    Note right of SL: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end
    Note right of SL: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(46, 204, 113, 0.14)
    Note right of RP: Phase 3: Cross-Credential Binding
    RP->>RP: Select same-User evidence:<br/>shared key, governed attributes,<br/>or presentation-level assurance
    opt Cryptographic binding proof present
        RP->>RP: Verify common-management proof<br/>for WSCA/WSCD or keystore<br/>and evaluate assurance class
    Note right of SL: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end
    Note right of SL: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(241, 196, 15, 0.14)
    Note right of RP: Phase 4: Attribute Extraction
    RP->>RP: Minimum validity = min(all exp)
    RP->>RP: Extract verified attributes
    Note right of SL: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end
```

<details>
<summary><strong>1. RP Instance decrypts JWE and extracts vp_token</strong></summary>

The RP receives the encrypted response payload (`direct_post.jwt`)—a JWE encrypted with the RP's ephemeral public key from `client_metadata.jwks`. It decrypts using `ECDH-ES` with the Wallet-selected `A128GCM` or `A256GCM` content encryption. After decryption, the RP extracts the DCQL-native `vp_token` result object and the `state` parameter used to correlate the original session. See §11.2 step 19 for the full decryption flow and payload example.

> **If decryption fails**: The RP returns an error and logs the failure. Common causes: ephemeral key mismatch (wrong session), JWE expired, or corrupted ciphertext. The RP should NOT attempt to re-request — the Wallet has already submitted and considers the transaction complete.

**Audit Telemetry:** On failure, the RP Instance MUST log a `PRESENTATION_DECRYPTION_FAILED` SIEM alert.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>2. RP Instance parses multiple attestations from vp_token</strong></summary>

The RP examines the `vp_token` structure. When the DCQL query requested multiple credentials through a combined-presentation request, the `vp_token` is a **JSON object** (not an array) where each key corresponds to a DCQL credential query ID:

```json
{
  "vp_token": {
    "pid_credential": ["&lt;Issuer-JWT>~&lt;Disclosure:family_name>~&lt;Disclosure:birth_date>~&lt;KB-JWT>"],
    "mdl_credential": ["&lt;CBOR-encoded DeviceResponse>"]
  }
}
```

The RP maps each `vp_token` key directly to the same credential-query `id` in the original DCQL request. Each array element is an independent presentation that must be verified individually (steps 3–8) before cross-credential binding is checked (steps 9–10). The RP must handle both SD-JWT VC format (`dc+sd-jwt`) and mdoc format (`mso_mdoc`) within the same response—see §19.5 for cross-format matching.

**Artifact Produced:** The decoupled `vp_token` structure mapping DCQL queries to disparate credential formats.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>3. RP Instance verifies issuer signature against LoTE trust anchor</strong></summary>

For each credential in the `vp_token`, the RP verifies the issuer's cryptographic signature. The verification method depends on the credential format:

- **SD-JWT VC**: The RP parses the issuer-signed JWT header to extract the `x5c` certificate chain (or `kid` referencing a key in the issuer's JWKS), then verifies the JWT signature (ES256 / P-256 ECDSA per HAIP 1.0). The trust anchor is the issuer's root CA certificate obtained from the LoTE (§5.5.10).
- **mdoc**: The RP verifies the `IssuerAuth` COSE_Sign1 signature in the MSO (Mobile Security Object) against the issuer's certificate from the LoTE.

In both cases, the RP must build a certificate chain from the credential's leaf certificate up to the LoTE-provided trust anchor and verify every link. See §14 for the full cryptographic verification procedure.

> **If signature verification fails**: The RP MUST reject the entire combined presentation — a single invalid credential invalidates the set, since the cross-credential binding (step 9) cannot be trusted if one credential is forged.

**Audit Telemetry:** On failure, the RP Instance MUST log a `CREDENTIAL_SIGNATURE_INVALID` SIEM alert.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>4. RP Instance validates standard claims (exp, iat, vct)</strong></summary>

The RP checks the temporal and type validity of each credential:

- **`exp` (Expiration)**: The credential must not have expired at the time of verification. The RP should apply a small clock skew tolerance (typically ≤ 60 seconds) to account for network latency.
- **`iat` (Issued At)**: The credential should have been issued before the current time. Credentials with `iat` in the future may indicate clock manipulation.
- **`nbf` (Not Before)**: If present, the credential is not yet valid before this timestamp.
- **`vct` (Verifiable Credential Type)** for SD-JWT VC / **`docType`** for mdoc: The credential type must match one of the types requested in the DCQL query. For SD-JWT VC PID, this is `urn:eudi:pid:1` or a domestic `urn:eudi:pid:*` value; for mdoc PID, the `docType` / namespace is `eu.europa.ec.eudi.pid.1`; for mDL, `org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL`.

> **Cross-reference**: HAIP 1.0 §6.3 defines the mandatory claims for SD-JWT VC. ISO 18013-5 §10.1.2.4 defines the MSO validity info structure for mdoc.

**Failure Path:** If the credential has expired, was issued in the future, or does not match the requested `vct`/`docType`, the RP MUST reject the presentation.

**Audit Telemetry:** The RP Instance logs a `CREDENTIAL_VALIDITY_CHECK_FAILED` event upon encountering expired or malformed metadata.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>5. RP Instance verifies selective disclosure hashes</strong></summary>

For SD-JWT VC credentials, the RP verifies that each selectively disclosed attribute is authentic by recomputing its hash and matching it against the `_sd` array in the issuer-signed JWT (SD-JWT §6.3):

1. For each `~`-delimited Disclosure in the SD-JWT presentation, decode the base64url string to obtain the JSON array `[salt, claim_name, claim_value]`
2. Compute `SHA-256(base64url(Disclosure))` to obtain the disclosure hash
3. Verify that this hash appears in the `_sd` array of the issuer-signed JWT payload (at the appropriate nesting level for nested disclosures)
4. If any disclosure hash is not found in `_sd`, reject the credential — it contains a tampered or fabricated attribute

For mdoc credentials, the equivalent check verifies data element digests: the RP computes `SHA-256` of each disclosed `DataElementValue` and matches it against the corresponding entry in the MSO's `ValueDigests` map (ISO 18013-5 §10.1.2.4).

**Failure Path:** If any data element digest or SD hash fails verification, it implies structural tampering.

**Audit Telemetry:** The RP Instance MUST trigger a `SELECTIVE_DISCLOSURE_TAMPERING_DETECTED` severe alert.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>6. RP Instance verifies device binding (KB-JWT or DeviceAuth)</strong></summary>

The RP verifies that the credential was presented by the device to which it was originally issued — preventing credential forwarding and replay attacks (§31.2, Cross-RP Collusion):

- **SD-JWT VC (KB-JWT)**: The RP verifies the Key Binding JWT signature using the `cnf.jwk` public key embedded in the issuer-signed JWT. It verifies `aud` against the audience defined by the selected presentation topology—the full `x509_hash:...` client identifier in the EUDI redirects branch, or the `origin:<Origin>` value for DC API—then verifies the request `nonce` and the `sd_hash` over the SD-JWT presentation (SD-JWT §10.3).
- **mdoc (DeviceAuth)**: The RP verifies the `DeviceSigned.DeviceAuth` COSE_Mac0 or COSE_Sign1 signature over the `SessionTranscript` using the `deviceKey` from the MSO (ISO 18013-5 §10.1.3.6). The `SessionTranscript` includes the session-specific handshake data, binding the response to this specific transaction.

> **If device binding fails**: This is a critical security failure — the credential may have been stolen, forwarded, or replayed. The RP MUST reject the presentation and SHOULD log an alert for fraud investigation.

**Audit Telemetry:** The RP Instance MUST trigger a `DEVICE_BINDING_VALIDATION_FAILED` SIEM alert.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>7. RP Instance selects and evaluates each credential's status mechanism</strong></summary>

The RP selects status handling independently for every credential. An SD-JWT VC branch is either short-lived or uses the CIR-selected Token Status List profile. An mdoc branch is short-lived or uses the MSO's Attestation Status List or Attestation Revocation/identifier-list reference. If the RP requires mdoc revocation checking, it implements both list mechanisms; it does not reinterpret identifier membership as a Token Status List bit.

> **Batch optimisation**: Credentials may reuse the same authenticated list object. Cache and internal distribution are keyed by credential class/profile, format mechanism, governing trust generation, list identity, authorized signer/chain, and endpoint. Reuse never crosses those boundaries merely because two URLs or issuers look alike.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>8. Status subsystem returns a profile-scoped result to RP Instance</strong></summary>

Steps 3–8 execute for **each credential** in the `vp_token`. For PID/QEAA/PuB-EAA, the status result is only **NOT_REVOKED** or permanently **REVOKED**; a suspension or other value is itself a profile failure. Another credential class may produce a profile-permitted suspension only when its controlling source defines that state. A required credential's revoked, permitted-suspension, prohibited-value, or evidence-incomplete result fails its dependent credential-set branch. An optional failed credential may be ignored only if another DCQL credential-set option remains fully satisfiable and the service policy does not consume its claims.

> **Partial-failure evidence**: Record every per-credential mechanism/result and the exact DCQL option that remains satisfiable. Do not convert "one valid credential exists" into whole-presentation success, and do not let a valid PID rescue a required revoked mDL, mandate, or other attestation.

**Failure Path:** If a required credential is revoked, suspended under a permitted profile, uses a prohibited state value, or lacks required reliable status evidence, the RP MUST abandon the dependent business logic.

**Audit Telemetry:** The RP Instance emits the format-specific leaf signal and records `combined_status_outcome` as `all_required_pass`, `required_failed`, `optional_ignored`, or `alternative_set_satisfied`.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>9. RP Instance performs identity matching across all attestations</strong></summary>

This is the **critical cross-credential binding check** that distinguishes a combined presentation from unrelated evidence. The RP selects the same-User evidence path required by the business decision and governing Rulebooks:

- **Shared-key evidence**: Matching `cnf.jwk` values across SD-JWT VCs, matching mdoc `deviceKey` values, or equivalent JWK/COSE representations prove possession of one key in the session. They do not by themselves prove that every credential describes the same legal subject.
- **Distinct-key evidence**: Different bound keys are valid input, not automatic failure. Apply a common subject identifier, another Rulebook-defined attribute match, or an expressly accepted presentation-based assurance path.
- **Common-management proof**: When profiled, verify a Topic 18 proof for the distinct keys and evaluate the stated WSCA/WSCD or keystore assurance. Pair it with the issuance-time User-binding conclusion required by `ACP_07`.

> **If the selected evidence path fails**: Reject the combined presentation when the RP cannot establish the required same-User relationship, or when subject evidence contradicts it. Log unexplained key/subject combinations as possible credential-cocktail abuse, but do not equate key inequality alone with fraud.

**Audit Telemetry:** The RP Instance MUST trigger a `CROSS_CREDENTIAL_BINDING_FAILED` SIEM alert, an indicator of potential synthetic identity abuse.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>10. RP Instance verifies WSCA proof of single WSCD management</strong></summary>

If the Wallet provided a Topic 18 binding proof—a cryptographic assertion that all relevant public keys are managed under the same WSCA/WSCD or keystore boundary—the RP verifies the proof, its algorithm/profile, session binding, and the assurance properties of that boundary. This is an evidence path for technically distinct keys, not merely an extra check after public-key equality.

> **Current status**: Topic 18 provides requirements (`ACP_01`-`ACP_07`) but not a deployed proof format. RPs should implement step 9's assurance-based decision across shared-key, attribute, and explicitly accepted presentation paths, then add proof verification when a concrete Topic 18/Topic 53-compatible profile arrives. Do not infer a universal hardware assurance merely from the word “keystore.”

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>11. RP Instance calculates minimum validity across all credentials</strong></summary>

The RP calculates the overall combined presentation validity window by taking the **minimum** `exp` value across all presented credentials. For example, if the PID expires at `2025-12-31T23:59:59Z` and the mDL expires at `2025-06-15T00:00:00Z`, the combined presentation is valid only until `2025-06-15`. This minimum validity determines how long the RP can rely on the combined presentation for session-based decisions (e.g., how long an authenticated session should last before requiring re-verification).

> **Session binding**: The RP should set the application session's `max-age` to no longer than this minimum validity, minus a safety margin. For time-sensitive transactions (SCA — §17), the validity window may be further constrained by the `transaction_data` expiry.

**Audit Telemetry:** The RP Instance logs a `COMBINED_PRESENTATION_EXPIRY_BOUND` event, recording the calculated minimum validity window.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>12. RP Instance extracts verified attributes into application logic</strong></summary>

Having cryptographically verified each individual credential (steps 3–8) and confirmed they belong to the same User and Wallet Unit (steps 9–10), the RP safely merges the disclosed attributes from all credentials into a unified attribute set for application consumption. For example, a combined PID + mDL presentation yields:

```json
{
  "pid": {
    "family_name": "Müller",
    "given_name": "Anna",
    "birthdate": "1990-03-15",
    "personal_administrative_number": "1234567890"
  },
  "mdl": {
    "driving_privileges": [{"vehicle_category_code": "B", "expiry_date": "2027-08-01"}],
    "portrait": "&lt;base64-encoded JPEG>"
  },
  "_meta": {
    "combined_validity_until": "2025-06-15T00:00:00Z",
    "credentials_verified": 2,
    "identity_binding": "cnf_jwk_match",
    "wsca_proof": false
  }
}
```

The `_meta` object is an RP-internal construct (not part of the protocol) that records the verification provenance — useful for audit trails (§33.3) and downstream policy decisions. The RP should feed this unified attribute set into its business rules engine (§26.1) for the final application-level decision (CDD, age gate, SCA, etc.).

**Artifact Produced:** Unified verified attribute dataset (JSON) fed to the business rules engine.

**Audit Telemetry:** On complete holistic verification success, the RP Instance logs a `COMBINED_PRESENTATION_VERIFIED` event, explicitly associating the grouped credential IDs.

</details>
<br/>

> **Key verification step**: Step 9 is the critical same-User decision. Shared public-key material is a strong transactional clue when present, but different keys are permitted. The RP must reach its required assurance through common-management proof, Rulebook-governed attributes, or a deliberately accepted presentation-based path; it rejects when that evidence is absent or contradictory.

#### 19.5 Cross-Format Identity Matching

Open Question #9 identifies the challenge of combined presentations that mix SD-JWT VC and mdoc credentials in a single response. When this occurs, the RP must bridge two different device binding mechanisms:

| Format | Device Binding Key | Location |
|:-------|:-------------------|:---------|
| **SD-JWT VC** | `cnf.jwk` (EC P-256 public key) | In the Issuer-signed JWT payload |
| **mdoc** | `deviceKey` (COSE_Key, EC P-256) | In the MSO's `deviceKeyInfo` |

For same-user verification in a cross-format combined presentation, the RP should:

1. **Extract both keys**: `cnf.jwk` from the SD-JWT VC and `deviceKey` from the mdoc MSO
2. **Compare canonical key material when the profile permits shared keys**: Convert both to a canonical form (for example, the same uncompressed EC point) and compare. Equality proves the same key was bound into both credentials; it is not required and is not a complete subject-identity proof.
3. **Apply the current same-User policy when the keys differ**: Use only Rulebook-permitted shared attributes or an expressly accepted presentation-based conclusion at the required assurance. Minimise identifying attributes and do not silently downgrade from cryptographic to name/date-of-birth matching.
4. **Consume cryptographic binding when profiled**: A future Topic 18 mechanism can provide format-agnostic proof that distinct keys are managed by the same WSCA/WSCD or keystore. Verify the proof and evaluate that boundary's security class rather than treating all storage types as equivalent.

> **Current limitation**: There is no guarantee that a Wallet Unit will use the same device key for SD-JWT VC and mdoc credentials, and no deployed Topic 18 proof format exists. Implementers should define the required same-User assurance per use case, prefer a privacy-preserving proof when it becomes available, and request identifying attributes only where a documented legal and risk basis justifies them.


### 20. Legal-Person Extension: EBW, LPID, and Mandates

Legal-person identity is a composition track on top of the natural-person baseline. A normal first-wave RP asks a Wallet User for PID or a narrow attestation, verifies the response, and converts the result into policy evidence. A B2B RP adds a second subject model: the legal person identified by LPID, the natural person interacting with the service, and any mandate or representation credential that proves authority to act.

:::important
Do not treat LPID as just a wider PID query. LPID has fewer mandatory attributes, a different subject identifier, a different issuer population, and a different binding problem. The RP must decide whether it is verifying a company, a representative, or a representative's authority over a specific operation.
:::

#### 20.1 Extension Boundary and Current Status

This document focuses on **natural person** PID presentation as the primary EUDI Wallet deployment baseline. Relying Parties operating in B2B contexts — financial onboarding, procurement, contract signing, VAT verification — will increasingly encounter **legal person** identity presentations, but those flows are not the first concept a retail or consumer RP should learn.

:::note[EBW is not the first rollout wave, but RP architecture should account for it early]
Legal-person flows are not the main implementation driver for the first EUDI Wallet deployment wave, but they reuse much of the same trust and registration infrastructure. RPs that expect B2B, procurement, or mandate-driven use cases should treat this chapter as a forward-compatibility design input rather than a distant add-on.
:::

ARF Topic 28 keeps wallet units for legal persons outside the current EUDI Wallet HLR baseline. All three rows for legal-person Wallet Units (`LP_01`–`LP_03`) are `Empty` in ARF v3.0.0. An empty row creates no current requirement and must not be used to infer the design of a separate business-wallet framework.

On 19 November 2025, the European Commission published **COM(2025) 838**, a proposal for a regulation establishing **European Business Wallets (EBWs)**. As of 26 July 2026, procedure `2025/0358(COD)` is ongoing. The proposal describes business wallets for economic operators and public bodies, but it is not enacted law; final roles, obligations, transition dates, and technical profiles may change during the ordinary legislative procedure.

> **Key architectural direction**: The EBW proposal is designed to reuse major EUDI trust-infrastructure concepts, but reuse does not prove identical provider roles, certificate policies, or issuer-assurance artifacts. RPs should extend their trust resolver for the final LPID/mandate provider and business-wallet profiles instead of assuming that EUDI WIA/KA or every existing trust anchor applies unchanged.

#### 20.2 EBW and Shared Trust Infrastructure

| Component | EUDI Wallet (Natural Person) | EBW (Legal Person) | Shared? |
|:----------|:----------------------------|:-------------------|:--------|
| **Trusted Lists / LoTE** | Commission-compiled EUDI provider-type lists | The proposal favours reuse and interoperability with EU digital infrastructure, but the final business-wallet trust-list profile is not established by the EUDI ARF | ⚠️ Proposed alignment; verify final law/profile |
| **Access Certificate Authority** | Issues EUDI WRPACs to RPs under the EUDI certificate profile | Do not assume the same CAs or certificate profile; resolve the final EBW relying-party/service authentication model | ⚠️ Unsettled |
| **Registrar** | Member-State Registrar under the EUDI RP-registration framework | Do not assume EUDI registration automatically covers EBW services, LPID types, or business-wallet purposes | ⚠️ Unsettled |
| **Wallet-unit assurance** | Issuance-side WIA/KA under the EUDI Wallet role and profile | Final EBW issuer-assurance role/profile is not yet settled; do not assume EUDI WIA/KA applies unchanged | ⚠️ Proposed alignment, not a settled shared mechanism |
| **Wallet Provider** | Notified per Member State; issues WIA/KA for EUDI Wallet issuance | EBW proposal anticipates business-wallet providers, but final designation, certification, and issuer-assurance boundaries remain profile-dependent | ❌ Role instances are not automatically shared |
| **PID / LPID Provider** | PID Providers (civil registries) | LPID Providers (business registers via BRIS) | ❌ No |
| **CAB certification** | Certifies EUDI Wallet Solutions under the notified eID-scheme framework | The proposal contains conformity and supervision concepts, but the final assessment scheme and its relationship to EUDI certification remain legislative/profile questions | ⚠️ Proposed |

Do not pre-register `EWC_LPID_Attestation` in the EUDI RP framework merely because the TS2/TS5/TS6 data model can represent legal entities. The EWC identifier is pilot evidence, not a final EBW registration entitlement. Keep the verifier and policy engine capable of adding a versioned LPID type, Service purpose, trust source, and certificate profile when the controlling EBW law and technical specifications establish them; until then, isolate pilot registrations from production EUDI authorization.

#### 20.3 LPID Attribute Model, EUID, and PID Comparison

**LPID** (Legal Person Identification Data) is the legal-person identity credential model used by the EUDI Wallet Consortium (EWC) pilot. EWC published its LPID specification in **RFC005** (October 2024), with business-register/BRIS-oriented issuer and source fields. Treat this as implementation evidence and a design input, not as the final COM(2025) 838 credential profile or proof that every national business register is already an LPID Provider.

LPID has a deliberately minimal mandatory attribute set — only two credential subject attributes:

| Attribute | Type | Mandatory | Description |
|:----------|:-----|:----------|:------------|
| `legal_person_id` | string | ✅ Yes | Unique identifier in EUID structure (§20.3.1) |
| `legal_person_name` | string | ✅ Yes | Official current legal person name as registered in the business register |

The LPID also includes mandatory metadata attributes:

| Attribute | Type | Mandatory | Description |
|:----------|:-----|:----------|:------------|
| `issuing_authority` | string | ✅ Yes | Name of issuing authority, or ISO 3166 Alpha-2 country code |
| `issuing_authority_id` | string | ✅ Yes | EUID of the issuing authority |
| `issuing_country` | string | ✅ Yes | ISO 3166-1 Alpha-2 country code |
| `issuing_jurisdiction` | string | Optional | ISO 3166-2:2020 subdivision code |
| `issuance_date` | datetime | ✅ Yes | Date/time of issuance |
| `expiry_date` | datetime | ✅ Yes | Date/time of expiry |
| `authentic_source_id` | string | Optional | EUID of the authentic source (can differ from issuing authority) |
| `authentic_source_name` | string | Optional | Name of the authentic source |
| `revocation_id` | string | Optional | Unique index in revocation list |
| `revocation_location` | string | Optional | URL to access revocation information |

> **RP impact**: The dramatically smaller attribute set means LPID verification is simpler per-credential, but RPs in B2B contexts will almost always need LPID **combined** with a natural person PID and potentially a mandate credential — making the overall verification flow more complex than natural-person-only scenarios.

##### 20.3.1 EUID: The Anchor Identifier for Legal Persons

The **European Unique Identifier (EUID)** is the EWC LPID model's primary cross-border business-register identifier and is specified for the BRIS context by Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/1042. It does not generally replace LEIs, VAT numbers, or national registration identifiers outside the use case and governing profile.

**Structure:**

```
&lt;CountryCode>&lt;BusinessRegisterCode>.&lt;DomesticRegistrationNumber>[_&lt;ValidationChar>]
```

**Examples:**
- `SEBOLREG.5560678965` — Swedish legal person registered at Bolagsverket
- `ESRMC.5789255_X` — Spanish legal person registered at Registro Mercantil Central

RPs receiving LPID should validate the `legal_person_id` (EUID) format:

```
Regex: ^[A-Z]{2}[A-Z0-9]+\.[A-Z0-9]+(_[A-Z0-9])?$
```

The country code is ISO 3166-1 Alpha-2, the business register code is MS-specific, and the validation character is optional.

Do not collapse LPID `legal_person_id` matching into raw X.509 subject-string matching. ETSI EN 319 412-1 V1.7.1 allows the legal-person `NTR` certificate prefix to carry either a national trade-register identifier or the BRIS/EUID form, but that is still a certificate-subject identifier interpreted through semantics identifiers, prefixes, country/scoping rules, and sometimes subdivision notation. An RP that compares an LPID claim to a WRPAC, WRPRC, QWAC, or QSealC subject field should parse the certificate semantics first and then compare within the relevant profile; it should not treat every EUID-looking value as the same legal-person assertion.

##### 20.3.2 LPID vs Natural Person PID: Comparison

| Dimension | Natural Person PID | LPID |
|:----------|:------------------|:-----|
| **Subject identifier** | Optional `personal_administrative_number` where issued; otherwise match on verified identity attributes under RP policy | `legal_person_id` (EUID from business register) |
| **Name attributes** | `family_name`, `given_name`, `birth_name` | `legal_person_name` (single field) |
| **Date attributes** | `birth_date` (mdoc) / `birthdate` (SD-JWT VC); no PID age predicates | None — legal persons have no birth date |
| **Address** | `resident_address`, `resident_city`, etc. | Not in base LPID — separate attestation |
| **Nationality** | `nationality` (mdoc) / `nationalities` (SD-JWT VC) | Not applicable — legal persons have jurisdiction |
| **Biometric** | `portrait` (optional) | Not applicable |
| **Mandatory count** | 5 mandatory attributes plus mandatory validity/issuer metadata | 2 mandatory attributes |
| **Type value** | SD-JWT VC `vct`: `urn:eudi:pid:1`; mdoc `docType` / namespace: `eu.europa.ec.eudi.pid.1` | `EWC_LPID_Attestation` (per RFC005 §6.10.4) |
