An organisation must first determine which instrument, national implementation, service, channel, and transition applies, then include RP-controlled Wallet entry, QR/deep-link, status, error, support, deletion, and reporting surfaces in the applicable accessibility assessment.

| EAA Scope Category | RP Example | Covered? |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Banking services** | Banks, PSPs using EUDI Wallet for SCA or CDD | ✅ Yes — Art. 2(2)(b) |
| **E-commerce services** | Online shops requesting age verification or identity attributes | ✅ Yes — Art. 2(2)(f) |
| **Electronic communications** | Telcos using EUDI Wallet for subscriber verification | ✅ Yes — Art. 2(2)(c) |
| **Transport services** | Airlines, railways using EUDI Wallet for passenger ID | ✅ Yes — Art. 2(2)(d) |
| **Public-sector websites/apps** | Government portals | Assess primarily under WAD/national law; EAA may apply only through a separately covered product/service |
| **Other private RPs** | Services outside the EAA Article 2 categories | Not automatically covered by EAA; assess sector/national law and adopt accessibility as a product requirement |

> **Micro-enterprise boundary**: The EAA exempts microenterprises **providing services** from the service accessibility requirements; it does not support a blanket statement that every small business, product, or other legal duty is exempt. Confirm the EU definition, the operator's role, national transposition, and any separately applicable WAD or equality/non-discrimination law.

**Do not collapse WAD and EAA harmonisation.** EN 301 549 V3.2.1 is cited as a harmonised standard for the WAD and maps its web requirements to WCAG 2.1. The Commission's current [WAD standards and harmonisation record](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/web-accessibility-directive-standards-and-harmonisation) also notes that WCAG 2.2 is not yet incorporated through that cited version. This does **not** establish V3.2.1 as an EAA presumption-of-conformity route. EAA-related EN 301 549 revision work remains a source-watch item until the applicable standard is final and cited in the Official Journal. RPs can adopt WCAG 2.2 as a current engineering baseline while keeping the legal evidence chain instrument- and version-specific.

ARF Topic 54 defines two accessibility HLRs — **ACC_01** and **ACC_02** — but both target **Wallet Providers**, not Relying Parties. There are no RP-specific accessibility HLRs in the ARF. The EAA fills this gap at the legal level: RPs in covered sectors must comply regardless of ARF coverage. The sections below bridge this gap with RP-specific implementation guidance.

> **⚠️ Legal obligation, not optional enhancement**: Where an RP-controlled surface is within the EAA, WAD, national accessibility, or equality-law scope, accessibility is enforceable. Remedies and penalties come from the applicable national implementation; do not quote an EU-wide maximum without jurisdiction-specific authority.

> **Design Guide source-status caveat**: Annex 5.02 is useful Wallet UX guidance, not a binding HLR or RP protocol specification. It still matters for RP planning because it describes how Wallets may present data-sharing requests, warnings, trust indicators, and optional pre-authorisation. Do not copy its stale illustrative age-attribute examples into PID requests; use the current PID Rulebook attributes from §6.

| Wallet UX Pattern | Design Guide Guidance | RP Integration Consequence |
|:------------------|:----------------------|:---------------------------|
| **Mandatory vs optional attributes** | Mandatory fields should be clearly marked and non-deselectable; optional fields should be grouped, collapsed, and unselected by default. | Design DCQL and service policy so mandatory attributes are truly necessary, and make optional attributes safe to omit without breaking the whole service. |
| **RP identity, purpose, and data use** | The Wallet should show the RP identity, purpose, how data will be used, storage information, and intent-to-store context in plain language. | Keep registered intended-use, privacy-policy, and intent-to-store text concise and user-facing; Wallet UI quality depends on RP metadata quality. |
| **Pre-authorisation setup** | A Wallet may let a User pre-authorise selected attributes for specific RPs only after the RP has been authenticated at least once. The setup should be friction-full, may require extra User authentication, and must never apply indiscriminately to all RPs or all attributes. | RPs must still support ordinary per-transaction approval and failure handling. Treat pre-authorisation as an optional Wallet feature, not as an RP entitlement or universal "remember my choice" baseline. |
| **Pre-authorised release** | Where pre-authorisation applies, the Wallet may release the selected attributes without first notifying the User, then immediately notify the User that release occurred. The notification should include withdrawal and intent-to-store information. | Services using recurring or low-friction flows need post-release transparency, withdrawal handling, and ordinary denial/retry paths when pre-authorisation is absent, expired, or withdrawn. |
| **Review and withdrawal** | Wallets should show a clear overview of active pre-authorisations, allow withdrawal, and apply validity limits or periodic review. | RPs should avoid assuming a durable consent state. Requests must remain valid when the Wallet returns to ordinary User approval. |
| **Untrusted-RP warning** | If the Wallet treats an RP as untrusted, the UI pattern includes warning, report, close, and learn-more outcomes. | Align "report" with Topic 50 / TS8 rather than an unspecified complaint action, and keep warnings consistent with the RP-authentication and registration-verification semantics in §13.1 and §22.2. |

##### 23.5.1 WCAG 2.2 and Accessible Authentication

[WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.8](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#accessible-authentication-minimum) evaluates the **complete authentication process** and restricts cognitive-function tests unless an exception applies, including an alternative method, an assistance mechanism, object recognition, or personal content. A Wallet can provide a useful possession/device-authenticator route, but it does not make the RP journey inherently conformant. PIN entry can involve recall; invocation, cross-device transfer, account selection, consent, fallback, recovery, transaction codes, CAPTCHA, timeout, and error recovery all remain in scope. Copy/paste, password-manager/autofill support, persistent display, and accessible alternative mechanisms matter.

| Scenario | SC 3.3.8 Status | RP Action |
|:---------|:-------------|:----------|
| RP uses a Wallet path (DC API or QR) | Requires full-path evaluation | Test invocation, local authentication, consent, cross-device handoff, fallback, recovery, timeout, and errors with assistive technology |
| RP uses Wallet + CAPTCHA | Fails if an unexcepted cognitive test is required | Provide an effective accessible alternative; do not treat an opaque “invisible” system as automatically accessible |
| RP offers Wallet + password fallback | May provide alternatives, but neither route is automatically conformant | Support paste/autofill/password managers and test every route needed to complete authentication |
| RP uses a displayed transaction code | Can qualify for an assistance exception when mechanisms avoid memorisation/transcription | Keep it visible and support copy/paste or automatic transfer; do not require recall |

##### 23.5.2 WCAG Success Criteria Mapping for RP UI Components

The following table maps the most critical WCAG 2.1 AA and WCAG 2.2 success criteria to concrete EUDI Wallet RP UI components. This is the practical compliance checklist that neither the ARF, the CIRs, nor EN 301 549 provide in RP-specific form.

| WCAG SC | Title | RP Component | Requirement |
|:--------|:------|:-------------|:------------|
| **1.1.1** | Non-text Content | QR code image | Provide descriptive `alt` text: e.g., `alt="QR code to initiate identity verification — scan with EUDI Wallet or use link below"`. Avoid generic `alt="QR code"` |
| **1.3.1** | Info and Relationships | Consent screen attribute list | Use semantic HTML (`<table>`, `&lt;dl>`, `<ul>`) to structure attribute lists; use `&lt;fieldset>`/`&lt;legend>` for grouped controls |
| **1.4.1** | Use of Colour | Verification result | Traffic-light indicators must be supplemented with text: "✅ Verified", "❌ Not verified", "⚠️ Partially verified" |
| **1.4.3** | Contrast (Minimum) | All RP UI text | Minimum 4.5:1 contrast ratio for normal text, 3:1 for large text (≥18pt or ≥14pt bold) |
| **1.4.11** | Non-text Contrast | QR code, buttons, form controls | QR code borders must have ≥3:1 contrast against background. All interactive controls must meet this threshold |
| **2.1.1** | Keyboard | All RP pages | All interactive elements (approve, reject, alternatives, deep-link buttons) must be operable via keyboard alone |
| **2.2.1** | Timing Adjustable | QR code with timeout | If the QR code expires, provide a mechanism to request a new one and warn before expiry |
| **2.4.3** | Focus Order | Consent screen | Tab order must be logical: RP identity → attribute list → purpose → approve → reject → cancel |
| **2.5.8** | Target Size (Minimum) | All interactive targets | Clickable/tappable targets must have a minimum size of **24×24 CSS pixels** (WCAG 2.2 AA). Mobile RP apps should aim for platform guidelines: 44×44pt (Apple) or 48×48dp (Material Design) |
| **3.1.1** | Language of Page | All RP pages | Declare the page language via `lang` attribute on `&lt;html>`. Essential for screen reader pronunciation |
| **3.1.2** | Language of Parts | Consent screen with translated attribute names | If attribute names are in a different language from the page, mark them with the `lang` attribute |
| **3.3.1** | Error Identification | Error pages | If verification fails, identify the error in text — not just a red border. "Verification timed out — the QR code has expired" |
| **3.3.3** | Error Suggestion | Error pages | Provide actionable suggestions: "Please request a new QR code" or "Try again using the direct link below" |
| **3.3.8** | Accessible Authentication (Minimum) | Complete Wallet-enabled authentication path | Evaluate every step and exception; Wallet/device authentication alone does not prove conformance. See §23.5.1 |
| **4.1.3** | Status Messages | Verification in progress | If verification updates asynchronously (polling for Wallet response), use `role="status"` or `aria-live="polite"` to announce updates to screen readers |

##### 23.5.3 QR Code Accessibility for Remote Flows

QR codes are inherently **visual**. The cross-device remote flow (§12) can exclude blind and low-vision users, people who cannot accurately aim or hold a second device, and users without a second compatible device unless the RP supplies an equivalent accessible route.

RPs MUST provide **at least one alternative invocation method** alongside the QR code:

| Alternative | How It Works | WCAG SC Addressed |
|:------------|:-------------|:------------------|
| **User-initiated Digital Credentials API action** | An "Open your identity wallet" button invokes `navigator.credentials.get()` with the versioned OpenID4VP Digital Credentials API protocol. The browser/OS can offer an eligible local Wallet or its supported secure cross-device branch without requiring the user to visually scan the RP's QR. | 1.1.1, 2.1.1, 2.5.8 |
| **Profiled compatibility deep link** | Where the deployed Wallet ecosystem explicitly supports it, a user-activated `haip-vp://` link invokes a same-device Wallet. Treat this as a compatibility path rather than a generic browser capability; do not encourage copying or forwarding the authorization URI because that turns it into a relayable bearer-like interaction reference. | 1.1.1, 2.1.1, 2.5.8 |
| **NFC tap** (proximity) | For in-person scenarios where a QR code is displayed on a terminal, NFC tap is the accessible alternative. Already covered in §15.11. | 1.1.1, 2.5.8 |

**Accessible QR code markup pattern:**

```html
&lt;figure role="img" aria-labelledby="qr-label" aria-describedby="qr-desc">
  <img src="/qr/session-abc123.svg"
       alt="QR code for identity verification with EUDI Wallet"
       style="min-width: 200px; min-height: 200px; border: 4px solid #000;" />
  &lt;figcaption id="qr-label">
    Scan this QR code with your EUDI Wallet to verify your identity
  &lt;/figcaption>
  <p id="qr-desc" class="visually-hidden">
    Alternatively, use one of the accessible options below.
  </p>
&lt;/figure>

&lt;!-- Accessible alternatives -->
<div role="group" aria-label="Alternative verification methods">
  &lt;button type="button" id="open-wallet" class="btn-primary">
    Open your identity wallet
  &lt;/button>
  <a href="haip-vp://authorize?client_id=x509_hash%3A...&amp;request_uri=..."
     class="btn-secondary">Use compatible Wallet link</a>
</div>
```

**Visual requirements**: QR code modules must maintain ≥4.5:1 contrast ratio against the background (black on white at 21:1 is optimal). Minimum recommended size is **200×200 CSS pixels**. Use error correction level **H** (30% recovery) for displayed codes. Maintain the standard 4-module quiet zone (white border) around the QR code. See §15.11 for proximity-specific QR considerations.

##### 23.5.4 Accessible Consent and Verification UX Patterns

**RP pre-consent pages** — the RP-controlled information page explaining what data will be requested and why — must comply with EAA/WCAG. The wallet-side consent dialog (showing exact attributes and approve/reject) is the **Wallet Provider's** responsibility under ACC_01/ACC_02; the RP cannot control the Wallet's UI.

| Pattern | Implementation | WCAG SC |
|:--------|:---------------|:--------|
| **Semantic structure** | Use `<h1>`→`<h2>` hierarchy for screen reader navigation. Use `&lt;dl>` for name-value pairs, `<table>` for attribute lists. | 1.3.1, 2.4.6 |
| **Focus management** (modal) | `role="dialog"`, `aria-modal="true"`, `aria-labelledby` pointing to dialog title. Trap focus inside dialog; restore on dismiss. | 2.1.2, 2.4.3 |
| **Descriptive labels** | Every interactive element must have a programmatic name. "Approve" and "Reject" must be `&lt;button>` elements with descriptive text, not icon-only. | 4.1.2, 2.4.6 |
| **No auto-action** | Do not automatically redirect to a Wallet app without user action. Let the user deliberately click "Open in EUDI Wallet". | 3.2.1 |
| **Clear language** | Avoid technical jargon on user-facing pages: "PID" → "Personal ID", "QEAA" → "Verified credential", "mDL" → "Digital driving licence". | 3.1.1 |

**Verification results** must use multi-modal presentation — text label, icon, and colour. Never use colour alone to convey outcome (WCAG 1.4.1):

| Outcome | Text Label | Icon | ARIA Role |
|:--------|:-----------|:-----|:----------|
| **Success** | "Identity verified successfully" | ✅ | `role="alert"` |
| **Failure** | "Verification failed — [specific reason]" | ❌ | `role="alert"` |
| **Partial** | "Partially verified — some attributes could not be confirmed" | ⚠️ | `role="alert"` |
| **Timeout** | "Verification timed out — please try again" | ⏱️ | `role="status"` |
| **In progress** | "Verifying your identity..." | 🔄 | `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` |

For **asynchronous status updates** (cross-device polling, §12): use `role="status"` with `aria-live="polite"` for non-urgent updates; use `role="alert"` with `aria-live="assertive"` for the final result. Set `aria-atomic="true"` so the entire region content is announced. Hide visual-only decorations (spinners, animated icons) with `aria-hidden="true"`.

##### 23.5.5 W3C Digital Credentials API Accessibility

The W3C DC API specification explicitly mandates that modal dialog content presented during credential requests must be labelled and made accessible to assistive technologies, and that interactive elements must be operable in a device-independent manner. The **credential chooser** is a browser-native dialog (comparable to the password manager or WebAuthn prompt) — its accessibility is the **browser vendor's** responsibility, not the RP's.

| RP Obligation | Details |
|:--------------|:--------|
| **Trigger via user gesture** | The DC API `get()` call must be triggered by a user activation (click/tap on a "Verify with EUDI Wallet" button). The button must be keyboard-operable, have visible focus, and meet target size requirements. |
| **Provide fallback** | If the browser does not support the DC API, the RP MUST provide an accessible fallback (QR code + deep link). The fallback itself must comply with §23.5.3. |
| **Handle result accessibly** | The RP's result page must follow §23.5.4 verification result patterns. |
| **Do not duplicate browser UI** | The RP must NOT implement its own wallet selector that competes with the browser's credential chooser. Duplicate dialog contexts confuse screen reader users. |

##### 23.5.6 Cross-Border Language Handling

Cross-border scenarios — e.g., a Spanish citizen verifying identity at a German bank's website — create language challenges for RP-controlled pages. The consent information, attribute labels, and error messages may be unintelligible to a foreign user.

| Aspect | Requirement | Standard |
|:-------|:------------|:---------|
| **Page language declaration** | Set `lang` attribute on `&lt;html>` to the page's primary language | WCAG 3.1.1 (Level A) |
| **Language of parts** | If attribute names or values are in a different language, wrap them in elements with the appropriate `lang` attribute | WCAG 3.1.2 (Level AA) |
| **Multi-language support** | RP SHOULD detect the user's browser language (`Accept-Language` header) and offer content in that language if available | ARF Design Guide §2.12 |
| **Attribute label translation** | Display PID attribute names as localised, user-facing labels — not raw schema identifiers like `family_name` | ARF user-centricity principle |
| **RTL text direction** | If supporting RTL languages (Arabic, Hebrew), apply CSS `direction: rtl` and `text-align: start` | WCAG 1.3.2 |

Example attribute label translations for standard PID identifiers:

| Schema Identifier | English | German | French | Spanish |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `family_name` | Family name | Nachname | Nom de famille | Apellidos |
| `given_name` | Given name | Vorname | Prénom | Nombre |
| `birth_date` | Date of birth | Geburtsdatum | Date de naissance | Fecha de nacimiento |
| `resident_address` | Address | Adresse | Adresse | Dirección |

##### 23.5.7 Accessibility Governance and Procurement Controls

ARF §8 and Annex Topic 54 do not create RP-specific HLRs; `ACC_01` and `ACC_02` remain Wallet Provider obligations for Wallet Units under Directive 2016/2102 and Directive 2019/882. The useful ARF contribution for RPs is the governance model: accessibility has to be built into technical specifications, UI design, testing, procurement, monitoring, feedback, and continuous improvement for every user-facing component in the ecosystem. RP-controlled wallet entry points therefore need lifecycle controls, not only a one-time WCAG audit.

| Control Gate | RP Evidence | Source Boundary |
|:-------------|:------------|:----------------|
| **Design and requirements** | User journeys identify keyboard, screen reader, language, timeout, QR alternative, and low-vision requirements before DCQL / flow implementation starts. | The legal evidence route depends on the applicable EAA, WAD, national-transposition, and harmonised-standard context; EN 301 549 and WCAG can supply version-specific engineering and test evidence but are not interchangeable legal shortcuts. ARF §8 is ecosystem governance context. |
| **Procurement and vendor due diligence** | Verifier SDKs, intermediary portals, hosted QR pages, support forms, and embedded SDK UI components have accessibility commitments, defect SLAs, VPAT / EN 301 549 evidence, and assistive-technology test results in the contract. | Do not treat Wallet Provider `ACC_01` / `ACC_02` compliance as proof that the RP's own pages or vendor front ends are accessible. |
| **Pre-production testing** | Automated WCAG scans are paired with manual keyboard, screen-reader, focus-order, timeout, and mobile assistive-technology tests across same-device, cross-device, error, deletion, and DPA-reporting flows. | Annex 5 Design Guide screenshots are useful UX context, not a substitute for RP-side EAA testing. |
| **Release and regression gates** | Accessibility checks run before each production release and after changes to browser DC API invocation, QR/deep-link layouts, verification result pages, support forms, or intermediary widgets. | Governance gate; no new protocol claim. |
| **Feedback and monitoring** | Support channels accept accessibility defects, tag them separately from ordinary verification failures, and feed recurring issues into §33 monitoring and vendor service reviews. | ARF §8.3 expects ongoing monitoring and feedback across user-facing components; RP evidence should be limited to RP-controlled surfaces. |
| **Expert and user involvement** | Periodic reviews include accessibility specialists and disabled users, especially before deploying kiosk/proximity flows or pre-authorisation UX. | Collaboration expectation is ecosystem-wide; RP implementation should document its own participation and remediation actions. |

#### 23.6 NIS2 Considerations for Critical-Sector RPs

The **NIS2 Directive** — Directive (EU) 2022/2555 — enhances cybersecurity requirements for critical infrastructure across the EU, applying from **17 October 2024** with full enforcement by Member State transposition deadlines. NIS2 applies to public or private entities of a type listed in **Annex I** (essential sectors) or **Annex II** (important sectors) that qualify as medium-sized enterprises or larger (≥50 employees or ≥€10M annual turnover), or are explicitly included regardless of size — trust service providers, DNS providers, public electronic communications networks, or sole national providers (Art. 2(2)). Many EUDI Wallet RPs in banking, healthcare, transport, energy, and digital infrastructure fall within scope.

| NIS2 Sector (Annex) | Typical EUDI Wallet RP | Entity Class |
|:-----|:-----|:-----|
| **Banking** (Annex I §3) | Banks performing CDD via EUDI Wallet (§24) | Essential |
| **Financial market infra** (Annex I §5) | Trading venue operators, CCPs | Essential |
| **Health** (Annex I §6) | Hospitals verifying patient identity | Essential |
| **Transport** (Annex I §2) | Airlines verifying passenger mDL (§15) | Essential |
| **Energy** (Annex I §1) | Energy companies verifying contractor identity | Essential |
| **Digital infrastructure** (Annex I §8) | A verifier/intermediary that itself qualifies as a listed cloud, data-centre, CDN, trust-service, or other digital-infrastructure entity | Essential only after entity-type and size/special-inclusion analysis |
| **Public administration** (Annex I §11) | Government portals performing eID verification | Essential |
| **Digital providers** (Annex II §6) | Online marketplaces, search engines, or social-network platforms that also act as RPs | Important only where the operator matches the listed entity type |

> **Scope boundaries**: Wallet integration does not determine NIS2 scope. Apply Articles 2–3, Annex I/II entity types, Recommendation 2003/361 size rules (including partner/linked-enterprise calculations), special inclusions regardless of size, Member State identification, and national transposition. A simple local headcount/turnover check or sector label is not sufficient.

NIS2 Art. 21(2) enumerates **10 mandatory cybersecurity risk-management measures**. DR-0002 already addresses the majority of these requirements through existing content — but without labelling them as NIS2-relevant. The following table makes these connections explicit:

| Art. 21(2) | NIS2 Measure | Existing DR-0002 Coverage |
|:-----------|:-------------|:--------------------------|
| **(a)** | Risk analysis and information system security | **§31** — Security Threat Model (19 threats, STRIDE + MITRE mapping, risk matrix) |
| **(b)** | Incident handling | **§33** — Monitoring (62 alert triggers in 6 categories, audit trail) |
| **(c)** | Business continuity and disaster recovery | **§36 Finding 4** — Trust anchor caching, Status List caching, WRPAC renewal, fallback flows |
| **(d)** | Supply chain security | **§29** — Vendor Ecosystem evaluation matrix; §27 — Intermediary Architecture |
| **(e)** | Security in acquisition, development, maintenance | **§13.8** — OIDF conformance testing; §7 implementation checklist |
| **(f)** | Effectiveness assessment of risk-management measures | **§13.8** — OIDF conformance suite; §7.1 step 20 |
| **(g)** | Cyber hygiene and training | *(Not directly covered — general training is out of scope for DR-0002)* |
| **(h)** | Cryptographic policies | **§12–§15** — ECDH-ES, SD-JWT, X.509, KB-JWT; §31.2 cryptographic threat model |
| **(i)** | HR security and access control | **§22** — RP Obligations (data handling); §23.3 — GDPR (purpose limitation) |
| **(j)** | Multi-factor authentication | **§23.2.2** — EUDI Wallet as SCA Method (two-factor analysis); §13.11 — LoA mapping |

**Incident reporting under NIS2 Art. 23**: The timelines apply to a **significant incident**, not to every EUDI verification signal. An in-scope entity first determines whether the event has caused or is capable of causing severe operational disruption or financial loss, or considerable material/non-material damage to others. If that threshold is met, the Article 23 sequence includes a 24-hour early warning, 72-hour incident notification, requested updates where applicable, and a final report normally within one month. WRPAC key compromise, trust-anchor poisoning, systemic verification failure, SDK compromise, or a data breach are classification inputs; none is automatically reportable without scope, impact, significance, and legal review. §33 should preserve the event, criteria, decision owner, classification time, rationale, and report identifiers.

**NIS2 vs DORA — sector-specific boundary**: NIS2 Article 4 gives precedence to sector-specific Union acts for equivalent risk-management or incident-reporting requirements. For DORA-covered financial entities, determine which entity, service, and obligation falls within that equivalence and how national transposition handles residual duties. Do not turn the relationship into a blanket exemption for every group company, service, or NIS2 provision.

```
NIS2:  [Event] → [Significance classification] → if significant: 24h early warning → 72h notification → normally 1-month final
DORA:  [Event] → [ICT-incident classification] → if major: initial ≤4h after major classification and ≤24h after awareness → intermediate/final stages
```

**EUDI Wallet as an MFA building block**: NIS2 Article 21(2)(j) requires MFA or continuous-authentication solutions **where appropriate**. A Wallet presentation can contribute a protected possession/device-key factor and evidence of local user authentication, but the RP must assess the credential/profile, holder and transaction binding, local-authentication policy, fallback/recovery, session lifecycle, channel risk, and service threat model. It is neither automatically MFA for every presentation nor proof that the entity has satisfied Article 21's proportional risk-management duty.

> **Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690** (in force 7 November 2024) provides concrete technical and methodological requirements for NIS2 Art. 21(2) measures. It is **mandatory** for DNS service providers, TLD name registries, cloud computing providers, CDN providers, managed service providers, online marketplaces, search engines, social networks, and trust service providers. Although most EUDI Wallet RPs are not directly subject, RPs that are themselves cloud/SaaS verification platforms (e.g., Intermediaries per §27) or trust service providers may be. All NIS2-covered RPs can use IR 2024/2690 as a **compliance benchmark** — it operationalises Art. 21(2) with 13 thematic sections covering governance, incident handling, supply chain security, cryptographic policies, and access control.

`ETSI EN 319 401 V3.2.1` is relevant here as the common policy/security baseline for a **trust-service provider**, including providers used by an RP or intermediary. It does not make an ordinary NIS2-covered RP an EN 319 401-conformant TSP. The RP-side control is supply-chain due diligence: request current conformity, qualification, audit, incident, continuity, and termination evidence for the specific service and its service-specific overlay, then map that evidence into the RP's NIS2 or DORA third-party-risk process.

#### 23.7 Wallet Solution Security Breach Response (CIR 2025/847)

[CIR 2025/847](https://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2025/847/oj) (in force 27 May 2025) establishes the regulatory framework for reactions to security breaches affecting wallet solutions, validation mechanisms, or electronic identification schemes. This is the first regulation creating **direct RP notification obligations** in the breach response chain — RPs registered under Art. 5b receive mandatory suspension and withdrawal notifications. Legal basis: Art. 5e(5) of Regulation 910/2014.

The ARF distinguishes three related but separate lifecycle surfaces: Wallet Provider notification status, Wallet Solution certification/availability status, and provider registration status for PID or attestation issuers. RPs should monitor all three, but they affect different verification decisions.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Wallet Provider" as WalletProvider {
        WPValid: Valid
        WPInvalid: Invalid
        [*] --> WPValid : Member State notifies Commission
        WPValid --> WPInvalid : Member State invalidates
        WPInvalid --> WPValid : Member State validates
    }

    state "Wallet Solution" as WalletSolution {
        SolutionValid: Valid
        SolutionSuspended: Suspended
        [*] --> Candidate : Wallet Provider publishes release candidate
        Candidate --> SolutionValid : validate / test / certify
        SolutionValid --> SolutionSuspended : suspend
        SolutionSuspended --> SolutionValid : re-establish
        SolutionValid --> Withdrawn : withdraw
        SolutionSuspended --> Withdrawn : withdraw
    }

    state "PID / Attestation Provider" as ProviderRegistration {
        [*] --> Registered : Registrar registers provider
        Registered --> Suspended : suspend
        Suspended --> Registered : unsuspend
        Registered --> Cancelled : cancel
        Suspended --> Cancelled : cancel
    }
```

For RP operations, Wallet Solution suspension or withdrawal is the most immediate availability concern because it can make presentations from a wallet family unacceptable or force fallback identity journeys. PID/Attestation Provider suspension affects issuer trust and new issuance paths; Wallet Provider invalidation affects downstream WIA/KA issuance assurance, while ordinary verifiers consume official solution notifications and credential evidence.

Do not equate Wallet Solution suspension with automatic Wallet Unit revocation. ARF §4.6.3 says the Member State must decide whether the corresponding Wallet Units also need to be revoked; if not, they can continue functioning while the solution-level issue is remediated. Withdrawal is different: it is terminal for the Wallet Solution, and the Wallet Provider revokes all associated Wallet Units. RP controls therefore need authoritative solution-status mapping plus each presented credential's trust, validity, status, and holder-binding results—not a generic WUA field or a single "wallet provider bad" switch.

The three status surfaces should be wired to different RP controls:

| Status surface | RP monitor | RP action when negative |
|:---------------|:-----------|:------------------------|
| **Wallet Provider notification status** | Wallet Provider LoTE / Commission notification state | Issuer-role systems suspend new WIA/KA trust decisions and evaluate credentials issued under the affected chain; ordinary verifiers refresh solution/credential policy rather than requesting WIA/KA. |
| **Wallet Solution certification or breach status** | Certified-wallet list, CIRAS/MS notifications, local suspension feed | Block or flag presentations from the affected solution, activate fallback journeys, and preserve incident/audit evidence. |
| **PID / Attestation Provider registration status** | Provider LoTE/Trusted List and provider registration status | Reject credentials from cancelled providers; apply suspension policy to new issuances and recently presented credentials according to issuer trust rules. |
| **RP registration status** | Registrar, Access CA status, WRPRC status list | Disable wallet initiation for affected RP services and rotate/revoke WRPAC/WRPRC material as required. |

The consolidated ARF state diagrams translate into an RP response matrix:

| ARF state surface | Negative state or event | RP response |
|:------------------|:------------------------|:------------|
| **Relying Party registration** | RP suspended or cancelled by the Registrar | Stop initiating wallet flows for the affected service, revoke or disable affected WRPAC/WRPRC material, and route users to fallback identity journeys. |
| **WRPAC / WRPRC status** | Access certificate or registration certificate revoked, suspended, expired, or stale | Reject request construction with that artifact; refresh from Access CA, Registration Certificate Provider, or Registrar before retrying. |
| **Wallet Solution** | Suspended or withdrawn after a security breach | Apply the official solution-status decision to mapped sessions, refresh issuer/credential status evidence, and activate fallback authentication paths. |
| **Wallet Unit** | Wallet Instance or WSCD/keystore revoked through the issuer-side WIA/KA status chain | PID and applicable EAA Providers apply their cascade policy. The RP rejects a cascaded credential when its own status evidence becomes negative; it does not obtain the WIA/KA directly. |
| **PID / attestation** | Credential revoked, expired, suspended where the controlling status profile permits that state, or outside the acceptable status policy | Apply credential-level rejection or step-up policy independently from wallet-solution status; never assume that every presentation status mechanism defines suspension. |
| **Provider registration** | PID Provider or Attestation Provider suspended or cancelled | Reject newly issued material from cancelled providers and re-evaluate cached trust anchors and recently accepted credentials under local risk policy. |

Topic 56 also matters because Wallet Providers monitor Wallet Instances for support, maintenance, and security posture. That telemetry is **provider-side** data, not an RP data feed.

| Topic 56 surface | Examples | RP boundary |
|:-----------------|:---------|:------------|
| `WPSM_01` maintenance monitoring | Runtime errors, UX telemetry, OS health, SDK/library versions, locale, wallet version, WSCA/WSCD capability, device identifiers, sensor patch levels, BLE/NFC support | Do not expect raw Wallet Provider telemetry; consume certified-wallet lists, breach notifications, and ordinary credential-verification results. WIA/KA status is consumed by issuers. |
| `WPSM_02` crash logs | Custom crash logs for provider analysis | Treat provider crash telemetry as outside the RP retention and incident pipeline unless a formal breach or outage notification is issued. |
| `WPSM_03` security posture monitoring | Root/jailbreak, emulator detection, OS health, wallet version, sensor and WSCA/WSCD posture | RP enforcement uses authoritative Wallet Solution status, credential status/holder binding, and lawful local risk signals—not direct device telemetry or presentation-time WIA/KA. |
| `WPSM_04` wallet updates | Provider updates Wallet Units for security and functionality | Track compatibility and breach posture, but avoid building flows that require users to disclose provider maintenance signals to the RP. |

##### 23.7.1 Breach Lifecycle

CIR 2025/847 defines a three-phase lifecycle for security breaches. The Member State assesses the breach against the Annex I criteria (§23.7.2), and based on proportionality decides whether to suspend the affected wallet solution. If suspended, the breach must be remedied within 3 months — otherwise withdrawal is automatic.

```mermaid
---
config:
  flowchart:
    nodeSpacing: 30
    rankSpacing: 40
---
flowchart TD
    A["`**Security Breach Detected**
    Wallet provider or MS identifies breach`"]
    B["`**Phase 1: Assessment**
    MS evaluates against Annex I criteria
    (life/health, malicious access, unavailability,
    impact scope, data compromise, certification)`"]
    C{"`Breach affects
    reliability?`"}
    D["`**Phase 2: Suspension**
    No new wallet units provided/activated
    24h notification to RPs, users, Commission
    MS evaluates Wallet Unit revocation`"]
    E{"`Breach remedied
    within 3 months?`"}
    F["`**Phase 3a: Re-establishment**
    New wallet units issued under new version
    New WIA/KA material
    Suspension measures repealed
    All parties notified`"]
    G["`**Phase 3b: Withdrawal**
    Associated Wallet Units revoked
    No new units or attestations
    72h notification after 3-month expiry
    Permanent — cannot revert to valid`"]

    A --> B
    B --> C
    C -->|Yes| D
    C -->|No — below threshold| A
    D --> E
    E -->|Yes| F
    E -->|No| G

    classDef default text-align:left
```

##### 23.7.2 Annex I Assessment Criteria

Member States assess whether a breach affects the **reliability** of a wallet solution based on the following criteria (CIR 2025/847, Annex I, paragraph 1). These inform — but do not automatically trigger — suspension decisions (Recital 5):

| Criterion | Threshold | RP Relevance |
|:----------|:----------|:-------------|
| **(a)** Life / health | Breach has caused or is capable of causing death or considerable health damage | Extreme — potential total service shutdown |
| **(b)** Malicious access | Successful suspected malicious/unauthorised access to critical network or information systems of wallet provider, validation mechanism provider, or eID scheme provider | High — trust infrastructure compromised |
| **(c)** Unavailability | Complete unavailability >12 consecutive hours, or >16 hours per calendar week | High — RP verification sessions fail |
| **(d)** Impact scope | >1% of wallet users or wallet-relying parties impacted by limited availability | Medium — RP availability degraded |
| **(e)** Physical access | Physical access to trusted-personnel-restricted locations compromised | Medium — HSM/WSCD integrity in question |
| **(f)** Data compromise | Privacy/integrity/confidentiality/authenticity compromised for >1% or >100K users (whichever smaller), or from malicious activity, or involving known vulnerabilities, or involving Art. 9(1)/Art. 10 GDPR special-category data, or impacting electronic communications, or posing high risk to fundamental rights, or impacting vulnerable persons | High — potential data breach notification cascade |
| **(g)** Certification cancelled | Certification of wallet solution cancelled or projected to be cancelled | High — WRPAC validity depends on wallet certification |
| **(h)** Financial loss | Direct financial loss >€500K or >5% annual turnover (whichever lower) | Informational |

> **Exclusion:** Planned maintenance operations that are pre-notified to users, RPs, and supervisory bodies are excluded from breach assessment (Annex I, paragraph 2).

##### 23.7.3 RP Notification Obligations

RPs registered under Art. 5b receive mandatory notifications at each phase of the breach lifecycle:

**Suspension notification** (Art. 5(1)(d)) — within **24 hours** of the suspension decision. The notification includes:
- Name of the wallet provider and wallet solution reference identifier (from the certified wallet list per CIR 2025/849)
- Date/time of breach detection and of the suspension
- Description of the security breach and of compromised data (including GDPR Art. 9(1)/Art. 10 special categories if applicable)
- Estimated number of affected wallet users
- **Description of potential impacts on wallet-relying parties** and user mitigation measures (Art. 5(2)(j))
- Planned remediation measures and deadline
- Planned user transition to alternative wallet solutions

**Re-establishment notification** (Art. 7) — remediation date/time, re-establishment date/time, description of remediation measures, description of residual impacts.

**Withdrawal notification** (Art. 9(1)(d)) — whether withdrawal is due to breach severity or to non-remediation within 3 months; date/time of withdrawal and effective revocation of all wallet unit attestations; user transition measures.

**Notification channel:** From May 2026, breach notifications to the Commission and Member State Single Points of Contact flow through **CIRAS** (Cyber Incident Reporting and Analysis System, operated by ENISA) per Art. 10. RP notification is via the registering MS's notification channel — RPs should proactively establish contact with their MS's Single Point of Contact (Art. 46c(1)) to confirm the delivery mechanism (email, API, push notification).

##### 23.7.4 RP Response Playbook

Upon receiving a breach notification, the RP must execute the following response sequence:

1. **Flag the suspended wallet solution** — mark the wallet solution reference identifier (from the certified wallet list per CIR 2025/849) as suspended in local verification configuration
2. **Reject or route new presentation requests** under the suspended solution using the official solution identifier and the applicable certified-list/breach-notification mapping; do not assume WIA/KA appears in a presentation or supplies that mapping
3. **Handle in-flight sessions gracefully** — inform users that their wallet solution is under review; offer alternative authentication methods (other wallet solutions, national eID, manual identification)
4. **Refresh affected credential and issuer evidence** — if the Member State also revokes associated Wallet Units, require fresh credential status and issuer-policy evaluation; issuer-role systems also process the WIA/KA cascade
5. **Monitor for resolution** — track the breach for re-establishment or withdrawal notification
6. **Upon re-establishment** — accept new-version wallet units from the remedied solution; update trust configuration; log the transition
7. **Upon withdrawal** — permanently remove the wallet solution from the accepted set, process the associated Wallet Unit and credential consequences from authoritative sources, and activate contingency authentication paths

> **Data portability:** Suspension or withdrawal must not hinder users' data portability rights (Art. 5a(4)(g) of Regulation 910/2014). However, this obligation applies to the **wallet provider**, not the RP. The RP should not attempt to export user data to the suspended wallet — its responsibility is to handle the presentation-side impact gracefully.

##### 23.7.5 NIS2 and DORA Cross-Reference

CIR 2025/847 Recital 4 states it operates "without prejudice to" NIS2 (Directive 2022/2555), the Cybersecurity Act (Regulation 2019/881), and the Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation 2024/2847). For NIS2-covered RPs (§23.6), a wallet solution security breach may trigger **parallel incident reporting obligations** under NIS2 Art. 23 — particularly if the breach materially affects the RP's service availability or data integrity. For DORA-covered financial RPs (§23.4), it may trigger ICT incident reporting under DORA Art. 17–23, especially if the RP treats the wallet integration infrastructure as a critical third-party ICT service.

> **⚠️ 3-Month Withdrawal Cliff:** If the breach is not remedied within **3 months**, withdrawal is automatic per Art. 8(1). Withdrawal **permanently** revokes all wallet unit attestations — they cannot revert to valid. RPs must have contingency plans for the sudden loss of an entire wallet solution from their accepted set. Single-wallet-solution dependency creates unacceptable residual risk; RPs should maintain multi-wallet verification capability and ensure fallback authentication paths exist for all user segments.

##### 23.7.6 Wallet Solution Certification Governance

ARF §7 treats Wallet Solution certification as a governance and assurance pipeline, not as an RP-side protocol exchange. Certification covers Wallet Solutions and the eID schemes under which they are provided; the certified object can include software components, hardware components provided directly or indirectly by the Wallet Provider, and operational processes such as Wallet Unit activation. The ordinary RP consumes the resulting status through certified-wallet lists, authoritative session-to-solution mapping, breach/suspension notifications, and issuer-mediated credential evidence. WIA/KA is consumed during issuance, not ordinary presentation. The RP does not inspect CAB working papers or component certificates during verification.

| Certification Surface | Source Model | RP Evidence Boundary |
|:----------------------|:-------------|:---------------------|
| **Wallet Solution / eID scheme object** | Certification evaluates the Wallet Solution and the eID scheme context, including relevant software, provider-provided hardware, WSCA/WSCD / keystore handling, and lifecycle processes. | Consume certified-list status, authoritative mapping/notifications, issuer-mediated credential evidence, and scheme/trusted-list state. Do not treat a vendor logo, SDK claim, or OIDF conformance report as a Wallet Solution certificate. |
| **National transitory schemes** | Before the dedicated Cybersecurity Act scheme is available, Member States operate national schemes using scheme owners, accredited CABs/Certification Bodies, ISO/IEC 17065 / 17067-style scheme frameworks, and possible reuse of EUCC, EUCS, EU5G, FITCEM, remote-ID, or private certification inputs. | Record which Member State / scheme source produced the status evidence and require certificate scope statements in procurement due diligence. Ordinary RPs should not attempt to replicate the CAB dependency analysis. |
| **Dedicated CSA-based scheme** | ENISA drafts the scheme with expert input, ECCG feedback, public consultation, and comitology adoption; once active, it replaces national schemes for cybersecurity certification while national schemes may remain for functional requirements. | Maintain a source-watch item for the transition. Procurement and rollout plans should distinguish cybersecurity certification status from functional / interoperability evidence. |
| **Composite certification and dependency analysis** | LoA High / Wallet Solution assurance can rely on component certifications and justified lower-assurance components where the overall composite certification still reaches the required level. | Trust the composite result surfaced through official lists and wallet/issuer evidence; do not downgrade or promote a presentation based only on a single component marketing claim. |
| **FCAF functional conformance** | ARF §7.5 introduces shared Functional Conformance Assessment Framework test cases for Wallet Solution certification and interoperability. The current framework is under active, incremental development; its initial and only SUT is the Wallet Solution. `WalletSolution_RelyingParty` tests the Wallet Solution's RP-facing interface—it is not an RP certification programme. | Record FCAF release/maturity, test class/case, SUT build, counterpart build, result, and evidence package. Do not claim an RP or vendor is “FCAF certified” from a WS_RP counterpart run. |
| **Other interoperability and protocol testing** | OIDF, reference-wallet, sandbox, and Launchpad results prove scoped technical interoperability and regression readiness; they are not the legal conformity assessment under CIR 2024/2981. | Keep each result's profile, versions, topology, and provenance as engineering/procurement evidence, separately from FCAF and legal certification artefacts. |

EC TS01 V1.2 exposes the certified state to the User through Wallet-side Trust Mark information and links to official certified-wallet information. `ETSI EN 319 487 V0.0.1` was still an early draft when checked on 2026-07-23. Neither artifact is an RP-presented credential or a substitute for certified-list, issuer, status, session-binding, and presentation checks; RPs should monitor the official status sources rather than scrape or infer assurance from the visual mark.

FCAF is deliberately **functional**. ARF §7.5 excludes performance, scalability, penetration testing, and availability testing and does not mandate a particular test tool or environment. It complements—not replaces—cybersecurity certification, non-functional assurance, accessibility evaluation, privacy/legal conformity, OIDF protocol tests, or multi-implementation interoperability exercises. The framework states that `v0.x` releases have partial coverage and that `v1.0.0` is intended to be the first full-scope certification-relevant baseline, so procurement evidence must preserve the exact release and maturity rather than cite only the moving `/latest/` page.

The adjacent TS02 provider-information publication feed should be monitored for provider additions, changes, invalidation, and publication-history events. It is an early-warning and discovery surface, not a replacement for the authenticated LoTE/Trusted List conclusion used by the affected verifier path.

---

### 24. AML/KYC Onboarding via EUDI Wallet

:::important
Treat wallet-based CDD as a regulated compliance workflow, not just a faster onboarding channel. The PID presentation is only one part of the decision; the RP still has to run the downstream screening, escalation, retention, and tipping-off controls required by AML law.
:::

> **Bank/PSP-specific guidance**: For the CDD/SCA dual-track compliance timeline, SCA bootstrapping via PID presentation, and supplementary identity verification (Portrait/PAD) guidance, see **§28**.

> **⚠️ Important: Proof of Age Is Not CDD Identity Evidence**
>
> A Proof of Age presentation (§21) supplies an age predicate, not the identity attributes and controls needed for customer due diligence or payment authentication. Do not substitute it for the applicable PID/CDD/SCA workflow. A financial institution may still use Proof of Age for a separate lawful age-only purpose under a separate policy.

#### 24.1 Customer Due Diligence (CDD) Flow (Direct RP Model)

Financial institutions subject to AMLD (Anti-Money Laundering Directive) must perform Customer Due Diligence during onboarding. The EUDI Wallet provides a streamlined digital CDD channel.
