Because this section is intentionally protocol-agnostic, the walkthrough focuses on session ownership, orchestration responsibilities, and decision boundaries rather than wire-level payloads.

<details>
<summary><strong>1. End User starts the journey in the first-party browser or native app</strong></summary>

The user starts a first-party journey such as onboarding, PID identification, pseudonym sign-in, SCA, recovery, credential re-binding, RP-controlled attestation issuance, or later attestation presentation / verification. The initiating channel may be a browser frontend or a native app, but in either case it remains the RP's own first-party experience rather than a direct handoff to a verifier or issuer console.

The important architectural fact is that the journey begins with **RP-owned purpose and product context already known**: what operation is being attempted, on which account or transaction, and what return experience the user expects. That first-party intent is what the orchestrator will later bind to the wallet result.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>2. First-party browser or native app starts the wallet-backed journey at the orchestrator</strong></summary>

The first-party channel calls the RP's own orchestration boundary rather than talking directly to a verifier or issuer API. In practice this call typically carries the RP's own journey identifiers and return intent: the browser or app session, operation class, account or transaction reference, and where the user should land when the wallet leg finishes.

This keeps the public contract stable even if the downstream wallet connector changes delivery mode, protocol role, or vendor. The frontend integrates once against an RP-owned journey API rather than learning connector-specific session creation semantics.

**Artifact Produced:** RP-owned journey initiation request bound to the first-party session.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>3. RP Orchestrator allocates session state</strong></summary>

The orchestrator creates the authoritative stateful envelope for the ceremony: correlation ID, product session linkage, nonce, timeout window, intended use, policy context, and the linkage back to the RP's own user, account, or transaction state. This is where the RP binds the wallet operation to its own business journey before any protocol message is emitted.

It is also where idempotency and replay boundaries begin. Later wallet messages are accepted only if they can be matched to this live RP-owned record. Without that envelope, a cryptographically valid wallet result could still be operationally unsafe because the RP would not know which business action it is authorising.

**Artifact Produced:** RP-controlled journey session envelope.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>4. RP Orchestrator creates a journey-specific connector session</strong></summary>

The orchestrator asks the wallet connector / protocol service to instantiate the protocol session for the journey branch that applies. In the **presentation / verification** branch, this means request construction, response-encryption setup, verifier-side handle creation, and preparation of the wallet entry artefact. In the **RP-controlled issuance** branch, it means issuer-side session preparation, offer / handle creation, and any issuance-specific setup needed before the wallet enters the ceremony.

The key boundary is that the connector owns the protocol-heavy mechanics, but the orchestrator decides **when** they are invoked and under **which RP purpose and policy context**. In a direct RP design the connector may run on RP infrastructure; in a SaaS-backed direct RP design the same call goes to a provider. The orchestrator does not need to expose that difference to the public-facing app.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>5. Wallet Connector returns request handle or wallet entry artefact</strong></summary>

The connector returns the material needed to reach or continue the wallet ceremony together with its own opaque session handle. In the **presentation / verification** case this might be a request URI, QR payload, deep link target, or other verifier-side entry artefact. In the **issuance** case it may be an offer handle, issuance entry handle, or other issuer-side wallet entry material.

The orchestrator receives this as an internal dependency, not as something that must be exposed verbatim to the frontend. That distinction matters because the RP may still want to wrap it, proxy it, or attach first-party routing and telemetry before the user-facing channel sees anything.

**Artifact Produced:** Connector session handle plus wallet entry artefact.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>6. RP Orchestrator returns a first-party wallet entry point to the browser or native app</strong></summary>

The orchestrator converts the connector output into a first-party launch contract for the browser or native app. That contract may proxy, wrap, or simply relay the wallet entry information, but from the app's perspective the RP still owns the journey surface, the return path, and the external contract.

This is the point where the RP can preserve first-party URL ownership (§26.8), keep internal services off the public internet, and avoid teaching attackers unnecessary details about connector topology. The frontend should learn how to continue the user journey, not how the connector is deployed.

**Artifact Produced:** First-party wallet launch contract returned to the app.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>7. First-party browser or native app invokes or exposes the wallet launch surface</strong></summary>

The first-party channel turns the launch contract into the concrete wallet-entry mechanism appropriate for the platform. In a same-device browser flow this may be a DC API / browser-mediated invoke. In a cross-device flow it may become a QR code carrying a `request_uri` or equivalent launch payload. In a native-app flow it may become a universal link, app link, or other OS-level handoff into the wallet.

This step is worth drawing explicitly because it is where the RP-controlled app stops being a normal product UI and becomes a wallet-entry surface. The browser or app is not yet sending a verified result; it is bridging the user from the RP's first-party context into the wallet ceremony while preserving the same RP-owned session envelope, return contract, and expiry semantics.

**Artifact Produced:** Wallet launch surface exposed to the user or platform mediator.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>8. End User reviews and approves the wallet action</strong></summary>

The user reviews the wallet prompt and explicitly approves the action that the journey requires: for example attribute disclosure, authentication, RP-controlled issuance acceptance, or another wallet-mediated authorization step. Making this approval explicit in the sequence matters because the wallet ceremony is not just a backend exchange; there is a user-consent or user-authorization moment inside the wallet before the next protocol message is sent.

Architecturally, this is the human confirmation point that must still line up with the RP purpose bound earlier. The wallet may present protocol-specific consent text, but the RP can interpret the result safely only if the approved wallet action still corresponds to the RP's intended business journey.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>9. Wallet sends a wallet-facing protocol message to the orchestrator edge</strong></summary>

This arrow stands in for the repeated wallet-facing interactions that may occur during the ceremony: request-object retrieval, protocol submission, token / credential retrieval, status advancement, or other wallet-facing steps. The internal OID4VP / OID4VCI and SD-JWT VC / mdoc details are abstracted away here on purpose.

What matters architecturally is that the RP-owned edge remains the first receiving boundary for those interactions when the chosen topology allows it. Even in a protocol-agnostic picture, that means the wallet is not talking directly to internal product code; it is talking to a controlled ingress point that can bind the message back to the RP's active session envelope.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>10. RP Orchestrator mediates the protocol step to the connector</strong></summary>

The orchestrator translates or forwards the wallet-facing step to the connector using the connector session established earlier. In a tightly integrated deployment this may look like a near pass-through. In other deployments it can include route normalization, session correlation, policy checks, or vendor-specific adaptation before the connector sees the request.

In a sync-inline topology (§26.6.4, §26.7.3) this can occur inside the same HTTP round-trip. In other topologies the connector may complete part of the work asynchronously, but from the first-party browser or native app's point of view that complexity is still hidden behind the orchestrator boundary.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>11. Wallet Connector returns a protocol result or internal failure</strong></summary>

The connector returns either a verified protocol outcome, a signal that another protocol turn is required, or a connector-internal failure such as duplicate `state`, nonce mismatch, malformed submission, expired session, or replay detection. Some of these protections may be implemented fully inside the connector rather than inside the orchestrator, and that is fine.

The architectural value is that the RP receives a structured internal outcome envelope rich enough for policy and telemetry, without exposing the low-level reason directly to the wallet or first-party app. This is the handoff point where protocol mechanics stop being the public concern and become RP decision input.

**Artifact Produced:** Internal protocol outcome envelope with result status, failure class, and next-action hint.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>12. RP Orchestrator returns protocol continuation or completion to the wallet</strong></summary>

If another wallet-facing interaction is needed, the orchestrator returns the next protocol step to the wallet. If the protocol is complete, the orchestrator returns the wallet-facing completion response that lets the wallet close its side of the ceremony.

This is distinct from the later RP business outcome returned to the first-party app: the wallet gets the protocol-level continuation or terminal response it needs to finish the exchange, while the app later gets the RP's own journey outcome. Keeping those two outputs separate avoids conflating protocol closure with business approval.

**Artifact Produced:** Wallet-facing continuation or completion response.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>13. RP Orchestrator sends verified result, HTTP context, and product state to policy / fraud / audit services</strong></summary>

Once the protocol result is sufficiently complete, the orchestrator enriches it with first-party context: product journey state, HTTP-layer observations, session history, and any required compliance metadata. This is where the RP combines connector output with VSI Layer 3 context (§32.5), product policy, AML / KYC / SCA logic, or other fraud controls.

That enrichment is what turns a cryptographically valid wallet result into an RP decision input. A valid wallet response is not automatically the same thing as an allowed business action; the RP still needs to evaluate it in the context of its own transaction, account, channel, and fraud posture.

**Artifact Produced:** Enriched decision input package combining protocol result and first-party context.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>14. Policy / Fraud / Audit services return a decision and internal reason</strong></summary>

The downstream policy stack returns the RP's internal decision record: business decision plus detailed internal reason. That reason may incorporate connector outcomes, replay / duplicate-state handling, HTTP-context anomalies, sanctions or fraud hits, and risk-scoring results.

This is the point where the RP decides whether the journey is allowed, denied, stepped up, or diverted into some other controlled handling path. The precise reason should be preserved for VSI, SIEM, and audit trails (§32.7, §33.3), even when the orchestrator intentionally suppresses it from the public response.

**Artifact Produced:** Internal policy decision record with rationale and audit linkage.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>15. RP Orchestrator returns a generic journey outcome to the first-party browser or native app</strong></summary>

The orchestrator converts the internal decision into the external RP-side journey outcome seen by the first-party browser or native app. This is separate from the wallet-facing protocol completion above. The app does not need the raw protocol failure details or fraud logic; it needs the RP-owned result surface that tells it how to continue the user journey.

The response can therefore remain intentionally generic: success, generic failure, or another controlled next action, while the detailed reason stays internal telemetry for monitoring, response, and investigation. This preserves a stable first-party completion contract without leaking attacker-useful diagnostics.

**Artifact Produced:** External first-party journey outcome linked to internal telemetry and session state.

</details>

<br/>

The practical design rule is therefore: **let the connector own connector mechanics, but let the orchestrator own the RP boundary around those mechanics**. That is the control point where first-party URL ownership, session binding, product context, fraud telemetry, generic external errors, and compliance evidence meet.

| Wallet Entry Variant | First-party launch surface | What the app exposes to the user or platform | What the wallet actually consumes | Primary reference |
|:---------------------|:---------------------------|:---------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------|:------------------|
| **Same-device browser** | Browser-mediated invoke | DC API / browser credential selector | RP-supplied request passed through the browser / OS credential API | §11, §30.1.1 |
| **Cross-device fallback** | Split-device handoff | QR code, copyable verification link, or equivalent launch payload | `request_uri`-based wallet entry artefact fetched by the wallet over its own channel | §12, §23.5.3 |
| **Native app** | OS-level app handoff | Universal link, app link, deep link, or platform-native invoke surface | Wallet launch target resolved by the mobile OS into the wallet app | §11.3, §30.1.2 |

The important boundary is that these are **entry variants of the same RP-owned journey**, not three unrelated architectures. The orchestrator still owns session linkage, expiry, return routing, and the business context bound to the wallet operation; only the user-facing launch surface changes by platform and channel.

##### 26.7.2 Deployment Topology: Proxy vs. Direct

With the first-party control boundary established, the next decision is whether the RP receives wallet traffic at its own gateway or lets the Wallet post directly to a verifier endpoint. That topology choice determines whether the RP can capture first-receiving-edge HTTP context and whether synchronous inline delivery is even available.

| Topology | Description | HTTP Context | VP Token Access | Enables |
|:---------|:------------|:-------------|:----------------|:--------|
| **Direct** | Wallet POSTs `direct_post` directly to verifier's `response_uri`. RP is not in the HTTP path — it receives results asynchronously via push/ping/poll/stream. | ❌ RP has no access to wallet's HTTP headers, IP, User-Agent, TLS fingerprint | ❌ RP never sees the raw `direct_post` — only processed results from verifier | Push, Ping, Poll, Stream, Event Bus |
| **Proxy** | RP's API gateway (reverse proxy) sits between Wallet and verifier. Gateway intercepts the `direct_post`, captures the full HTTP context (origin IP, User-Agent, cookies, TLS fingerprint, request timing), and forwards to verifier. | ✅ Full HTTP context captured at gateway | ✅ Gateway sees raw VP Token (encrypted JWE) before forwarding to verifier | All of Direct's modes **plus** Sync Inline |

> **Key insight**: Proxy deployment is a **prerequisite** for HTTP context capture and VSI Layer 3 signal extraction (§32.5) — regardless of whether the RP processes the verification result synchronously or asynchronously. An RP can deploy a proxy to capture HTTP context for VSI evaluation and *still* receive verification results via push webhook. The proxy and the delivery mode are independent decisions.
>
> **SaaS compatibility**: Proxy topology is **straightforward** with self-hosted or on-prem verifiers — the RP controls the deployment and can route `response_uri` through any gateway. With SaaS verifiers, proxy topology is **still achievable**: the RP configures the `response_uri` to point to its own gateway domain (§26.6.4), which captures HTTP context and forwards traffic to the SaaS backend. This requires the SaaS vendor to support custom domain configuration for the `response_uri`, or the RP to handle DNS-level routing. For the orchestrator pattern described above, wrapping only the SaaS verifier's session API (creation, polling, webhook ingestion) is **not sufficient** if the wallet-facing `direct_post` still lands on a vendor-owned domain: the RP would still lose first-receiving-edge HTTP context and first-party control of the wallet-facing URL surfaces in §26.8. No vendor in the EUDI ecosystem provides a dedicated "synchronous verify" API endpoint (POST VP token → receive result in response body) — the OpenID4VP `direct_post` flow places the *wallet* as the HTTP client, and the RP is always a third party. Library/SDK embeds (Spruce ID, Scytáles) are inherently synchronous since verification executes in-process.
>
> **Security recommendation**: The verifier's `response_uri` should never be directly internet-facing on a vendor-owned domain in banking-grade deployments. The minimum expectation is that the RP owns the wallet-facing receiving edge and the relevant RP-bindable URL surfaces in §26.8, so that `direct_post` traffic, request-object fetches, verifier identity material, and result retrieval remain first-party. Routing through the RP's API gateway enables rate limiting (per-IP, per-session), WAF rules, DDoS mitigation (e.g., Cloudflare, AWS Shield), request size limits, TLS termination with the RP's own certificates, and capture of source IP / User-Agent / TLS context for VSI. Without that RP-owned edge, the verifier's endpoint is exposed to the open internet with whatever protection the vendor provides, and the RP loses the HTTP context needed for high-assurance fraud and audit handling.
>
> See §26.6.4 for the full reverse proxy integration pattern, architecture diagram, and security considerations.

##### 26.7.3 Result Delivery Mode Taxonomy

This subsection is the canonical delivery-mode taxonomy for the chapter. §26.5.2 keeps the narrower asynchronous L2 view, and §26.6.5.1 applies the same mechanisms specifically to callback architectures.

Six distinct delivery modes are discussed for the verification result, three of which correspond to the token delivery modes defined by OpenID Connect Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication (CIBA) Core 1.0 (§14–§16):

| Mode | Mechanism | Direction | Latency | RP Infrastructure Required | Data in Transit | CIBA Equivalent | Requires Proxy? |
|:-----|:----------|:----------|:-------:|:--------------------------|:---------------|:---------------:|:---------------:|
| **Push** | Connector POSTs **complete** result (status + disclosed attributes + verification breakdown) to RP's `statusCallbackUri` | Connector → RP | ~100ms | RP exposes authenticated webhook endpoint | Full attribute payload traverses network | CIBA §14 (Push) | No |
| **Ping** | Connector POSTs **thin notification** (session ID + status only) to RP's callback endpoint; RP fetches full result via `GET /session/{id}` | Connector → RP → Connector | ~200ms | RP exposes webhook endpoint + calls session API | Attributes remain on connector until RP fetches via authenticated API | CIBA §13 (Ping) | No |
| **Poll** | RP periodically calls `GET /session/{id}` until status transitions | RP → Connector | 1–5s (interval) | No RP endpoint needed — RP initiates all requests | Attributes remain on connector until RP fetches | CIBA §12 (Poll) | No |
| **Stream** | RP holds a persistent connection (SSE or WebSocket); connector pushes status events in real-time | Connector → RP (persistent) | ~50ms | RP maintains persistent HTTP connection | Events + attributes traverse persistent channel | — | No |
| **Sync Inline** | RP's proxy gateway forwards `direct_post` to verifier, waits for verification result in the HTTP response, and processes the result before returning the response to the wallet — all in a single round-trip | Wallet → Gateway → Verifier → Gateway → Wallet | ~0ms (synchronous) | RP deploys an RP-owned proxy / orchestrator edge in front of verifier (§26.6.4) | RP has full result within the wallet's HTTP request lifecycle | — | **Yes** |
| **Event Bus** | Connector publishes verification events to a message broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ, AWS EventBridge); RP subscribes | Connector → Broker → RP | ~100–500ms | RP runs message consumer; broker infrastructure | Attributes traverse broker; encryption at rest recommended | — | No |

> **CIBA alignment**: The push, ping, and poll modes correspond directly to the three token delivery modes in OpenID Connect CIBA Core 1.0 (§12 Poll, §13 Ping, §14 Push). While CIBA governs **authentication token** delivery from an OpenID Provider to a client, the same patterns apply to **verification result** delivery from a wallet connector to an RP. Adopting this terminology provides a shared vocabulary for architects familiar with the OIDC ecosystem.
>
> **Sync Inline is the only mode that requires proxy deployment.** All other modes work with both direct and proxy topologies. When the RP deploys a proxy but uses push/ping/poll for result delivery, the proxy provides HTTP context capture as a side-channel benefit — the result delivery itself is no different from the direct topology.

##### 26.7.4 Two-Axis Selection

The RP makes two independent decisions — one for each axis:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start(["`**RP Integration Architecture**`"]) --> D1["`**Decision 1**
    **Deployment Topology**
    _Independent of result delivery_`"]
    Start --> D2["`**Decision 2**

    D1 --> TQ1{"`Does the RP need any of:
    • HTTP context capture

    TQ1 -- "Yes to any" --> ProxyT["`**Proxy Topology**

```

###### 26.7.4.1 Common Topology × Delivery Combinations

| Combination | Use Case | Example |
|:------------|:---------|:--------|
| **Proxy + Push** | RP needs HTTP context for VSI Layer 3 signals (§32.5) but processes verification results asynchronously via webhook | Banking RP: gateway captures wallet's IP/TLS fingerprint for VSI composition; verification result delivered via push webhook to RP's event-driven backend |
| **Proxy + Sync Inline** | RP needs both HTTP context capture AND real-time inline VSI decisions (rate limiting, signal-based blocking) before the wallet's HTTP response | High-assurance banking: gateway captures HTTP context, waits for verifier result, invokes VSI composition engine (§32.7), returns Allow/Flag/Step-up/Block decision to wallet — all in one round-trip |
| **Direct + Push** | Simple deployment, no gateway infrastructure, event-driven result delivery | Low-volume RP: SaaS verifier receives `direct_post`, pushes result to RP's webhook |
| **Direct + Poll** | Simplest possible deployment — no webhook endpoint, no gateway | Development/testing; low-volume deployments; RP polls verifier session API |
| **Proxy + Ping** | RP needs HTTP context but wants high-PII protection — attributes stay off webhook channel | Healthcare RP: gateway captures HTTP context; verifier sends thin notification; RP fetches attributes via authenticated API |
| **Direct + Stream** | Frontend-driven same-device flow — no server-side webhook infrastructure | Cross-device browser flow: RP's frontend subscribes to SSE events while QR code is displayed |

> **Hybrid deployments**: Production RPs rarely use a single combination. A common pattern is **Proxy + Push + batch polling fallback** (§26.6.7) — the gateway captures HTTP context from every wallet interaction, the verifier pushes results via webhook in the normal case, and a periodic batch poll sweeps for any missed callbacks. For cross-device browser flows, this is often combined with **SSE** on the frontend to provide real-time UX updates while the backend processes the push callback.

##### 26.7.5 Mode Deep Dives

###### 26.7.5.1 Push vs. Ping: The Payload Trade-Off

The key architectural decision for webhook-based delivery is whether to use **push** (full payload) or **ping** (thin notification + fetch):

| Dimension | Push | Ping |
|:----------|:-----|:-----|
| **Network exposure** | Disclosed attributes (PII) traverse the webhook channel | Only `session_id` and `status` traverse the webhook; PII stays on the connector until fetched via authenticated API |
| **Latency** | Single round-trip: connector → RP | Two round-trips: connector → RP (notification) → connector → RP (fetch) |
| **Freshness** | Payload reflects state at time of emission; may be stale if RP processes slowly | Fetch returns current state — guaranteed freshness |
| **Webhook security burden** | RP must protect endpoint against payload injection (§26.6.7) — a forged push with fabricated attributes is a direct data integrity attack | Reduced impact — a forged ping only triggers a fetch against the authentic API; the attacker would need to compromise both the notification channel and the session API |
| **Vendor examples** | walt.id (default), MATTR, Vidos | Procivis (default), Paradym |

> **Recommendation**: For RPs processing **sensitive PII** (banking KYC, healthcare) in environments where webhook endpoint hardening is complex, **ping mode** reduces the attack surface by keeping attributes off the webhook channel. For high-throughput, low-sensitivity use cases (age verification, basic identity confirmation), **push mode** is simpler and faster.

###### 26.7.5.2 Poll: When Simplicity Wins

Polling is the lowest-complexity integration — the RP needs no webhook endpoint, no persistent connections, and no message broker. It is the default delivery mode in the OpenID4VP reference design (the Verifier's frontend polls the Response URI using a `transaction-id`).

**Sub-variants:**

- **Short polling** — `GET /session/{id}` at fixed intervals (typically 1–3 seconds). Simple but wasteful; each poll is a full HTTP request-response cycle.
- **Long polling** — `GET /session/{id}?wait=30` with server-side hold. The server keeps the connection open until the session state changes or a timeout expires. Reduces request volume while maintaining low latency. The server responds immediately when the state transitions.
- **Batch polling** — `GET /sessions?status=fulfilled&since={timestamp}` sweeps for all completed sessions since a timestamp. Useful as a complementary mechanism alongside push/ping to catch missed webhooks (§26.6.7 "Polling fallback"). Not suitable as a primary delivery mode due to higher latency.

> **Interval guidance**: For short polling, use 2-second intervals during the first 30 seconds (user is actively waiting), then back off to 5-second intervals. Implement a maximum poll duration (e.g., 10 minutes per §26.5.1 session expiry) after which the RP stops polling and displays a timeout error. The verifier may include a recommended `interval` in the session creation response.

###### 26.7.5.3 Stream: Real-Time Frontend Integration

Server-Sent Events (SSE) and WebSocket provide real-time delivery without requiring the RP to expose a server-side endpoint:

| Variant | Protocol | Direction | Browser-Native | Use Case |
|:--------|:---------|:----------|:--------------:|:---------|
| **SSE** | HTTP/1.1 (`text/event-stream`) | Server → Client (unidirectional) | ✅ `EventSource` API | Cross-device browser flows: the RP's frontend listens for session status events while the QR code is displayed |
| **WebSocket** | `ws://` / `wss://` | Bidirectional | ✅ `WebSocket` API | Same-device flows requiring bidirectional communication; real-time dashboards; mobile app integration |

Stream delivery is primarily a **frontend** integration pattern — the RP's browser-based UI subscribes to events to update the user-facing state (e.g., transitioning from "Waiting for Wallet..." to "Verification complete"). It typically complements a backend delivery mode (push or ping) rather than replacing it. The backend still receives the full verification result for server-side processing; the stream provides the frontend with real-time awareness of the state transition.

###### 26.7.5.4 Event Bus: Enterprise Pub-Sub

For high-throughput enterprise RPs — particularly those subject to DORA (Art. 9 ICT risk management framework documentation) —verification events can be published to a message broker instead of or in addition to point-to-point webhooks:

- **Guaranteed delivery** — message persistence ensures no verification event is lost, even if the RP's consumer is temporarily unavailable
- **Fan-out** — multiple consumers can subscribe to the same event stream: audit logging, VSI evaluation (§32), CRM update, session management, SIEM integration
- **Replay** — events can be replayed for incident investigation, regulatory audit, or recovery from processing failures
- **Backpressure** — the broker absorbs traffic spikes; consumers process at their own rate

The 17 March 2026 vendor-documentation snapshot used for this chapter did not establish a connector with a native enterprise-broker delivery option. That is historical evidence, not a claim about current products. Unless a current, version-pinned vendor contract or API reference establishes native broker delivery, treat it as `Unassessed` and use the **bridge pattern** where appropriate: receive push or ping webhooks from the connector, then publish the event to an internal message broker for downstream processing. This decouples the webhook endpoint (which must respond quickly to avoid retry storms) from the business logic processing (which may be slow or multi-step).

###### 26.7.5.5 Vendor Ecosystem Landscape

The push model (full-payload webhook) is the dominant integration delivery mode across the EUDI vendor ecosystem. Only **Procivis** defaults to the ping model (thin notification → fetch), and **MATTR** supports a hybrid push/ping pattern via its backend retrieval architecture. The **synchronous inline** mode — where the RP forwards the VP token and receives the verification result in the same HTTP response — is **natively straightforward** with self-hosted or on-prem vendors (walt.id, Procivis) and library/SDK embeds (Spruce ID, Scytáles). With SaaS providers, sync inline requires the RP to proxy the `response_uri` through its own gateway and depends on whether the SaaS backend returns the verification result in the `direct_post` HTTP response — most SaaS vendors process asynchronously and deliver results via webhook, making sync inline impractical without vendor-specific support. Proxy topology for HTTP context capture (without sync inline) is achievable with **any** vendor if the RP routes `response_uri` traffic through its own gateway (§26.6.4).

No vendor natively offers SSE or WebSocket as a server-to-server L2 delivery mechanism — these remain RP-side frontend technologies for cross-device session status (via SDKs like MATTR's Verifier Web SDK). Polling is universally available as a fallback. See §29.8.1 for the full vendor-by-vendor delivery mode matrix.

#### 26.8 URL Surface Ownership, Facade Deployment, and RP-Bindability

The preceding sections establish **where the RP control boundary sits** and **where messages move**. This subsection addresses a different but equally important architectural question: **which party owns the URLs that define those movements**. For verifier products claiming white-label, façade, proxy, or RP-owned-edge deployment, URL ownership is a first-class capability domain rather than a branding afterthought.

In `DR-0002`, a URL surface counts as **RP-bindable** only if all three conditions are true:

1. The RP can choose or constrain the host / origin at product-configuration time.
2. The chosen value is the one actually emitted in the protocol artefact, trust document, callback, or follow-up API response seen by wallets, browsers, or the RP backend.
3. The emitted value remains consistent with the verifier's authenticated identity model — for example the EUDI/HAIP `x509_hash` certificate path, `verifier_attestation`, `openid_federation`, or DID-based trust resolution where the selected non-EUDI profile actually permits it.

This is stricter than a generic “custom domain” checkbox. A product is not meaningfully façade-deployable if it offers a branded callback or landing page but still exposes vendor-owned `request_uri`, verifier metadata, JWKS, polling, audit, or export URLs.

| ID | Surface | Representative parameters / endpoints | Why it matters |
|:---|:--------|:-------------------------------------|:---------------|
| **URL-01** | **Wallet submission target control** | `response_uri`, wallet POST target, verifier `direct_post` endpoint | Determines where the Wallet sends the VP Token or signing artefact. This is the first RP-visible receiving edge in remote presentation. |
| **URL-02** | **Post-wallet return target control** | `redirect_uri`, `wallet_response_redirect_uri_template`, native-app return URL, app link / universal link | Controls where the browser or native app lands after Wallet completion and whether the user returns to RP-owned navigation surfaces. |
| **URL-03** | **Callback / webhook target control** | `statusCallbackUri`, `callBackUrl`, `callbackUrl`, approval/completion callback URL | Determines whether asynchronous vendor-to-RP notifications terminate on RP-controlled infrastructure. |
| **URL-04** | **Request-object host control** | `request_uri`, QR / deep-link host, authorization-request fetch host | Controls where the Wallet retrieves the Request Object or invitation payload. This is a distinct surface from the final `response_uri`. |
| **URL-05** | **Verifier identity URL control** | `did:web`, DID Document URL, `jwks_uri`, `signed_jwks_uri`, `/.well-known/openid-federation`, and explicitly labelled product-specific metadata endpoints | Defines where verifier identity and trust material resolves. OpenID4VP 1.0 does not define `/.well-known/openid-credential-verifier`; a product endpoint of that kind is proprietary. In façade claims, identity URLs must align with the selected trust model rather than leak vendor hosting. |
| **URL-06** | **Follow-up URL control** | session polling URL, result retrieval API, audit / event retrieval, export / download endpoints | Determines whether post-verification data access stays on RP-owned surfaces or shifts to vendor APIs after the initial exchange. |
| **URL-07** | **Document fetch origin control** | `documents[].uri`, document download host, remote-signing document retrieval URL | Relevant in QES / document-retrieval flows where the Wallet fetches unsigned source documents from RP-controlled infrastructure before signing. |
| **URL-08** | **Front-channel authorization host control** | `/authorize`, PAR/browser-facing authorization host, approval / consent host | Relevant where the product exposes browser-visible or wallet-visible authorization pages and claims a branded or RP-owned front channel. |

The standards base supports treating these as separate control surfaces rather than a single roll-up:

- In OpenID4VP, `redirect_uri` / `response_uri` values are part of the Authorization Request state and, for signed requests, come from the signed Request Object rather than from an out-of-band console setting.
- In the EUDI/HAIP profile, `x509_hash` authenticates the signed request against the WRPAC leaf certificate hash; it does not turn a callback hostname into a certificate hash. The exact `request_uri` and `response_uri` still have to be signed, registered, tenant-bound, and accepted by the Wallet/RP policy. Other OpenID4VP profiles may define different Client Identifier Prefix rules, but those must not be imported into the EUDI branch.
- For `openid_federation`, verifier identity is not whatever the platform happens to render in `client_metadata`; it is the metadata obtained from the trust chain, including entity configuration and key-discovery URLs.
- Under RFC `9101`, `request_uri` is a security-sensitive capability URL surface: it must be `https` when client-hosted, should have high entropy, and carries its own anti-rewrite / anti-DoS considerations.

This yields a practical procurement rule: **do not score “custom domain support” as a single capability**. Score the relevant URL classes separately.

| Deployment claim | Minimum URL surfaces that must bind to the RP-owned edge | What breaks if they do not |
|:-----------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------|
| **RP-owned verifier edge** | `URL-01`, `URL-04`, `URL-05`, `URL-06` | Wallets still talk to vendor infrastructure even though the product is presented as RP-hosted. |
| **Reverse-proxy / synchronous-inline model** | `URL-01`, `URL-04`, plus any `URL-06` result endpoints surfaced to operators | A proxy in front of one callback path does not by itself make the verifier identity or result surface RP-owned. |
| **White-label / façade SaaS** | At minimum `URL-01`, `URL-02`, `URL-04`, `URL-05`; add `URL-08` if browser-visible auth pages are in scope | The user may see RP branding, while wallets and operators still resolve trust or fetch results on vendor domains. |
| **RP-channelled QES / document retrieval** | `URL-01`, `URL-04`, `URL-07`, and any applicable `URL-08` | The RP may own the signing journey superficially, but the Wallet still fetches documents or request objects from vendor infrastructure. |

Two implementation cautions follow from this model:

- **A proxy is not proof of identity ownership.** Routing `response_uri` through the RP's gateway is valuable for telemetry and inline controls, but it does not prove RP ownership if the verifier metadata, request-object host, or result APIs still terminate on vendor infrastructure.
- **Self-hosted / in-process products differ structurally from SaaS connectors.** For self-hosted or embedded products, many URL surfaces are RP-owned by construction. For SaaS connectors, the RP must verify that the emitted artefacts — not just the admin console — actually carry RP-owned hosts.

---

### 27. Intermediary Architecture and Trust Flows

:::caution
An intermediary is not just a convenience wrapper around direct integration. It changes who holds the WRPAC, who decrypts and verifies the presentation, what the user sees on the consent screen, and where liability and data-handling constraints attach.
:::

#### 27.1 Intermediary Role vs Direct Integration

When establishing a connection to the Wallet ecosystem, Relying Parties must decide between a **Direct RP Model** (as diagrammed in [§11](#11-same-device-remote-presentation) and [§12](#12-cross-device-remote-presentation)) or relying on an **Intermediary RP Model**.

> **Embedded wallet SDK — a third integration model**: For RP-specific credentials (SCA attestations, loyalty cards), an **embedded wallet SDK** (§11.4) offers an alternative to both the direct and intermediary models. The RP embeds wallet holder functionality directly in its app, using the same OID4VP/OID4VCI protocol stack. This does not replace the intermediary for external EUDI Wallet verification — but it eliminates the need for an intermediary for RP-issued credentials. See §11.4 for the full analysis.

An intermediary is a first-class RP in the EUDI Wallet ecosystem. It connects multiple "intermediated RPs" to the Wallet ecosystem, abstracting away the technical complexity of:

- OpenID4VP / ISO 18013-5 protocol implementation
- WRPAC management and certificate chain maintenance
- Trust anchor refresh (LoTE/Trusted List synchronisation)
- Credential format parsing and verification (SD-JWT VC, mdoc)
- Revocation checking infrastructure
- DCQL query construction
- SCA flow orchestration (for PSP intermediaries)

ARF Topic 52 makes the certificate split precise. The intermediary registers as an RP with intermediary intent (`RPI_01`) and obtains access certificates containing its own RP and Service identity. Under `Reg_34a`, the applicable intermediary WRPAC also carries the associated end-RP identifier and end-RP Service identifier, so a separate access-certificate set is needed for each intermediated `(RP, Service)` relationship. The intermediated RP remains registered in its Member State of establishment and receives a separate WRPRC for each `(Service, intended use)`; each such certificate carries the reciprocal intermediary identifier and intermediary Service identifier under `RPRC_04`. The intermediary's own WRPRC, if it has one, is not used for intermediated transactions.

The same legal entity can be both an intermediary and a direct RP. The operational rule is certificate-path separation: when acting directly, it uses its own direct-RP WRPAC/WRPRC material; when acting as intermediary, it uses the WRPAC carrying the applicable end-RP association plus the single end-RP WRPRC selected by that end RP for the current Service and intended use. Empty `RPRC_19a`, `RPRC_20a`, and `RPI_07a` supply no extra metadata or online-lookup path.

##### 27.1.1 Deployment Architecture and Legal Implications

The decision between Direct and Intermediary integration carries severe regulatory consequences:

1. **Direct RP Model (SaaS / Self-Hosted Connector)**: The RP maintains its own Access Certificate and integrates directly with the Wallet ecosystem. If the RP uses a vendor's "SaaS Connector" to facilitate this, the vendor is legally a **Data Processor** (subject to GDPR Article 28 and DORA third-party risk management) but is *not* an eIDAS Relying Party. A self-hosted connector reduces the vendor's runtime role, but does not eliminate software supply-chain, support and update, cloud/HSM, organisational, or DORA-relevant third-party dependencies; the RP must inventory and assess the dependencies that remain.
2. **Intermediary RP Model**: The vendor acts as the RP on behalf of the organisation. Under **Article 5b(10) of Regulation (EU) 910/2014**, these intermediaries are *"deemed to be relying parties"* but are subjected to a strict **no-storage mandate**: they *"shall not store data about the content of the transaction"*.

Because an Intermediary stands between the End-RP and the Wallet users, the trust flow and sequence diagrams diverge critically from the direct model.

#### 27.2 End-to-End Intermediary Flow (Intermediary RP Model)

```mermaid
---

  themeVariables:
    noteBkgColor: "transparent"
    noteBorderColor: "transparent"
  sequence:
    messageAlign: left
    noteAlign: left
    actorMargin: 250
---
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant User as 👤 User
    participant WU as 📱 Wallet Unit
    participant INT as 🔄 Intermediary<br/>(registered as RP)
    participant IRP as 🏦 Intermediated RP
    participant REG as 🏛️ Registrar

    rect rgba(148, 163, 184, 0.14)
    Note right of User: Precondition: Both entities registered
    IRP->>REG: Register Service/intended use<br/>and intermediary relationship
    REG-->>INT: Relationship registered and<br/>end-RP WRPRCs made available
    Note right of INT: Applicable WRPAC carries<br/>end-RP + end-Service association
    Note right of IRP: Each WRPRC carries reciprocal<br/>intermediary + intermediary-Service association
    Note right of REG: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀

    Note right of User: Flow: Presentation via Intermediary
    IRP->>INT: Request presentation + select<br/>one Service/intended-use WRPRC
    INT->>INT: Build JAR with:<br/>- applicable intermediary WRPAC<br/>  carrying end-RP association<br/>- selected end-RP WRPRC by value
    INT->>WU: OpenID4VP request
    Note right of REG: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀

    WU->>WU: Verify selected end-RP WRPRC<br/>by value
    WU->>WU: Evaluate requested scope<br/>against registered scope
    WU->>WU: Match reciprocal RP/Service<br/>certificate associations
    WU->>WU: Prepare separate approval<br/>and transaction-log projections
    WU->>User: Display end RP + end-RP Service<br/>(do not display intermediary)
    User->>WU: Approve
    WU->>WU: Commit end RP and intermediary<br/>identity/Service log evidence
    WU->>WU: Build encrypted response
    WU->>INT: POST response to Intermediary
    Note right of REG: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(241, 196, 15, 0.14)
    Note right of User: Response Forwarding

    INT->>INT: Extract attributes<br/>(MUST NOT store content data)
    INT->>IRP: Forward verified attributes
    IRP->>IRP: Process attributes
    Note right of REG: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end
```

<details>
<summary><strong>1. Intermediated RP registers its Service, intended use, and intermediary relationship</strong></summary>

Before any presentation, the end RP registers in its Member State of establishment, defines the end-RP Service and intended use, and provides legally valid evidence of its relationship with the intermediary. The Registrar verifies that evidence and records the association; a private routing configuration alone does not establish the Topic 52 relationship.

**Artifact Produced:** Registrar-verified end-RP Service, intended-use, and intermediary-association record.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>2. Registrar confirms the relationship and makes end-RP registration certificates available</strong></summary>

After registration succeeds, the authorized registration-certificate path issues the end-RP WRPRCs for the registered `(Service, intended use)` combinations and records the reciprocal intermediary identifier and intermediary Service. The intermediary separately holds an association-specific WRPAC carrying the end-RP and end-RP Service identifiers.

**Artifact Produced:** Reciprocal WRPAC/WRPRC association evidence available before session initiation.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>3. Intermediated RP requests presentation from Intermediary</strong></summary>

The Intermediated RP (e.g., an e-commerce platform or a small bank without its own EUDI integration) calls the Intermediary's session initiation API to request a credential presentation. Under Topic 52 `RPI_05`, the end RP selects the **single WRPRC** applicable to the active end-RP Service and intended use and supplies that certificate with the minimum private-API routing data and DCQL query. The intermediary must not choose a broader certificate on the tenant's behalf.

The Intermediary acts as a **technical proxy**—it has the WRPAC whose `Reg_34a` association names that end RP and end-RP Service and manages the OpenID4VP protocol on the end RP's behalf. The Intermediated RP does not need its own WRPAC, ECDH response key management, or SD-JWT/mdoc verifier for this transaction, but it remains registered in its establishment Member State. Its selected WRPRC carries the reciprocal `RPRC_04` association to the intermediary and intermediary Service.

**Artifact Produced:** Intermediary session-initiation payload containing the end-RP-selected WRPRC by value, DCQL scope, end-RP/Service routing identifiers, callback binding, and agreed verification set.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>4. Intermediary builds JAR with WRPAC and Intermediated RP identity</strong></summary>

The Intermediary constructs the OpenID4VP Authorization Request (JAR). It signs the JAR with the private key corresponding to its applicable WRPAC and includes the end RP's selected WRPRC by value using the `RPRC_20` / ETSI TS 119 472-2 presentation extension. The two certificates, not a parallel self-declared metadata object, carry the identities, Services, intended-use scope, and reciprocal association that the Wallet validates.

**Artifact Produced:** Signed OpenID4VP Authorization Request containing the intermediary WRPAC chain and one end-RP WRPRC by value.

```json
{
  "iss": "https://verifier.signicat.com",
  "aud": "https://self-issued.me/v2",
  "exp": 1750089600,
  "iat": 1750003200,
  "jti": "b8d4e1f2-3c5a-6d7b-8e9f-0a1b2c3d4e5f",
  "client_id": "x509_hash:Lm4nP9qRsT2uVwXy1zA3bC5dEfGhJ7kK8lO0pI6jHgF",
  "response_type": "vp_token",
  "response_mode": "direct_post.jwt",
  "response_uri": "https://verifier.signicat.com/oid4vp/callback",
  "nonce": "kYzM4NTY3ODkwMTIzNDU2Nz",
  "state": "int-session-abc",
  "client_metadata": {
    "jwks": {
      "keys": [{
        "kty": "EC",
        "crv": "P-256",
        "alg": "ECDH-ES",
        "use": "enc",
        "kid": "intermediary-enc-01",
        "x": "...",
        "y": "..."
      }]
    },
    "encrypted_response_enc_values_supported": ["A128GCM", "A256GCM"]
  },
  "verifier_info": [
    {
      "format": "registration_cert",
      "data": "eyJ...<single end-RP WRPRC selected for this Service and intended use>..."
    }
  ],
  "dcql_query": {
    "credentials": [
      {
        "id": "pid",
        "format": "dc+sd-jwt",
        "meta": { "vct_values": ["urn:eudi:pid:1"] },
        "claims": [
          {"path": ["family_name"]},
          {"path": ["given_name"]},
          {"path": ["birthdate"]}
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

> **Carriage boundary**: The example uses the `ETSI TS 119 472-2` OpenID4VC-side registration-certificate element already described in §9.2. `RPRC_19` requires one certificate by value in remote and proximity requests, and `RPRC_20` points to the applicable ETSI extension. Empty `RPRC_19a` and `RPRC_20a` add no intermediary-specific self-declared metadata carrier.

JWS header — signed with the **Intermediary's** WRPAC:

```json
{
  "alg": "ES256",
  "typ": "oauth-authz-req+jwt",
  "x5c": [
    "&lt;Intermediary WRPAC certificate DER>",
    "&lt;Access CA intermediate>"
  ]
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>5. Intermediary sends OpenID4VP request to Wallet Unit</strong></summary>

The Intermediary delivers the signed JAR to the User's Wallet Unit using the same mechanisms as direct RP flows: DC API (same-device, §11.2 step 6), QR code (cross-device, §12.2 step 6), or push notification. The `response_uri` points to the **Intermediary's** backend (`https://verifier.signicat.com/oid4vp/callback`), not the Intermediated RP — all presentation responses flow through the Intermediary.

> **response_uri domain**: The `response_uri` must match the domain authorised by the Intermediary's WRPAC SAN. The Intermediated RP's domain is irrelevant for response routing — the Wallet sends the JWE to the Intermediary, which then forwards verified attributes to the Intermediated RP.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>6. Wallet Unit authenticates Intermediary via WRPAC chain</strong></summary>

The Wallet verifies the Intermediary's WRPAC certificate chain (from the JAR's `x5c` header) against the Access CA LoTE trust anchor, identical to §11.2 steps 8–10. The WRPAC identifies the **Intermediary** entity (e.g., *"Signicat AS"*), not the end Intermediated RP — this is a key distinction. The Wallet knows it is interacting with a third-party verification service, not the business the User is actually engaging with.

The Wallet also verifies the JAR's `client_id` matches the Intermediary's WRPAC SAN, checks the WRPAC's revocation status, and validates the JAR's temporal claims (`iat`, `exp`, `nbf`).

**Failure Path:** If the WRPAC signature or chain is invalid, the Wallet terminates the flow and warns the User.

**Audit Telemetry:** The Wallet logs an `INTERMEDIARY_WRPAC_VALIDATION_FAILED` alert locally.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>7. Wallet Unit identifies End RP and Service from the selected WRPRC</strong></summary>

The Wallet parses the mandatory end-RP WRPRC carried in the request. The certificate supplies the end RP's trade name and unique identifier, the end-RP Service identifier and trade name, registered intended use and requested-attribute scope, intermediary association, privacy information, and other registered fields. The Wallet uses the end RP and end-RP Service for the approval view in step 12.

> **Trust model**: The intermediary WRPAC authenticates the live presenter and request, but it does not self-assert the end RP's registered scope. The signed WRPRC is the portable end-RP registration artifact; no live Registrar lookup substitutes for it.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>8. Wallet Unit verifies WRPRC for Intermediated RP</strong></summary>

The Wallet verifies the end-RP WRPRC as the portable authorization and transparency artifact defined by ETSI TS 119 475. The certificate is issued by an authorized Registration Certificate Provider associated with the Registrar and carries the final RP's registered Service and intended-use scope. The Wallet checks:

1. WRPRC provider signature validity and chain
2. WRPRC status-list validity and current status
3. Presence of one certificate by value for the current end-RP Service and intended use
4. The WRPRC intermediary identifier and intermediary Service match the WRPAC subject and Service
5. The WRPAC end-RP identifier and end-RP Service match the WRPRC subject and Service
6. The requested DCQL credentials and claims fit within the WRPRC's registered scope

**Failure Path:** Missing, malformed, inauthentic, expired, revoked, mismatched, or over-scoped registration evidence produces the applicable `RPRC_17`, `RPRC_17a`, or `RPRC_21` warning/policy outcome. It is not repaired with `RPRC_19a`, `RPI_07a`, or an online relationship lookup.

**Audit Telemetry:** The Wallet logs a `WRPRC_POLICY_VIOLATION` event.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>9. Wallet Unit evaluates requested scope against the selected WRPRC</strong></summary>

The Wallet compares each requested credential type and attribute with the registered scope in the selected WRPRC. A fully registered request continues. If the intermediary has injected, merged, or routed claims outside that scope, the Wallet applies the `RPRC_21` warning and Wallet Provider policy: permit the complete request, permit only the registered subset, or reject the request. The intermediary must independently enforce the end RP's registered scope before building the JAR; Wallet checking is not a reason to accept arbitrary tenant input.

**Failure Path:** Any claim outside the selected certificate's scope is recorded as an overasking result and cannot silently pass as registered.

**Artifact Produced:** Requested-versus-registered scope comparison bound to the end-RP WRPRC fingerprint.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>10. Wallet Unit matches the reciprocal RP and Service certificate associations</strong></summary>

The Wallet compares both directions of the relationship: the intermediary WRPAC must name the end RP and end-RP Service, while the selected end-RP WRPRC must name the intermediary and intermediary Service. Identifier or Service disagreement is a certificate-association failure, not a prompt for a live `RPI_07a` lookup.

**Failure Path:** A missing or asymmetric association terminates the request before approval.

**Artifact Produced:** Reciprocal `(intermediary, intermediary Service, end RP, end-RP Service)` association result.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>11. Wallet Unit prepares separate approval and transaction-log projections</strong></summary>

The same authenticated request evidence feeds two different User surfaces:

- **Approval projection (`RPI_07`)**: end-RP trade name, end-RP Service trade name, intended use, and requested attributes. The intermediary and intermediary Service are deliberately omitted.
- **Transaction-log projection (`DASH_03`)**: end-RP trade name, identifier, Service identifier, establishment Member State and registered request data from the WRPRC, plus intermediary trade name, available contact data, identifier, and Service identifier from the WRPAC.

**Artifact Produced:** Approval-view model and transaction-log record draft derived from the two validated certificates without a live Registrar response.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>12. Wallet Unit displays End RP and End-RP Service to User</strong></summary>

The Wallet constructs the approval screen required by `RPA_06` and `RPI_07`:

- **Relying Party**: 🏦 *"Example Bank AG"* (from the end-RP WRPRC)
- **Service**: *"Retail Customer Onboarding"* (the end-RP Service from the same WRPRC)
- **Requested attributes**: `family_name`, `given_name`, `birthdate`
- **Purpose**: *"KYC customer onboarding"* (from the selected registered intended use)
- **Registration result**: the applicable certificate/scope warning or success state

The Wallet **must not display** the intermediary trade name or intermediary Service in this approval view. The intermediary is still authenticated as the live presenter and recorded in the transaction log; suppressing it here does not remove that audit evidence.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>13. User approves presentation to the named End-RP Service</strong></summary>

The User reviews the end-RP/Service approval screen and approves the registered attribute release. The User authenticates through the applicable Wallet/WSCA ceremony to authorize holder-bound presentation. The protocol route still sends the encrypted response to the intermediary, but the approval object is the named end-RP Service and requested disclosure—not a three-party consent statement invented from the transport topology.

> **Transparency boundary**: The end RP remains responsible for applicable privacy/process transparency in its own journey, while the Wallet preserves intermediary identity and Service evidence in the transaction log under `DASH_03`. Neither duty overrides `RPI_07` by putting the intermediary back on the Wallet approval screen.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>14. Wallet Unit commits end-RP and intermediary identity and Service evidence to the transaction log</strong></summary>

After approval, the Wallet commits the `DASH_03` transaction record. It records the end RP, end-RP Service, requested and presented attribute identifiers, intended use, and applicable contact/privacy fields, plus the intermediary identity, available contacts, unique identifier, and intermediary Service. It does not log disclosed attribute values.

**Artifact Produced:** Topic 19 transaction-log entry whose evidence projection remains distinct from the approval UI.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>15. Wallet Unit builds encrypted response with vp_token</strong></summary>

The Wallet builds the `vp_token` (SD-JWT VC with selected disclosures and KB-JWT, or mdoc `DeviceResponse`), encrypts it into a JWE using the Intermediary's ephemeral ECDH-ES public key from `client_metadata.jwks`, identical to §11.2 steps 16–17. In a redirects branch, the KB-JWT's `aud` claim is set to the **Intermediary's** full `client_id` (not the Intermediated RP's), since the Intermediary is the authenticated Verifier that validates the presentation.

> **Encryption recipient**: The JWE is encrypted to the **Intermediary's** ephemeral key. The Intermediated RP cannot decrypt the response directly — it relies on the Intermediary to decrypt, verify, and forward the attributes.

**Artifact Produced:** JWE-encrypted `vp_token` (SD-JWT VC or mdoc) structurally addressed to the Intermediary's ephemeral key.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>16. Wallet Unit POSTs encrypted response to Intermediary</strong></summary>

The Wallet POSTs the JWE to the Intermediary's `response_uri` (`https://verifier.signicat.com/oid4vp/callback`), identical to §11.2 step 18. The response goes to the **Intermediary**, not the Intermediated RP. The Intermediary's backend correlates the response with the pending session using the `state` parameter.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>17. Intermediary decrypts JWE and verifies presentation</strong></summary>

The Intermediary performs the complete verification pipeline — the same verification an RP would do in the Direct model:

1. Decrypt the JWE using the session's ephemeral private key (then destroy it)
2. Parse the SD-JWT VC and verify the Issuer-JWT signature against the PID Provider LoTE trust anchor (§5.5.10)
3. Verify the KB-JWT signature against the `cnf.jwk` bound in the credential
4. Validate `aud` (matches the Intermediary's `client_id`), `nonce`, `sd_hash`, and `iat` recency
5. Check the credential's revocation status via the Token Status List
6. Verify the disclosed claims' SHA-256 digests against the Issuer-JWT `_sd` array

The Intermediary bears the full verification responsibility — the Intermediated RP trusts the Intermediary's verification result and does not re-verify the cryptographic proofs.

**Failure Path:** Any failure in signature validation or cryptographic binding immediately terminates the intermediary verification.

**Audit Telemetry:** The Intermediary MUST log an `INTERMEDIARY_VERIFICATION_FAILED` alert to its SIEM.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>18. Intermediary extracts attributes (MUST NOT store content data)</strong></summary>

The Intermediary extracts the verified attribute values (e.g., `family_name: "Müller"`, `given_name: "Anna"`, `birthdate: "1990-03-15"`) into an in-memory data structure. **Article 5b(10)** of Regulation 910/2014 imposes a strict legal obligation: the Intermediary *"shall not store the content of the transaction data"*. This means:

- The extracted attributes MUST NOT be persisted to disk, database, or any durable storage
- The attributes should exist in memory only for the duration of the forwarding operation (step 19)
- The Intermediary MUST purge the attributes from memory immediately after forwarding
- Log entries may record metadata (timestamp, credential type, verification result, session ID) but MUST NOT include attribute values

> **Audit compliance**: The Intermediary may retain proof-of-verification metadata (e.g., *"PID verified successfully at 2026-07-15T14:32:00Z, 3 attributes disclosed, forwarded to Example Bank AG"*) but not the actual values *"Müller", "Anna"*. This balance allows audit trails without violating Art. 5b(10).

**Artifact Produced:** Ephemeral in-memory attribute object (purged immediately after forwarding per Art. 5b(10)).

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>19. Intermediary forwards verified attributes to Intermediated RP</strong></summary>

After every agreed `RPI_09` verification succeeds, the Intermediary transmits the verified attributes **only** to the Intermediated RP on whose behalf this request was made. Tenant routing is bound to the end-RP/Service session and selected WRPRC; the attributes must not be forwarded to another RP, affiliate, analytics service, or any other entity. Common delivery mechanisms (see §26.6.1 for full analysis):

- **Webhook** — the Intermediary POSTs a signed JWT (containing the verified attributes) to the Intermediated RP's callback URL. The JWT is signed with the Intermediary's key, and the Intermediated RP trusts this signature as proof of verification.
- **SSE (Server-Sent Events)** — the Intermediated RP maintains a persistent connection to the Intermediary and receives events in real-time.
- **Polling** — the Intermediated RP periodically queries the Intermediary's session status endpoint.

The forwarded payload typically includes: the verified attribute values, a verification timestamp, the credential type, and a session reference. The Intermediated RP trusts the Intermediary's assertion — it does not receive the raw SD-JWT or KB-JWT.

**Artifact Produced:** L2 Callback Payload (Signed JWT) containing verified attributes and verification dimensions.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>20. Intermediated RP processes received attributes</strong></summary>

The Intermediated RP receives the verified attributes from the Intermediary and processes them within its business logic layer — CDD onboarding (§24), account creation, age verification, or identity matching. From this point, the flow continues identically to a Direct RP model: the RP creates an authenticated session, updates its records, and redirects the User.

The Intermediated RP's data retention obligations (GDPR Art. 5(1)(e), Art. 6) are independent of the Intermediary — the RP stores and processes the attributes according to its own privacy policy and the User's consent. The Intermediary's Art. 5b(10) deletion obligation does not apply to the Intermediated RP.

> **Trust delegation trade-off**: The Intermediated RP fully trusts the Intermediary's verification. If the Intermediary's verification was flawed (e.g., failed to check revocation), the Intermediated RP has no way to detect this. RPs should select Intermediaries with contractual SLAs covering verification completeness and liability.

</details>

#### 27.3 Intermediary Constraints (Art. 5b(10))

| Constraint | Requirement |
|:-----------|:------------|
| **Registration** | Intermediary must register as an RP itself |
| **No content storage** | Must NOT store the content of the transaction data (User attributes) |
| **Attribution** | Applicable intermediary WRPAC and selected end-RP WRPRC carry reciprocal RP/Service associations |
| **Approval UI** | Wallet displays only the end RP and end-RP Service; it suppresses the intermediary and intermediary Service |
| **Transaction log** | Wallet records both end-RP and intermediary identity/Service evidence under `DASH_03`, even though the approval UI differs |
| **Certificate** | Intermediary holds the association-specific WRPAC; end RP selects one by-value WRPRC for the active Service and intended use |
| **Forwarding** | After every agreed verification succeeds, forward only to the RP on whose behalf the request was made; otherwise forward to neither that RP nor any other entity |
| **Compliance** | Subject to all RP obligations (TS7, TS8, GDPR) |

ARF Topic 52 adds the current operational checklist for the intermediary model:

| Requirement | Current Topic 52 rule | RP / intermediary consequence |
|:------------|:----------------------|:------------------------------|
| `RPI_01` | Intermediary registers as an RP and indicates intermediary intent; it obtains its own WRPAC. Its own WRPRC, if any, is not used for intermediated transactions. | Separate the intermediary WRPAC path from the end-RP registration-certificate path. A vendor using its own WRPAC is not merely a transparent SaaS connector. |
| `RPI_02` | Empty. | Do not cite it as a live requirement. |
| `RPI_03` | Intermediary ensures each end RP is registered in its establishment Member State and receives the required end-RP WRPRCs; every certificate shows the intermediary relationship. | End-RP registration and current `(Service, intended use)` certificates remain mandatory even when the end RP never talks directly to the Wallet. |
| `RPI_04` | Intermediary provides legally valid evidence, such as a contract, that the intermediated RP uses the intermediary; the Registrar verifies and registers the relationship. | Do not rely on a private commercial agreement alone. The relationship needs Registrar-visible evidence. |
| `RPI_05` | Intermediated RP indicates which single registration certificate the intermediary must include. | The end RP owns deterministic certificate selection for the current Service and intended use; the intermediary must not widen it. |
| `RPI_06` | Intermediary sends the request with its applicable WRPAC and the end-RP WRPRC selected under `RPI_05`. | The two certificate associations let the Wallet authenticate the presenter and registered recipient/purpose target without `RPRC_19a` metadata or Registrar fallback. |
| `RPI_06a` | Empty. | Do not use it for intermediary semantics; CT/SCT failure references belong to the access-certificate profile. |
| `RPI_07` | Wallet does **not** display the intermediary or intermediary Service when asking for approval. | Display the end RP and end-RP Service only; retain intermediary identity and Service evidence in the transaction log instead. |
| `RPI_07a` | Empty. | Do not cite it as a live relationship-verification or User-requested lookup requirement. |
| `RPI_07b` | Empty. | Do not cite it as a live requirement. |
| `RPI_08` | After successful agreed verifications, the intermediary forwards the attributes only to the RP on whose behalf the request was made; if any verification fails, it forwards no attributes to that RP **or to any other entity**. | Tenant routing and callback configuration must prevent accidental or malicious cross-RP, affiliate, or auxiliary-service forwarding. |
| `RPI_09` | Intermediary verifies PID/attestation authenticity, revocation, device binding, User binding, and combined-presentation checks where applicable and as agreed with the end-RP. | The verification set is contractual and per-RP; do not add a WUA gate or write "all five checks are always mandatory" into the service model. |
| `RPI_10` | Intermediary completely and immediately deletes the PIDs or attestations it obtained, including their User attributes, after forwarding—or after completing necessary verification when nothing is forwarded. | The no-storage obligation covers raw credential material and failed-verification paths, not just extracted attribute values after success. |

#### 27.4 Intermediary-to-Intermediated-RP Attribute Forwarding

The intermediary's role doesn't end at Wallet interaction. It must securely forward verified attributes to the intermediated RP. The ARF and CIR do not prescribe a specific protocol for this leg — it is a private API contract between intermediary and intermediated RP, typically implemented via webhook push, SSE, or polling (§26.6.5 specifies the callback payload requirements for both SaaS and intermediary models).

##### 27.4.1 Verification Gates and Forwarding Requirements (`RPI_08`/`RPI_09`)

Before forwarding any data, the intermediary acts as a verification gateway. Current Topic 52 `RPI_09` defines the verification dimensions the intermediary carries out, with the important qualifier that some checks apply **if agreed with the Relying Party**. `RPI_08` then supplies the forwarding rule: forward attributes only after the agreed verifications succeed, and forward nothing if any agreed verification fails.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Gate["`**Verification&nbsp;Dimensions&nbsp;(RPI_09)**`"]
        V1["`**1.&nbsp;Authenticity**
        Check&nbsp;signature&nbsp;vs&nbsp;LoTE&nbsp;chain`"]
        V2["`**2.&nbsp;Revocation&nbsp;Status**
        Check&nbsp;Status&nbsp;List/OCSP`"]
        V3["`**3.&nbsp;Device&nbsp;Binding**
        Verify&nbsp;WSCD&nbsp;proof`"]
        V4["`**4.&nbsp;User&nbsp;Binding**
        Trust&nbsp;or&nbsp;verify&nbsp;rightful&nbsp;user`"]
        V5["`**5.&nbsp;Combined&nbsp;Presentation**
        Check&nbsp;cross-credential&nbsp;binding<br/>where&nbsp;applicable`"]
    end

    Cond{"`**Conditional&nbsp;Forwarding**
    Did&nbsp;ALL&nbsp;agreed&nbsp;verifications&nbsp;pass?`"}

    Reject["`**❌&nbsp;Drop&nbsp;Payload**
    Forward&nbsp;to&nbsp;no&nbsp;entity`"]

    subgraph Transmit["`**Payload&nbsp;Transmission&nbsp;Rules**`"]
        direction LR
        T1["`1.&nbsp;Authenticate&nbsp;Intermediated&nbsp;RP`"]
        T2["`2.&nbsp;Encrypt&nbsp;payload&nbsp;(TLS&nbsp;1.3+)`"]
        T3["`3.&nbsp;NO&nbsp;STORAGE&nbsp;of&nbsp;content&nbsp;data`"]
        T4["`4.&nbsp;Include&nbsp;provenance&nbsp;metadata`"]
        T5["`5.&nbsp;Forward&nbsp;only&nbsp;to&nbsp;named&nbsp;end&nbsp;RP`"]
        T1 ~~~ T2 ~~~ T3 ~~~ T4 ~~~ T5
    end

    Gate --> Cond
    Cond -- "No" --> Reject
    Cond -- "Yes" --> Transmit

    style V1 text-align:left
    style V2 text-align:left
    style V3 text-align:left
    style V4 text-align:left
    style V5 text-align:left
```

**The "As Agreed" Qualification**: Topic 52 explicitly notes that the ARF does not mandate every Relying Party to carry out all verification dimensions. The intermediary and the intermediated RP must agree contractually on which verifications the intermediary will carry out. This creates a per-RP configuration requirement and an audit requirement: the callback should tell the end-RP which agreed checks passed.

> **Meaning of "User binding" here**: Per ARF §6.6.3.9, this does **not** always mean a separate cryptographic artifact beyond device binding. For device-bound credentials, the intermediary may verify device binding and then **trust** the Wallet Unit / WSCA/WSCD user-auth ceremony as the baseline user-binding result. For higher-friction journeys, the agreed verification package may additionally include portrait/selfie comparison, PAD-backed live-person checks, or supervised document comparison. See §13.9 for the trust model and §28.5.3 for the portrait/PAD escalation path.

**Conditional Forwarding (`RPI_08`)**: If any of the *agreed* verifications fail, the intermediary `SHALL NOT` forward any attributes to the end RP **or to any other entity**. If they all succeed, it forwards only to the RP on whose behalf this exact presentation request was made. Beyond the verification gate, the intermediary should: (1) authenticate the end RP and bind delivery to its RP/Service session, (2) encrypt in transit, (3) not store content data, (4) include provenance metadata, and (5) forward promptly.

## Sector Integration Blueprints

This Part contains sector-specific integration blueprints that translate the general RP integration guidance from preceding Parts into compliance-oriented implementation roadmaps for regulated industries. Each blueprint consolidates the mandatory obligations, conditional requirements, and recommended best practices relevant to a specific sector, cross-referencing the detailed technical sections elsewhere in this specification.

---

### 28. Bank and PSP Integration Blueprint: EUDI Wallet Compliance Hub

:::important
Banks and PSPs should treat this as a single linked compliance programme, not as separate optional workstreams. RP registration, PID-based CDD, wallet-based SCA, and resilience/privacy controls all have to come online in a coherent sequence to avoid regulatory and delivery failure.
:::

This chapter consolidates all Bank/PSP-specific integration requirements into a single compliance-oriented navigation hub. It cross-references the detailed technical guidance found elsewhere in this specification, overlays the exact regulatory basis for each obligation, and classifies requirements as **mandatory** (regulatory), **conditional** (triggered by specific use case), or **recommended** (architectural best practice).

Bank and PSP readers should also keep two adjacent trust stacks separate throughout this chapter. The **Wallet RP stack** covers national Registrar registration, `WRPAC` / `WRPRC`, wallet-facing OpenID4VP presentation, and TS12 SCA flows. The **PSD2/open-banking institution certificate stack** covers `QWAC` / `QSealC`, the open-banking `QCStatement`, `organizationIdentifier` authorization-number syntax, `NCAName` / `NCAId`, and NCA/EBA register-backed role interpretation. `ETSI TS 119 495` sharpens that second stack; it complements, but does not replace, the Wallet RP trust model.
