The flow above is a better mental model for RP architects than "selfie check" alone. It shows why a supplementary remote-proofing ceremony is really a **pipeline of separate control objectives** rather than one biometric yes/no decision.

That same control model also needs a hard distinction between **presentation attacks** and **injection attacks** in the capture pipeline. Presentation attacks involve artefacts shown to the sensor (printed photos, masks, replayed documents on a screen); injection attacks bypass the sensor path entirely via virtual cameras, deepfakes, or modified video streams. For RPs, the practical consequence is simple: if the RP invokes remote selfie/video-ident as a stronger ceremony, the control set should cover **both** PAD and IAD / capture-integrity checks rather than treating a face-match score as sufficient.

OCR-heavy document capture is also fragile and can itself become an integrity risk, whereas chip reading is materially stronger where legally and operationally possible. So if an RP's fallback ceremony asks for a physical identity document in addition to Wallet data, **NFC chip reading should be preferred over OCR-only extraction** when available; otherwise the RP should classify the ceremony accordingly and compensate with stronger supervision or manual review.

Those three RP-side attack families are modelled explicitly later in the threat section: biometric presentation attacks in D.2.42, capture-pipeline injection attacks in D.2.43, and fallback document-authenticity failures in D.2.44. Teams designing supplementary proofing should treat those sections as the concrete attack and mitigation companion to this policy discussion.

The current standards landscape is useful to summarise here in adapted form:

| Domain | Ongoing Activity | Current Gap / Constraint |
|:-------|:-----------------|:-----------------------------|
| **Remote identity proofing** | `ETSI TS 119 461` | Still too abstract on its own; needs clearer mapping to **LoA High** |
| **Injection-specific threats** | `CEN TS 18099` | Technical specificity is still needed for implementation validation |
| **Security testing & evaluation** | `ETSI TS 119 461` references both `CEN TS 18099` and `ISO/IEC 19989-3` | Test specifications are not yet widely available or harmonised across Europe |
| **EUDI Wallet onboarding** | `CEN TS 18098` (`CEN TC 224 WG20`) | Still evolving; lacks detailed conformance guidance |
| **Biometric security** | `CEN TC 224 WG18` work on biometric product requirements | Still under development |

The practical RP reading of that matrix is:

- `ETSI TS 119 461` is an important umbrella baseline, but RPs should not treat it as meaning that every live-person step-up path is already fully harmonised or equally testable across Europe.
- `CEN TS 18099` matters because a strong selfie/video-ident ceremony must address **injection attacks** and capture-integrity threats, not just presentation attacks or passive liveness.
- This matrix does not eliminate the separate **remote document authenticity** problem: if the RP asks for an additional identity document, document validation remains its own control domain rather than a by-product of face matching.
- The broader conclusion is that **chip reading is stronger than OCR-only extraction** where legally and operationally possible; OCR-only fallback should therefore be classified as a weaker or more supervised ceremony.

Article 5b(8) explicitly permits supplementary security measures:

> **eIDAS Reg. Art. 5b(8):** *"Nothing in this Article shall prevent a relying party from applying a higher level of security in the authentication of the user than the level of security applied to the European Digital Identity Wallet, or from applying a different level of security to the authentication of the user for the provision of an online service."*

This means requesting a supplementary biometric liveness check is **not an obstruction** of eIDAS 2.0, provided it is justified under the bank's AML risk framework and applied uniformly (not penalising EUDI Wallet users). It does **not** mean that every wallet-based onboarding flow must request `portrait` by default.

**The `portrait` PID attribute**: CIR 2024/2977 defines `portrait` as an **optional** PID attribute — a facial image compliant with ISO 19794-5. Its best reading in light of CIR 2026/798 is as a **supplementary RP-side control**, not as the universal mechanism by which all RPs must establish user binding. To request it:

1. Declare `portrait` in the RP registration (eIDAS Reg. Art. 5b(2)(c))
2. State the intended use as "Biometric liveness matching for AML/CDD compliance"
3. Present the CIR 2026/1731 biometric-use warning and obtain the User's specific approval before portrait processing
4. Default to session-only processing and deletion; retain only where necessary for the identification/authentication purpose under Union data-protection law or expressly provided by Union or national law
5. Do not transfer the portrait to a third country or international organisation unless Union data-protection law permits the transfer

<details>
<summary><strong>Liability distribution — why supplementary checks matter</strong></summary>

| Scenario | Attack Vector | Liable Party | Rationale |
|:---------|:-------------|:-------------|:----------|
| **Coerced mule** | Citizen physically forced to unlock EUDI Wallet and share PID | **Bank (RP)** | AMLR requires detection of suspicious onboarding (CDD obligation). PID was authentic — Issuer is blameless. Bank failed to apply adequate CDD friction. |
| **Relay / phishing** | Fraudster tricks user into approving a PID presentation from the fraudster's device | **Bank (RP)** | PSD2 SCA liability falls on PSP if it fails to bind transaction to user intent. |
| **Deepfake injection** | Fraudster bypasses camera sensor, injects AI-generated synthetic video derived from stolen `portrait` | **Bank (RP)** | Bank's selfie check was insufficient — no Presentation Attack Detection (PAD). |
| **Forged PID** | MS registry compromised; PID issued to imposter | **Issuer (MS)** | eIDAS Art. 11 — Issuer liable for authentication failures due to its negligence. |

**Key finding**: eIDAS 2.0 shifts **document forgery / issuer-side identity-proofing** liability to the Issuer (Art. 11), but PSD2/AMLR keeps **transaction fraud and onboarding-channel risk** on the PSP. The bank does not have to recreate the issuer's identity proofing in every session, but it does own the decision whether additional live-person friction is needed for the specific risk profile.

**Required check quality — ETSI TS 119 461 PAD**:

A vanilla selfie comparison against the `portrait` attribute is **insufficient**. Modern generative AI defeats simple photo matching. If a bank chooses to use portrait-based live-person matching, it should implement **Presentation Attack Detection (PAD)** per ETSI TS 119 461:

| Approach | Coercion Defence | Deepfake Defence | RP Liability Risk |
|:---------|:----------------|:----------------|:-----------------|
| EUDI Wallet only (no selfie) | None | N/A | Depends on use case — acceptable where upstream proofing + holder binding are sufficient; weak for high-fraud remote onboarding |
| EUDI + basic selfie comparison | Low | None | 🟡 High |
| EUDI + ETSI-grade PAD (active/passive liveness + injection detection) | High | High | 🟢 Low |

</details>

**Operational guidance for PSPs**:

| # | Action | Priority |
|:-:|:-------|:---------|
| 1 | Treat verified PID + trust-chain validation + holder/device binding as the **baseline**; do not request `portrait` by default | 🔴 Critical |
| 2 | Register `portrait` only for specific intended uses where a supplementary live-person check is justified under the AML risk framework | 🔴 Critical |
| 3 | Implement ETSI TS 119 461-compliant PAD for high-risk onboarding, fallback, or exception flows that actually use portrait/selfie matching (see Remote Live-Person Step-Up: Biometric Presentation Attack (D.2.42)) | 🔴 Critical |
| 4 | For low-risk re-verification or flows relying on upstream high-assurance proofing, PID-only may suffice — apply risk-based approach | 🟢 Medium |
| 5 | Ensure the capture pipeline also covers injection attack detection, randomized challenge-response, and tamper checks — not just liveness (see Remote Live-Person Step-Up: Capture-Pipeline Injection Attack (D.2.43)) | 🟡 High |
| 6 | Apply the progressive assurance pattern (§18.13): PID-only for browsing → full PID, and only add portrait/PAD where the risk model demands it | 🟡 High |
| 7 | If a fallback path asks for an additional identity document, treat document authenticity as a separate control and prefer NFC chip reading over OCR-only extraction where possible (see Fallback Document Proofing: OCR and Document Authenticity Failure (D.2.44)) | 🟡 High |
| 8 | Give the required portrait warning, record specific approval separately from ordinary Wallet disclosure, purge the portrait after the session by default, and gate any retention or third-country/international-organisation transfer on the applicable legal exception | 🔴 Critical |

> **⚠️ Data minimisation tension**: Requesting `portrait` increases the PID attribute set and must be justified. Register it exclusively for the CDD intended use — never for SCA or general authentication. The GDPR DPIA (§23.3) must assess the proportionality of biometric collection against the specific AML risk being mitigated.

> **Source**: Analysis based on eIDAS Reg. Art. 5b(8), CIR 2026/798, the July 2025 ANSSI/BSI joint paper on remote identity proofing for EUDI Wallet onboarding, AMLR CDD obligations, ETSI TS 119 461, and EC EUDIW FAQ liability clarifications.

#### 28.6 Operational Resilience, Privacy, and Incident Handling

##### 28.6.1 DORA Compliance

🔴 **Mandatory** — All financial entities under DORA (credit institutions, payment institutions, EMIs, investment firms)

The **Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA)** — Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 — applies to all financial entities, including credit institutions, payment institutions, electronic money institutions, and investment firms. EUDI Wallet integration components fall within DORA's scope as ICT systems supporting critical business functions.

| # | Obligation | Regulatory Basis | DR-0002 Reference |
|:-:|:-----------|:-----------------|:------------------|
| 1 | Include EUDI Wallet integration in digital resilience testing programme | DORA Art. 24–27 | DORA Considerations for Financial RPs (§23.4) |
| 2 | If using an intermediary (§28.7.5): classify it as ICT third-party service provider | DORA Art. 28–30 | DORA Considerations for Financial RPs (§23.4); Intermediary Architecture and Trust Flows (§27) |
| 3 | Report EUDI-related ICT incidents (WRPAC failure, LoTE unavailability, mass verification failure) | DORA Art. 17–23 | DORA Considerations for Financial RPs (§23.4); Monitoring, Observability, and Operational Readiness (§33) |
| 4 | Include trust infrastructure events in cyber threat intelligence sharing | DORA Art. 45 | DORA Considerations for Financial RPs (§23.4) |

> **DORA Art. 28(1)(a)** — Third-party risk management:
>
> Financial entities shall manage ICT third-party risk as an integral component of ICT risk within their ICT risk management framework [...], and in accordance with the following principles: (a) financial entities that have in place contractual arrangements for the use of ICT services to run their business operations shall at all times remain fully responsible for compliance with, and the discharge of, all obligations under this Regulation and applicable financial services law.

**Bank-specific application**: If a PSP outsources EUDI Wallet verification to a SaaS Verifier (e.g., via the intermediary model in §27), the PSP retains full responsibility under DORA. The SaaS Verifier must be assessed as a critical ICT third-party service provider:

- **DORA Art. 28(3)**: The contractual arrangement must address data security, business continuity, incident reporting, and subcontracting chains
- **DORA Art. 30**: The contract must specify SLA metrics for verification latency, availability, and data handling
- **Vendor assessment**: Use §29.7 (Vendor Decision Matrix) with the DORA Art. 28–30 overlay

> **NIS2 lex specialis**: DORA is lex specialis for financial entities. Financial RPs complying with DORA Art. 6–16 (ICT risk management) and Art. 17–23 (incident reporting) satisfy the equivalent NIS2 Art. 21 and Art. 23 obligations. However, NIS2 Art. 29 (cybersecurity information sharing) has no direct DORA equivalent and may still apply. See §23.4 for the complete lex specialis mapping.

##### 28.6.2 Privacy and Data Protection

🔴 **Mandatory** — All banks and PSPs processing EUDI Wallet data

| # | Obligation | Regulatory Basis | DR-0002 Reference |
|:-:|:-----------|:-----------------|:------------------|
| 1 | Process EUDI Wallet-received data in full GDPR compliance | GDPR Art. 5; eIDAS Art. 2(4) | GDPR Obligations for RPs (§23.3) |
| 2 | Request only attributes necessary and proportionate for the specific service | eIDAS Reg. Art. 5b(3); GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) | GDPR Obligations for RPs (§23.3) |
| 3 | Perform DPIA before processing wallet data at scale | GDPR Art. 35; Recital 17 | GDPR Obligations for RPs (§23.3) |
| 4 | Support selective disclosure while designing mandatory requests for all-or-none approval; accept partial attribute sets only under explicit low-risk policy | eIDAS Reg. Art. 5a(4)(a); CIR 2024/2982 Art. 5(4); ARF Topic 6 | Edge Cases and Error Handling (§13.5); OpenID4VP Error Responses (§13.6) |
| 5 | Prevent cross-service tracking/correlation of wallet presentations | eIDAS Reg. Art. 5a(16)(a) | Linkability-Resistant Verification Practices (§13.10) |
| 6 | Register URL/email/phone deletion channels and operate TS7 data deletion handling behind them | CIR 2024/2982 Art. 6; GDPR Art. 17 | Data Deletion Requests (TS7) (§22.1) |
| 7 | Comply with embedded disclosure policies on attestations | CIR 2024/2979 Art. 10(3) | Trust Boundaries: User Binding, Wallet Trust, Device Binding, and ZKP Roadmap (§13.9) |
| 8 | Retain identity matching logs for 6–12 months | CIR 2025/846 Art. 5 | Identity Matching Normalisation (CIR 2025/846) (§25.6) |
| 9 | For `portrait`, provide the biometric-use warning and specific approval; default to session-only processing, apply the narrow retention exception, and restrict third-country/international-organisation transfers | CIR 2026/1731; GDPR Arts. 5, 9, 35, 44–49 | Supplementary Identity Verification (§28.5.3); supervised proximity flow (§15.4) |

> **eIDAS Reg. Art. 5a(16)(a) — Anti-linkability mandate**:
>
> The technical framework of the European Digital Identity Wallet shall: (a) not allow providers of electronic attestations of attributes or any other party, after the issuance of the attestation of attributes, to obtain data that allows transactions or user behaviour to be tracked, linked or correlated, or knowledge of transactions or user behaviour to be otherwise obtained, unless explicitly authorised by the user.

**Bank-specific application**: Anti-linkability is architecturally significant for PSPs. Do NOT persist unique attestation elements (salts, hash arrays, SD-JWT disclosures, signature values) beyond the verification session. Use application-level session tokens instead. Store only verification *results* (e.g., `cdd_verified: true`, `sca_passed: true`), not raw PID attributes. See §13.10 for the complete anti-linkability implementation guide.

> **TS10 Transaction Log Warning**: Attribute requests are recorded in the Wallet Unit's transaction log (TS10) under retention, export, deletion, and migration rules. Over-requesting creates a **forensically discoverable trail** of non-compliance while the relevant entries are retained, exported, or restored. See §23.3 for the complete TS10 implications.

##### 28.6.3 Security Breach Response

🔴 **Mandatory** — All banks and PSPs accepting EUDI Wallet presentations

| # | Obligation | Regulatory Basis | DR-0002 Reference |
|:-:|:-----------|:-----------------|:------------------|
| 1 | Receive and act on wallet suspension notifications (within 24h) | CIR 2025/847 Art. 5(1)(d) | Wallet Solution Security Breach Response (CIR 2025/847) (§23.7); Breach Notification Monitoring (CIR 2025/847) (§33.4) |
| 2 | Receive wallet re-establishment notifications | CIR 2025/847 Art. 7(1) | Wallet Solution Security Breach Response (CIR 2025/847) (§23.7) |
| 3 | Receive wallet withdrawal notifications (within 24h) and stop accepting | CIR 2025/847 Art. 9(1)(d) | Wallet Solution Security Breach Response (CIR 2025/847) (§23.7); Breach Notification Monitoring (CIR 2025/847) (§33.4) |
| 4 | Establish notification channel with MS Single Point of Contact before go-live | eIDAS Reg. Art. 46c(1) | Wallet Solution Security Breach Response (CIR 2025/847) (§23.7) |
| 5 | Subscribe to CIRAS (from May 2026) or MS interim notification mechanism | CIR 2025/847 Art. 10 | Breach Notification Monitoring (CIR 2025/847) (§33.4) |
| 6 | Check wallet solution certification status before accepting presentations | CIR 2025/849 | Wallet Solution Certification Status Check (§13.13.1) |
| 7 | Classify wallet-SCA outages, verification failures, certificate-status failures, and TPP-interface failures under payment-service incident processes | PSD2 Art. 95-96; DORA Art. 17-23 | PSD2/RTS Wrapper: Lifecycle, Monitoring, Exemptions, Evidence, and TPP Parity (§28.4.6); Monitoring, Observability, and Operational Readiness (§33) |
| 8 | Preserve customer-impact and transaction-impact evidence for major operational or security incident reporting | PSD2 Art. 96; EBA major incident reporting guidance | Alert Triggers (§33.2); Breach Notification Monitoring (CIR 2025/847) (§33.4) |
| 9 | Feed wallet verification failures, exemption use, confirmed fraud, and attempted fraud into fraud-reporting and fraud-risk analytics | PSD2 Art. 96(6); EBA fraud reporting guidance; RTS Art. 2 | Verification Signal Intelligence (§32); Monitoring, Observability, and Operational Readiness (§33) |
| 10 | Maintain a DORA/PSD2 incident taxonomy mapping so one wallet event can be classified consistently for ICT, payment-service, fraud, and customer-notification purposes | DORA Art. 17-23; PSD2 Art. 95-96 | DORA Considerations for Financial RPs (§23.4); PSD2/RTS Wrapper: Lifecycle, Monitoring, Exemptions, Evidence, and TPP Parity (§28.4.6) |

**PSD2/DORA boundary**: DORA supplies the financial-sector ICT incident framework, but PSPs should not collapse every Wallet event into an ICT-only classification. A Wallet SCA outage may also be a payment-service incident; a dynamic-linking manipulation attempt may be a fraud signal; an AISP/PISP redirect failure may be an open-banking interface issue. The incident record should preserve all relevant classifications so competent-authority reporting, fraud reporting, user notification, and post-incident remediation can be reconstructed from the same evidence base.

#### 28.7 Conditional and Extended Banking Use Cases

These obligations are triggered only when a PSP enters specific use cases.

##### 28.7.1 Corporate Onboarding (Legal Person Wallets)

🟡 **Conditional** — PSPs accepting corporate accounts where an applicable LPID, representation, digital EU PoA, or final EBW profile is available

If a PSP accepts corporate accounts, it should prepare a profile-gated path for Legal Person Identification Data (LPID) and representation evidence. Current inputs come from the EUDI LPID work, plural Topic 29 representation Rulebooks, the scoped digital EU PoA established by Directive (EU) 2025/25, and the still-proposed EBW framework; none establishes a universal production date or a single corporate-mandate profile.

| # | Obligation | Trigger | DR-0002 Reference |
|:-:|:-----------|:--------|:------------------|
| 1 | Support LPID (`legal_person_id`, `legal_person_name`) credential type | Corporate account opening | Legal-Person Extension: EBW, LPID, and Mandates (§20); LPID Credential Format and Profile Gaps (§20.5); Cross-Entity Binding and Verification Delta (§20.7) |
| 2 | Validate EUID format for `legal_person_id` claims | Receiving LPID presentations | EUID: The Anchor Identifier for Legal Persons (§20.3.1); EUID Format Validation (§20.7.2) |
| 3 | Implement triple-credential DCQL queries (LPID + PID + mandate) | Corporate representative onboarding | Legal-Person Request Patterns (§20.6); Mandate Verification Flow (§20.8.5) |
| 4 | Verify relationship binding: mandate representative identifier ↔ representative PID subject identifier and `represented_entity_id` ↔ `legal_person_id` under the applicable profile; evaluate any cryptographic holder-binding proof each credential format/profile actually requires, without assuming one shared key | Combined presentations | Cross-Entity Binding and Verification Delta (§20.7); Mandate Verification Flow (§20.8.5) |
| 5 | Apply the selected profile's validity, status, register-evidence, and freshness rules; re-evaluate before final authorization when earlier evidence no longer meets signed freshness and risk policy | Mandate verification | Mandate Revocation Model (§20.8.7) |

##### 28.7.2 Qualified Electronic Signatures for Contract Signing

🟡 **Conditional** — PSPs using EUDI Wallet for contract signing (loans, investment mandates)

If a PSP uses EUDI Wallet for contract signing (loan agreements, investment mandates), it must integrate with QES infrastructure.

| # | Obligation | Trigger | DR-0002 Reference |
|:-:|:-----------|:--------|:------------------|
| 1 | Select signing flow pattern (web portal / wallet-channelled / RP-channelled) | Contract signing requirement | Three Signing Flow Patterns (§34.2) |
| 2 | If wallet-channelled (Scenario B): integrate QES document context through the signing request / approval model, not the payment SCA `transaction_data` profile | Combined signing approval | Scenario B: Wallet-Channelled Remote QES (§34.2.2); What You See Is What You Sign (WYSIWYS) (§35.4.5) |
| 3 | If RP-channelled (Scenario C): comply with QES_24a (ETSI TS 119 101 for RP-provided SCAs) | RP manages SCA creation | QES_24a: The RP's Core Signing Obligation (§35.4.2) |
| 4 | Implement PAdES signature validation for incoming signed documents | Receiving signed documents | Mandatory Format: PAdES (§35.3.1) |
| 5 | For representative signing: embed mandate metadata in signatures | Authorized representative signing | Representative Signing: Mandate and QES (§35.7) |

##### 28.7.3 Embedded Wallet SDK (Dual-Wallet Model)

🟡 **Conditional** — PSPs embedding a wallet SDK within their mobile banking app

If a PSP issues its own SCA attestations into a Wallet embedded within the banking app, the dual-wallet architecture applies.

| # | Consideration | DR-0002 Reference |
|:-:|:-------------|:------------------|
| 1 | Issue SCA attestations via OID4VCI directly into the embedded SDK | OID4VCI Issuance Flow for SCA Attestations (§17.4); Embedded Wallet SDK Integration Pattern (§11.4) |
| 2 | Evaluate SDK vendors: Verimi (EUDI-certified), walt.id (open-source), Ping Identity (enterprise IAM) | Embedded Wallet SDK Capability Assessment (§29.7) |
| 3 | Test Android CredentialManager dual-registration: both wallets appear in OS credential picker | Protocol Reuse: Single QR Code, Dual Wallet (§11.4.2) |
| 4 | Maintain a single OID4VP verification backend for both external EUDI Wallet and embedded SDK | Recommended Architecture: The Dual-Wallet Model (§11.4.5) |

##### 28.7.4 Corporate Group RP Registration

🟡 **Conditional** — Banking groups with multiple legal entities or cross-border operations

Banking groups typically operate multiple legal entities (retail bank, investment arm, insurance subsidiary, payment institution) across multiple Member States. The eIDAS 2.0 framework requires per-entity registration but accommodates shared infrastructure through the intermediary pattern.

**Core rule: Each legal entity registers separately.**

> **eIDAS Reg. Art. 5b(1):** *"Where a relying party intends to rely upon European Digital Identity Wallets [...], the relying party shall register in the Member State where it is established."*

The registration number ties RP registration to a **specific legal entity** (eIDAS Reg. Art. 5b(2)(a)(ii)) — a parent company's KvK/Handelsregister number is not its subsidiary's. A group-level registration is architecturally prohibited.

**The intermediary pattern for banking groups (eIDAS Reg. Art. 5b(10))**:

The regulation provides a shared infrastructure mechanism. A typical banking group architecture:

```
Banking Group N.V. (Holding — NOT an RP)
│
├── Group IT Services B.V. (Intermediary RP)
│   ├── RPAC: own certificate as intermediary
│   ├── RPRC for Retail Bank N.V.  → intended use: CDD onboarding
│   ├── RPRC for Retail Bank N.V.  → intended use: SCA for payments
│   ├── RPRC for Insurance N.V.   → intended use: claims verification
│   └── RPRC for Leasing B.V.     → intended use: contract signing
│
├── Retail Bank N.V. (End-RP, registered separately)
├── Insurance N.V. (End-RP, registered separately)
└── Leasing B.V. (End-RP, registered separately)
```

The Wallet User sees **both names** (CIR 2025/848 Annex V point 3(j)): "Group IT Services B.V. acting on behalf of Retail Bank N.V." — preserving transparency about which entity processes their data.

**Key constraints for banking groups**:

| Constraint | Rule | Source |
|:-----------|:-----|:-------|
| **Flat two-layer only** | Max 2 layers (intermediary + End-RP). No chaining through regional hubs. | ARF Topic 52 |
| **No-storage mandate** | The intermediary (Group IT) cannot store transaction content data | eIDAS Reg. Art. 5b(10) |
| **Per-entity RPRC** | Each End-RP gets its own RPRC per intended use | CIR 2025/848 Art. 7 |
| **Single trade name** | CIR 2025/848 Annex I provides one `tradeName` per registration — multi-brand entities must choose | Annex I Point 2 |
| **TR40 threat** | Multi-unit RPs risk scope creep — one unit accessing data beyond its authorised scope | CIR 2024/2981 Annex I (TR40) |

**What can be shared within the group**:

| Shareable | Not Shareable |
|:----------|:-------------|
| Technical infrastructure (wallet integration platform) | RP registration (per entity) |
| Development & maintenance (one engineering team) | RP certificates (RPAC/RPRC per entity) |
| Centralised monitoring & incident response | Intended use declarations (per entity) |
| Core compliance assessment (platform-level VCQ) | Privacy policies (per entity, GDPR) |

<details>
<summary><strong>Passported institutions and RP registration</strong></summary>

Financial institutions operating cross-border under passporting regimes (CRD IV, PSD2, Solvency II, MiFID II) face a specific question: does passporting exempt from RP registration?

**No — the obligations run in parallel.** eIDAS Reg. Art. 5b(4) states that RP registration is "without prejudice to" sectoral law. However, a passported entity registers in its **home MS only** — cross-border service provision does not trigger host-MS registration. Art. 4(2) of CIR 2025/848 allows MSs to **reuse existing sectoral registration** (EBA register, LEI) to streamline the process.

| Passporting Mode | RP Registration MS |
|:---------------- |:------------------|
| Home MS authorisation only | Home MS |
| Branch in host MS | Likely home MS; host MS per national policy (CIR 2025/848 Art. 4) |
| Cross-border services (no establishment) | Home MS only |
| PSD2 agent in host MS | Agent registers independently |

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Dual-role entities (RP + Attestation Provider)</strong></summary>

Banks may operate as both RP (consuming PID for KYC) and QEAA Provider (issuing payment account attestations). CIR 2025/848 Annex I Point 12 supports multiple entitlements per registration (`Service_Provider` + `QEAA_Provider`). However, eIDAS Reg. Art. 45h imposes **functional separation**: KYC data obtained through the RP role cannot be combined with attestation issuance data, even for the same customer.

</details>
<br/>

> **Source**: Analysis based on eIDAS Reg. Art. 5b(1)/(10), CIR 2025/848 Annex I, ARF Topic 52, sectoral passporting regimes, and dual-role registration requirements.

##### 28.7.5 Intermediary Obligations

🟡 **Conditional** — PSPs using a commercial SaaS Verifier (Art. 5b(10) intermediary)

Most banks will not build wallet verification infrastructure in-house. Instead, they will procure a commercial integration product (e.g., Signicat, Authada, iDenfy, walt.id) that acts as an **intermediary** under Art. 5b(10). This creates obligations on both sides: the bank as the **delegating relying party** (the "end-RP" in ARF terminology) and the vendor as the **intermediary relying party** (Art. 5b(10)).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph WU["EUDI Wallet Unit"]
        PID["PID / SCA Attestation"]
    end

    subgraph INT["Intermediary RP (SaaS Verifier)"]
        direction TB
        WRPAC["WRPAC: intermediary Service<br/>+ end-RP/Service association"]
        RPRC1["Selected WRPRC:<br/>Bank Service → CDD"]
        RPRC2["Selected WRPRC:<br/>Bank Service → SCA"]
        VP["OID4VP Verification Engine"]
        WRPAC ~~~ RPRC1 ~~~ RPRC2
    end

    subgraph BANK["Bank N.V. (End-RP)"]
        direction TB
        REG["RP Registration (home MS)"]
        AUTH["Authorisation Engine"]
        CDD["CDD / AML Screening"]
    end

    WU -- "VP Token (encrypted)" --> INT
    INT -- "Verified attributes +<br/>verification result" --> BANK
    INT -. "❌ No transaction content data storage (Art. 5b(10))" .-> INT

```

> **Key architectural constraint**: The intermediary receives and processes VP Tokens but **must not store transaction content data** (Art. 5b(10)). Verified attributes may flow only to the bank on whose behalf the request was made, and only after every agreed Topic 52 check passes; on any failed check, none may flow to the bank or another entity. The intermediary must then delete the PIDs or attestations and all contained User attributes completely and immediately. WIA/KA is not presented to the intermediary. The Wallet approval UI shows *Bank N.V.* and its selected Service, not the intermediary; the Wallet transaction log nevertheless records both the bank and intermediary identifiers/Services.

**A. Obligations for the Bank (delegating RP)**:

When a PSP delegates wallet verification to a commercial intermediary, it retains full regulatory responsibility and must:

| # | Obligation | Regulatory Basis | DR-0002 Reference |
|:-:|:-----------|:-----------------|:------------------|
| 1 | Declare reliance on intermediary in the national register | CIR 2025/848 Annex I point 14 | TS6 Mandatory and Role-Dependent Registered Data (§4.2.2) |
| 2 | Provide formal association to the specific intermediary | CIR 2025/848 Annex I point 15 | TS6 Mandatory and Role-Dependent Registered Data (§4.2.2) |
| 3 | Verify intermediary registration, the association-specific WRPAC path, reciprocal WRPAC/WRPRC relationship setup, and deterministic end-RP certificate selection before delegation | CIR 2025/848; ARF Topic 52 `RPI_01`-`RPI_05`; `Reg_34a`; `RPRC_04` | Intermediary Architecture and Trust Flows (§27); Callback Integration Architecture (§26.6) |
| 4 | Establish Data Processing Agreement (DPA) and DORA outsourcing controls with intermediary | GDPR Art. 28(3) + eIDAS Reg. Art. 5b(10) + DORA Art. 28 | DORA Considerations for Financial RPs (§23.4); Intermediary Architecture and Trust Flows (§27) |
| 5 | Monitor and act on intermediary breach/suspension notifications | CIR 2025/847 Art. 5(1)(d) | Wallet Solution Security Breach Response (CIR 2025/847) (§23.7); Breach Notification Monitoring (CIR 2025/847) (§33.4) |
| 6 | Classify intermediary as ICT third-party service provider under DORA | DORA Art. 28 | DORA Considerations for Financial RPs (§23.4) |

> **Liability clarification**: The intermediary executes the agreed verification set under Topic 52, but the bank still owns the business decision that relies on the result. The contract should therefore name the exact `RPI_09` verification dimensions, callback evidence, breach-notification duties, and liability allocation instead of treating the intermediary's signed assertion as a black box.

**B. Obligations for the Intermediary vendor** (Art. 5b(10) intermediary relying party):

These obligations apply to the **vendor** providing the integration product, not to the bank purchasing it. Listed here for completeness — PSPs should verify their chosen vendor meets these requirements during procurement due diligence:

| # | Obligation | Regulatory Basis | DR-0002 Reference |
|:-:|:-----------|:-----------------|:------------------|
| 1 | Register as an RP while indicating intermediary intent | Topic 52 `RPI_01` | Intermediary Role vs Direct Integration (§27.1) |
| 2 | Obtain and manage own Wallet-Relying Party Access Certificate (WRPAC) | Topic 52 `RPI_01`; CIR 2025/848 Art. 7 | Access Certificates (WRPAC) (§5.2); End-to-End Intermediary Flow (Intermediary RP Model) (§27.2) |
| 3 | Ensure each downstream RP relationship is registered, use the WRPAC carrying the matching end-RP/Service association, and carry the single end-RP WRPRC selected for the current Service and intended use | Topic 52 `RPI_03`-`RPI_06`; `Reg_34a`; `RPRC_04` | End-to-End Intermediary Flow (Intermediary RP Model) (§27.2); Intermediary Constraints (§27.3); Callback Integration Architecture (§26.6) |
| 4 | Ensure the Wallet approval path displays only the end RP and end-RP Service while the transaction log retains the intermediary's trade name, contact data, identifier, and Service identifier | Topic 52 `RPI_07`; Topic 19 `DASH_03` | End-to-End Intermediary Flow (Intermediary RP Model) (§27.2); Audit Trail Requirements (§33.3) |
| 5 | Implement immediate deletion of PIDs or attestations and their User attributes after forwarding or failed verification | Topic 52 `RPI_10`; eIDAS Reg. Art. 5b(10) | Intermediary Constraints (§27.3) |
| 6 | Maintain audit trail demonstrating agreed verification, forwarding, and data non-storage compliance without retaining content data | Topic 52 `RPI_08`-`RPI_10`; eIDAS Reg. Art. 5b(10) | Intermediary-to-Intermediated-RP Attribute Forwarding (§27.4); Audit Trail Requirements (§33.3) |
| 7 | Support multi-wallet interoperability across all certified EUDI Wallets | CIR 2024/2982 Art. 5(1) | First-Party Control Boundary and Delivery Architecture (§26.7) |

<details>
<summary><strong>Bank procurement checklist</strong> — vendor evaluation criteria for intermediary selection</summary>

| # | Procurement Check | What to Look For |
|:-:|:------------------|:-----------------|
| 1 | **Registration status** | Vendor is registered as RP in at least one MS; holds valid WRPAC |
| 2 | **No-storage architecture** | SOC2/ISO 27001 report confirming stateless transaction processing |
| 3 | **Multi-wallet testing** | Vendor has tested against ≥2 wallet implementations (EU Reference Wallet + national) |
| 4 | **Certificate and association management** | Vendor can keep association-specific WRPACs isolated and accept the one end-RP WRPRC selected per client Service/intended use, without using its own WRPRC or a Registrar fallback |
| 5 | **UI/log separation** | Conformance evidence shows only bank + bank Service in Wallet approval, while the Wallet log retains vendor identity/contact/Service evidence |
| 6 | **Incident response** | Vendor has &lt;24h breach notification SLA aligned with CIR 2025/847 |
| 7 | **DORA compatibility** | Contract includes DORA Art. 28–30 third-party risk management clauses |

</details>

##### 28.7.6 Electronic Trust Services (Signatures, Seals, Timestamps)

🟡 **Conditional** — PSPs whose business processes involve document signing, sealed attestation verification, or regulatory timestamping (note: seal verification is effectively mandatory for any PSP verifying PIDs/EAAs)

The eIDAS Regulation imposes general obligations on all RPs regarding electronic signatures, seals, and timestamps. For PSPs, these are **conditional** — they apply only when the PSP's business processes involve document signing or sealed attestation verification.

**Classification for PSPs**:

| Trust Service | PSP Relevance | Trigger | Typical Use Case |
|:-------------|:-------------|:--------|:----------------|
| **Qualified Electronic Signatures (QES)** | 🟡 Conditional | PSP requires contract signing | Loan agreements, investment mandates, account opening documents |
| **Advanced Electronic Signatures** | 🟡 Conditional | PSP accepts digitally signed documents | Customer-submitted declarations, mandate confirmations |
| **Electronic Seals** | 🟢 Common | Verifying issuer seals on EAAs | Validating PID issuer seals, SCA attestation seals |
| **Qualified Timestamps** | 🟡 Conditional | PSP needs legal timestamping | Transaction audit trails, regulatory reporting timestamps |
| **Electronic Archiving** | 🟡 Conditional | Long-term record preservation | Regulatory record-keeping (AML, MiFID II) |

**Mandatory requirements when applicable**:

| # | Obligation | Regulatory Basis | Trigger |
|:-:|:-----------|:-----------------|:--------|
| 1 | Accept electronic signatures regardless of electronic form | eIDAS Reg. Art. 25(1) | Any document acceptance |
| 2 | Recognise qualified e-signatures as equivalent to handwritten | eIDAS Reg. Art. 25(2) | Contract signing flow |
| 3 | Recognise qualified e-signatures from all Member States | eIDAS Reg. Art. 25(3) | Cross-border acceptance |
| 4 | Validate qualified e-signatures correctly (certificate, revocation, integrity) | eIDAS Reg. Art. 32(1) | Receiving signed documents |
| 5 | Accept electronic seals regardless of form | eIDAS Reg. Art. 35(1) | EAA issuer seal verification |
| 6 | Recognise qualified seal presumptions (integrity + origin) | eIDAS Reg. Art. 35(2) | EAA verification pipeline |
| 7 | Accept electronic timestamps regardless of form | eIDAS Reg. Art. 41(1) | Transaction ordering |
| 8 | Recognise qualified timestamp presumptions (accuracy + integrity) | eIDAS Reg. Art. 41(2) | Regulatory timestamping |
| 9 | Accept electronic attestations of attributes regardless of form | eIDAS Reg. Art. 45b(1) | All EAA processing |
| 10 | Recognise legal effect of qualified EAA and public-sector EAA | eIDAS Reg. Art. 45b(2) | EAA-based onboarding |
| 11 | Recognise public-sector EAA from all Member States | eIDAS Reg. Art. 45b(3) | Cross-border EAA acceptance |

> **Bank-specific note**: Even PSPs that do not implement a contract signing flow (§28.7.2) will encounter electronic seals and EAAs during normal wallet verification. Every PID and EAA is sealed by its issuer — the PSP's verification pipeline must validate these seals as part of the standard presentation processing. The seal validation requirements are therefore effectively **mandatory** for all PSPs accepting EUDI Wallet presentations, even though the corresponding eIDAS articles are general-purpose.

> **DR-0002 Reference**: Signature and seal validation patterns are covered in §13 (core verification pipeline), §34 (QES integration), and §14 (trust infrastructure — seal certificate chain validation).

**Provider assurance boundary:** `ETSI EN 319 401 V3.2.1` is the general TSP policy/security floor behind these services; the applicable certificate, validation, timestamp, EAA, or remote-signing standard supplies the service-specific controls. A PSP procuring the service should retain evidence for both layers. This is provider due diligence and service acceptance, not a claim that the PSP itself conforms to EN 319 401.

#### 28.8 Financial-Sector High-Assurance Profile, Threats, and Architecture

##### 28.8.1 Financial-Sector High-Assurance Wallet Profile

For banks, PSPs, and similarly fraud-sensitive RPs, the threat and architecture guidance in this subsection should be governed by an explicit **high-assurance wallet policy profile** rather than left as ad hoc design choices. This profile is the **financial-sector instantiation** of the broader assurance-profile model in §26.1.2, while §37.2 translates the same profile into an implementation-facing recommendation set. The goal is not to force proximity for every presentation, but to define which flows require a stronger ceremony by default and which flows should escalate when signals indicate elevated risk.

The row-level references below point to the detailed treatment elsewhere in this document; the table is the policy summary, not the full argument.

| Policy Dimension | Recommended Financial-Sector Profile | Primary DR References |
|:-----------------|:-------------------------------------|:----------------------|
| **Browser presentation channel** | Use the **W3C Digital Credentials API** for supported same-device and secure local cross-device paths where the exact browser/OS/protocol capability is established. Prefer the `OIA_08g` local-channel branch cross-device; treat redirects-based QR as a compatibility path with `OIA_08d` mitigations rather than the normative default. | ARF OIA_08 Privacy and Support Boundary (§7.7.4); Same-Device Remote Presentation (§11); Cross-Device vs. Same-Device Decision Logic (§12.6); Assurance Profiles and Channel Policy (§26.1.2) |
| **Cross-device remote presentation** | Permit cross-device remote presentation for compatibility and accessibility, but attach stricter session TTLs, replay protections, and step-up triggers than for same-device origin-bound flows. | Security Considerations for Cross-Device Flows (§12.4); Cross-Device UX Patterns and Failure Recovery (§12.5); Session Management and Result Delivery (§26.5); Relay Attack: Cross-Device (D.2.4); Layer 3 Contextual and Behavioural Signals (§32.5) |
| **Sensitive lifecycle events** | For **issuance, recovery, credential re-binding, and other fraud-sensitive lifecycle events**, use **supervised or otherwise controlled proximity flows** where operationally feasible. This is especially relevant when a bank issues its own high-risk credentials such as SCA attestations. | Proximity Presentation Flows (§15); Account Recovery Flow After Device Loss (§18.11.2); Progressive Assurance (§18.13); SCA Attestation Bootstrap and Issuance (§28.4.2); Remote Proofing Step-Up Signals (§32.4.5) |
| **RP-issued credentials** | For credentials under RP control, make **device binding a policy requirement at issuance time** for high-assurance use cases. This is an RP/issuer policy choice, not merely a verifier preference. | Trust Boundaries and Device Binding (§13.9); SCA Attestation Bootstrap and Issuance (§28.4.2); Unbound Credential Forwarding (D.2.39); SD-JWT VC Verification Signals (§32.4.1) |
| **Externally issued credentials** | Accept that some external credentials may be non-device-bound. Do not treat those presentations as assurance-equivalent to device-bound ones; instead, shorten session duration, limit downstream actions, or require step-up when the assurance gap matters. | Device Binding Is Format- and Profile-Dependent (§13.9.3); Assurance Profiles and Channel Policy (§26.1.2); Unbound Credential Forwarding (D.2.39); Financial-Sector RP Recommendations (§37.2) |
| **Signal-triggered escalation** | Use Verification Signal Intelligence (§32) not only to score or block a session, but to **change the required ceremony**: same-device to supervised flow, remote to proximity, low-friction presentation to stronger re-verification. | VSI Overview (§32.1); Signal Composition and Risk Scoring (§32.7); Alert Triggers (§33.2); Audit Trail Requirements (§33.3) |

This profile matters because the main hardening levers operate at different layers. **DC API-first** reduces QR / out-of-band invocation exposure in browser flows. **Proximity** reduces relay opportunity for the lifecycle events where it is invoked. **Device binding** reduces forwarding and credential-sharing risk when the RP controls issuance. These controls should therefore be expressed as one coherent policy set rather than as isolated recommendations.

For financial-sector deployments, the same profile has concrete architecture consequences:

| Design Rule | Operational Consequence | Primary DR References |
|:------------|:------------------------|:----------------------|
| **Front the wallet journey with a stateful first-party orchestrator** | Do not expose wallet-verifier mechanics directly to product frontends or internal systems. The orchestrator binds wallet sessions to the RP's product session, journey purpose, fraud policy, and audit evidence before downstream systems consume the result. | Session Lifecycle States (§26.5.1); Concurrent Session Management (§26.5.3); First-Party Orchestrator Rationale (§26.7.1) |
| **Keep connector credentials inside the RP security domain** | Backend API keys, OAuth client credentials, access tokens, mTLS client certificates, and connector-specific secrets must not be distributed to browser or mobile frontend code. | Reverse Proxy Integration Pattern (§26.6.4); Callback Payload Requirements (§26.6.5); First-Party Orchestrator Rationale (§26.7.1) |
| **Hide connector delivery mechanics behind the orchestrator** | If a connector uses push, ping, polling, or callback-style result delivery internally, those mechanics should stay behind the first-party boundary rather than defining the public frontend contract. | Result Delivery: Polling vs. Callbacks (§26.5.2); Callback Payload Requirements (§26.6.5); Callback Security and Error Handling (§26.6.7); Result Delivery Mode Taxonomy (§26.7.3) |
| **Keep wallet-facing URL surfaces first-party and RP-bindable** | The wallet submission target, request-object host, verifier identity and trust-material URLs, follow-up result surfaces, post-wallet return target, and browser-visible authorization host should resolve to RP-controlled surfaces where the topology supports it. | First-Party Orchestrator Rationale (§26.7.1); URL Surface Ownership and RP-Bindability (§26.8) |
| **Reject vendor-owned `direct_post` as the high-assurance default** | A vendor-owned first receiving edge causes the RP to lose source IP, User-Agent, TLS fingerprint, request timing, and wallet-facing trust-surface control. That weakens VSI, fraud detection, and RP-bindability for banking-grade deployments. | Reverse Proxy Integration Pattern (§26.6.4); First-Party Orchestrator Rationale (§26.7.1); URL Surface Ownership and RP-Bindability (§26.8); Layer 3 Contextual and Behavioural Signals (§32.5) |

For financial-sector RPs, the practical rule is: **do not require proximity for routine presentation by default, but do require stronger ceremony for credential issuance, recovery, re-binding, and signal-triggered escalation paths.** For the abstract policy model, see §26.1.2; for the prioritised financial-sector action list, see §37.2.

##### 28.8.2 PSP-Specific Threat Profile

The following threats from the Security Threat Model (§31) and Appendix D threat-card catalogue are particularly relevant to Bank and PSP integration scenarios. This is not an exhaustive list — consult §31 for the model and Appendix D for the complete card catalogue.

| Threat / Attack Surface | PSP-Specific Risk | Profile / Control Response | VSI / Evidence Hooks | Primary DR References |
|:------------------------|:------------------|:---------------------------|:---------------------|:----------------------|
| **Credential / SCA attestation replay** | Replayed SCA response authorises a second payment or reuses a prior authentication result. | Enforce nonce and audience binding, consumed-nonce storage, short TTLs, and `transaction_data_hashes` verification. | `KBJWT_NONCE_REUSE`, `KBJWT_NONCE_MISMATCH`, `KBJWT_EXPIRED` | Credential Replay (D.2.2); Transactional Data HLRs (§17.15); SD-JWT VC Verification Signals (§32.4.1) |
| **Dynamic-linking request tampering** | The amount, payee, IBAN, merchant identity, or transaction hash seen by the Wallet no longer matches the PSP's authorisation decision. | Sign and verify the request object; validate end-to-end `transaction_data` integrity before authorisation. | `PROTO_INVALID_TRANSACTION_DATA`, `JARM_SIG_INVALID`, `SESSION_STATE_MISMATCH` | Transactional Data HLRs (§17.15); JAR Modification in Transit (D.2.8); Protocol Error Signals (§32.3) |
| **Cross-device relay / proxy attack** | Fraudster relays a Wallet interaction to a legitimate device and lands the result in the attacker's RP session. | Prefer DC API where available; use controlled proximity for selected lifecycle events; correlate TLS fingerprint, timing, velocity, and geolocation. | `KBJWT_AUD_MISMATCH`, `CTX_TLS_FINGERPRINT_ANOMALY`, `CTX_SESSION_DURATION_ANOMALY` | Security Considerations for Cross-Device Flows (§12.4); Relay Attack: Cross-Device (D.2.4); Layer 3 Contextual and Behavioural Signals (§32.5) |
| **Unbound or forwarded credential sharing** | Shared or bearer-style credentials are reused across users, devices, accounts, or fraud-ring infrastructure. | Require device binding for RP-issued high-risk credentials; downgrade or step up externally issued credentials that lack holder binding. | `SDJWT_CNF_MISSING`, `KBJWT_MISSING`, `CTX_VELOCITY_EXCEED` | Device Binding Is Format- and Profile-Dependent (§13.9.3); Unbound Credential Forwarding (D.2.39); SD-JWT VC Verification Signals (§32.4.1) |
| **WRPAC private key compromise** | Attacker impersonates the bank or PSP to Wallet Users and obtains valid wallet presentations. | Store WRPAC keys in HSM-backed infrastructure; monitor certificate transparency and revocation; preserve signing and request-object audit evidence. | WRPAC / CT alerts, trust-material audit trail, anomalous `invalid_client` patterns | WRPAC Private Key Compromise (D.2.3); Trust Management and PKI Anchors (§33.2.2); Audit Trail Requirements (§33.3) |
| **Status/revocation outage or stale evidence** | RP treats unavailable evidence as `not_revoked`, accepts a revoked PID/SCA/other attestation, or conflates the SD-JWT VC and mdoc mechanisms. | Validate signed freshness and authority-bound caching; bounded Token Status List decompression; mdoc Attestation Status List trust bridge/indexing; exact identifier-list membership; and the VCR_14 risk-analysis outcome per credential class. | `STATUS_EVIDENCE_FETCH_FAILED`, `SDJWT_STATUS_REVOKED`, `MDOC_STATUS_REVOKED`, `MDOC_IDENTIFIER_LIST_REVOKED`, `STATUS_VALUE_NOT_ALLOWED_FOR_PROFILE`, mechanism-specific freshness/unavailable deltas | Status List Denial of Service (D.2.6); Status List Verification Deep-Dive (§B); format-specific signals (§32.4.1–§32.4.2) |
| **Intermediary over-retention, over-requesting, or injection** | SaaS verifier stores PID data, over-requests attributes, or mutates query / forwarding semantics in violation of Art. 5b(10) and the end-RP contract. | Contractually bind deletion, forwarding, audit, and DORA Art. 28 controls; verify Topic 52 relationship setup and forwarding gates. | Intermediary audit trail, DCQL policy logs, forwarding-result evidence | Intermediary Constraints (§27.3); Intermediary Attribute Forwarding (§27.4); RP-Side Data Breach (D.2.19); DCQL Query Injection via Intermediary (D.2.32) |

**PSP-Specific Verification Signal Intelligence (VSI):**

The VSI pipeline (§32) is particularly valuable for PSPs because payment fraud detection benefits directly from wallet verification signals. The following signal families are most relevant to PSD2 Transaction Risk Analysis (TRA):

| VSI Signal / Evidence Family | Layer | PSP Application | Primary DR References |
|:-----------------------------|:------|:----------------|:----------------------|
| `KBJWT_NONCE_REUSE`, `KBJWT_NONCE_MISMATCH`, `SESSION_STATE_MISMATCH` | L2 | Detect replay, session fixation, and payment-authorisation reuse. | SD-JWT VC Verification Signals (§32.4.1); JWE/JARM Response Encryption Signals (§32.4.3); Alert Triggers (§33.2) |
| `PROTO_INVALID_TRANSACTION_DATA` and `transaction_data_hashes` verification | L1 / L2 | Detect dynamic-linking mismatch between the Wallet ceremony and the PSP authorisation decision. | Transactional Data HLRs (§17.15); Protocol Error Signals (§32.3) |
| `SDJWT_CNF_MISSING`, `KBJWT_MISSING`, `ISSUANCE_WIA_KA_INVALID` in the PSP's issuer pipeline | L2 / issuer | Feed presentation binding strength and separately retained issuance-assurance outcomes into SCA exemption and TRA scoring without inventing a presentation WUA check. | Trust Boundaries and Device Binding (§13.9); SD-JWT VC Verification Signals (§32.4.1); Trust Infrastructure Signals (§32.4.4) |
| `CTX_GEO_MISMATCH` | L3 | Cross-reference source geography with customer baseline, beneficiary geography, and travel / VPN context. | Layer 3 Contextual and Behavioural Signals (§32.5); Signal Composition and Risk Scoring (§32.7) |
| `CTX_TLS_FINGERPRINT_ANOMALY` | L3 | Detect automated attacks, relay tooling, or headless clients that do not resemble known wallet implementations. | Reverse Proxy Integration Pattern (§26.6.4); Layer 3 Contextual and Behavioural Signals (§32.5) |
| `CTX_VELOCITY_EXCEED` | L3 | Rate-limit suspicious account access patterns and detect credential sharing where a lawful correlation basis exists. | Layer 3 Contextual and Behavioural Signals (§32.5); Signal Composition and Risk Scoring (§32.7) |

Deploy an API gateway in the `direct_post` path to capture Layer 3 signals. Without it, the VSI composition engine operates on L1/L2 only — significantly reducing detection capability for relay attacks and bot farms. See §32.5 for the full signal taxonomy and §32.7 for the composition engine architecture.

The following implementation patterns translate the profile and threat model above into Bank/PSP engineering work. They are not all standalone legal obligations, but they are the controls most likely to determine whether the integration is defensible in production.

|:-:|:--------------|:---------|:------------------|
| 1 | Adopt the financial-sector high-assurance wallet profile as the policy baseline for browser channel selection, lifecycle ceremony strength, device-binding posture, and signal-triggered escalation | 🔴 Critical | Financial-Sector High-Assurance Wallet Profile (§28.8.1); Assurance Profiles and Channel Policy (§26.1.2); Financial-Sector RP Recommendations (§37.2) |
| 2 | Front wallet journeys with a stateful first-party orchestrator and RP-bindable URL surfaces | 🔴 Critical | Financial-Sector High-Assurance Wallet Profile (§28.8.1); First-Party Orchestrator Rationale (§26.7.1); URL Surface Ownership and RP-Bindability (§26.8) |

| 4 | Deploy a pluggable verification architecture supporting SD-JWT, mdoc, and ZKP proof types | 🟡 High | RP Authentication and Presentation Verification (§13); Age Verification Attestation Pipelines (§21) |
| 5 | Implement the Verification Signal Intelligence (VSI) pipeline as a first-class SIEM integration | 🟡 High | Verification Signal Intelligence (§32) |
| 6 | Implement an API gateway in the `direct_post` path for Layer 3 signal capture | 🟡 High | Layer 3 Contextual and Behavioural Signals (§32.5); First-Party Control Boundary and Delivery Architecture (§26.7) |
| 7 | Test against at least two different Wallet implementations before production | 🟡 High | RP Pre-Production Testing Checklist (§13.8.5); Wallet Interoperability Testing (§30.3) |
| 8 | Revalidate current German and French programme test-environment access before planning, and enrol in available Member State or Launchpad interoperability exercises | 🟡 High | Wallet Interoperability Testing (§30.3) |
| 9 | Map EUDI integration security controls to DORA Art. 25 resilience testing framework | 🟡 High | DORA Considerations for Financial RPs (§23.4) |
| 10 | Implement identity matching normalisation (CIR 2025/846): Unicode NFC, whitespace collapse, hyphen equivalence | 🟡 High | Identity Matching Normalisation (§25.6) |
| 11 | Design attestation processing to be entity-type-agnostic (natural person PID + LPID + mandate) | 🟡 High | Legal-Person Extension: EBW, LPID, and Mandates (§20); Cross-Entity Binding and Verification Delta (§20.7) |

#### 28.9 Industry Interpretation Disputes and Open Questions

The obligation for banks/PSPs has been a major point of contention since eIDAS 2.0 was published in April 2024. The most prominent industry challenge came from the **Dutch Payment Association** (*Betaalvereniging Nederland*), whose Taskforce eIDAS (TFeIDAS) published a feasibility assessment in May 2025 entitled *"The EU Digital Identity Wallet in payments: Interpretation of legislators' intention and feasibility assessment."* The paper argued that EUDI Wallet acceptance for PSPs was "impossible" under the current RTS on SCA. This section examines each major objection and its regulatory resolution.

| # | Dispute | Status | Resolution Source |
|:-:|:--------|:------:|:-----------------|
| 1 | SUA ≠ SCA: "The wallet is just a 2FA tool" | ✅ Settled | EC FAQ + TS12 |
| 2 | Banks do not control the EUDIW / wallet-local SCA factors | ⚠️ Boundary clarified | EC FAQ + PSD2 RTS + wallet certification |
| 3 | The EUDIW lacks dynamic linking | ✅ Settled | TS12 v1.0 |
| 4 | PSPs are not required to issue EAAs | ⚠️ Partial | EC FAQ + Use Case Manual 11 |
| 5 | POS/contactless out of scope; LSPs voluntary | ⚠️ Partial | Art. 5f(2) scope analysis |
| 6 | TPPs must have equal SCA exemption access | 🔵 Open | Pending PSR/PSD3 |
| 7 | Card payments need separate EMV 3DS flow | 🔄 In progress | EMVCo/Mastercard pilots |
| 8 | Wallet is just for SCA, not KYC/onboarding | ✅ Settled | AMLR Art. 22(6)(b) + SUA=SCA bridge |

<details>
<summary><strong>Dispute 1 ✅ SETTLED: "SUA ≠ SCA: The wallet is just a 2FA tool"</strong></summary>

The Dutch PA argued that eIDAS 2.0's "strong user authentication" (SUA) merely refers to two-factor authentication (2FA), which is "only a small part of the complex concept that is SCA." They concluded that the EUDI Wallet can only serve as a "2FA tool" — not a complete SCA solution — and that PSPs cannot meet RTS requirements using it.

**Resolution — SETTLED by EC FAQ and TS12:**

The EC FAQ explicitly confirms SUA and SCA are synonyms (full quote in §28.2, "Terminology clarification" box).

The EC's SUA/SCA synonymy clarification directly undercuts the Dutch PA's framing. Furthermore, TS12 v1.0 demonstrates that the wallet *can* satisfy full SCA requirements — including **dynamic linking** (via `transaction_data_hashes` in KB-JWT), **possession** (private key in WSCD), **knowledge** (PIN), and **inherence** (biometric). The Dutch PA's "2FA tool" characterisation ignored the SCA Attestation model, which was developed and piloted by EWC and NOBID *after* their paper was drafted.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Dispute 2 ⚠️ BOUNDARY CLARIFIED: "Banks do not control the EUDIW: RTS requires PSP control over PSCs"</strong></summary>

The Dutch PA argued that the RTS on SCA (Art. 22–27) requires PSPs to "ensure the safety, security, confidentiality of personalised security credentials" — but since the wallet falls outside the PSP's domain, they cannot fulfil this obligation.

**Resolution — delegation settled; RTS evidence still required:**

The EC FAQ confirms that outsourcing agreements are not required in the SCA Attestation model where the PSP acts as both issuer and verifier. The wallet acts as a "secure carrier," not a delegated authentication provider (full quote in §28.4.4, "No outsourcing or delegation required" box). That settles the delegation question: the PSP does not need to treat the Wallet Provider as the entity performing authentication merely because the Wallet Unit stores and presents the attestation.

However, the FAQ should not be overread as a blanket PSD2 RTS certification of every Wallet Unit implementation. The RTS does not use an ownership test; it uses an **ensure** test. The PSP must be able to demonstrate that wallet-based SCA satisfies the requirements for secure credential creation, delivery, association, renewal/reactivation, factor protection, factor independence, authentication-code generation, and dynamic linking.

The Dutch PA objection would remain valid for an unmanaged wallet flow where the PSP merely receives a "success" result from an opaque PIN or biometric ceremony and cannot evidence how that factor was enrolled, protected, invoked, or bound to the payment transaction. The objection is answered only by the TS12 control model: PSP-issued SCA Attestation, PSP-side provider-certificate plus WIA/KA issuance gates, KA-admitted holder-bound key material, later KB-JWT verification, `amr` traceability, `transaction_data_hashes`, nonce/freshness checks, and revocation. In that model, the PSP does not physically control the user's wallet PIN or biometric template, but it can evidence the security properties that the RTS requires it to ensure.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Dispute 3 ✅ SETTLED: "The EUDIW lacks dynamic linking functionality"</strong></summary>

The Dutch PA claimed that "EUDIWs lack certain functionality" such as dynamic linking (RTS Art. 5), and therefore cannot fulfil SCA requirements for payment initiation.

**Resolution — SETTLED by TS12 v1.0 (published December 2024):**

TS12 explicitly implements dynamic linking through `transaction_data_hashes` in the KB-JWT. When a user confirms a payment:
1. The wallet displays the amount and payee (RTS Art. 5(1)(a) — payer awareness)
2. The wallet hashes `transaction_data` (amount + payee) using SHA-256
3. The hash is included in the KB-JWT signed by the WSCD private key
4. The PSP verifies the signature and the hash — ensuring the authentication code is dynamically linked to the specific transaction

The Dutch PA's paper was published in May 2025, five months **after** TS12 v1.0 was released, yet still claimed the EUDIW "lacks" this functionality. This was incorrect at the time of publication. The EWC and NOBID Large Scale Pilots successfully demonstrated dynamic-linked SCA attestation flows in production.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Dispute 4 ⚠️ PARTIAL: "PSPs are not required to issue EAAs"</strong></summary>

The Dutch PA argued that "there is no requirement for relying parties to issue EAAs" and that "if a payment use case necessitates that PSPs issue EAAs to function, it will always be considered a beyond-compliance use case."

**Resolution — PARTIALLY CORRECT, but misleading:**

While eIDAS 2.0 does not *generally* mandate that RPs issue EAAs, the SCA Attestation model — as described in the EC FAQ and TS12 — requires PSPs to issue a dedicated SCA attestation into the wallet. Whether this attestation is technically classified as an "EAA" is a definitional question; what matters is that the PSP **must issue a payment-authentication credential** into the wallet for the wallet-based SCA flow to work. The EC FAQ describes issuance as standard practice (full quote in §28.4.2, "EC-confirmed practical fulfilment model").

The Use Case Manual 11 (*Payment Authentication*) confirms: PSPs issue SCA attestations via OID4VCI, and users present them via OID4VP. This is the established model.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Dispute 5 ⚠️ PARTIAL: "POS/contactless are out of scope; LSP solutions are voluntary"</strong></summary>

The Dutch PA argued two related points: (1) only transactions "online from both a technical and user experience perspective" are in scope, excluding POS terminals and contactless; (2) LSP solutions are voluntary and cannot be imposed on the ecosystem.

**Resolution — LARGELY CORRECT on both counts, but neither provides a compliance escape:**

On **scope**: The Art. 5f(2) obligation applies to "online identification." Pure contactless POS payments using EMV chip authentication without an online SCA trigger are not captured. However, POS transactions with online authentication (PIN-online, EMV 3DS) *are* in scope, and the regulation is technology-neutral — if a PSP's proximity flow routes through an online backend for SCA, Art. 5f(2) applies.

On **LSP solutions**: The LSP solutions are not legally binding. However, the EC FAQ explicitly describes the SCA Attestation flow developed by LSPs as the recommended compliance path. PSPs deviating from the EC-endorsed model bear the burden of demonstrating their alternative satisfies both eIDAS 2.0 and PSD2/RTS — creating regulatory risk with no clear upside.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Dispute 6 🔵 OPEN: "TPPs must have equal access to SCA exemptions via the wallet"</strong></summary>

The **European Third Party Providers Association** (ETPPA) has argued that PISPs and AISPs must be able to use, in a non-discriminatory manner, the same SCA exemptions available to the account-servicing PSP (ASPSP) when using the wallet flow. Their core position is that SCA should attach to the *execution* phase (controlled by the ASPSP) rather than the *initiation* phase (triggered by the TPP), and that the wallet must not create new friction for TPP-mediated flows.

**Resolution — OPEN, pending PSR/PSD3:**

The ETPPA's concern is legitimate but legislative. eIDAS 2.0 does not itself define SCA exemptions — those are governed by RTS Art. 10-18 and will be revised under PSR Art. 89. The current-law duties are already clear: PSPs must operate transaction monitoring, traceability, secure communication, and TPP access controls (§28.4.6). The open question is narrower: whether future EBA RTS will require Wallet SCA to expose exactly the same TRA-exemption and exemption-request mechanics as native ASPSP SCA. Until then, PSPs should design their Wallet SCA integration to produce the same TRA-scoring signals as their native SCA (session risk, authenticator binding strength, transaction amount, payee risk, and verification signals) — preserving exemption-eligibility parity where the RTS conditions are satisfied.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Dispute 7 🔄 IN PROGRESS: "Card payments need a separate flow: EMV 3DS integration"</strong></summary>

The card payment industry (EMVCo, Visa, Mastercard) has identified the need for a "**merchant-captured authentication**" flow where the EUDI Wallet integrates with the EMV 3-D Secure protocol. In this model, the merchant (not the issuer) initiates wallet authentication on their website; the cardholder authenticates via the wallet; and the merchant relays the outcome to the card issuer via 3DS for final validation.

**Resolution — IN PROGRESS (EMVCo/Mastercard active development):**

EMVCo has confirmed that EUDI Wallets can fulfil SCA within EMV 3DS transactions. Mastercard is actively building "enriched transaction" flows where payment credentials are combined with verified identity attributes (e.g., age, residency) through 3DS rails. This model differs from the TS12 SCA Attestation flow (which targets SEPA/account-based payments):

| Aspect | TS12 SCA Attestation | EMV 3DS Merchant-Captured |
|:-------|:--------------------|:------------------------|
| **Payment type** | SEPA credit transfer, account access | Card-not-present (CNP) |
| **SCA attestation issuer** | ASPSP (account-servicing bank) | Card issuer |
| **Protocol** | OID4VP → `direct_post` | EMV 3DS → ACS |
| **Rulebook owner** | EPC | EMVCo / card schemes |
| **Current status** | TS12 v1.0 published | Pilot phase (EWC LSP) |

PSPs with card-issuing operations must plan for **both** integration paths. The SCA Attestation Rulebook (EPC) and EMVCo specifications will converge on a common wallet authentication interface, but timing is uncertain.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Dispute 8 ✅ SETTLED: "The wallet is just for SCA: banks don't need it for KYC/onboarding"</strong></summary>

Some banking industry voices have argued that the Art. 5f(2) obligation is narrowly scoped to SCA, and that banks are not required to accept the wallet for Customer Due Diligence (CDD) / Know Your Customer (KYC) onboarding.

**Resolution — MISLEADING. CDD and SCA are not separable in practice, and PID presentation is itself a form of SCA.**

The AMLR Art. 22(6)(b), applicable from **10 July 2027**, explicitly lists eIDAS electronic identification (including EUDI Wallet) as a *permitted* CDD verification method. Recital 66 goes further: the wallet "should be taken into account and accepted by obliged entities." While this is not a standalone "shall accept" mandate, a deeper analysis reveals that the CDD and SCA tracks are architecturally inseparable:

**The SUA = SCA bridge for authenticator binding:**

PID presentation from the EUDI Wallet is not merely identification — it is **strong user authentication** (SUA). The wallet PID flow requires at least two independent factors: **possession** (WSCD private key) and **knowledge** (PIN) or **inherence** (biometric). Since SUA = SCA (Dispute 1, confirmed by EC FAQ), a PID presentation satisfies the SCA requirement under PSD2.

This has a critical consequence for **SCA Attestation issuance**: RTS Art. 24(2)(b) requires SCA for PSC Association (authenticator binding). Issuing an SCA Attestation into the wallet IS a form of PSC association — the PSP is binding the user's identity to a new authentication credential. Therefore, the SCA required for this binding can be satisfied by the PID presentation itself.

This creates **two valid bootstrapping paths** for SCA Attestation issuance:

| Path | Scenario | SCA Method for PSC Association | Regulatory Basis |
|:-----|:---------|:------------------------------|:----------------|
| **A. Existing customer** | Customer already has a banking relationship and existing SCA methods | Existing SCA (banking app, SMS OTP, hardware token, or existing SCA Attestation from another device) | RTS Art. 24(2)(b) — PSC association via existing SCA |
| **B. New customer (CDD + SCA bootstrap)** | Customer onboards via EUDI Wallet PID presentation for CDD | PID presentation itself (SUA = SCA) | RTS Art. 24(2)(b) + eIDAS Art. 3(51) — PID presentation satisfies SCA via SUA equivalence |

**Path B is the key insight**: during wallet-based CDD onboarding, the PID presentation simultaneously satisfies:
1. **CDD identity verification** (AMLR Art. 22(6)(b)) — the bank verifies the customer's identity via PID attributes
2. **SCA for PSC association** (RTS Art. 24(2)(b)) — the PID presentation's multi-factor authentication satisfies the SCA requirement for binding a new credential
3. **SCA Attestation issuance** — the PSP can immediately issue an SCA Attestation into the same wallet, bootstrapping the payment SCA capability in a single flow

This means a **single wallet interaction** can accomplish: identity verification → AML screening → SCA attestation issuance — collapsing what was previously a multi-day, multi-channel process into one session. Banks that argue "the wallet is just for SCA" miss this convergence: refusing wallet-based CDD forces the bank to maintain a separate, inferior onboarding flow, only to later ask the same customer to re-authenticate for SCA attestation issuance.

Once a bank has built the PID verification infrastructure for the mandatory SCA track (eIDAS Art. 5f(2), 24 December 2027), refusing wallet-based CDD is both technically unjustifiable and strategically irrational — the same verification pipeline serves both purposes. See **§28.2** for the full dual-track analysis.

</details>
<br/>

> **Compliance position**: Despite the open questions below, the core obligation is legally certain: eIDAS Reg. Art. 5f(2) **mandates** wallet acceptance for SCA by **24 December 2027**. The AMLR additionally *enables and recommends* wallet-based CDD from **10 July 2027** (Art. 22(6)(b), Recital 66) — creating a de facto dual-track where CDD readiness precedes SCA go-live. The EC's FAQ, TS12, Use Case Manual 11, EMVCo's 3DS alignment work, and the LSP results collectively demonstrate that the technical path exists and is viable. PSPs that delay implementation pending "further clarity" on peripheral issues assume significant regulatory risk. The Dutch PA's May 2025 position paper, while raising legitimate operational questions, is now materially outdated on SUA/SCA synonymy and dynamic linking, and its control objection has narrowed to an evidence question: PSPs must prove the TS12 wallet-based flow satisfies PSD2 RTS properties, not prove that they physically operate every wallet-local factor.
>
> For non-banking RPs facing the same acceptance obligation under different sector regulation, see **§28** (General RP Integration Blueprint).

| # | Issue | Status | Expected Resolution |
|:-:|:------|:------:|:-------------------|
| 1 | **SCA Attestation Rulebook** — no SCA Rulebook appears in the pinned EC catalogue snapshot of 20 July 2026 | 🟡 Not catalogued in the audited snapshot | Monitor the EC catalogue and the applicable EPC/EMVCo profile sources; do not infer a publication date or production schema from pilot material |
| 2 | **PSD3/PSR technical-standard alignment** — the provisional package points toward further EBA work, but the final mandate, scope, timing, and Wallet-specific content remain unestablished until adoption | 🟡 Pre-legislative | Monitor Council position, final OJ texts, enacted mandates, and EBA consultations |
| 3 | **Liability in case of wallet compromise** — if a certified wallet is compromised, how is liability allocated between PSP, Wallet Provider, and user? | 🟡 Open | Reassess against final PSD3/PSR texts, national law, contracts, and case facts |
| 4 | **mDOC dynamic linking** — TS12 v1.0 covers SD-JWT-VC only; mDOC format lacks `transaction_data_hashes` equivalent | 🟡 Specification gap | Awaiting TS12 extension |
| 5 | **Batch payment authentication** — corporate batch payments requiring SCA for multiple transactions are not addressed in TS12 | 🟡 Open | Industry proposal (Merkle tree approach) under discussion |
| 6 | **TPP (PISP/AISP) verification** — how a PSP verifies the identity of a Third Party Provider in the wallet flow is not fully specified | 🟡 Open | GitHub Discussion #439 |
| 7 | **SCA exemption parity** — whether future technical standards require Wallet SCA to expose identical TRA/exemption mechanics as native ASPSP SCA | 🟡 Open | Current PSD2/RTS controls in §28.4.6; monitor final PSD3/PSR mandate and later EBA work |
| 8 | **Privacy vs. fraud detection** — the wallet's unlinkability and selective disclosure features conflict with banks' behavioural analytics and cross-session fraud scoring models | 🟡 Architectural | Industry guidance needed on consent-based data sharing for fraud prevention |
| 9 | **Cold start / adoption risk** — mandatory acceptance by December 2027 does not guarantee user adoption; banks face investment risk if wallet uptake is low | 🟡 Market | Member State rollout quality; first-mover competitive dynamics |
| 10 | **Cross-border wallet fragmentation** — 27 Member States may produce non-uniform wallet implementations; PSPs operating cross-border face a "pyramid of complexity" | 🟡 Interoperability | Certification mutual recognition (CIR 2024/2981); reference implementation convergence |
| 11 | **RTS evidence package for wallet-local factors** — exact artefacts PSPs should retain to prove wallet PIN/biometric, WSCD/WSCA, `amr`, and dynamic-linking controls satisfy RTS Art. 6-9 and 22-26 | 🟡 Governance | Baseline evidence in Outsourcing, Delegation, and PSD2 RTS Control Boundary (§28.4.4) and PSD2/RTS Wrapper: Lifecycle, Monitoring, Exemptions, Evidence, and TPP Parity (§28.4.6); further detail from Wallet certification schemes, TS12/SCA Attestation Rulebooks, and EBA RTS under PSR Art. 89 |
| 12 | **SCA success and fraud liability** — how the final PSD3/PSR package will address the EBA concern that SCA success alone should not prove authorisation, fraud, or gross negligence in social-engineering disputes | 🟡 Pre-legislative | Provisional package direction; revalidate against final texts and resulting standards |

### 29. Vendor Evaluation

:::caution
Treat this chapter as evidence-weighted procurement input, not as a certification register or a timeless ranking. Public documentation quality, deployment model, and feature-surface visibility materially affect the scores, so any shortlist still needs direct technical and contractual validation with the vendor.
:::

The tables in §29.1–§29.8 preserve the **17 March 2026 research snapshot** that informed the original market scan. They are not a current product catalogue, certification register, or procurement recommendation. Product names, feature claims, deployment modes, roadmap entries, and documentation-quality labels were not comprehensively revalidated on 26 July 2026; every vendor's current readiness is therefore `Unassessed` until confirmed through dated, version-pinned primary documentation, contract terms, conformance evidence, and RP-run tests. Pilot participation alone never proves a product capability.

> **Vendor selection criteria for RPs**: When evaluating vendors, prioritise:
> 1. **HAIP 1.0 compliance** — mandatory for EUDI ecosystem
> 2. **Both format support** — SD-JWT VC AND mdoc
> 3. **DCQL support** — required by HAIP 1.0, replacing legacy presentation_definition
> 4. **Certificate management** — WRPAC lifecycle, trust anchor refresh
> 5. **Intermediary support** — if the RP plans to use an intermediary model
> 6. **SCA integration** — critical for PSPs and banks
> 7. **Conformance certification** — the OpenID Foundation launched self-certification for HAIP 1.0, OpenID4VP 1.0, and OID4VCI 1.0 on February 26, 2026; prefer vendors with verified conformance status
> 8. **FCAF evidence handling** — require the vendor to state the exact FCAF release/maturity, Wallet Solution SUT, WS_RP test cases, counterpart build, result, and evidence package; reject “FCAF-certified RP” claims because the initial SUT is the Wallet Solution
> 9. **Verification policy engine** — configurable policies (static, parameterized, dynamic) for auditable verification decisions (§26.1)
> 10. **Status-profile dispatch** — verify the SDK selects short-lived, SD-JWT VC Token Status List, mdoc Attestation Status List, mdoc identifier list, or Rulebook-defined handling from the credential's controlling profile rather than using one default parser (Appendix B)
> 11. **Webhook/callback support** — server-to-server push notification and webhook delegation for AML/business-rule integration (§26.2)
> 12. **Verification result granularity** — per-credential, per-policy result objects for audit trail compliance (§33.3.1)
> 13. **EUDI Reference Wallet tested** — documented interoperability with the EU Reference Wallet or active LSP participation; see the unified capability matrix in §29.6

#### 29.3 Ecosystem Vendor Landscape

Beyond the RP-facing verifier platforms listed in §29 and §29.1, the EUDI Wallet ecosystem includes infrastructure providers, QTSPs, and identity proofing services that RPs may interact with indirectly. This section maps the broader vendor landscape for ecosystem awareness.
