Verification signals originate from three distinct layers of the RP's infrastructure, each with different producers, latencies, and security semantics:

```mermaid
---
config:
  flowchart:
    nodeSpacing: 40
    rankSpacing: 40
---
flowchart TB
    subgraph L1["Layer 1 — Protocol Errors"]
        direction LR
        P1["Wallet Response Handler"]
        P2["OID4VP error codes (§13.6)"]
        P3["mdoc status codes (ISO 18013-5)"]
        P1 --> P2
        P1 --> P3
    end

    subgraph L2["Layer 2 — Verification Pipeline"]
        direction LR
        V1["Verification Engine"]
        V2["SD-JWT VC Signals"]
        V3["mdoc Signals"]
        V4["JWE/JARM Signals"]
        V5["Trust Infra Signals"]
        V6["Remote Step-up Signals"]
        V1 --> V2
        V1 --> V3
        V1 --> V4
        V1 --> V5
        V1 --> V6
    end

    subgraph L3["Layer 3 — Contextual & Behavioural"]
        direction LR
        G1["API Gateway (§26.6.4)"]
        G2["HTTP Context Signals"]
        G3["Temporal Signals"]
        G1 --> G2
        G1 --> G3
    end

    L1 --> AGG["Signal Aggregator"]
    L2 --> AGG
    L3 --> AGG
```

| Layer | Producer | When | Signal Source | Example Signals |
|:------|:---------|:-----|:-------------|:----------------|
| **Layer 1** — Protocol Errors | Wallet Response Handler | On receiving a Wallet error through the selected response channel | OID4VP §6.3/§10.5 error codes; mdoc ISO 18013-5 status codes | `access_denied`, `invalid_request`, `wallet_unavailable` |
| **Layer 2** — Verification Pipeline | RP's Verification Engine (§13.3/§13.4/§14) | During VP Token validation | SD-JWT VC signature, disclosure, temporal, revocation, KB-JWT checks; mdoc MSO, IACA, DeviceAuth checks; JWE decryption; trust infrastructure; optional supplementary remote proofing checks | `SDJWT_SIG_INVALID`, `KBJWT_NONCE_REUSE`, `MDOC_DEVICE_SIG_INVALID`, `STEPUP_CAPTURE_INJECTION_DETECTED` |
| **Layer 3** — Contextual & Behavioural | API Gateway (§26.6.4) | On receiving a direct-post HTTP request or browser-forwarded API result | HTTP headers, TLS fingerprint, IP geolocation, device fingerprint, velocity counters, temporal patterns | `CTX_GEO_MISMATCH`, `CTX_VELOCITY_EXCEED`, `CTX_TLS_FINGERPRINT_ANOMALY` |

**Layer 1 signals are wallet-emitted** — the RP receives them passively through DC API, native OS API, direct-post, or proximity response handling. **Layer 2 signals are RP-generated** — the RP's own verification engine produces them during VP Token validation. **Layer 3 signals are infrastructure-generated** — the RP's API gateway captures them from the HTTP context it actually sees. Direct-post branches expose Wallet-to-RP HTTP context; browser/OS API-mediated branches expose the RP frontend-to-backend context instead, so their Layer 3 signal set is different.

The three layers are **independent signal sources**: a single presentation can produce signals from all three layers simultaneously. For example, a wallet might return a valid VP Token (no Layer 1 errors), but the RP's verification engine detects a revoked credential (Layer 2: `SDJWT_STATUS_REVOKED`), and the gateway observes a geo-mismatch (Layer 3: `CTX_GEO_MISMATCH`). The signal composition engine (§32.7) aggregates signals across all three layers to produce a composite risk score.

#### 32.3 Signal Inventory: Layer 1: Protocol Errors

Layer 1 signals originate from the **wallet's error response** to the RP's presentation request. These are returned through the selected response channel when the wallet cannot or will not fulfil the request: a DC API promise/error path for browser-mediated flows, an OS credential result for native-app flows, or `response_uri` (`direct_post` / `direct_post.jwt`) for direct-post branches. The protocol-level error codes are defined in OID4VP §6.3 and documented in §13.6 of this specification.

> **Key distinction from Layer 2**: Layer 1 signals mean the wallet **declined to submit a VP Token at all** — the RP never receives a credential to verify. Layer 2 signals mean the wallet **submitted a VP Token** but the RP's verification pipeline found a problem with it. The security semantics are fundamentally different: Layer 1 failures are usually user-driven or configuration-driven; Layer 2 failures indicate possible tampering, replay, or compromise.

| Signal ID | OID4VP Error Code | Source | VSI Severity | Fraud/Security Interpretation | §31 Threat Ref |
|:----------|:-----------------|:-------|:------------:|:------------------------------|:---------------|
| `PROTO_ACCESS_DENIED` | `access_denied` | OID4VP §6.3 | S4 | User declined consent. Benign in isolation. **Spike from same RP instance = possible consent screen manipulation or social engineering campaign** (D.2.16). Monitor decline rate per RP Instance. | User Device Malware: Consent Manipulation (D.2.16) |
| `PROTO_TEMPORARILY_UNAVAILABLE` | `temporarily_unavailable` | OID4VP | S4 | Wallet temporarily busy. Benign. **Sustained spike from same IP range = possible DoS probe against wallet infrastructure.** | — |
| `PROTO_INVALID_CLIENT` | `invalid_client` | OID4VP | S1 | RP's client authentication failed at wallet side. **Critical misconfiguration or WRPAC compromise** — the wallet does not recognise the RP's credentials. Immediate investigation required. | WRPAC Private Key Compromise (D.2.3) |
| `PROTO_INVALID_REQUEST` | `invalid_request` | OID4VP | S2 | Malformed JAR or request parameters. Isolated = RP bug. **Pattern from unknown sources = fuzzing/probing attempt** against the RP's OID4VP endpoint. | — |
| `PROTO_VP_FORMATS_NOT_SUPPORTED` | `vp_formats_not_supported` | OID4VP | S3 | Wallet doesn't support the requested VP format. Benign if from heterogeneous wallet ecosystem. **Repeated pattern = probing for format-specific vulnerabilities.** | — |
| `PROTO_INVALID_SCOPE` | `invalid_scope` | OID4VP | S3 | Wallet cannot satisfy the requested credential scope. Benign if isolated. **Spike = credential harvesting probe** testing which credential types the RP accepts. | Over-Identification (D.2.15) |
| `PROTO_SERVER_ERROR` | `server_error` | OID4VP | S2 | Internal wallet error. **Spike associated with the same officially mapped Wallet Solution = possible exploit attempt or rollout defect.** Correlate through authoritative solution/session mapping or provider notifications, not a WUA field. | — |
| `PROTO_INVALID_TRANSACTION_DATA` | `invalid_transaction_data` | OID4VP §6.3 | S1 | Wallet rejected the `transaction_data` binding. **Critical for SCA flows (§17)**: possible dynamic linking manipulation — the transaction amount, IBAN, or merchant identity in the signed request may have been tampered with. | JAR Modification in Transit (D.2.8) |
| `PROTO_INVALID_REQUEST_URI_METHOD` | `invalid_request_uri_method` | OID4VP | S2 | The `request_uri_method` value is neither the case-sensitive value `get` nor `post`. Usually an RP implementation or parameter-serialization defect; repeated malformed values can indicate protocol fuzzing. | — |
| `PROTO_WALLET_UNAVAILABLE` | `wallet_unavailable` | OID4VP §8.5 | S3 | Wallet app not reachable — platform cannot invoke it, or an intermediary component received the request instead. **Spike per platform/channel = wallet adoption or deployment issue, not a security concern.** Monitor per platform type for operational visibility. | — |

#### 32.4 Signal Inventory: Layer 2: Verification Pipeline

Layer 2 signals are produced by the RP's own verification engine (§13.3, §13.4, §14) during VP Token validation. The wallet has **submitted** a VP Token — these signals represent the RP's findings about the credential's cryptographic integrity, temporal validity, revocation status, holder binding, and trust chain.

> **Implementation note**: Every check in the §13.3 (SD-JWT VC) and §11.4 (mdoc) verification checklists implicitly produces a signal. A passing check produces a `signal_result: "pass"` entry in the verification record (§33.3.1); a failing check produces a named VSI signal with the severity and interpretation defined below. RPs SHOULD emit both pass and fail signals to build complete behavioural baselines for UEBA.

##### 32.4.1 SD-JWT VC Verification Signals

| Signal ID | Failure Mode | STRIDE | Severity | Fraud/Security Interpretation | §31 Threat Ref |
|:----------|:-------------|:-------|:--------:|:------------------------------|:---------------|
| `SDJWT_SIG_INVALID` | Issuer JWT signature fails verification against the issuer's public key from the LoTE trust anchor | Tampering | **S0** | **Forged credential or tampered payload.** The signature over the JWT body does not match the issuer's key. This is the highest-severity signal — it means either the credential was manufactured outside a legitimate PID/QEAA Provider, or the payload was modified after issuance. Quarantine source IP; log the raw JWT for forensic analysis. | Credential Forgery (D.2.36) |
| `SDJWT_SIG_ALG_UNEXPECTED` | JWS `alg` header value not in RP's algorithm allowlist (e.g., `RS256` instead of `ES256`) | Tampering | **S0** | **Algorithm confusion attack** (CVE-2015-9235 class). The credential uses an algorithm the RP does not expect. HAIP mandates `ES256`; any other algorithm is suspicious. Block and alert security team. | Algorithm Confusion/Type Confusion (D.2.23) |
| `SDJWT_SIG_ALG_NONE` | `alg: "none"` in JWS header | Tampering | **S0** | **Critical exploit attempt.** The `alg: none` attack bypasses signature verification entirely. Immediate block; this is always malicious. Log full request context for incident response. | Algorithm Confusion/Type Confusion (D.2.23) |
| `SDJWT_DISCLOSURE_HASH_MISMATCH` | Disclosure hash does not match the corresponding `_sd` digest in the JWT body | Tampering | **S1** | **Tampered selective disclosure.** An attacker has modified a disclosed attribute value after issuance — the hash of the disclosure (salt + claim name + value) no longer matches the digest committed in the issuer-signed JWT body. This indicates targeted attribute manipulation. | Selective Disclosure Tampering (D.2.37) |
| `SDJWT_DISCLOSURE_DUPLICATE_SALT` | Duplicate salt values detected across disclosures in the same SD-JWT | Tampering | **S1** | **Fuzzing or manipulation attempt.** Salt values MUST be unique per disclosure (SD-JWT VC §5.2.5). Duplicates indicate either a faulty issuer implementation or deliberate structure manipulation. Reject and log raw disclosure array. | Selective Disclosure Tampering (D.2.37) |
| `SDJWT_EXP_EXPIRED` | `exp` claim is in the past (beyond RP's clock skew tolerance) | — | **S3** | **Stale credential.** Benign if isolated — the user's PID may have expired naturally. **Spike from multiple sources = possible credential database leak** being tested against RPs. Monitor for patterns. | — |
| `SDJWT_NBF_NOT_YET_VALID` | `nbf` claim is in the future | — | **S3** | **Premature credential or clock manipulation.** The credential is not yet valid. Could indicate a time zone issue, clock skew, or a credential issued for future activation. Flag for review. | — |
| `SDJWT_IAT_FUTURE` | `iat` claim is in the future (beyond clock skew tolerance) | Spoofing | **S2** | **Clock manipulation.** The issuance timestamp is in the future, suggesting an emulated wallet environment with a manipulated system clock, or a rogue issuer backdating credentials for future use. | Clock Manipulation/Environment Emulation (D.2.40) |
| `SDJWT_ISSUER_UNTRUSTED` | Issuer `iss` claim does not match any entry in the RP's LoTE trust anchor cache | Spoofing | **S1** | **Unknown issuer.** The credential claims to be from an issuer not in the RP's trusted set. Could be a legitimate new Member State PID Provider not yet cached, or a spoofed issuer. Cross-check against a fresh LoTE fetch before blocking. | OID-FED Trust Chain Spoofing (D.2.27) |
| `SDJWT_ISSUER_CHAIN_INVALID` | Issuer's X.509 certificate chain does not validate to any LoTE root anchor | Spoofing | **S0** | **Certificate chain attack.** The issuer presents a certificate chain that doesn't terminate at a trusted root. Critical — possible MITM, rogue CA, or self-signed chain. Block immediately. | OID-FED Trust Chain Spoofing (D.2.27) |
| `SDJWT_VCT_UNKNOWN` | `vct` (Verifiable Credential Type) value not recognised by the RP's credential type registry | — | **S3** | **New or unknown credential type.** Could be a legitimate new attestation type (e.g., a newly published QEAA schema) or probing to discover which types the RP accepts. Log and review against TS11 registry. | — |
| `SDJWT_STATUS_REVOKED` | CIR-profiled Token Status List check returns bit/value `1` (`REVOKED`) for the credential's `status.idx` | — | **S1** | **Permanently revoked credential being presented.** Reject the dependent branch and preserve the definitive issuer lifecycle result; a risk score cannot turn it back into allow. Alert on anomalous presentation patterns without assuming the issuer's revocation reason. | — |
| `CREDENTIAL_STATUS_SUSPENDED_PROFILE_ALLOWED` | A controlling attestation profile other than PID/QEAA/PuB-EAA expressly defines a temporary suspended state and the selected status mechanism returns it | — | **S1** | **Profile-permitted temporary invalidity.** Reject or route to the stronger ceremony/fallback expressly defined by that profile; do not treat suspension as an ordinary elevated-risk allow. Re-check only under the profile's reactivation semantics. | — |
| `STATUS_VALUE_NOT_ALLOWED_FOR_PROFILE` | A status mechanism returns suspension, a reserved value, or another state outside the selected credential class/Rulebook vocabulary | Tampering / Repudiation | **S1** | **Profile-semantic failure.** PID, QEAA, and PuB-EAA admit only not-revoked and permanently-revoked. Reject rather than interpreting the unknown value as a temporary state or trying a different status parser. | — |
| `SDJWT_CNF_MISSING` | SD-JWT issuer-signed body contains no `cnf` claim — the credential was issued without key binding information | Spoofing | **S2** | **Credential issued without device binding.** Unlike `KBJWT_MISSING` (which means the presentation omits the KB-JWT), this signal means the **credential itself** was issued without a `cnf.jwk` claim — no device key was bound at issuance. This can be legitimate for low-assurance EAAs that do not require device binding, but is unexpected for PIDs (which mandate `cnf`). Flag and evaluate against the RP's binding policy for this credential type. | Unbound Credential Forwarding (D.2.39) |
| `SDJWT_JSON_PARSE_ERROR` | SD-JWT structure is syntactically malformed — not valid Base64URL encoding, wrong number of `~`-separated segments, or JSON body fails parsing | Tampering | **S1** | **Malformed payload.** The SD-JWT string is structurally invalid. SD-JWT equivalent of `MDOC_CBOR_PARSE_ERROR`. Possible fuzzing attempt against the RP's SD-JWT parser, corrupted transmission, or a crafted payload exploiting parser vulnerabilities. Reject; log raw string for analysis. | VP Token Parser Exploitation (D.2.38) |
| `KBJWT_MISSING` | No Key Binding JWT (`~` delimiter) appended to the SD-JWT presentation | Spoofing | **S1** | **No holder binding.** The presenter has not proven possession of the device key bound to the credential (`cnf.jwk`). If the RP's policy requires KB-JWT (recommended for all high-assurance flows), reject. Without KB-JWT, the credential could be forwarded from another device. | Credential Replay (D.2.2) |
| `KBJWT_SIG_INVALID` | KB-JWT signature does not verify against the `cnf.jwk` public key embedded in the issuer-signed JWT | Spoofing | **S0** | **Stolen credential replay.** The presenter is **not** the credential holder — the device key signature doesn't match. The credential was likely extracted from the holder's wallet and presented from a different device. Block; alert SOC; correlate with source IP for ring detection. | Credential Replay (D.2.2) |
| `KBJWT_NONCE_MISMATCH` | KB-JWT `nonce` claim does not match the nonce issued by the RP in the authorization request | Replay | **S0** | **Replay attack.** The VP Token is being presented with a nonce from a different session. The credential may be valid, but it was captured in a prior session and is being replayed. Block immediately. | Credential Replay (D.2.2) |
| `KBJWT_NONCE_REUSE` | The nonce in the KB-JWT was already consumed by the RP in a previous session | Replay | **S0** | **Definitive replay attack.** Block and alert the SOC; for a DORA-scoped service route the event through Art. 18 / 2024/1772 classification and report only if it is major. | Credential Replay (D.2.2) |
| `KBJWT_AUD_MISMATCH` | KB-JWT `aud` claim does not match the RP's `client_id` (WRPAC `client_id` or OID-FED Entity Identifier) | Spoofing | **S0** | **Relay attack.** The credential was bound to a **different RP** — the holder authenticated to RP-A, but the VP Token is being presented to RP-B. This is a textbook relay/proxy attack (D.2.4). Block; log both the expected and actual `aud` values. | Relay Attack: Cross-Device (D.2.4) |
| `KBJWT_CLOCK_SKEW` | KB-JWT `iat` timestamp differs from the RP's server time by more than the configured tolerance (recommended: 60 seconds) | — | **S3** | **Network latency or replay delay.** Minor clock skew is normal in cross-device flows. **Skew > 300 seconds combined with other signals** (e.g., geo-mismatch) elevates to suspicious. Log for pattern analysis; build per-wallet-provider skew baselines. | — |
| `KBJWT_EXPIRED` | KB-JWT `exp` claim is in the past | Replay | **S2** | **Stale proof of possession.** The KB-JWT was generated too long ago. Could indicate a delayed replay attempt — the attacker captured the VP Token and is presenting it after the KB-JWT's validity window. | Credential Replay (D.2.2) |

##### 32.4.2 mdoc (ISO 18013-5) Verification Signals

| Signal ID | Failure Mode | STRIDE | Severity | Fraud/Security Interpretation | §31 Threat Ref |
|:----------|:-------------|:-------|:--------:|:------------------------------|:---------------|
| `MDOC_MSO_SIG_INVALID` | Mobile Security Object (MSO) signature verification fails against the issuer's IACA-chained public key | Tampering | **S0** | **Forged or tampered mdoc.** The MSO signature is the mdoc equivalent of the SD-JWT issuer signature. Failure indicates the document was manufactured outside a legitimate Document Signer or the MSO was modified after issuance. Critical — block immediately. | mdoc DeviceSignature Skip: RP Accepts Replayed Credentials (D.2.29) |
| `MDOC_IACA_CHAIN_INVALID` | Issuing Authority Certificate Authority (IACA) certificate chain does not validate to a trusted IACA root in the RP's trust store | Spoofing | **S0** | **Certificate chain bypass attempt.** The issuer presents a certificate chain that doesn't terminate at a trusted IACA root. Possible self-signed chain attack or rogue Document Signer. Block; log the full certificate chain for forensic analysis. | mdoc IACA Chain Validation Bypass (D.2.30) |
| `MDOC_IACA_REVOKED` | IACA certificate appears on the Certificate Revocation List (CRL) | Spoofing | **S0** | **Revoked issuer authority.** The IACA certificate itself has been revoked — all credentials issued under this chain are suspect. Reject **all** credentials from this chain until the RP's IACA trust store is refreshed. | mdoc IACA Chain Validation Bypass (D.2.30) |
| `MDOC_DIGEST_MISMATCH` | Data element hash does not match the corresponding digest in the MSO's `ValueDigests` | Tampering | **S1** | **Selective disclosure tampering.** An individual claim value within a disclosed namespace has been modified after the MSO was signed. The attacker computed a new data element but could not update the MSO digest (which requires the issuer's key). | Selective Disclosure Tampering (D.2.37) |
| `MDOC_DEVICE_SIG_INVALID` | `DeviceSignature` (COSE_Sign1) verification fails against the device public key in the MSO's `DeviceKeyInfo` | Spoofing | **S0** | **Replayed or cloned credential.** The device key signature does not match — the presenter is not the device that holds the original mdoc. The credential may have been cloned from a compromised WSCD or extracted and replayed from a different device. | mdoc DeviceSignature Skip: RP Accepts Replayed Credentials (D.2.29) |
| `MDOC_DEVICE_SIG_MISSING` | No `DeviceSignature` or `DeviceMAC` present in the `DeviceAuth` structure | Spoofing | **S1** | **No device authentication.** The mdoc was presented without any proof that the presenting device holds the device private key. Critical if the RP requires device binding (proximity supervised flows per §15). Without DeviceAuth, the mdoc could be forwarded from any device. | mdoc DeviceSignature Skip: RP Accepts Replayed Credentials (D.2.29) |
| `MDOC_DEVICE_MAC_INVALID` | `DeviceMAC` (COSE_Mac0) verification fails | Spoofing | **S1** | **Session transcript mismatch.** The MAC was computed over a `SessionTranscript` that doesn't match the current session. Possible relay attack — the mdoc was presented in a different session context. | Relay Attack: Cross-Device (D.2.4) |
| `MDOC_SESSION_TRANSCRIPT_MISMATCH` | The `encodedSessionTranscript` reconstructed by the RP does not match the one used to compute `DeviceSignature` or `DeviceMAC` | Replay/Spoofing | **S0** | **Relay attack.** The session context (nonce, RP identifier, session establishment) used to sign the device response does not match the current session. This is a textbook relay attack (D.2.4) — the mdoc was presented to a different reader and the response is being relayed to this RP. | Relay Attack: Cross-Device (D.2.4) |
| `MDOC_READER_AUTH_REJECTED` | Wallet returned ISO 18013-5 status code 20 (Reader Authentication Error) | — | **S2** | **RP's reader certificate rejected by wallet.** The wallet could not validate the RP's reader authentication certificate (the mdoc equivalent of WRPAC validation). Check IACA root inclusion within the wallet's trust store and certificate expiry. | mdoc ReaderAuth Skip: Wallet Accepts Unauthenticated Reader (D.2.28) |
| `MDOC_REQUEST_REJECTED` | Wallet returned ISO 18013-5 status code 21 | — | **S3** | **Wallet policy block.** The wallet refused the request based on its internal policy. Log and monitor for patterns. | — |
| `MDOC_VALIDITY_EXPIRED` | MSO `validityInfo.validUntil` is in the past | — | **S3** | **Stale credential.** The mdoc's validity period has expired. Equivalent to SD-JWT `exp` expiry. Benign if isolated; spike = possible expired credential database being tested. | — |
| `MDOC_STATUS_REVOKED` | The authenticated mdoc Attestation Status List marks the credential's bounded index invalid/revoked | — | **S1** | **Permanently revoked mdoc.** Reject the dependent branch. Preserve list identity, signer/chain authorization, freshness, and a redacted index hash; never pass this definitive result through a score that can allow it. | — |
| `MDOC_IDENTIFIER_LIST_REVOKED` | The credential's complete opaque revocation identifier is present in the authenticated, fresh mdoc identifier list | — | **S1** | **Permanently revoked mdoc by exact membership.** Reject the dependent branch. Absence is usable only after list authorization and freshness succeed; a failed fetch is not “not present.” | — |
| `MDOC_NAMESPACE_NOT_FOUND` | Requested namespace (e.g., `org.iso.18013.5.1`) not present in the `DeviceResponse` | — | **S4** | **Missing credential type.** The wallet does not hold an mdoc with the requested namespace. Benign in most cases. | — |
| `MDOC_DATA_REQUEST_DENIED` | Wallet returned ISO 18013-5 error code 3 for specific data elements | — | **S4** | **Partial consent.** User declined to share specific attributes. Expected behaviour — not a security signal. Log for analytics only. | — |
| `MDOC_CBOR_PARSE_ERROR` | CBOR structure is syntactically malformed — cannot be decoded per RFC 8949 | Tampering | **S1** | **Malformed payload.** The `DeviceResponse` CBOR is structurally invalid. Possible fuzzing attempt against the RP's CBOR parser, or a corrupted transmission. Reject; log raw bytes for analysis. | VP Token Parser Exploitation (D.2.38) |

##### 32.4.3 JWE/JARM Response Encryption Signals

These signals arise from the response encryption and authentication layer — the encrypted response envelope, carried through DC API / OS mediation or through `direct_post.jwt`, that wraps the VP Token during transmission from wallet to RP.

| Signal ID | Failure Mode | STRIDE | Severity | Fraud/Security Interpretation | §31 Threat Ref |
|:----------|:-------------|:-------|:--------:|:------------------------------|:---------------|
| `ENVELOPE_KID_UNKNOWN` | JWE header `kid` does not match any ephemeral response-encryption key retained for the active session | Tampering | **S3** | **Unknown encryption key.** The JWE was encrypted with a `kid` that the RP does not recognise for any active session. Could be a stale session, misrouted response, or probing attempt. Lower severity than full decryption failure — the key mismatch is the root cause. | Ephemeral Key Interception: Response Encryption (D.2.7) |
| `ENVELOPE_JWE_DECRYPT_FAILED` | JWE decryption fails using the RP's ephemeral private key (key found, but decryption produces invalid output) | Tampering | **S1** | **Decryption failure with known key.** The `kid` matched an active session key but decryption failed — the JWE was encrypted with a different public key than the one corresponding to this `kid`. Session integrity is compromised — possible MITM during key exchange or JWE tampering. | Ephemeral Key Interception: Response Encryption (D.2.7) |
| `ENVELOPE_JWE_ALG_UNSUPPORTED` | JWE `alg` or `enc` header value not in the RP's algorithm allowlist | Tampering | **S1** | **Downgrade attack on response encryption.** HAIP requires `ECDH-ES` on P-256 support; the Verifier lists both `A128GCM` and `A256GCM`, while the Wallet supports one or both and should select `A256GCM` when it supports both. Reject values outside the negotiated allowlist. | Ephemeral Key Interception: Response Encryption (D.2.7) |
| `JARM_SIG_INVALID` | JARM JWT signature verification fails | Tampering | **S1** | **Modified response in transit.** The signed authorization response has been tampered with after the wallet signed it. Possible MITM between wallet and RP during `direct_post` delivery. | JAR Modification in Transit (D.2.8) |
| `SESSION_STATE_MISMATCH` | `state` parameter in the JARM response does not match the `state` issued by the RP in the authorization request | Replay | **S0** | **Session fixation attack.** The response is being injected into a session that it was not intended for. The attacker may have captured a valid response and is replaying it in a different user's session. Critical — block immediately. | Session Fixation (D.2.11) |

##### 32.4.4 Trust Infrastructure Signals

These signals arise from failures in trust infrastructure used by verifier and issuer pipelines: the LoTE cache, the authenticated `LOTL` / national trusted-list state used for qualified-status conclusions where relevant, issuer-side WIA/KA validation, and certificate-profile parsing for WRPAC/WRPRC, provider-registration/access certificates, bank/PSP certificates, and remote-signing certificate models.

| Signal ID | Failure Mode | STRIDE | Severity | Fraud/Security Interpretation | §31 Threat Ref |
|:----------|:-------------|:-------|:--------:|:------------------------------|:---------------|
| `LOTE_FETCH_FAILED` | Cannot retrieve the LoTE from the Member State or EU-level publication endpoint | DoS | **S2** | **Trust infrastructure outage.** The RP cannot refresh its notified-entity trust-anchor cache. If the cached LoTE is still within TTL, continue with degraded confidence for LoTE-backed issuer checks. If cache is expired, the RP cannot verify issuer signatures for those entities — apply fail-open/fail-closed policy. Possible DNS hijacking or BGP manipulation (D.2.22). | LoTE Cache Poisoning (D.2.22) |
| `LOTE_SIG_INVALID` | LoTE signature verification fails against the expected signing key | Tampering | **S0** | **LoTE cache poisoning attack.** The RP received a LoTE response that is not authentically signed by the expected authority. **Critical** — if the RP accepts this poisoned LoTE, all subsequent issuer signature verifications operate against attacker-controlled trust anchors. Block the LoTE update; retain the previously verified cache; alert SOC immediately. | LoTE Cache Poisoning (D.2.22) |
| `LOTE_EXPIRED` | LoTE cache is beyond its signed/policy freshness window and a fresh fetch is unavailable | — | **S2** | **Trust evidence unavailable.** Use only a still-valid last-known-good snapshot permitted by policy and containing no known-invalid material; otherwise stop the affected trust path. | — |
| `TRUST_ANCHOR_FLEET_DIVERGENCE` | Relevant RP Instances report different active LoTE/TL snapshot versions after the convergence deadline, or a required removal is incomplete | Tampering / DoS | **S1** | **Fleet trust split.** Different Instances can reach different issuer/status decisions. Isolate non-converged Instances and prove that every invalidated anchor was removed before restoring traffic. | LoTE Cache Poisoning (D.2.22) |
| `STATUS_SIGNER_UNAUTHORIZED` | A status/revocation object has a valid signature, but the signer is absent from the separately authorized anchor class for the selected provider/profile/source generation | Spoofing / Tampering | **S1** | **Status-authority substitution.** Reject even if an embedded `x5c`/`kid` validates or the same key signs credentials; investigate unauthorized rollover or cache/context confusion. | Status List Denial of Service (D.2.6) |
| `STATUS_EVIDENCE_FETCH_FAILED` | The format/profile-selected Token Status List, mdoc Attestation Status List, or mdoc identifier list cannot be retrieved safely and no still-authorized, signed-fresh cache entry is usable | DoS | **S2** | **Revocation evidence unavailable.** Preserve the mechanism-specific `evidence_unavailable` result and apply the documented VCR_14 risk-analysis decision. Acceptance, where that analysis permits it, is explicitly evidence-incomplete and never `NOT_REVOKED`. | Status List Denial of Service (D.2.6) |
| `CERT_SUBJECT_SEMANTICS_UNKNOWN` | Certificate subject uses `serialNumber` or `organizationIdentifier` without a recognised ETSI EN 319 412-1 semantics identifier or profile context | Spoofing / Tampering | **S2** | **Ambiguous certificate subject.** The RP cannot tell which natural-person or legal-person identifier family the value belongs to. Do not compare the raw value to WRPRC `sub`, LPID `legal_person_id`, PSP authorization numbers, or local register identifiers until the profile semantics are resolved. | RP authentication material, trust anchors, and certificate/federation spoofing |
| `CERT_SUBJECT_ID_PREFIX_UNSUPPORTED` | Parsed subject identifier prefix is deprecated, unsupported for the certificate surface, or inconsistent with the declared semantics identifier | Spoofing / Tampering | **S2** | **Identifier-family mismatch.** Examples include treating `PSD` as a generic organization identifier outside the bank/PSP profile, accepting deprecated natural-person prefixes where policy forbids them, or mixing `LEI`, `NTR`, `VAT`, and local schemes as if they were interchangeable. Block or step up to register validation. | RP authentication material, trust anchors, and certificate/federation spoofing |
| `CERT_LOCAL_SCHEME_AUTHORITY_MISSING` | A local `XX:` subject identifier is present but the certificate lacks a usable `nameRegistrationAuthorities` URI or equivalent local-scheme authority binding | Spoofing | **S2** | **Unscoped local identifier.** Local schemes are not globally meaningful without their registration authority. Comparing the identifier as if it were EU-wide creates false matches across Member States or sector registers. | RP authentication material, trust anchors, and certificate/federation spoofing |
| `CERT_VALASSURED_ST_POLICY_UNMET` | A short-term certificate path relies on ETSI EN 319 412-1 validity-assured short-term semantics, but the extension, policy, CPS, or issuer conditions are absent or not accepted by RP policy | Tampering / Repudiation | **S1** | **Unsafe revocation shortcut.** The RP is about to skip or weaken leaf revocation checking without evidence that the certificate qualifies for validity-assured short-term treatment. Continue normal revocation validation unless the issuing policy and certificate extension meet the configured rule. | Status List Denial of Service (D.2.6) |
| `ISSUANCE_WIA_KA_INVALID` | Issuer pipeline rejects WIA or KA because the role/transport is wrong, a mandatory artifact is absent, signature/trust/status/freshness fails, the requested maintenance/security level is unmet, or the proof key does not match the KA | Spoofing / Tampering | **S1** | **Issuance-only failure.** Deny token or credential issuance, preserve the typed sub-result, and correlate with Wallet Provider/issuer incidents. This signal must never be emitted by an ordinary presentation verifier. | Invalid or Wrong-Role WIA/KA Accepted During Issuance (D.2.41) |
| `WALLET_SOLUTION_SUSPENDED` | An official status source identifies the Wallet Solution as suspended | — | **S1** | **Wallet Solution under security investigation.** Apply the authoritative solution policy and any separately available Wallet Unit revocation decision; do not infer universal Wallet Unit revocation from suspension alone. | Wallet Solution Suspension or Withdrawal (D.2.21) |

> **Qualified-status boundary**: The signals above are primarily about LoTE-backed issuer trust and wallet-environment integrity. Where the RP later needs to state a trusted-list-backed qualified conclusion, it should maintain a **separate** authenticated `LOTL` / national trusted-list state and treat outages in that path as loss of qualified-status evidence — not as something silently substituted by LoTE success. Under `ETSI TS 119 615`, the qualified-status leg may therefore degrade to unavailable or `Indeterminate` even when ordinary LoTE-backed issuer trust remains usable.

##### 32.4.5 Remote Proofing Step-Up Signals

These signals apply only when the RP deliberately invokes a **supplementary remote proofing ceremony** in addition to the wallet presentation — for example selfie / portrait comparison, video-ident, or extra-document capture during onboarding, recovery, or rebinding. They should be kept distinct from the main wallet verification pipeline so the RP can tell whether risk comes from the credential itself or from the RP's own extra ceremony.

Routine **face-match mismatch** outcomes should also be logged separately in implementations, but the table below focuses on the attack-oriented step-up failures that map directly to the new threat cards in D.2.42–D.2.44.

| Signal ID | Failure Mode | STRIDE | Severity | Fraud/Security Interpretation | §31 Threat Ref |
|:----------|:-------------|:-------|:--------:|:------------------------------|:---------------|
| `STEPUP_PRESENTATION_ATTACK_DETECTED` | PAD / biometric-genuineness or document-liveness controls detect printed photos, masks, projected faces, screen replays, or other presentation attack instruments during remote step-up | Spoofing | **S1** | **Remote live-person spoof detected.** The RP's supplementary selfie / portrait / document ceremony observed a non-genuine presentation artefact. The session must not be treated as stronger user binding. | Remote Live-Person Step-Up: Biometric Presentation Attack (D.2.42) |
| `STEPUP_CAPTURE_INJECTION_DETECTED` | Injection-attack / capture-integrity controls detect virtual cameras, stream substitution, deepfake insertion, media-pipeline tampering, or challenge-response inconsistency | Spoofing / Tampering | **S1** | **Capture path compromised.** The proofing engine is no longer evaluating trusted live-sensor input. Treat as an active bypass attempt against the RP's supplementary proofing stack. | Remote Live-Person Step-Up: Capture-Pipeline Injection Attack (D.2.43) |
| `STEPUP_DOCUMENT_AUTH_FAILED` | Remote document fallback cannot establish document authenticity or current possession — e.g., OCR succeeded but chip read was absent, signed chip-data validation was not performed, optional anti-cloning checks were not run where required, or replay detection failed | Tampering | **S2** | **Weak documentary fallback.** The RP extracted fields from a document but did not obtain enough evidence to trust the document as genuine. Do not silently upgrade assurance on the basis of OCR-only success or a raw NFC read without enforced validation. | Fallback Document Proofing: OCR and Document Authenticity Failure (D.2.44) |

**Adjacent governance and lifecycle signals.** These events sit next to the verifier pipeline but do not describe credential-cryptography failure. Emit them from the Wallet, RP privacy gateway, or lifecycle controller that owns the decision:

| Signal ID | Failure Mode | Severity | Required interpretation and action |
|:----------|:-------------|:--------:|:-----------------------------------|
| `PORTRAIT_RETENTION_POLICY_INVALID` | A component attempts to retain a disclosed portrait based only on generic disclosure approval or internal policy, or route it to a third country/international organisation without the required Union-data-protection-law permission | **S1** | Block persistence/transfer, purge session copies, preserve the denied policy decision, and route repeated or successful violations into privacy-incident assessment. This is a data-governance failure, not proof that the credential was invalid. |
| `PHYSICAL_CREDENTIAL_DELETE_SCOPE_INVALID` | Wallet deletion would omit another physical copy in the selected Credential Dataset or delete a different same-type Dataset | **S1** | Abort the destructive operation before it becomes partial or over-broad. Recompute the set using type + Provider + Credential Dataset, authenticate the User where required, and retry atomically. |
| `DELETION_CONTACT_UNAVAILABLE` | The selected presentation-log entry has no usable URL, email address, or phone number for the RP deletion request | **S2** | Explain that common TS7 initiation is unavailable, preserve non-sensitive transaction context for user-led support, and do not claim that a request was initiated. Empty `DATA_DLT_02a` does not authorize an invented live Registrar repair lookup. |
| `QES_PROFILE_VERSION_MISMATCH` | A signing integration advertises or assumes a QES protocol, method, or signature-format profile that does not match the CIR-selected clauses or the explicitly negotiated broader provider profile | **S1** | Stop before document or credential authorization, record the selected ETSI/CSC/signature profile and observed metadata, and route to an explicit compatibility decision. Do not silently fall back to the superseded CSC API v2.0 legal thesis. |

These signals are intentionally absent from §C: §C catalogues verifier-engine failures, while these events govern portrait processing, Wallet-local destructive lifecycle operations, rights-request initiation, and QES integration compatibility.

##### 32.4.6 Relationship to §C Signal Registry

The signal tables in §32.4.1–§32.4.5 are representative deep-dives for the most operationally critical signals. They are **not** an exhaustive registry. **§C (Verifier Failure Catalogue)** is the comprehensive signal registry — 175 failure scenarios across 11 populated pipeline stages plus the cross-reference stage, each with a stable `VERIFY-{STAGE}-{NNNN}` identifier, fine-grained signal name, severity, STRIDE classification, test fixture, and cross-references to §31 threats and §14 implementation.

Every signal in §32.4 maps to one or more §C entries, but §C covers additional signals not individually detailed in §32 (e.g., rare edge cases, format-specific parser failures, release/ops gates). Conversely, Layer 1 (§32.3) and Layer 3 (§32.5) signals are operational observations rather than verifier-engine failures — they appear in §32 but not in §C.

The architectural principle: **§32 provides the framework** (classification layers, severity taxonomy, composition model, SIEM schema); **§C provides the implementation reference** (what to emit, when, with what severity, against which threat).

##### 32.4.7 Signal Aggregation Guidance for Consumers

RPs emit signals at the **finest granularity** available — the individual signal names listed in §32.4 and §C. Downstream consumers (SIEM, UEBA, fraud engines) aggregate these fine-grained signals into families that match their operational workflows. The aggregation is a **consumption-time decision**, not an emission-time one.

| Aggregation Family | Member Signals | Typical Consumer |
|:-------------------|:---------------|:-----------------|
| Decryption Failure | `ENVELOPE_KID_UNKNOWN`, `ENVELOPE_JWE_DECRYPT_FAILED` | SIEM correlation |
| Replay Detection | `SESSION_NONCE_REUSE`, `KBJWT_NONCE_REUSE`, `SESSION_DUPLICATE_SUBMISSION` | SOC playbook |
| Algorithm Downgrade | `ENVELOPE_JWE_ALG_UNSUPPORTED`, `SDJWT_SIG_ALG_NONE`, `SDJWT_SIG_ALG_UNEXPECTED`, `SDJWT_SIG_ALG_SYMMETRIC_CONFUSION` | Fraud engine rule |
| Trust Chain Failure | `LOTE_SIG_INVALID`, `TRUST_ANCHOR_FLEET_DIVERGENCE`, `MDOC_IACA_CHAIN_INVALID`, `SDJWT_ISSUER_CHAIN_INVALID`, `TRUST_SIGNATURE_INVALID` | SOC playbook |
| Credential Forgery | `SDJWT_SIG_INVALID`, `MDOC_MSO_SIG_INVALID`, `ISSUANCE_ATTESTATION_SIG_INVALID` | Fraud engine |
| Status Check Failure | `STATUS_SIGNER_UNAUTHORIZED`, `STATUS_EVIDENCE_FETCH_FAILED`, `STATUS_EVIDENCE_FETCH_BLOCKED`, `SDJWT_STATUS_REVOKED`, `MDOC_STATUS_REVOKED`, `MDOC_IDENTIFIER_LIST_REVOKED`, `CREDENTIAL_STATUS_SUSPENDED_PROFILE_ALLOWED`, `STATUS_VALUE_NOT_ALLOWED_FOR_PROFILE`, `SDJWT_STATUS_DECOMPRESSION_BOMB` | Dashboard / SOC playbook for signer substitution, lifecycle rejection, profile drift, and dependency outage |
| Release Quality Gate | `RELEASE_KNOWN_BAD_ACCEPTED`, `RELEASE_KNOWN_GOOD_REGRESSION`, `RELEASE_FUZZING_REGRESSION` | CI/CD dashboard |

> **Note**: These aggregation families are non-normative guidance. Each RP's operational context determines the optimal grouping. The signal names are stable; aggregation is a deployment-time decision.

#### 32.5 Signal Inventory: Layer 3: Contextual and Behavioural

Layer 3 signals are **not credential-verification errors**. Most are contextual observations captured by the RP's API gateway (§26.6.4) from the HTTP request context of `direct_post`; channel-selection signals can also come from the RP-controlled browser/session snapshot before the credential response exists.

> **Evidence prerequisite**: IP, TLS, and Wallet-to-endpoint timing signals require an RP-controlled gateway in the `direct_post` path (§26.6.4, §26.7). An API-mediated DC API response may instead expose only browser-origin/session and negotiated-channel evidence; do not claim the Wallet's source IP or TLS fingerprint when the response returned locally through browser mediation.

| Signal ID | Source | VSI Severity | Fraud/Security Interpretation | Composition Notes |
|:----------|:-------|:------------:|:------------------------------|:-----------------|
| `CROSS_DEVICE_LOCAL_BINDING_UNAVAILABLE` | RP/browser session snapshot records that the preferred CTAP 2.3 local channel was unavailable or not negotiated | **S2** | **Channel downgrade.** The transaction cannot claim the preferred local proximity-plus-transfer path. This is not proof of attack: the deployment may legitimately support only CTAP 2.2 Hybrid or a policy-approved redirects fallback. | Route to topology policy; record the actual Hybrid/redirects branch and apply its controls |
| `CTX_GEO_MISMATCH` | IP geolocation of the `direct_post` request vs. the PID's issuing Member State | **S3** | **Possible relay or VPN.** The presentation originates from an IP geolocated to a different country than the PID's issuing Member State. **Not malicious alone** — legitimate for tourists, business travellers, and VPN users. Becomes significant when combined with other signals (e.g., `KBJWT_CLOCK_SKEW`, `CTX_VELOCITY_EXCEED`). | Correlated — never block on this signal alone |
| `CTX_TLS_FINGERPRINT_ANOMALY` | JA3/JA4 TLS fingerprint of the `direct_post` connection does not match known EUDI Wallet user agent fingerprints | **S2** | **Emulated or scripted client.** The TLS handshake characteristics do not match any known wallet implementation. Possible automated replay tool, headless browser, or custom HTTP client. Correlate with User-Agent and other independently available evidence. | Correlated within presentation traffic; do not mix it with issuer-only WIA/KA signals unless a separately correlated issuer event exists |
| `CTX_VELOCITY_EXCEED` | Same lawful identity key or pseudonym presented more than N times within T minutes (RP-configured thresholds) | **S2** | **Credential sharing, bot activity, or account farming.** Legitimate users rarely present the same credential at high velocity to the same RP. Correlate with IP diversity — same IP + high velocity = bot; diverse IPs + high velocity = credential sharing ring. | Configurable; requires lawful correlation basis |
| `CTX_DEVICE_UNKNOWN` | Device fingerprint (browser fingerprint, app attestation) not previously seen for this lawful identity key or account pseudonym | **S3** | **New device.** The user is presenting from a device not previously associated with this identity at this RP. Expected after device changes or wallet migration. Becomes significant when combined with velocity or geo signals. | Correlated — baseline-dependent |
| `CTX_TIME_OF_DAY_ANOMALY` | Presentation occurs at an unusual hour relative to the user's historical presentation pattern at this RP | **S4** | **Possible account takeover.** Weak signal — many legitimate reasons for unusual-hour access. Only actionable when combined with other elevated signals. Requires ≥ 10 prior presentations to establish a meaningful baseline. | Noise unless combined; requires baseline |
| `CTX_SESSION_DURATION_ANOMALY` | Time between authorization request issuance and `direct_post` submission is outside expected bounds (&lt; 2s or > 120s) | **S3** | **Automated submission or delayed replay.** Sub-2-second submission suggests an automated tool bypassing the user consent screen. Over-120-second submission suggests a delayed replay or manual credential forwarding. Correlate with KB-JWT `iat` for consistency. | Correlated — compare with `KBJWT_CLOCK_SKEW` |

> **Anti-linkability boundary (§13.10)**: Layer 3 signals that build per-user behavioural baselines (velocity, device fingerprint, time-of-day) inherently create linkability across sessions for the same lawful identity key or account correlation key. This is acceptable for RPs that maintain an identified user account model (e.g., banks performing CDD per §24). However, RPs that accept **pseudonyms** (§18) MUST NOT build linkable behavioural profiles across pseudonymous sessions — the VSI composition engine must operate in a **stateless mode** for pseudonymous presentations, evaluating only within-session signals (Layer 1, Layer 2, and single-session Layer 3 signals like geo-mismatch and TLS fingerprint) without cross-session correlation.

#### 32.6 Signal Severity Classification

Every VSI signal is assigned a severity level from S0 (Critical) through S4 (Noise). The severity determines the RP's automated response and regulatory escalation obligation.

| Severity | Label | Automated Response | Manual Follow-up | Example Signals |
|:---------|:------|:-------------------|:-----------------|:----------------|
| **S0** | **Critical — Active Attack** | **Block** presentation immediately. Quarantine source IP. Emit SIEM alert with `priority: critical`. Trigger SOAR playbook. | SOC investigation required within 1 hour. Preserve full request payload for forensic analysis. Evaluate DORA Art. 17 incident classification. | `KBJWT_NONCE_REUSE`, `SDJWT_SIG_ALG_NONE`, `LOTE_SIG_INVALID`, `KBJWT_SIG_INVALID`, `KBJWT_AUD_MISMATCH`, `MDOC_SESSION_TRANSCRIPT_MISMATCH`, `SESSION_STATE_MISMATCH` |
| **S1** | **High — Reject / Probable Attack or Definitive Lifecycle Failure** | **Block** the affected credential branch, presentation, issuance transaction, signing transaction, destructive lifecycle action, or prohibited data operation. Increment source IP risk only where that inference is justified. Emit SIEM event with `priority: high`. | Security review within 4 hours for attack-indicative patterns; lifecycle, privacy-policy, interoperability, and profile-semantic failures follow their owning operations without automatically becoming reportable incidents. | `PROTO_INVALID_CLIENT`, `SDJWT_DISCLOSURE_HASH_MISMATCH`, `KBJWT_MISSING`, `MDOC_DEVICE_SIG_MISSING`, `ISSUANCE_WIA_KA_INVALID` (issuer pipeline), `SDJWT_STATUS_REVOKED`, `STATUS_VALUE_NOT_ALLOWED_FOR_PROFILE`, `STEPUP_PRESENTATION_ATTACK_DETECTED`, `PORTRAIT_RETENTION_POLICY_INVALID`, `PHYSICAL_CREDENTIAL_DELETE_SCOPE_INVALID`, `QES_PROFILE_VERSION_MISMATCH` |
| **S2** | **Medium — Suspicious or Evidence/Operational Route Unavailable** | Apply the named signal's policy. Suspicious contextual signals may allow with elevated risk; a missing required trust/status fact produces `evidence_incomplete`, and an unavailable rights route stays explicitly unavailable. Emit SIEM event with `priority: medium`. | Review clustered suspicious signals within 24 hours; restore or investigate unavailable evidence or operational routes according to the owning runbook. | `SDJWT_IAT_FUTURE`, `CTX_TLS_FINGERPRINT_ANOMALY`, `CTX_VELOCITY_EXCEED`, `STATUS_EVIDENCE_FETCH_FAILED`, `LOTE_FETCH_FAILED`, `MDOC_READER_AUTH_REJECTED`, `STEPUP_DOCUMENT_AUTH_FAILED`, `DELETION_CONTACT_UNAVAILABLE` |
| **S3** | **Low — Informational** | **Allow** normally. Log signal in verification record. Update UEBA behavioural baseline. | No manual review required. Aggregate for weekly trend analysis. | `SDJWT_EXP_EXPIRED`, `CTX_DEVICE_UNKNOWN`, `CTX_GEO_MISMATCH`, `MDOC_VALIDITY_EXPIRED`, `KBJWT_CLOCK_SKEW`, `PROTO_WALLET_UNAVAILABLE` |
| **S4** | **Noise — Operational** | **Allow** normally. Log for diagnostics only. Do not feed into risk score. | No review. Use only for operational dashboards and debuggability. | `CTX_TIME_OF_DAY_ANOMALY`, `MDOC_NAMESPACE_NOT_FOUND`, `MDOC_DATA_REQUEST_DENIED`, `PROTO_ACCESS_DENIED`, `PROTO_TEMPORARILY_UNAVAILABLE` |

##### 32.6.1 Severity × STRIDE Matrix

The intersection of severity level and STRIDE classification reveals the most dangerous signal combinations:

| STRIDE Category | S0 (Critical) | S1 (High) | S2 (Medium) | S3 (Low) |
|:----------------|:--------------|:----------|:------------|:---------|
| **Spoofing** | `KBJWT_SIG_INVALID`, `KBJWT_AUD_MISMATCH`, `SDJWT_ISSUER_CHAIN_INVALID`, `MDOC_IACA_CHAIN_INVALID`, `MDOC_DEVICE_SIG_INVALID` | `SDJWT_ISSUER_UNTRUSTED`, `KBJWT_MISSING`, `MDOC_DEVICE_SIG_MISSING`, `MDOC_DEVICE_MAC_INVALID`, `ISSUANCE_WIA_KA_INVALID`, `STEPUP_PRESENTATION_ATTACK_DETECTED` | `SDJWT_IAT_FUTURE`, `SDJWT_CNF_MISSING`, `CTX_TLS_FINGERPRINT_ANOMALY` | — |
| **Tampering** | `SDJWT_SIG_INVALID`, `SDJWT_SIG_ALG_NONE`, `SDJWT_SIG_ALG_UNEXPECTED`, `LOTE_SIG_INVALID`, `MDOC_MSO_SIG_INVALID` | `SDJWT_DISCLOSURE_HASH_MISMATCH`, `SDJWT_DISCLOSURE_DUPLICATE_SALT`, `SDJWT_JSON_PARSE_ERROR`, `ENVELOPE_KID_UNKNOWN`, `ENVELOPE_JWE_DECRYPT_FAILED`, `ENVELOPE_JWE_ALG_UNSUPPORTED`, `JARM_SIG_INVALID`, `MDOC_DIGEST_MISMATCH`, `MDOC_CBOR_PARSE_ERROR`, `STEPUP_CAPTURE_INJECTION_DETECTED` | `STEPUP_DOCUMENT_AUTH_FAILED` | — |
| **Replay** | `KBJWT_NONCE_REUSE`, `KBJWT_NONCE_MISMATCH`, `SESSION_STATE_MISMATCH`, `MDOC_SESSION_TRANSCRIPT_MISMATCH` | — | `KBJWT_EXPIRED` | `KBJWT_CLOCK_SKEW` |
| **DoS** | — | — | `STATUS_EVIDENCE_FETCH_FAILED`, `LOTE_FETCH_FAILED`, `LOTE_EXPIRED` | — |

> **Key observation**: Tampering and Spoofing signals concentrate at S0/S1, because they indicate active credential manipulation or identity spoofing. Replay signals are exclusively S0 — any nonce/session reuse is unambiguous evidence of attack. DoS signals cap at S2 because they degrade service without compromising credentials.

##### 32.6.2 Regulatory Escalation Paths

| VSI Severity | Regulatory Trigger | Reporting Timeline | Applicable Regulation |
|:-------------|:-------------------|:-------------------|:---------------------|
| **S0** | DORA major-incident candidate | Classify under Art. 18 / 2024/1772; if major, initial report ≤4h after major classification and ≤24h after awareness, then applicable intermediate/final stages under 2025/301 | DORA-scoped financial entities/services |
| **S0** | NIS2 significant-incident candidate | Apply entity/service scope and Art. 23 significance criteria; only if significant start the 24h early warning → 72h notification → normally 1-month final sequence | NIS2-scoped essential/important entities |
| **S0** | GDPR personal-data-breach candidate | Determine whether Art. 4(12) is met and assess risk; notify under Art. 33 within 72h after awareness unless unlikely to result in risk | Controllers subject to GDPR |
| **S0–S1** | PSD2 RTS Art. 18 — TRA fraud rate monitoring | Elevate TRA risk score; re-evaluate SCA exemption thresholds | PSD2/PSR (PSPs) |
| **S1** | eIDAS Art. 5b — RP integrity obligations | Internal incident log; pattern analysis for supervisory body reporting | eIDAS 2.0 (all RPs) |
| **S2+** | AML/6AMLD — Suspicious activity reporting | SAR to Financial Intelligence Unit if pattern indicates money laundering | AML (obliged entities) |

#### 32.7 Signal Composition and Risk Scoring

Individual VSI signals are generally inputs to a composed decision, but a severity label does not erase the verifier's deterministic semantics. **S0 signals and definitive reject signals**—including permanent credential revocation, a status value prohibited by the controlling profile, and failed mandatory cryptographic verification—are independently actionable. Other S1–S4 observations may be composed into a risk score where their definitions permit it.

For RPs using explicit assurance profiles (§26.1.2), the composition engine should not treat `STEP_UP` as a generic placeholder. It should map elevated-risk outcomes to a **stronger predefined ceremony**: for example, prefer same-device DC API over cross-device fallback, require supervised or controlled proximity for a recovery or rebinding event, or restrict a non-device-bound presentation to lower-risk operations until stronger evidence is obtained.

##### 32.7.1 Scoring Model

```
composite_risk = Σ (base_weight[signal_i] × severity_multiplier[signal_i] × recency_factor[signal_i])
                 + Σ (context_modifier[j])

Decision:
  composite_risk &lt; 20   → ALLOW
  composite_risk 20–49  → FLAG (allow + mark for review)
  composite_risk 50–79  → STEP-UP (require additional authentication)
  composite_risk ≥ 80   → BLOCK (reject + alert SOC)
  any S0 or definitive reject signal present → BLOCK affected branch/presentation
                                              (override, regardless of composite score)
```

| Parameter | Description | Example Values |
|:----------|:------------|:---------------|
| `base_weight` | RP-calibrated illustrative weight for composable signals; deterministic reject signals bypass weighting | `CTX_GEO_MISMATCH` = 10, `CTX_VELOCITY_EXCEED` = 20 |
| `severity_multiplier` | Numeric multiplier mapped from severity level | S0 = 10.0, S1 = 5.0, S2 = 2.0, S3 = 1.0, S4 = 0.1 |
| `recency_factor` | Decay function for historical signals from previous sessions | 1.0 (current session), 0.5 (last 24h), 0.2 (last 7d), 0.0 (> 7d) |
| `context_modifier` | Additive score from environmental factors not captured by named signals | High-risk jurisdiction = +15, known VPN exit IP = +10, first-ever presentation = +5 |

> **Implementation note**: The specific thresholds (20/50/80) and weights above are **illustrative, not prescriptive**. RPs MUST calibrate these values against their own transaction volumes, risk appetite, and regulatory tier. Financial RPs subject to PSD2 TRA should align thresholds with their reference fraud rate monitoring data (§17, RTS Art. 19).

##### 32.7.2 Fail-Fast vs Aggregate Validation

RPs should not collapse VP Token validation into a single undifferentiated `verification_failed` result. A verifier can be implemented in two broad modes:

- **Fail-fast**: stop at the first failed check and return only that error.
- **Aggregate**: continue running all remaining **safe and meaningful** checks for the same presentation, then return the full set of failures and passes.

For VSI, aggregate validation is operationally superior. A fail-fast verifier may report only `signature_invalid` or only `aud_mismatch`, even though the same VP Token also fails nonce freshness, revocation status, holder binding, or trust-chain validation. That throws away useful security detail. The RP still blocks the presentation, but it loses the richer failure map that explains **how many controls were violated simultaneously** and whether the failure looks like ordinary implementation drift, a malformed submission, or an actively hostile payload.

The goal is therefore not "keep validating forever regardless of prerequisites." It is: **collect every failure that can still be evaluated correctly after the first error**. If a prerequisite failure makes later checks meaningless, the verifier should emit `not_evaluated` or `skipped_due_to_prerequisite_failure` rather than inventing results. For example:

- If JWE decryption fails, downstream credential checks cannot run and should be marked not evaluated.
- If the token is structurally parseable, the RP may still be able to report multiple independent failures such as `KBJWT_AUD_MISMATCH`, `KBJWT_NONCE_REUSE`, and `SDJWT_STATUS_REVOKED` from the same presentation.
- If trust material is temporarily unavailable, the verifier should distinguish `issuer_trust_indeterminate` from a definitive cryptographic failure.

This is why vendors and in-house verification stacks should preserve:

- **Per-check outcomes**, including `pass`, `fail`, `indeterminate`, and `not_evaluated`.
- **Aggregate failure arrays** listing all failed checks from the same validation pass, not just the first one encountered.
- **Per-policy result objects** showing which checks passed even though the overall presentation failed.
- **Decision rationale** explaining which failures were decisive for the final `FLAG`, `STEP_UP`, or `BLOCK` outcome.

Without that granularity, the RP can still reject the single presentation, but it loses the most useful part of VSI: the ability to inspect the full failure surface of one suspicious VP Token instead of only the first error a library happened to report.

##### 32.7.3 Composite Scenario Walkthroughs

The following worked examples demonstrate how multi-signal composition drives decisions that differ from any individual signal's standalone action:

<details>
<summary><strong>Scenario 1: Tourist presenting foreign PID — ALLOW</strong></summary>

**Context**: A German PID holder presents their credential at a Spanish online retailer while on holiday.

| Signal | Severity | Base Weight | Multiplier | Score |
|:-------|:--------:|:------------|:-----------|:------|
| `CTX_GEO_MISMATCH` (DE PID, ES IP) | S3 | 10 | 1.0 | 10 |

**Composite score: 10** → **ALLOW**

A geo-mismatch alone is expected for cross-border scenarios. No additional signals → no escalation.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Scenario 2: Replay attack with expired KB-JWT — BLOCK</strong></summary>

**Context**: An attacker captured a valid VP Token from a café WiFi session and replays it 45 minutes later from a different IP.

| Signal | Severity | Base Weight | Multiplier | Score |
|:-------|:--------:|:------------|:-----------|:------|
| `KBJWT_NONCE_REUSE` | **S0** | 100 | 10.0 | 1000 |
| `KBJWT_EXPIRED` | S2 | 30 | 2.0 | 60 |
| `CTX_GEO_MISMATCH` | S3 | 10 | 1.0 | 10 |

**Composite score: 1070** → **BLOCK** (S0 override triggers regardless of score)

The `KBJWT_NONCE_REUSE` S0 signal alone triggers an immediate block. The additional S2/S3 signals confirm the attack pattern and enrich the forensic record. If the entity/service is DORA-scoped, the event becomes a classification candidate under Article 18 and Delegated Regulation 2024/1772; it is not automatically major or reportable.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Scenario 3: Credential database leak — FLAG escalating to STEP-UP</strong></summary>

**Context**: A batch of expired PIDs from a compromised issuer database are being tested against multiple RPs. The RP sees an unusual spike in expired credential presentations from diverse IPs.

| Signal | Severity | Base Weight | Multiplier | Score |
|:-------|:--------:|:------------|:-----------|:------|
| `SDJWT_EXP_EXPIRED` | S3 | 15 | 1.0 | 15 |
| `CTX_VELOCITY_EXCEED` (same lawful identity key, 5× in 10 min) | S2 | 25 | 2.0 | 50 |
| `CTX_DEVICE_UNKNOWN` | S3 | 10 | 1.0 | 10 |

**Composite score: 75** → **STEP-UP** (require additional authentication)

No individual signal crosses S1, but the combination of expired credential + velocity anomaly + unknown device pushes the composite into step-up territory. The RP requests a fresh PID presentation or WebAuthn confirmation.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Scenario 4: Automated issuance probing with invalid WIA/KA — BLOCK</strong></summary>

**Context**: An automated tool is repeatedly driving the organisation's issuer endpoints with untrusted or revoked WIA/KA and machine-speed sessions. This is an issuer-pipeline scenario, not an ordinary OpenID4VP presentation.

| Signal | Severity | Base Weight | Multiplier | Score |
|:-------|:--------:|:------------|:-----------|:------|
| `ISSUANCE_WIA_KA_INVALID` | S1 | 50 | 5.0 | 250 |
| `CTX_VELOCITY_EXCEED` (10× in 2 min) | S2 | 25 | 2.0 | 50 |
| `CTX_SESSION_DURATION_ANOMALY` (&lt; 1s) | S3 | 10 | 1.0 | 10 |

**Composite score: 310** → **BLOCK**

The typed WIA/KA failure, high velocity, and impossibly fast issuance session together create a strong automation signature. The issuer denies the token or credential, applies issuance-endpoint rate controls, and investigates Wallet Provider/issuer rollout state before attributing a device compromise. No presentation-time WUA signal is created.

</details>

##### 32.7.4 Signal Flow: VP Token to Decision

```mermaid
---
config:
  themeVariables:
    noteBkgColor: "transparent"
    noteBorderColor: "transparent"
  sequence:
    messageAlign: left
    noteAlign: left
    actorMargin: 250
---
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant W as Wallet
    participant GW as API Gateway<br/>(§26.6.4)
    participant VE as Verification<br/>Engine
    participant CE as Composition<br/>Engine
    participant SM as SIEM / SOAR

    W->>GW: direct_post (VP Token)
    Note over GW: Layer 3: Capture HTTP context<br/>(geo, TLS, velocity, device)

    GW->>VE: Forward VP Token + HTTP context
    Note over VE: Layer 1: Check for protocol errors<br/>(OID4VP error codes)
    Note over VE: Layer 2: Verify VP Token<br/>(signature, disclosure, temporal,<br/>revocation, holder binding,<br/>trust chain)

    VE->>CE: Signal array<br/>[L1 signals, L2 signals, L3 signals]
    Note over CE: Compute composite_risk<br/>= Σ(weight × severity × recency)<br/>+ context_modifiers

    alt Low risk, score below 20, or all pass
        CE->>GW: ALLOW
        GW->>W: HTTP 200 (redirect_uri)
    else Moderate risk, score 20 to 49
        CE->>GW: FLAG (allow + review)
        GW->>W: HTTP 200 (redirect_uri)
        CE->>SM: VSI event (priority: low)
    else High risk, score 50 to 79
        CE->>GW: STEP-UP
        GW->>W: HTTP 200 (step-up challenge)
    else Critical risk, score 80 or higher, or any S0
        CE->>GW: BLOCK
        GW->>W: HTTP 403
        CE->>SM: VSI event (priority: critical)
        Note right of SM: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end
```

<details>
<summary><strong>1. Wallet or browser-origin channel submits VP Token to API gateway</strong></summary>

In direct-post branches, the Wallet sends the VP Token to the RP's API gateway endpoint via `direct_post` / `direct_post.jwt`. In browser/OS API-mediated branches, the Wallet returns the encrypted response through the platform API, and the RP frontend forwards the opaque result to the same backend verification boundary. This is the gateway entry point for remote presentation processing, but the available HTTP context differs by branch: direct-post exposes Wallet-to-RP network context, while DC API exposes the RP origin's frontend-to-backend request context.

```http
POST /oidc/response HTTP/1.1
Host: rp.example.eu
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

response=eyJhbGciOiJFQ0RILUVTI...[Encrypted JWE]...
```

After decryption, the Authorization Response contains a DCQL-native result such as `{"vp_token":{"pid":["eyJ...~disclosures~kb-jwt"]},"state":"session_abc123"}`. API-mediated branches instead deliver the result through the platform API and do not assume redirect-style `state`.

**Artifact Produced:** Opaque remote-presentation submission arriving at the API gateway.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>2. API gateway forwards VP Token and HTTP context to verification engine</strong></summary>

The gateway captures Layer 3 environmental context before forwarding: source IP (for geo-lookup), TLS fingerprint (JA3/JA4 hash), HTTP headers (User-Agent, Accept-Language), and increments the velocity counter for the lawful identity key or account correlation key when the RP has one. The gateway bundles the raw VP Token with this environmental metadata and forwards both to the verification engine as an internal service call.

```json
// Internal gateway → verification engine payload
{
  "response": "eyJhbGciOiJFQ0RILUVTI...[Encrypted JWE]...",
  "gateway_request_id": "gw_req_88f9a2b",
  "http_context": {
    "source_ip": "198.51.100.42",
    "geo_country": "NL",
    "tls_fingerprint": "cd09ab3f...",
    "user_agent": "EUDI Wallet/1.2.3 (Android 15)",
    "velocity_count_10min": 2
  }
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** VP Token + HTTP context metadata forwarded to the verification engine.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>3. Verification engine emits signal array to composition engine</strong></summary>

The verification engine processes the VP Token through two verification layers. **Layer 1** checks for OID4VP protocol errors — if the submission is an error response rather than a VP Token, Layer 1 signals are generated and Layer 2 is skipped. **Layer 2** runs the full credential verification pipeline: issuer signature (D.2.36), disclosure hashes (D.2.37), temporal validity (`iat`/`exp`), revocation status (D.2.8), holder binding via KB-JWT (D.2.2–D.2.5), trust chain resolution via LoTE, authoritative Wallet Solution policy where mapped, and, where the RP explicitly invokes it, supplementary remote proofing controls (D.2.42–D.2.44). WIA/KA failures are emitted by the separate issuer pipeline and correlated only at the organisation's decision layer. The complete applicable signal array is sent to the composition engine.

**Artifact Produced:** Signal array containing all Layer 1, Layer 2, and Layer 3 signals with severity classifications.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>4. Composition engine sends ALLOW decision to gateway</strong></summary>

When the composite risk score is below 20 and no S0 (Critical) signal is present, the composition engine sends an **ALLOW** decision to the API gateway. This is the happy path — all verification checks passed, environmental context is normal, and no anomalies were detected. The RP can proceed with the business transaction using the verified credential attributes.

**Artifact Produced:** ALLOW decision dispatched to the API gateway.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>5. API gateway returns HTTP 200 with redirect_uri to wallet (ALLOW)</strong></summary>

The gateway returns HTTP 200 to the Wallet with a `redirect_uri` that continues the user's session. The redirect URI typically points to the RP's success page or the next step in the business flow (e.g., account creation confirmation, age-gated content access, KYC completion). The Wallet opens the redirect URI in the device browser to complete the user journey.

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "redirect_uri": "https://rp.example.eu/verify/success?session=abc123"
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** HTTP 200 response with `redirect_uri` for session continuation.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>6. Composition engine sends FLAG decision to gateway</strong></summary>

When the composite risk score falls between 20 and 49, the composition engine sends a **FLAG** decision — the presentation is accepted (the user's session proceeds) but marked for post-hoc review. This threshold captures low-confidence anomalies that do not warrant blocking or step-up: minor clock skew, first-time device, unusual but not impossible geo-location.

**Artifact Produced:** FLAG decision dispatched to the API gateway (allow + review marker).

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>7. API gateway returns HTTP 200 with redirect_uri to wallet (FLAG)</strong></summary>

The gateway returns the same HTTP 200 with `redirect_uri` as in the ALLOW path — the user experience is identical. The FLAG decision is invisible to the Wallet and the user. The RP processes the credential attributes normally; the review marker is handled asynchronously by the security operations team.

**Artifact Produced:** HTTP 200 response with `redirect_uri` — user session proceeds normally despite FLAG.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>8. Composition engine sends low-priority VSI event to SIEM</strong></summary>

The composition engine emits a VSI event to the SIEM/SOAR platform with `priority: low`. The event contains the full signal array, composite risk score, contributing signals with individual weights, and the FLAG decision rationale. Security analysts review these events in batch — typically during daily or weekly triage. The event follows the §32.8 VSI Event JSON Schema, enabling correlation with previous presentations from the same `subject_correlation_hash` where correlation is lawful for the journey.

```json
{
  "event_type": "vsi_signal",
  "composition": {
    "composite_risk": 35,
    "decision": "FLAG",
    "contributing_signals": ["CTX_DEVICE_UNKNOWN", "SDJWT_EXP_NEAR"]
  },
  "priority": "low"
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Low-priority VSI event ingested into SIEM for batch review.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>9. Composition engine sends STEP-UP decision to gateway</strong></summary>

When the composite risk score falls between 50 and 79, the composition engine sends a **STEP-UP** decision. The presentation is conditionally accepted — the credential attributes are tentatively available, but the RP requires additional authentication before granting full access. Step-up challenges include: re-authentication with WebAuthn (§17), presentation of an additional credential (e.g., a QEAA on top of the PID), or a fresh biometric confirmation. The specific challenge type is determined by the RP's risk policy configuration.

**Artifact Produced:** STEP-UP decision dispatched to the API gateway with challenge type specification.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>10. API gateway returns HTTP 200 with step-up challenge to wallet</strong></summary>

The gateway returns HTTP 200 with a response body that directs the Wallet to a step-up challenge rather than a simple redirect. The challenge payload specifies what additional authentication is required. The Wallet or device browser presents the challenge to the user — the session remains active but access is gated until the challenge is satisfied.

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "redirect_uri": "https://rp.example.eu/verify/step-up?session=abc123",
  "step_up": {
    "challenge_type": "webauthn",
    "reason": "elevated_risk_score"
  }
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** HTTP 200 response with step-up challenge payload.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>11. Composition engine sends BLOCK decision to gateway</strong></summary>

When the composite risk score exceeds 80 **or** any S0 (Critical) signal is present, the composition engine sends an immediate **BLOCK** decision. The S0 override is absolute — a single critical signal such as `KBJWT_AUD_MISMATCH` or `SDJWT_SIG_INVALID` triggers BLOCK regardless of how low the other signals score. An issuer-side `ISSUANCE_WIA_KA_INVALID` is S1 and denies the affected issuance transaction; it is not injected into an unrelated presentation. Credential attributes are discarded when the final presentation decision is BLOCK.

**Artifact Produced:** BLOCK decision dispatched to the API gateway.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>12. API gateway returns HTTP 403 to wallet (BLOCK)</strong></summary>

The gateway returns HTTP 403 Forbidden to the Wallet. The response body contains a generic error message — the RP does not disclose the specific signal(s) that triggered the block to avoid leaking information to potential attackers. The Wallet displays an error to the user indicating that verification was unsuccessful.

```http
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "error": "verification_failed",
  "error_description": "The credential presentation could not be verified."
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** HTTP 403 response terminating the verification session.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>13. Composition engine sends critical-priority VSI event to SIEM</strong></summary>

The composition engine emits a VSI event to the SIEM/SOAR platform with `priority: critical`. Unlike the low-priority FLAG events, critical events trigger automated incident response playbooks: the source IP range is added to a quarantine watchlist, the `subject_correlation_hash` is flagged for enhanced monitoring on subsequent presentations where lawful, and an alert is dispatched to the on-call security analyst. The event contains the full signal array, composite risk score, the S0 signal(s) that triggered the block, and correlation data from the past 24 hours.

```json
{
  "event_type": "vsi_signal",
  "composition": {
    "composite_risk": 1025,
    "decision": "BLOCK",
    "s0_trigger": "KBJWT_AUD_MISMATCH",
    "contributing_signals": [
      "KBJWT_AUD_MISMATCH",
      "CTX_GEO_MISMATCH",
      "KBJWT_CLOCK_SKEW"
    ]
  },
  "priority": "critical",
  "correlation": {
    "subject_correlation_hash": "sha256:a1b2c3...",
    "presentation_count_24h": 3
  }
}
```

**Audit Telemetry:** Critical VSI event triggers SOAR playbook execution. Source IP quarantined. On-call analyst alerted. Full signal array preserved for forensic correlation.

**Artifact Produced:** Critical-priority VSI event ingested into SIEM/SOAR, triggering automated incident response.

</details>

#### 32.8 SIEM Integration Event Schema

Each VSI signal emits a structured event suitable for SIEM ingestion. The schema extends the §33.3.1 Verification Result Object with per-signal event data, enabling correlation across multiple presentations and drill-down from aggregate dashboards to individual signal detail.

##### 32.8.1 VSI Event JSON Structure

```json
{
  "event_type": "vsi_signal",
  "event_version": "1.0",
  "timestamp": "2026-03-17T14:30:00.123Z",
  "session_id": "abc-123-def",
  "signal": {
    "signal_id": "KBJWT_AUD_MISMATCH",
    "layer": 2,
    "severity": "S0",
    "severity_label": "Critical — Active Attack",
    "stride": "Spoofing",
    "threat_ref": "D.2.4",
    "description": "KB-JWT aud claim does not match RP client_id"
  },
  "context": {
    "credential_format": "dc+sd-jwt",
    "credential_type": "urn:eudi:pid:1",
    "issuer_country": "DE",
    "source_ip": "198.51.100.42",
    "geo_country": "NL",
    "tls_fingerprint": "cd09ab...",
    "user_agent": "EUDI Wallet/1.2.3 (Android 15)"
  },
  "composition": {
    "base_weight": 100,
    "severity_multiplier": 10.0,
    "recency_factor": 1.0,
    "signal_score": 1000,
    "composite_risk": 1025,
    "decision": "BLOCK"
  },
  "correlation": {
    "subject_correlation_hash": "sha256:a1b2c3...",
    "presentation_count_24h": 3,
    "previous_signals_24h": ["CTX_GEO_MISMATCH", "KBJWT_CLOCK_SKEW"]
  },
  "verification_result_ref": "abc-123-def"
}
```

> **GDPR compliance (§33.3)**: The event schema logs `subject_correlation_hash` (a one-way hash of the RP's lawful account or identity correlation key), not raw PID attributes. The `source_ip` is included for security incident response (GDPR Art. 6(1)(f) legitimate interest) and must be subject to the RP's IP address retention policy. No attribute values (family_name, birthdate) are included in VSI events — only the credential type, format, and signal metadata.

##### 32.8.2 Field Reference

| Field | Type | Description | Retention |
|:------|:-----|:------------|:----------|
| `event_type` | string | Always `"vsi_signal"` — distinguishes VSI events from other SIEM events | N/A |
| `signal.signal_id` | string | The VSI signal identifier from §34.3–§34.5 | Per audit policy |
| `signal.layer` | integer | 1, 2, or 3 — the signal's origin layer | Per audit policy |
| `signal.severity` | string | S0–S4 | Per audit policy |
| `signal.stride` | string | STRIDE classification (Spoofing/Tampering/Replay/DoS or null) | Per audit policy |
| `signal.threat_ref` | string | Cross-reference to §31 threat catalogue entry (e.g., `"D.2.4"`) | Per audit policy |
| `context.credential_format` | string | `"dc+sd-jwt"` or `"mso_mdoc"` | Per audit policy |
| `context.source_ip` | string | Client IP from `direct_post` request | IP retention policy |
| `context.tls_fingerprint` | string | JA3/JA4 hash of the TLS connection | Per audit policy |
| `composition.composite_risk` | integer | Aggregate risk score at time of decision | Per audit policy |
| `composition.decision` | string | `"ALLOW"`, `"FLAG"`, `"STEP_UP"`, or `"BLOCK"` | Per audit policy |
| `correlation.subject_correlation_hash` | string | SHA-256 hash of the RP's lawful account or identity correlation key for cross-session correlation | Per data retention policy |
| `correlation.previous_signals_24h` | array | Signal IDs from prior sessions in the last 24 hours | 24h rolling window |
| `verification_result_ref` | string | `session_id` linking to the full §33.3.1 verification result object | Per audit policy |

##### 32.8.3 CEF Compatibility

For SIEM platforms that ingest Common Event Format (CEF), the VSI event maps to:

```
CEF:0|EUDI-RP|VSI|1.0|KBJWT_AUD_MISMATCH|KB-JWT audience mismatch|10|
  src=198.51.100.42 shost=wallet.example.com
  cs1=S0 cs1Label=VSI_Severity
  cs2=Spoofing cs2Label=STRIDE
  cs3=D.2.4 cs3Label=ThreatRef
  cs4=BLOCK cs4Label=Decision
  cn1=1025 cn1Label=CompositeRisk
  cs5=abc-123-def cs5Label=SessionID
```

##### 32.8.4 Sample SIEM Queries

**Splunk** — Top 10 signals in the last hour:
```spl
index=eudi_vsi event_type="vsi_signal" earliest=-1h
| stats count by signal.signal_id, signal.severity
| sort -count
| head 10
```

**Elasticsearch (KQL)** — All S0 signals with BLOCK decision:
```
event_type: "vsi_signal" AND signal.severity: "S0" AND composition.decision: "BLOCK"
```

**Elasticsearch** — Credential leak pattern (expired + velocity):
```
event_type: "vsi_signal" AND signal.signal_id: ("SDJWT_EXP_EXPIRED" OR "CTX_VELOCITY_EXCEED")
| aggs by correlation.subject_correlation_hash having count > 3
```

#### 32.9 Cross-Reference Map: Signal to Threat to Alert to Regulation

The following table connects each representative signal to its originating threat, operational alert, and **candidate legal/control routing**. A signal is not a reportability conclusion.
