The organisation must first establish entity/service scope, determine whether an incident or personal-data breach occurred, apply the relevant significance/materiality/risk criteria, document the accountable decision, and start an external clock only when the applicable threshold is met.

| Signal | Description | §31 Threat | §33.2 Alert Trigger | Regulatory Provision | Decision |
|:-------|:------------|:-----------|:--------------------|:---------------------|:---------|
| `KBJWT_NONCE_REUSE` | Definitive replay attack — nonce already consumed | Credential Replay (D.2.2) | §33.2.3 Nonce/state replay detected | Security event; for DORA-scoped services classify under Art. 18 + Delegated Regulation 2024/1772 before Art. 19 reporting | BLOCK |
| `KBJWT_AUD_MISMATCH` | Relay attack — credential bound to different RP | Relay Attack: Cross-Device (D.2.4) | §33.2.3 Audience mismatch | eIDAS Art. 5b (RP integrity) | BLOCK |
| `SDJWT_SIG_ALG_NONE` | Algorithm confusion — `alg: none` exploit | Algorithm Confusion/Type Confusion (D.2.23) | §33.2.3 Algorithmic downgrade | Internal security event; apply the scoped incident/significance workflow | BLOCK |
| `SDJWT_STATUS_REVOKED` / `MDOC_STATUS_REVOKED` / `MDOC_IDENTIFIER_LIST_REVOKED` | Permanently revoked credential presented through its format-selected mechanism | none directly; issuer lifecycle fact, with misuse patterns assessed separately | §33.2.5 Revoked credential spike | Internal lifecycle enforcement; external incident/reporting classification assessed from surrounding evidence | BLOCK |
| `STATUS_VALUE_NOT_ALLOWED_FOR_PROFILE` | Status vocabulary contradicts the selected credential class or Rulebook | none directly; profile/conformance failure | §33.2.2 Status-profile mismatch | Applicable EUDI credential profile; investigate issuer/verifier drift | BLOCK |
| `MDOC_IACA_CHAIN_INVALID` | IACA certificate chain bypass | mdoc IACA Chain Validation Bypass (D.2.30) | §33.2.2 Trust anchor failure | Internal trust-control event; NIS2 Art. 23 only after entity scope and significant-incident classification | BLOCK |
| `MDOC_SESSION_TRANSCRIPT_MISMATCH` | Relay attack via session transcript manipulation | Relay Attack: Cross-Device (D.2.4) | §33.2.3 Session mismatch | eIDAS Art. 5b (RP integrity) | BLOCK |
| `ENVELOPE_KID_UNKNOWN` / `ENVELOPE_JWE_DECRYPT_FAILED` | Response encryption key mismatch or decryption failure | Ephemeral Key Interception: Response Encryption (D.2.7) | §33.2.3 Threat detection | Diagnose protocol/key failure; GDPR Art. 33 only if a personal-data breach occurred and its notification threshold is met | BLOCK |
| `LOTE_SIG_INVALID` | LoTE cache poisoning — trust anchor compromise | LoTE Cache Poisoning (D.2.22) | §33.2.2 Trust anchor key rotation | Internal trust incident; NIS2 Art. 23 only after significant-incident classification | BLOCK |
| `TRUST_ANCHOR_FLEET_DIVERGENCE` | Relevant RP Instances disagree on the active trust snapshot or removal state | LoTE Cache Poisoning (D.2.22) | §33.2.2 Trust snapshot fleet divergence | Internal trust-control incident; external classification assessed separately | ISOLATE / BLOCK AFFECTED PROFILE |
| `STATUS_SIGNER_UNAUTHORIZED` | Status object is signed validly by a key not authorized for that list role | Status List Denial of Service (D.2.6) | §33.2.2 Unauthorized or unresolved status signer | Internal trust-control incident; external classification assessed separately | BLOCK |
| `ISSUANCE_WIA_KA_INVALID` | Issuer rejected WIA/KA role, trust, status, freshness, security level, maintenance period, or proof/key binding | Invalid or Wrong-Role WIA/KA Accepted During Issuance (D.2.41) | §33.2.3 issuer WIA/KA gate failure | ARF Topics 9–10; EC TS03 | DENY ISSUANCE |
| `STEPUP_PRESENTATION_ATTACK_DETECTED` | Remote proofing presentation attack detected during selfie / portrait / document step-up | Remote Live-Person Step-Up: Biometric Presentation Attack (D.2.42) | §33.2.5 Biometric presentation-attack spike in remote step-up | eIDAS Art. 5b(8); GDPR Arts. 9 & 35 | BLOCK |
| `STEPUP_CAPTURE_INJECTION_DETECTED` | Remote proofing capture-pipeline injection or virtual-camera attack detected | Remote Live-Person Step-Up: Capture-Pipeline Injection Attack (D.2.43) | §33.2.3 Capture-pipeline injection detected | eIDAS Art. 5b(8); DORA ICT third-party / incident controls where applicable | BLOCK |
| `STEPUP_DOCUMENT_AUTH_FAILED` | OCR / document fallback failed to establish document authenticity or current possession | Fallback Document Proofing: OCR and Document Authenticity Failure (D.2.44) | §33.2.5 Fallback document-authenticity anomaly | eIDAS Art. 5b(8); GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) | STEP-UP / BLOCK |
| `CTX_VELOCITY_EXCEED` | High-velocity credential reuse | Cross-RP Collusion (D.2.13) | §33.2.5 Velocity anomaly | Fraud/AML triage input where entity and activity are in scope; suspicion and reporting decisions remain with the accountable function | STEP-UP |
| `SDJWT_ISSUER_CHAIN_INVALID` | Issuer X.509 chain doesn't validate to LoTE root | OID-FED Trust Chain Spoofing (D.2.27) | §33.2.2 Trust anchor failure | Internal trust-control event; NIS2 Art. 23 only after significant-incident classification | BLOCK |
| `PROTO_INVALID_TRANSACTION_DATA` | Transaction data binding rejected by wallet | JAR Modification in Transit (D.2.8) | §33.2.5 SCA integrity failure | PSD2 RTS (dynamic linking) | BLOCK |
| `SDJWT_SIG_INVALID` | Forged credential — issuer signature fails verification | Credential Forgery (D.2.36) | §33.2.3 Threat detection | Internal security/fraud signal; DORA reporting only after Art. 18 / 2024/1772 major-incident classification | BLOCK |
| `SDJWT_DISCLOSURE_HASH_MISMATCH` | Selective disclosure tampered post-issuance | Selective Disclosure Tampering (D.2.37) | §33.2.3 Threat detection | eIDAS Art. 5b (RP integrity) | BLOCK |
| `SDJWT_JSON_PARSE_ERROR` | Malformed VP Token exploiting parser vulnerabilities | VP Token Parser Exploitation (D.2.38) | §33.2.3 Threat detection | NIS2 Art. 21(2)(a) (risk analysis) | BLOCK |
| `SDJWT_CNF_MISSING` | Credential issued without device binding — unbound forwarding | Unbound Credential Forwarding (D.2.39) | §33.2.5 Device binding anomaly | eIDAS Art. 5b (RP integrity) | BLOCK |
| `SDJWT_IAT_FUTURE` | Future-dated issuance — clock manipulation / emulation | Clock Manipulation/Environment Emulation (D.2.40) | §33.2.5 Temporal anomaly | eIDAS Art. 5b (RP integrity) | FLAG |

> **How to read this table**: Each row traces a signal from verification to threat/alert handling and then to a **classification queue**. The pipeline preserves evidence and assigns an accountable decision; it never converts a protocol failure directly into “major,” “significant,” “personal-data breach,” or “suspicious activity report.”

#### 32.10 Vendor Signal Exposure Assessment

Not all verifier vendors expose the same level of signal granularity. Some return rich per-check failure data; others return opaque pass/fail results. The RP's ability to implement a VSI pipeline depends on the vendor's signal exposure.

This assessment evaluates vendor capabilities across six VSI-relevant dimensions (cross-references §29.6 Unified Vendor Capability Matrix and §29.8 Delivery Mode Selection Guide):

| Capability | Description | What to Ask the Vendor |
|:-----------|:------------|:----------------------|
| **Granular failure codes** | Does the API/webhook return a named failure reason per check (e.g., `signature_invalid`, `revoked`, `holder_binding_failed`), or just a boolean `pass` / `fail`? | "When verification fails, does your API response include the specific check that failed and the reason?" |
| **Per-policy result array** | Does the response include a per-check result array (signature ✅, revocation ✅, holder-binding ❌), or a single aggregate boolean? | "Does your verification result include a breakdown of individual policy checks, as described in §33.3.1?" |
| **Raw VP Token access** | Can the RP access the raw VP Token (JWT string or CBOR bytes) for independent verification and signal extraction, or only vendor-processed results? | "Can we receive the raw VP Token in addition to your verification result, to run our own verification pipeline?" |
| **Webhook event types** | Does the vendor distinguish between `verification_failed` (check failed), `verification_error` (infrastructure error), `verification_timeout`, and `user_cancelled`? | "Does your webhook payload differentiate between verification failure, system error, timeout, and user cancellation?" |
| **SIEM-friendly event format** | Does the vendor produce structured events (JSON with consistent schema) suitable for SIEM ingestion, or are events only available via a vendor-specific dashboard? | "Can we export verification events as structured JSON via webhook or API for ingestion into our SIEM?" |
| **Aggregate validation output** | When a presentation fails, does the verifier stop at the first error, or does it return the full set of applicable failed / passed / indeterminate checks from the same validation pass? | "Can your verifier return all applicable policy failures for one VP Token, rather than only the first error encountered?" |

##### 32.10.1 Vendor Assessment Matrix

> **Evidence rule**: Delivery mode determines what the RP may be able to observe or implement; it does not prove what a current product actually exposes. A local library can still be fail-fast, omit policy results, or lack stable event schemas. A hosted verifier may expose rich results. Assign a VSI rating only from version-pinned primary vendor documentation, response/schema samples, contractual commitments, and RP-run negative tests covering all six dimensions. Until then, `Unassessed` is the only defensible readiness conclusion.

### 33. Monitoring, Observability, and Operational Readiness

:::important
Treat this chapter as the operating system for the RP's wallet integration, not as dashboard ornament. If trust-anchor state, verification failures, fraud patterns, and breach notifications are not wired into live alerting and response paths, the RP cannot sustain either regulatory compliance or production reliability.
:::

> **Incident-handling boundary**: Monitoring can support NIS2 Article 21(2)(b), DORA incident management, GDPR breach response, and sector fraud controls, but this chapter is not proof of compliance. A Wallet event enters an accountable classification workflow. NIS2 Article 23 reporting applies only to a significant incident; DORA reporting only to a major ICT-related incident; GDPR Article 33 only to a personal-data breach meeting its notification rule.

#### 33.1 Key Metrics

Financial RPs integrating with the EUDI Wallet should monitor the following metrics:

| Metric | Description | Alert Threshold |
|:-------|:------------|:----------------|
| **Presentation success rate** | Ratio of successful verifications to total presentation requests | &lt; 95% → investigate |
| **Verification latency (p95)** | Time from receiving encrypted response to verification complete | > 500ms → investigate |
| **Revocation-check latency by mechanism** | Fetch, authentication, and evaluation time split across SD-JWT VC Token Status List, mdoc Attestation Status List, and mdoc identifier list | > 2s or material baseline shift → inspect endpoint, chain validation, decoding/member lookup, and cache freshness |
| **Status-evidence cache hit rate by mechanism/profile** | Percentage of list-backed revocation checks served from a still-authorized, signed-fresh cache entry | &lt; 80% → investigate cache-key fragmentation and refresh cadence; do not lengthen past signed freshness merely to improve the metric |
| **Status evidence unavailable rate** | Percentage of required checks ending `evidence_incomplete`, split by credential class, mechanism, provider, and unavailable-policy outcome | Any sustained increase or high-assurance occurrence → investigate dependency and confirm no unavailable result was counted as `NOT_REVOKED` |
| **WRPAC expiry countdown** | Days until WRPAC certificate expires | &lt; 30 days → trigger renewal |
| **LoTE freshness** | Time since last LoTE update was fetched | > 24h → force refresh |
| **Trust snapshot fleet convergence** | Percentage of relevant RP Instances reporting the currently activated LoTE/TL version and hash | &lt; 100% after the configured convergence deadline → isolate lagging Instances |
| **Authorized status-signer failures** | Count of status/revocation objects whose signature validates mathematically but not to the authorized signer class for the provider/profile/source generation | > 0 → reject and investigate rollover/substitution |
| **Authenticated `LOTL` / national TL freshness** | Time since the last successfully authenticated trusted-list refresh used for qualified-status conclusions | > 24h → review qualified-output path and refresh |
| **Error rate by type** | Breakdown: `access_denied`, `invalid_request`, `expired_credential`, etc. | Spike in any category → investigate |
| **Cross-border presentation ratio** | Percentage of presentations from foreign MS PIDs | Unexpected spike → possible attack vector |

#### 33.2 Alert Triggers

Operating an RP in a pan-European, federated, cryptographic ecosystem requires observability across application and infrastructure layers. Tooling is an implementation choice. Each applicable trigger should create a structured internal event with evidence, ownership, and a response playbook; it must not automatically label the event a DORA major incident, NIS2 significant incident, GDPR personal-data breach, or AML report.

The alert triggers in this section consume signals classified by the **Verification Signal Intelligence taxonomy (§32)**. Each named signal ID referenced in the tables below (e.g., `KBJWT_NONCE_REUSE`, `LOTE_SIG_INVALID`) maps to a specific entry in the §32 signal inventory, with a defined severity level (S0–S4) and SIEM event schema (§32.8). The §32.9 cross-reference map provides a complete Signal → Alert → Regulation traceability table.

The alert triggers are organised into six operational pillars. Before the individual trigger tables, every implementation needs the same legal-classification handoff:

| Stage | Required action | Evidence to retain |
|:------|:----------------|:-------------------|
| **1. Detect and contain** | Reject/isolate the affected request or component, preserve relevant logs, and avoid expanding collection without need | Signal IDs, raw/derived evidence under retention policy, timestamps, affected component, containment action |
| **2. Establish scope** | Determine entity, service, jurisdiction, data, users, third parties, and whether DORA, NIS2, GDPR, sector fraud/AML, or another framework applies | Scope owner, legal entities/services, jurisdictions, applicable-framework rationale |
| **3. Characterise the event** | Distinguish protocol rejection, vulnerability attempt, ICT incident, service outage, security compromise, and personal-data breach | Facts, confidence, cause hypothesis, confidentiality/integrity/availability impact |
| **4. Apply statutory criteria** | DORA: Art. 18 + Delegated Regulation 2024/1772; NIS2: Art. 23 significance; GDPR: Art. 4(12) and Art. 33 risk; sector regimes: their own thresholds | Criterion-by-criterion assessment, impact/materiality, affected clients/transactions, decision time |
| **5. Decide and start clocks** | Accountable incident, legal/privacy, and regulatory owners approve the classification; start an external clock only when its legal trigger occurs | Decision, approver, rationale, classification/awareness times, competent authority |
| **6. Report and update if required** | Submit the applicable initial/intermediate/final notifications and keep engineering containment/remediation running | Submission IDs, content/version, updates, remediation, lessons learned |

##### 33.2.1 Compliance, Governance and Incident Mapping

Triggers can have legal consequences, but the bridge is **technical event → accountable classification → report if threshold met**, not technical event → automatic external report.

| Event | Severity | Threshold | Regulatory Mapping & Action |
|:------|:---------|:----------|:----------------------------|
| DORA major-incident candidate | 🔴 Critical | Verification bypass, WRPAC key compromise, or other high-impact ICT event | Preserve and contain, then classify under DORA Art. 18 and Delegated Regulation 2024/1772. If major, report under Art. 19 / Delegated Regulation 2025/301 using the correct awareness and classification timestamps |
| GDPR personal-data-breach candidate | 🔴 Critical | Confirmed or suspected compromise of PID/presentation data confidentiality, integrity, or availability | Determine whether a personal-data breach occurred; document risk. Notify under Art. 33 within 72 hours after awareness unless unlikely to result in risk; assess Art. 34's separate high-risk threshold |
| Cross-RP correlation/collusion indicator | 🔴 Critical | Presentation artefacts or correlation keys match an external dataset or unauthorised sharing pattern | Investigate provenance, purpose, authorisation, and data roles; stop unauthorised sharing. Determine GDPR/eIDAS consequences from facts rather than treating every duplicate as a proven violation |
| Certification / conformance evidence drift | 🟠 High | Wallet Solution certified-list status, CAB certificate scope statement, OIDF conformance report, sandbox evidence, or vendor accessibility evidence is missing, stale, or contradicted before a production release | Block go-live or downgrade readiness until evidence is refreshed. Keep OIDF conformance / Launchpad readiness evidence separate from CIR 2024/2981 Wallet Solution certification (§23.7.6, §30.3) |
| Trust Mark / certified-list inconsistency | 🟠 High | Wallet-side TS01 information or a vendor claim conflicts with the official certified-wallet or breach/suspension status | Treat the official status source as controlling, investigate the stale/misleading Trust Mark information, and do not use the visual mark as a runtime acceptance signal (§30.5) |
| Accessibility regression gate failed | 🟠 High | Critical defect against the RP's selected WCAG/EN 301 549 baseline or applicable EAA/WAD/national requirement | Release block or emergency remediation depending on user/legal impact. Keep the engineering baseline and the instrument-specific conformity evidence separate (§23.5) |

##### 33.2.2 Trust Management and PKI Anchors

Monitors the foundational anchors tying the RP to the European federation. Failures in this layer result in systemic verification outages or immediate regulatory non-compliance.

| Event | Severity | Threshold | Edge Cases & Action |
|:------|:---------|:----------|:--------------------|
| WRPAC expiry countdown | 🟡 Warning / 🔴 Critical | &lt; 30 days (Warning); &lt; 7 days (Critical) | Initiate automated certificate renewal pipeline with the National Access CA. Edge case: the replacement WRPAC may be issued before the applicable CT / transparency evidence is available — treat that as an evidence-readiness / deployment-policy issue distinct from rogue issuance, and verify your Access CA profile before deployment (§5.2.4) |
| WRPAC SCT missing or invalid | 🔴 Critical | Any production WRPAC in a Topic 55 CT profile lacks at least one valid SCT | Do not deploy the certificate for Wallet-facing presentation. Topic 55 maps missing valid SCT evidence to Wallet-side RP-authentication failure under `RPA_06a`; resolve with the Access CA before traffic cutover (§5.2.4) |
| Unauthorised WRPAC detected in CT log | 🔴 Critical | > 0 unauthorised issuances observed | A rogue or mistaken certificate appears to have been issued for the RP's domain. Treat CT as the detection/evidence layer, not the revocation authority: confirm the signal, escalate immediately to the Access CA / Registrar / supervisory contacts, and initiate certificate-status action through the authority that actually controls revocation or suspension (§5.2.4) |
| HSM / KMS latency spikes | 🔴 Critical | > 500ms for signing operations | Evaluate hardware security module health; scale signing capacity. If offline, the RP cannot execute `client_assertion` authentication or sign JARs |
| LoTE staleness or fetch failure | 🟡 Warning | > 24 hours since last successful fetch | Force manual cache refresh; investigate outbound network rules preventing LoTE synchronisation. Edge case: network partition isolating the RP from the EU Trust Framework infrastructure |
| Trust snapshot fleet divergence | 🟠 High | Any relevant RP Instance reports the wrong version/hash after the convergence deadline, or any Instance retains an invalidated anchor | Remove non-converged Instances from the affected traffic pool; reconcile additions/changes/removals and prove that invalidated anchors cannot be used before restoring service |
| Authenticated `LOTL` / national Trusted List stale or unavailable | 🟠 High | > 24 hours since last successful authenticated refresh for a path where the RP consumes qualified outputs | Do not silently substitute LoTE success for trusted-list-backed qualification. Keep ordinary issuer checks running where appropriate, but treat the qualified-output leg as unavailable or `Indeterminate` until the authenticated trusted-list path is healthy again |
| Issuer metadata fetch failure | 🟡 Warning | > 3 consecutive failures from the same Issuer `iss` | Activate temporary cache fallback; raise network-level alert if a specific Member State's `.well-known/openid-credential-issuer` endpoint is persistently down |
| Status / revocation endpoint outage | 🟠 High | > 5 minutes HTTP 5xx or timeout for a Token Status List, mdoc Attestation Status List, or mdoc identifier list | Use only a still-authorized, signed-fresh cache entry. Otherwise return the documented `evidence_incomplete` outcome for the affected branch and notify on-call. If a provider rotates a reference, refresh the governing profile/metadata without purging the last-known-good entry until the new object and authority binding validate |
| Unauthorized or unresolved status signer | 🔴 Critical | > 0 `STATUS_SIGNER_UNAUTHORIZED` events | Reject the list even when its signature is mathematically valid. Compare provider/profile, list identity, active LoTE/TL generation, and rollover notification; never accept an embedded signer or credential-signing key by convenience |
| Status-profile mismatch | 🟠 High | > 0 `STATUS_VALUE_NOT_ALLOWED_FOR_PROFILE` events | Reject the affected credential. Compare credential class, format router, Rulebook/profile version, and returned status vocabulary; never reinterpret PID/QEAA/PuB-EAA suspension or a reserved value as temporary validity |
| Trust Anchor key rotation failure | 🔴 Critical | LoTE signature or authenticated `LOTL` / national TL signature unverifiable against cached bootstrap keys / `LOTLSO` material | The EU or a Member State rotated their signing keys, but the RP's local trust store failed to synchronise. Halt the affected trust path until the trust store is updated — accepting credentials or qualified outputs against an unverified list is a critical security gap |
| Provider publication feed changed or stale | 🟡 Warning | TS02 / future EN 319 482-5 feed shows an unexpected provider lifecycle change, or no authenticated refresh succeeds within the RP's policy window | Reconcile the change against the controlling LoTE/Trusted List and service status before changing acceptance. Treat the feed as discovery/monitoring evidence, not a substitute trust anchor (§5.5.1) |

##### 33.2.3 Threat Detection and Verification Engine

Deep inspection of the EUDI cryptographic constructs. Alerts in this layer almost universally indicate a direct, active attack against the RP's core security controls.

| Event | Severity | Threshold | Edge Cases & Action |
|:------|:---------|:----------|:--------------------|
| KB-JWT / SD-JWT signature verification spike | 🔴 Critical | Spike > 5% failure rate above baseline | Sudden spike indicates forged credentials testing the perimeter, or a supply-chain bug in the verification SDK (D.2.20). Quarantine source IP and escalate to security team |
| Nonce / `state` replay detection | 🔴 Critical | > 0 duplicate nonces utilised across independent sessions | Active replay attack (D.2.2) or session fixation (D.2.11). The exact same attestation payload is being replayed across distinct HTTP sessions. Invalidate all sessions sharing the nonce |
| Audience (`aud`) mismatch | 🔴 Critical | > 0 instances | Relay attack detected (D.2.4). The user is presenting a credential whose `aud` claim does not match the RP's registered `client_id`. Drop presentation and log all client metadata |
| Issuer WIA/KA gate failure | 🟠 High | Any failure denies the issuance; alert when failure rate exceeds 1% or a trust/status pattern emerges | Check artifact role/transport, Wallet Provider LoTE chain, signature/PoP, status, freshness, requested maintenance/security levels, and KA-to-proof key binding. Keep this alert on Token/Credential Endpoint telemetry; it must not trigger from an ordinary presentation |
| Capture-pipeline injection detected in remote step-up | 🔴 Critical | > 0 confirmed detections | Active bypass attempt against the RP's supplementary proofing stack — virtual camera, stream substitution, or tampered media pipeline. Block the session immediately. If the capture workflow is vendor-operated, review capture-SDK integrity, vendor incident handling, and DORA third-party processes where applicable |
| Algorithmic downgrade attempt | 🟠 High | > 5% of presentations using unexpected algorithms | Attacker attempting to force weak cryptographic algorithms (e.g., RS256 instead of ES256, or non-standard ECDH curves). Deny presentation and log the attempted algorithm |
| KB-JWT clock skew | ℹ️ Info | KB-JWT `iat` > 60 seconds from server receipt time | Indicator of extreme network lag, Wallet clock desynchronisation, or potential replay delay. Log for pattern analysis |
| Selective Disclosure salt collision | 🟠 High | > 0 instances of duplicate salts within a single disclosure array | Malformed SD-JWT structure. Edge case: attacker fuzzing the disclosure array to manipulate hash verification logic. Reject payload and log the raw structure for forensic analysis |

##### 33.2.4 Network Perimeter and Integration Protocol

Operates at the OpenID4VP / DC API protocol integration surface, detecting infrastructure stress, fuzzing, and volumetric attacks.

| Event | Severity | Threshold | Edge Cases & Action |
|:------|:---------|:----------|:--------------------|
| PAR endpoint resource exhaustion | 🟠 High | HTTP 429 responses > 2% of total PAR requests | Potential Denial-of-Wallet (DDoS) attack flooding the backend with pending authorisation session states. Implement rate limiting per source IP and per `client_id` |
| Callback URI origin mismatch | 🔴 Critical | Any instance | Attempted cross-origin redirect manipulation. The presentation response is returning to a mismatched or unauthorised origin. Log IP aggressively and reject |
| Malformed payload parsing failures | 🟡 Warning | > 100 parse faults per minute | Automated fuzzing of the JWE/JWS presentation endpoints. Drop traffic at the WAF level based on IP reputation scoring |
| App-to-app deep link timeout | 🟡 Warning | > 15% timeout rate for cross-device flows | User taps the authentication button on mobile, the Wallet app opens, but the presentation never returns via the `redirect_uri`. Indicates OS-level deep-link breakage or Wallet-side rendering failure |
| Token vs. authorisation asymmetry | 🟡 Warning | Ratio deviation > 10% | The PAR endpoint allocates sessions, but the token/response endpoint never receives the corresponding payload. Indicates session dropping, UX abandonment, or intermediary network failures |
| TLS cipher downgrade attempts | 🟠 High | > 5% of TLS handshakes using unexpected cipher suites | Attacker attempting to force weak TLS configurations. Deny handshake and investigate TLS termination proxy configuration |

##### 33.2.5 Fraud, Abuse and Continuous Evaluation

Application-layer heuristics applied to cryptographically valid presentations, detecting systemic abuse of the identity system.

| Event | Severity | Threshold | Edge Cases & Action |
|:------|:---------|:----------|:--------------------|
| Presentation velocity anomaly | 🟠 High | > 5 presentations from the same PID or pseudonym within 10 minutes | Bot activity, shared credential abuse, or aggressive account enumeration. Implement temporary soft-lock or step-up re-authentication challenge |
| Revoked credential submission spike | 🟠 High | > 3 `SDJWT_STATUS_REVOKED`, `MDOC_STATUS_REVOKED`, or `MDOC_IDENTIFIER_LIST_REVOKED` events within 1 hour | Possible testing of leaked or extracted credentials, but do not infer the issuer's revocation reason from the bit/member result alone. Route the pattern—not ordinary isolated lifecycle enforcement—to fraud intelligence and correlate before IP-level action |
| Biometric presentation-attack spike in remote step-up | 🟠 High | > 1% of remote step-up attempts or > 3 attempts from the same account / IP within 1 hour | Printed-photo, mask, or screen-replay pressure against the RP's selfie / portrait ceremony. Escalate the affected flow to a stronger supervised path or manual review; review PAD thresholds and challenge randomness |
| Fallback document-authenticity anomaly | 🟠 High | > 3 failures from the same account / IP within 1 hour or > 2% of fallback document flows | Indicates forged, altered, or screen-replayed documents, or an OCR-heavy fallback that is being over-trusted. Prefer NFC chip reading with cryptographic validation where possible; do not treat OCR-only success or a raw NFC extraction as equivalent to upstream LoA High proofing |
| Data minimisation / oversharing violation | 🟡 Warning | Wallet returns claims not present in the RP's DCQL query | The Wallet implementation has a privacy bug (e.g., returning `address` when only `age_over_18` was requested), or a compromised Wallet is dumping all available data. Discard unrequested data immediately per GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) and log the incident |
| Portrait retention/transfer policy blocked | 🟠 High | Any `PORTRAIT_RETENTION_POLICY_INVALID`, or a successful prohibited operation | Stop persistence or routing immediately, purge session copies, and investigate whether any portrait reached durable storage or an unauthorised third-country/international-organisation service. A successful operation triggers privacy-incident assessment |
| Wallet physical-deletion scope rejected | 🟠 High | Any `PHYSICAL_CREDENTIAL_DELETE_SCOPE_INVALID` | Abort before deletion, recompute the selected Credential Dataset, and verify that all and only physical copies sharing type + Provider + Dataset will be removed atomically |
| Deletion contact unavailable | 🟡 Warning | Any `DELETION_CONTACT_UNAVAILABLE`; escalate if > 0.5% of deletion attempts | Inspect log migration/corruption and registration-certificate population. Preserve the user's selected transaction context, but do not claim initiation or add an unmandated live Registrar repair path |
| QES profile/version mismatch | 🟠 High | Any `QES_PROFILE_VERSION_MISMATCH` | Stop before document/credential authorization. Compare the CIR-selected ETSI clauses, observed `/info` metadata, requested signature profile, and provider conformance statement; require an explicit compatibility decision rather than silent CSC-version fallback |
| Test environment credential leakage | 🔴 Critical | Presentation of credentials issued by staging or test Issuers to the production RP endpoint | Reject immediately. Edge case: a Wallet Provider may deploy test credentials with production-like `iss` URIs during pilot programmes — maintain an explicit blocklist of known test Issuer identifiers |
| Continuous access evaluation — mid-session revocation | 🟠 High | Status List check reveals revocation for a credential backing an active session | A previously authenticated user's credential has been revoked while their web session remains active. Sever the session token immediately and redirect to re-authentication. This is critical for financial RPs where DORA Art. 9 mandates continuous access controls |
| Cross-border geolocation skew | ℹ️ Info | Source IP geolocation does not match the Issuer Member State | A German PID presented from a non-European VPN exit node. Contextual signal to elevate the transaction's internal fraud risk score — not necessarily malicious (legitimate travel, VPN usage), but correlated with relay and phishing attacks |
| Expired credential submission spike | ℹ️ Info | Spike in `exp` claim validation failures | Monitor for UX implications — the user may not realise their Wallet credential requires manual re-issuance or renewal from the PID Provider |

##### 33.2.6 UX Flow and Conversion Observability

Product-level alerts ensuring the RP is not losing legitimate users due to friction, Wallet-side latency, or schema compatibility errors.

| Event | Severity | Threshold | Edge Cases & Action |
|:------|:---------|:----------|:--------------------|
| Authorisation abandonment rate | 🟡 Warning | > 15% drop-off after QR code display or redirect initiation | Users generate the authorisation challenge but never submit the presentation payload. Suggests poor Wallet-side UX, deep-link failure, QR rendering issues, or user confusion about the flow |
| `access_denied` volumetric spike | 🟠 High | > 10% of standard presentation volume | Users are explicitly tapping "Decline" on the Wallet consent screen. Edge case: the RP may be requesting an intimidating array of sensitive attributes in its DCQL query — review the attribute set for data minimisation compliance (D.2.15) |
| Verification SLA breaches | 🟡 Warning | p95 verification pipeline latency > 1000ms | End-to-end decryption, SD-JWT parsing, or future Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) evaluation is CPU-starved. Scale verification worker processes horizontally |
| Presentation from unknown `vct` or `docType` | 🟡 Warning | Spikes or recurring pattern | A Member State may have deployed a new credential schema, or attackers are spoofing experimental credential types. Log and review; update the RP's supported credential type registry if the new `vct` is legitimate |
| Format deprecation usage | ℹ️ Info | Spike in legacy credential formats (e.g., pure mDoc where SD-JWT VC is preferred) | Users with outdated Wallet software are attempting presentations in deprecated formats. Track for graceful deprecation scheduling and user communication |
| Presentation payload assembly delay | 🟡 Warning | > 500ms for payload reassembly | The Wallet transmits large credential fragments, and the RP backend struggles to reassemble them within acceptable latency. Monitor memory buffers and consider payload size limits |
| Sudden drop in overall presentation success rate | 🔴 Critical | Success rate drops below 95% | Systemic failure indicator. Check WRPAC validity, JAR construction logic, Status List availability, and verification SDK health in parallel. Correlate with deployment timestamps to identify regression |

#### 33.3 Audit Trail Requirements

GDPR Art. 30 and DORA Art. 28 require RPs to maintain records of processing. For EUDI Wallet integrations, the audit trail should capture:

| Field | Description | Retention |
|:------|:------------|:----------|
| `timestamp` | ISO 8601 timestamp of presentation | Per data retention policy |
| `session_id` | Internal correlation ID | Per data retention policy |
| `flow_type` | `same-device`, `cross-device`, `proximity-supervised`, `proximity-unsupervised` | Per data retention policy |
| `credential_type` | VCT or docType | Per data retention policy |
| `issuing_country` | MS that issued the credential | Per data retention policy |
| `attributes_requested` | List of claims in DCQL query | Per data retention policy |
| `attributes_received` | List of claims actually received (may differ if partial) | Per data retention policy |
| `verification_result` | `success`, `failed_signature`, `failed_revocation`, `user_denied`, etc. | Per data retention policy |
| `revocation_status` | Mechanism-specific result: not revoked, permanently revoked, profile-permitted suspension, profile-prohibited value, not required, unavailable, or not evaluated | Per data retention policy |
| `status_mechanism` | `short_lived`, `sdjwt_token_status_list`, `mdoc_attestation_status_list`, or `mdoc_identifier_list`, selected from format and controlling profile | Per security evidence policy |
| `status_profile_result` | Credential class, Rulebook/profile version, allowed state vocabulary, and the state-machine result applied | Per security evidence policy |
| `status_trust_context` | List identity, authorized signer/chain fingerprint, governing trust source and anchor generation; hash or redact correlating indices and opaque identifiers | Per security evidence policy |
| `status_unavailable_policy` | Whether status was required, last signed-fresh evidence used, terminal `evidence_incomplete` decision, and User/provider/RP risk-analysis rationale; absent for definitive revocation | Per security evidence policy |
| `trust_snapshot` | Active LoTE/TL version and hash used by the RP Instance, plus fleet-convergence result | Per security evidence policy |
| `wrpac_serial` | Serial number of the WRPAC used | Per data retention policy |
| `end_rp_id` / `end_rp_service_id` | End-RP and Service identifiers selected for the journey | Per data retention policy |
| `intermediary_id` / `intermediary_service_id` | Intermediary and Service identifiers for an intermediated journey; absent for direct presentation | Per data retention policy |
| `end_rp_wrprc_fingerprint` | Fingerprint of the one end-RP WRPRC selected for the Service/intended use | Per security evidence policy |
| `intermediary_wrpac_fingerprint` | Fingerprint of the WRPAC carrying the reciprocal end-RP/Service association | Per security evidence policy |
| `intermediary_association_result` | Reciprocal RP/Service match, agreed verification set, performed results, and bound callback recipient | Per security evidence policy |
| `qes_profile` | For signing events only: CIR-selected ETSI TS 119 432 version/clauses, Annex A vs Annex B/provider-specific branch, negotiated CSC/service-profile version and methods, and profile-compatibility result | Per security evidence policy |
| `qes_signature_profile` | For signing events only: format standard/version, conformance level, algorithm, result shape (`documentWithSignature` / `signatureObject`), and trusted-list/QSCD qualification result—without document content | Per security evidence policy |
| `policy_results` | Per-credential, per-policy pass/fail breakdown (§33.3.1) | Per data retention policy |
| `verification_duration` | ISO 8601 duration of the verification pipeline execution (e.g., `PT0.012S`) | Per data retention policy |
| `policies_evaluated` | Count of verification policies executed | Per data retention policy |

> **GDPR note**: The general audit trail should NOT store the attribute values themselves (e.g., not the family name or date of birth). Store only attribute names and verification results; keep any legally required CDD evidence in a separately governed record set. A portrait is session-only by default and must not leak into logs, debug payloads, or telemetry; any exceptional retention and any third-country/international-organisation transfer need the separate legal decision described in §28.5.3.

> **Wallet-log distinction for intermediated presentations:** `RPI_07` suppresses the intermediary from the Wallet approval screen, but `DASH_03` still requires the Wallet transaction log to record the end RP's trade name, identifier, Service identifier, and establishment Member State from the WRPRC, plus the intermediary's trade name, available contact data, identifier, and Service identifier from the WRPAC. The RP/intermediary operational audit fields above preserve the matching cryptographic and routing evidence; they are not a reason to expose the intermediary in the approval UI or retain credential values.

> **Wallet presentation/issuance log distinction:** Current `DASH_03` also retains the privacy-policy URL, Registrar URL, deletion contacts, supervising-DPA contacts, intended use, and requested/presented attribute **identifiers** for presentation entries. `DASH_05` is a separate issuance entry: it identifies the PID/Attestation Provider and its Service, requested/issued type and count, failure reason or reissuance trigger, and Registrar URL. Neither schema authorises logging disclosed attribute values or confusing the Attestation Provider Service with the Wallet Provider.

##### 33.3.1 Verification Result Object Structure

The canonical verifier-engine result object is defined in Canonical Verification Result and Audit Evidence (§14.11). This section covers the **audit and SIEM projection** of that object: the fields that should be preserved when the result is exported into monitoring, incident response, GDPR processing records, or DORA evidence. Audit systems may redact or aggregate the canonical result, but they should not invent a separate truth about terminal state, policy version, credential-check outcomes, or evidence completeness.

```json
{
  "session_id": "abc-123-def",
  "canonical_result_id": "vr_01HQ7Y4N8K",
  "timestamp": "2026-03-17T14:30:00Z",
  "topology": "intermediated",
  "end_rp_id": "5299001GCLKH6FPVJW75",
  "end_rp_service_id": "urn:eudi:service:de:example-bank:retail-onboarding",
  "intermediary_id": "urn:eudi:rp:de:intermediary-001",
  "intermediary_service_id": "urn:eudi:service:de:intermediary:verification",
  "end_rp_wrprc_fingerprint": "sha256:...",
  "intermediary_wrpac_fingerprint": "sha256:...",
  "intermediary_association_result": "matched",
  "transaction_state": "verified",
  "verified": true,
  "policy_id": "pid-login-high-v3",
  "result_schema_version": "verification-result-v1",
  "policy_results": [
    {
      "credential_index": 0,
      "credential_type": "urn:eudi:pid:1",
      "credential_format": "dc+sd-jwt",
      "policies": [
        {
          "policy": "signature",
          "description": "Cryptographic signature verification",
          "result": "pass"
        },
        {
          "policy": "expiry",
          "description": "Credential not expired (exp claim)",
          "result": "pass"
        },
        {
          "policy": "not_before",
          "description": "Credential validity period started (nbf claim)",
          "result": "pass"
        },
        {
          "policy": "revocation_status",
          "description": "SD-JWT VC Token Status List check (CIR-pinned draft-20 profile)",
          "result": "pass"
        },
        {
          "policy": "holder_binding",
          "description": "KB-JWT presenter matches credential subject (cnf.jwk)",
          "result": "pass"
        },
        {
          "policy": "issuer_trust",
          "description": "Issuer trust resolves through the applicable LoTE or authenticated trusted-list path",
          "result": "pass"
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "status_evidence": [
    {
      "credential_index": 0,
      "credential_class": "PID",
      "mechanism": "sdjwt_token_status_list",
      "profile_version": "CIR-2026-1731",
      "profile_state_result": "not_revoked",
      "list_identity_hash": "sha256:...",
      "index_hash": "sha256:...",
      "authorized_signer_fingerprint": "sha256:...",
      "anchor_generation": "lote-ms-example-2026-07-25",
      "signed_freshness": "valid",
      "unavailable_policy": null
    }
  ],
  "redaction": {
    "attribute_values_logged": false,
    "raw_credential_stored": false,
    "evidence_bundle_ref": "sha256:..."
  },
  "verification_duration": "PT0.045S",
  "policies_evaluated": 6
}
```

Key design principles for the audit projection:

1. **Per-credential granularity** — Combined presentations (§19.5) may contain multiple credentials; each gets its own policy result array. A partial failure (one credential passes, another fails) should be logged with per-credential detail.

2. **Canonical result linkage** — Audit records should link back to the §14 result id/schema version and preserve the same terminal state. A SIEM alert, webhook, operator UI, and audit export may redact different fields, but they should not disagree about whether the presentation was verified.

3. **Policy descriptions** — Human-readable descriptions enable audit reviewers to understand what was checked without needing to consult implementation documentation. This supports DORA's requirement for "clear and comprehensive" ICT incident records.

4. **No attribute values in results** — The projection records the credential *type* and policy *outcomes*, not the attribute values (family_name, birth_date, etc.). This maintains the GDPR principle from §33.3: log attribute *names*, not *values*.

5. **Execution timing** — ISO 8601 duration enables performance monitoring and SLA tracking (§33.1 key metrics). Abnormally long verification times may indicate revocation list fetch failures or certificate chain issues.

#### 33.4 Breach Notification Monitoring (CIR 2025/847)

CIR 2025/847 requires RPs to receive and act on wallet solution security breach notifications within 24 hours (§23.7). The §33.2 monitoring framework should integrate breach notification processing as an additional alert category:

| Category | Alert | Severity | Source |
|:---------|:------|:---------|:-------|
| **Breach Notification** | Wallet solution suspension received | 🔴 Critical | CIRAS / MS notification channel |
| **Breach Notification** | Wallet solution withdrawal received | 🔴 Critical | CIRAS / MS notification channel |
| **Breach Notification** | Wallet solution re-establishment received | 🟡 Medium | CIRAS / MS notification channel |
| **Trust Config** | Wallet solution certification status changed in certified wallet list | 🟡 Medium | Periodic certified list poll |

**CIRAS integration**: From May 2026, breach notifications to the Commission and MS Single Points of Contact flow through CIRAS (Art. 10). RP notification is via the registering MS's notification channel. RPs should proactively establish contact with their MS's Single Point of Contact (Art. 46c(1)) to confirm the notification delivery mechanism (email, API, push notification) and ensure integration with the §33 monitoring pipeline.

**Audit trail extension**: When a presentation is rejected due to a suspended or withdrawn wallet solution, the §33.3 audit trail should include `breach_notification_id` and `breach_notification_timestamp` fields — linking the rejection to the specific breach notification. This provides regulatory compliance evidence demonstrating that the RP acted on the notification within the required timeframe.

## Document Signing and Remote QES

This group covers the integration of Qualified Electronic Signatures (QES) with the EUDI Wallet. It details the three primary signing flow patterns (QTSP Web Portal, Wallet-Channelled, RP-Channelled), the CIR 2026/1731-selected ETSI TS 119 432 V1.3.1 RP-to-Wallet profile, the companion CSC service surface used in concrete deployments, and the RP's obligations when verifying or handling PAdES signatures.

---

### 34. QES Signing Flow Patterns

:::important
Treat the signing-flow choice as a control-boundary decision, not just an integration preference. The selected scenario determines who operates the CSC client, who owns the signing UX and document path, and whether the RP itself inherits deeper ETSI and operational obligations.
:::

#### 34.1 Overview

Document signing is one of three core capabilities of the EUDI Wallet — alongside identification (PID presentation) and attestation presentation (QEAA/PuB-EAA). While the earlier RP-verification sections focus on how RPs verify identity and attributes, this chapter covers the RP's role when the Wallet creates **Qualified Electronic Signatures (QES)** — legally binding signatures equivalent to handwritten signatures under eIDAS 2.0.

The regulatory foundation for document signing is established across multiple instruments:

| Instrument | Key Provisions | RP Relevance |
|:-----------|:---------------|:-------------|
| **eIDAS 2.0, Art. 5a(4)(e)** | Wallet functional requirement to enable qualified electronic signatures and seals | Core capability |
| **CIR 2024/2979, Arts. 11–12, as amended** | Qualified certificates may bind to local/external/remote QSCDs; SCAs may be Wallet Provider-, trust-service-provider-, or **RP-provided**; Wallet Units support the Annex IV interface | Defines the actor split and when an RP becomes an SCA provider |
| **[CIR 2026/1731](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202601731), Annex VI** | From **11 August 2026**, Annex IV selects **PAdES EN 319 142-1 V1.2.1** and **ETSI TS 119 432 V1.3.1 clauses 6.4.3, A.6, A.7, and A.8** | Current implementation target for the Wallet-facing signing interface |
| **ETSI TS 119 432 V1.3.1** | Clause 6.4.3 defines the EUDIW-participating model; Annex A.6–A.8 defines the RP request, Wallet response, integrity processing, and UX rendering | Binding selected profile; its broader clauses remain useful only with their own source/status labels |
| **CIR 2025/1567** | ETSI TS 119 431-1 V1.3.1 for remote QSCD management | QTSP conformance standard |
| **ARF v3 Topic 16** | `QES_06` retains the three remote flow options; `QES_07` is empty; `QES_08` updates signature profiles; `QES_23`-`QES_24a` split QTSP and RP duties | Current Wallet Provider, QTSP, and RP responsibility boundary |

> **Transition note (publication date 2026-07-22):** the former Annex IV text naming CSC API v2.0 remains the pre-amendment rule only until CIR 2026/1731 enters into force on **11 August 2026**. New implementations should target the published replacement now. The replacement is not a generic instruction to relabel every old flow “CSC v2.2”: it selects specific ETSI TS 119 432 clauses.

The RP participates in signing flows in three distinct configurations retained by `QES_06`, each with different responsibilities and integration complexity. This chapter therefore walks through the three actor patterns, then separates three source layers that the earlier edition blurred:

1. **selected legal profile** — ETSI TS 119 432 V1.3.1 clauses 6.4.3 and A.6–A.8;
2. **broader ETSI deployment profile** — client registration/security and remote-signing-service APIs elsewhere in TS 119 432, cited only where a deployment actually adopts them;
3. **reference-library behavior** — concrete `/csc/v2` endpoints and Document Retrieval code, useful as interoperability evidence but not itself the legal floor.

Within the selected profile, Annex A uses OpenID4VP 1.0: `dcql_query` selects an X.509 signing credential, base64url-encoded `transaction_data` carries a `qesRequest`, and the result returns either inline in the VP Token or out of band to `responseURI`. The Wallet verifies any by-reference document checksum, renders the QES transaction and RP origin, obtains explicit consent, and returns a `qesResponse`. TS 119 432's broader architecture also contemplates `openid4vp://` and Digital Credentials API invocation, but exact browser/OS deployment support remains a separately tested channel capability.

TS 119 432 V1.3.1 normatively references CSC API v2.2 and records alignment with v2.2 in its change history. That fact explains the CSC-shaped data and service calls used by the standard; it does **not** make all CSC v2.2 endpoints part of the CIR-selected clause set. `ETSI TR 119 462` remains complementary architecture taxonomy for `Driving Application` / `SCA` / `SCDev` and certificate placement.

> **Disambiguation — SCA**: In this chapter, "SCA" refers to **Signature Creation Application** (ETSI TS 119 432), not Strong Customer Authentication (PSD2) and not the SCA Attestation credential defined by TS12 (§17). These are three entirely different concepts despite sharing the same acronym. Where ambiguity exists, this chapter uses "SCA (Signature)" or "SCA (Payment)". For the full SCA/SUA terminology frame, see §17.1.

##### 34.1.1 ETSI TR 119 462 Functional Model

Alongside the selected ETSI TS 119 432 profile, `ETSI TR 119 462` is useful as **informative architecture guidance**. It does not replace the CIR-selected clauses or the current ARF HLRs. Its value is that it decomposes a signing integration into four wallet-facing interfaces — `signing initiation`, `signature attributes`, `signature activation`, and `identity data` — and separates the business application from the signing application and the signing device.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    signer["Signer"]
    wallet["EUDI Wallet"]
    signer --> wallet

    subgraph stack[" "]
        direction TB
        da["Driving Application"]
        sca["Signature Creation Application"]
        scdev["Signature Creation Device"]
        ca["Certification Authority"]
        da <--> sca
        sca <--> scdev
        scdev <--> ca
    end

    wallet -->|"A. Signing initiation"| da
    wallet -->|"B. Signature attributes"| sca
    wallet -->|"C. Signature activation"| scdev
    wallet -->|"D. Identity data"| ca
```

From the RP perspective, this model is valuable because it explains why the same "QES flow" can still imply different ownership and compliance boundaries:

| Layer | Typical interpretation in `DR-0002` | RP-facing consequence |
|:------|:------------------------------------|:----------------------|
| `Driving Application` | The business application initiating the transaction — in this chapter, typically the RP service itself | Owns document selection, business context, and the decision to start the signature flow |
| `Signature Creation Application` | QTSP portal in Scenario A, wallet-linked component in Scenario B, or RP-controlled application/server in Scenario C | Determines who assembles the signing request, who carries signature attributes, and whether ETSI TS 119 101 obligations can fall on the RP |
| `Signature Creation Device` | Local QSCD or remote QSCD that actually creates the signature | Determines whether the chosen model is local or remote and how much of the key lifecycle sits outside RP control |
| `Certification Authority` / identity-data path | Certificate issuance and onboarding layer feeding certificate and identity data into the signing stack | Explains why certificate model selection and QTSP/issuer relationships matter even when the RP only sees the runtime signing flow |

`ETSI TS 119 432` Figure 22 is a useful complement to that taxonomy because it shows the end-to-end interaction surface between the Wallet, the driving application, the authorization server, and the signature creation service in a single sequence. For browser-based same-device flows, the `User agent -> EUDIW` handoff in this model should be read together with the W3C Digital Credentials API mediation layer discussed in `§11`: `ETSI TS 119 432` explicitly allows the Wallet-facing invocation to happen through Digital Credentials API methods or `openid4vp://`, rather than leaving that browser/OS bridge as an unstated implementation detail.

```mermaid

config:
  themeVariables:
    noteBkgColor: "transparent"
    noteBorderColor: "transparent"
  sequence:
    messageAlign: left
    noteAlign: left
    actorMargin: 250
---
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor User
    participant UA as User agent
    participant EUDIW as EUDIW<br/>SCA + SIC<br/>OAuth2 client
    participant WRP as Wallet Relying Party<br/>Driving application
```

<details><summary><strong>1. User browses the document set in the user agent</strong></summary>

The flow begins in the RP-facing browsing context, where the user agent is already showing the document or transaction the user may later sign. At this point there is no wallet or QTSP state yet; this is still purely the business-document surface controlled by the RP.

**Artifact Produced:** Human-visible unsigned document context in the RP/user-agent surface.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>2. User agent asks the driving application to start signing</strong></summary>

The RP-side `Driving Application` receives the sign request and becomes the main business orchestrator for the rest of the flow. In `DR-0002` terms, this is the point where a generic browser session turns into a signing session with explicit remote-QES context.

```json
{
  "documentId": "contract-2026-07-001",
  "requestedSignatureFormat": "PAdES",
  "requestedConformanceLevel": "AdES-B-B"
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Local RP-side signing-session context.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>3. Driving application asks the EUDIW for document-signing support</strong></summary>

The RP-side driving application pushes the request into the wallet-signing surface so the `SCA`/`SIC` components can prepare the credential-authorization leg. In this generic Figure 22 model, the wallet is not yet creating the signature; it is preparing the user-facing approval and wallet-bound authorization path.

```json
{
  "client_id": "contracts.example-bank.de",
  "transaction_data": [
    "<base64url(qesRequest)>"
  ],
  "response_mode": "direct_post.jwt"
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Wallet-facing signing request handle and transaction context.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>4. Driving application requests an authorization code from the authorization server</strong></summary>

The RP-side client starts the authorization-server interaction needed to reach the signature creation service. This first leg establishes the browser-to-authorization-server path before the user-facing wallet approval is completed.

```http
GET /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=rp-signing-client HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev
```

**Artifact Produced:** Pending authorization transaction at the authorization server.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>5. Driving application submits the richer authorization request</strong></summary>

This is the request carrying the signing and authorization context to the authorization server. In the stronger `ETSI TS 119 432` profile, this is where `PAR`, signed request objects, and `RAR`-style authorization details naturally sit.

```http
POST /par HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

client_id=rp-signing-client&
request=<signed-jar-jwt>&
authorization_details=%5B%7B%22type%22%3A%22https%3A%2F%2Fcloudsignatureconsortium.org%2F2025%2Fcredential%22%7D%5D
```

**Artifact Produced:** Authorization request carrying signing-specific transaction context.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>6. User agent asks the EUDIW for credential authorization</strong></summary>

The browser or user-agent surface now hands the credential-use prompt to the EUDIW side of the flow. This is the transition from RP-side orchestration into wallet-mediated user approval.

**Artifact Produced:** Wallet-visible credential-authorization prompt.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>7. User authorizes credential use in the user agent / wallet flow</strong></summary>

The signer explicitly confirms that the selected signing credential may be used for this transaction. Depending on the deployment, the visible confirmation may be rendered in the browser while the actual approval logic is anchored in the wallet interaction component.

**Artifact Produced:** User-approved credential-use decision.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>8. User agent returns the credential authorization to the EUDIW</strong></summary>

The approved credential-use context is handed back into the wallet-side interaction path so the wallet can produce the approval evidence expected by the authorization server.

```json
{
  "approval": "granted",
  "credentialId": "credential-001",
  "transactionHash": "R7T3KLmP9Qs2Vx..."
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Wallet-side approval evidence tied to the selected credential and transaction.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>9. Driving application confirms the authorization state with the authorization server</strong></summary>

After wallet-side approval, the RP-side client confirms the authorization with the authorization server. This is the bridge from user approval into the server-side code/token path that will finally authorize signature creation.

```http
POST /authorize/confirm HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "state": "credential-state-02",
  "approvalEvidence": "vp_token_or_equivalent"
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Confirmed authorization state at the authorization server.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>10. Authorization server returns the authorization code to the driving application</strong></summary>

The RP-side client now has the code it needs for token exchange. This code represents completion of the user-approved authorization leg and is the pivot into the service/token side of the flow.

```http
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://rp.example.eu/callback?code=cred_auth_code_789&state=credential-state-02
```

**Artifact Produced:** Authorization code bound to the approved signing transaction.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>11. Driving application exchanges the code for an access token</strong></summary>

The RP-side client redeems the returned code at the token endpoint to obtain the token that authorizes the downstream signing-service call.

```http
POST /token HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code&
code=cred_auth_code_789&
client_id=rp-signing-client&
code_verifier=pkce-verifier-02
```

**Artifact Produced:** Token request for signature-service access.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>12. Authorization server returns the access token to the driving application</strong></summary>

The driving application receives the token that authorizes the downstream signing-service call. In stronger profiles this may be sender-constrained and short-lived.

```json
{
  "access_token": "cred_at_eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9",
  "token_type": "DPoP",
  "expires_in": 120
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Access token for the signature-creation service.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>13. Driving application requests the signature operation from the signature creation service</strong></summary>

Using the access token, the RP-side client calls the signature creation service with the actual signing request. Depending on the deployment, this can be `signHash` or `signDoc`; Figure 22 is generic enough to cover both.

```http
POST /signatures/signHash HTTP/1.1
Host: walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev
Authorization: DPoP cred_at_eyJhbGciOi...
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "credentialID": "credential-001",
  "hash": [
    "I8Ck9u/eLZXvbqpxKLX+rFftEzhy6MF61IJCfIUKq02o="
  ],
  "signAlgo": "1.2.840.113549.1.1.11"
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Signature-creation request at the QTSP-side signing service.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>14. Signature creation service returns the signature result to the driving application</strong></summary>

The QTSP-side signing service returns the generated signature output to the driving application. Depending on the model, this may be a detached signature object or material ready to be assembled into a full signed document.

```json
{
  "signatures": [
    "MIIByAYJKoZIhvcNAQcCoIIBuTCCAbUCAQExDzANBglghkgBZQMEAgEFADALBgkqhkiG9w0BBwGg..."
  ]
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Remote-signing result returned from the signature creation service.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>15. Driving application returns the signed document to the user agent</strong></summary>

The RP-side flow completes by handing the signed document back to the user-facing browsing context. In some deployments this means returning a complete `documentWithSignature`; in others it means returning a locator or download response for the assembled signed document.

```json
{
  "documentId": "contract-2026-07-001",
  "resultType": "documentWithSignature",
  "signatureFormat": "PAdES",
  "signedDocumentUri": "https://rp.example.eu/signing/session/abc123/result"
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** User-consumable signed document or signed-document locator returned to the user-agent surface.

</details>

#### 34.2 Three Signing Flow Patterns

ARF HLR QES_06 mandates that Wallet Providers support at least one of three remote QES creation flows. Each flow assigns a different orchestration role to the RP, the Wallet, and the QTSP.

`ETSI TR 119 462` does not replace these three ARF scenarios. It adds a cleaner ownership model for them. Across the three flows below, the RP is always the business initiator of the signing transaction, but it is not always the full **Driving Application** in the strict `ETSI TS 119 432` sense. In Scenario A, the RP mostly hands off to the QTSP portal. In Scenario B, the RP usually remains the business `Driving Application` while the wallet-linked component operates the signing application. In Scenario C, the RP is most clearly the `Driving Application` and may also host or operate the `Signature Creation Application`.

The “CSC client” labels below describe where a concrete remote-signing deployment places its QTSP-facing client. They are **not** a claim that CIR 2026/1731 selects every CSC service endpoint in that leg. The selected legal interface is the RP-to-Wallet profile in TS 119 432 clause 6.4.3 and Annex A.6–A.8; Wallet-to-QTSP or RP-to-QTSP calls must be sourced separately from the broader TS 119 432/CSC profile and the chosen provider's conformance evidence.

| Scenario | Typical Driving Application Placement | Signature Creation Application | Signature Creation Device | Main RP consequence |
|:---------|:--------------------|:-------------------------------|:--------------------------|:--------------------|
| **A — QTSP Web Portal** | RP initiates the business transaction, but the QTSP portal owns the effective end-user driving/signing journey | QTSP online service / portal | Remote QSCD at QTSP | RP initiates and receives the result, but does not operate the CSC client or the signing UX |
| **B — Wallet-Channelled** | RP business application | Wallet-linked signing component | Remote QSCD at QTSP | RP owns the document source and retrieval channel, but the Wallet operates the CSC client and most of the signing UX |
| **C — RP-Channelled** | RP business application / RP server | RP-controlled application or server | Remote QSCD at QTSP | RP operates the CSC client and signing orchestration, so actor-boundary discipline and ETSI TS 119 101 obligations are strongest here |

`ETSI TS 119 432` Figure 12 is the clearest architecture view for the most common wallet-authenticated remote-signing placement: the RP-side `Driving Application`, QTSP-side `SCA`/`SSA`, and the Wallet split across browser/user-agent and wallet-resident interaction components.

