| **SCAL1** | EN 419 241-1 §6 | Authorization grants access to credential for N signatures | ❌ Hashes NOT bound to authorization | Not acceptable for QES |
| **SCAL2** | EN 419 241-1 §7 | Authorization is bound to specific document hashes | ✅ RSSP verifies signHash hashes match authorized hashes | **Required** by QES_23 |

In the EUDI reference implementation, SCAL2 is enforced at the type level — the `signHash` method on `CredentialAuthorized.SCAL2` does not require the caller to re-specify document hashes (they are already bound in the token):

```kotlin
// SCAL2 signHash — hashes already bound at credential authorization time
suspend fun CredentialAuthorized.SCAL2.signHash(
    signingAlgorithmOID: SigningAlgorithmOID,
    signingAlgorithmParams: String? = null,
): Result&lt;SignaturesList>

// SCAL1 signHash — caller must specify hashes (no binding guarantee)
suspend fun CredentialAuthorized.SCAL1.signHash(
    documentDigestList: DocumentDigestList,
    signingAlgorithmOID: SigningAlgorithmOID,
    signingAlgorithmParams: String? = null,
): Result&lt;SignaturesList>
```

##### 35.1.5 Reference Implementation

The EUDI RQES library ecosystem consists of four packages:

| Library | Platform | Purpose |
|:--------|:---------|:--------|
| `eudi-lib-jvm-rqes-csc-kt` | Kotlin/JVM (Android) | CSC client whose current metadata parser requires `specs == "2.2.0.0"`; also provides document hashing and assembly |
| `eudi-lib-ios-rqes-csc-swift` | Swift (iOS) | CSC client with explicit CSC API 2.2 feature tests; some repository prose still uses older “v2.0” / “version 2” wording |
| RQES UI SDK (Android) | Android | Pre-built signing UI screens + flow |
| `EudiRQESUi` | Swift (iOS) | Pre-built signing UI screens + flow |

The core `CSCClient` interface composes 8 capability traits via Kotlin delegation — each trait maps to a distinct phase of the signing flow:

```kotlin
interface CSCClient :
    AuthorizeService,         // Tier 1: Service-level OAuth2
    AuthorizeCredential,      // Tier 2: Credential-level OAuth2 (SCAL2 hash-binding)
    ListCredentials,          // POST /credentials/list
    GetCredentialInfo,        // POST /credentials/info
    SignHash,                 // POST /signatures/signHash
    SignDoc,                  // POST /signatures/signDoc
    CreateSignedDocuments,    // Local: embed signature into PDF (PodofoManager)
    CalculateDocumentHashes   // Local: compute document hash (PodofoManager)
```

The reference wallets configure a demo QTSP endpoint:

```kotlin
// From eudi-ref-android RQESConfigImpl.kt
QtspData(
    name = "Wallet-Centric",
    endpoint = "https://walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev/csc/v2",
    tsaUrl = "https://timestamp.sectigo.com/qualified",
    hashAlgorithm = HashAlgorithmOID.SHA_256,
)
```

Key integration points in the reference wallets:
- **Android**: `DocumentSign` navigation screen, `QrScanFlow.Signature` flow type, `DeepLinkType.RQES` and `DeepLinkType.RQES_DOC_RETRIEVAL` deep link handlers
- **iOS**: `EudiRQESUi` Swift Package, `rqes://oauth/callback` deep link scheme

These libraries are implementation evidence, not legal-profile authorities. The observations above were verified in locally cloned repository snapshots (JVM commit `b5881df1d405492c0f012b88bb47a0dd15db30ea`; iOS commit `c5e2abe51eaad8920aa1d7a8a35dc2b8cddd001a`). A deployment still has to trace its selected endpoints and controls to CIR 2026/1731, ETSI TS 119 432 V1.3.1, the applicable ARF requirements, and its provider agreement.

##### 35.1.6 ETSI TS 119 432 OAuth/FAPI Reference Sequence

The sequence below comes from the **broader** ETSI TS 119 432 V1.3.1 runtime and client-security profile, not from the narrower clauses selected by CIR 2026/1731 Annex VI. Figure 19 provides a concrete OAuth2 Authorization Code + `PAR` / `RAR` deployment model for a high-assurance remote-signing client. It also contemplates the EUDIW being invoked through `openid4vp://` or the **W3C Digital Credentials API**. In browser-based same-device deployments, the `User agent -> EUDIW` transition can therefore map onto the `navigator.credentials.get()` mediation layer covered in `§11`. Treat this as an ETSI-profiled implementation pattern that must be selected in the provider/deployment profile—not as a mandatory Annex VI wire sequence.

```mermaid
---
config:
  themeVariables:
    noteBkgColor: "transparent"
    noteBorderColor: "transparent"
  sequence:
    messageAlign: left
    noteAlign: left
    actorMargin: 250
---
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor User
    participant UA as User agent
    participant EUDIW
    participant DA as Driving Application / SCA
    participant AS as Authorization Server
    participant SCS as Signature Creation Service

    rect rgba(148, 163, 184, 0.14)
    Note over User,SCS: Phase 1 — User initiation and service access bootstrap
    User->>UA: Browse documents
    UA->>DA: Sign document(s) request to remote service
    DA->>AS: Request authorization code for authentication to SCS
    AS-->>DA: Authorization code
    DA->>AS: Exchange code for service access token
    AS-->>DA: Service access token
    Note right of SCS: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(52, 152, 219, 0.14)
    Note over DA,SCS: Phase 2 — Credential discovery and PAR setup
    DA->>SCS: POST credentials/list and credentials/info
    SCS-->>DA: Supported methods and signing credential info
    DA->>AS: Pushed Authorization Request with signed JAR and RAR
    AS-->>DA: request_uri
    Note right of SCS: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(241, 196, 15, 0.14)
    Note over UA,AS: Phase 3 — Wallet-facing approval and credential authorization
    DA-->>UA: Redirection to authorization endpoint
    UA->>EUDIW: Read Authorization Request URI
    EUDIW->>DA: Retrieve request object and qesApprovalRequest
    EUDIW->>AS: Authorization response with VP token
    AS-->>DA: Authorization code
    DA->>AS: Exchange code for credential access token
    AS-->>DA: Credential access token
    Note right of SCS: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(46, 204, 113, 0.14)
    Note over DA,SCS: Phase 4 — Signature creation and result return
    DA->>SCS: Request signatures via signHash or signDoc
    SCS-->>DA: Return signature(s)
    DA-->>UA: Signed document
    Note right of SCS: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end
```

<details><summary><strong>1. User browses the document in the user agent</strong></summary>

The sequence starts in the RP-facing browsing surface before any OAuth, wallet, or QTSP state exists. This separation matters because `ETSI TS 119 432` models the later signing client as a distinct runtime actor rather than as an invisible extension of the browser session.

**Artifact Produced:** Human-visible document context in the RP/user-agent surface.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>2. User agent asks the driving application to start remote signing</strong></summary>

The user agent hands control to the `Driving Application` or `SCA`-side client that will orchestrate the remote-signing flow. In the RP-channelled model this is typically the RP-side signing client; in other deployments it may be another signing application that the RP delegates to.

```json
{
  "documentId": "contract-2026-07-001",
  "signatureFormat": "PAdES",
  "conformanceLevel": "AdES-B-B",
  "qtspId": "walletcentric-sign-service"
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Local signing-session context in the driving application.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>3. Driving application requests a service authorization code from the authorization server</strong></summary>

This first authorization leg is about establishing authenticated access to the remote signing service. It is intentionally separate from the later credential-scoped authorization that will bind the user-approved signing transaction.

```http
GET /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=rp-signing-client&scope=service HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev
```

**Artifact Produced:** Pending service-authentication transaction at the authorization server.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>4. Authorization server returns the service authorization code</strong></summary>

The authorization server returns the first code that the client can redeem for a service-scoped token. This code still represents service discovery access only, not permission to invoke `signHash` or `signDoc`.

```http
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://rp.example.eu/callback?code=srv_auth_code_123&state=service-state-01
```

**Artifact Produced:** Service authorization code bound to the client and redirect context.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>5. Driving application exchanges the service code for a service access token</strong></summary>

The client redeems the first code at the token endpoint so it can call service-discovery APIs. This is the first of the two token exchanges that the article now treats explicitly rather than collapsing into a single OAuth blur.

```http
POST /token HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code&
code=srv_auth_code_123&
client_id=rp-signing-client&
code_verifier=pkce-verifier-01
```

**Artifact Produced:** Service-token request for signing-service discovery.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>6. Authorization server returns the service access token</strong></summary>

The returned token lets the client inspect credentials and supported methods. If this exchange fails with `401` or `invalid_client`, the flow should terminate before the user is pushed into any wallet approval step.

```json
{
  "access_token": "srv_at_eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 300,
  "scope": "service"
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Service access token for credential discovery.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>7. Driving application queries the signature creation service for credentials and methods</strong></summary>

With service access in hand, the client interrogates the remote signing service to discover which credentials, signature methods, and profile features are actually exposed. This is where the stronger `ETSI TS 119 432` runtime profile becomes operationally relevant.

```http
POST /credentials/list HTTP/1.1
Host: walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev
Authorization: Bearer srv_at_eyJhbGciOi...
Content-Type: application/json

{}
```

```http
POST /credentials/info HTTP/1.1
Host: walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev
Authorization: Bearer srv_at_eyJhbGciOi...
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "credentialID": "credential-001",
  "certificates": "chain",
  "authInfo": true
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Credential-discovery requests against the remote signing service.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>8. Signature creation service returns credential metadata and supported methods</strong></summary>

The service answers with credential metadata, supported methods, and capability indicators that shape the next authorization request. In `DR-0002` terms, this is also where the client can discover whether the service exposes the stronger `ETSI TS 119 432`-aligned profile, for example through `oauth2FAPIsupport`.

```json
{
  "credentialID": "credential-001",
  "multisign": 10,
  "SCAL": 2,
  "oauth2FAPIsupport": true,
  "signatures": [
    "signHash",
    "signDoc"
  ]
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Credential metadata and capability surface for the selected credential.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>9. Driving application sends a pushed authorization request with signed JAR and RAR details</strong></summary>

This second authorization leg is the richer one. The client packages the credential-scoped request into a signed request object, pushes it to the authorization server, and carries the `RAR`-style authorization details that bind the later signing action to a specific transaction context.

```http
POST /par HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev
Authorization: Bearer srv_at_eyJhbGciOi...
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

client_id=rp-signing-client&
request=<signed-jar-jwt>&
authorization_details=%5B%7B%22type%22%3A%22https%3A%2F%2Fcloudsignatureconsortium.org%2F2025%2Fcredential%22%2C%22credentialID%22%3A%22credential-001%22%7D%5D
```

**Artifact Produced:** Pushed authorization request carrying the signed JAR and credential-scoped authorization details.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>10. Authorization server returns the request URI</strong></summary>

The authorization server materializes the pushed request as a short-lived `request_uri`. That handle is what the browser and wallet will later resolve, instead of carrying the whole sensitive request through the front channel.

```json
{
  "request_uri": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:request_uri:9c4f2a1e",
  "expires_in": 90
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Short-lived `request_uri` for the wallet-facing authorization leg.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>11. Driving application redirects the user agent to the authorization endpoint</strong></summary>

The client now switches from the back-channel `PAR` phase to the front-channel user interaction phase. The redirect carries the `request_uri` reference rather than restating the full request inline.

```http
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://auth.walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev/authorize?client_id=rp-signing-client&request_uri=urn:ietf:params:oauth:request_uri:9c4f2a1e
```

**Artifact Produced:** Browser redirect into the wallet-facing approval leg.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>12. User agent lets the EUDIW read the authorization request URI</strong></summary>

The user agent hands the authorization request to the EUDIW, which becomes the user-controlled approval surface. In a same-device browser deployment, this is the moment where the RP-side page crosses into the W3C Digital Credentials API / browser mediation layer instead of a plain application redirect. `ETSI TS 119 432` is explicit that this wallet-facing invocation may use Digital Credentials API methods or `openid4vp://`, so the browser-to-wallet bridge here is part of the standards-backed signing flow rather than an article-local convenience assumption.

**Artifact Produced:** Wallet-visible authorization-request handle.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>13. EUDIW retrieves the request object and approval payload</strong></summary>

The wallet resolves the request handle and fetches the approval payload, such as the `qesApprovalRequest` model from `ETSI TS 119 432` Annex `B` when the authorization-server/QTSP side is orchestrating approval. This is where the wallet learns which credential and transaction context it is being asked to approve.

```json
{
  "transaction_data": [
    "eyJ0eXBlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9jbG91ZHNpZ25hdHVyZWNvbnNvcnRpdW0ub3JnLzIwMjUvcWVzLWFwcHJvdmFsIiwicWVzQXBwcm92YWxSZXF1ZXN0Ijp7ImNyZWRlbnRpYWxJRCI6ImNyZWRlbnRpYWwtMDAxIiwibnVtU2lnbmF0dXJlcyI6MX19"
  ],
  "client_id": "rp-signing-client",
  "request_uri": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:request_uri:9c4f2a1e"
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Wallet-resolved approval payload and transaction context.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>14. EUDIW submits the authorization response with the VP token</strong></summary>

After user approval, the wallet returns the authorization response together with the approval evidence. In the wallet-integrated model this can include a `vp_token` carrying the evidence or wallet presentation that the authorization server expects.

```http
POST /authorize/response HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

vp_token=eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiJ9...&
state=credential-state-02
```

**Artifact Produced:** Wallet approval evidence submitted to the authorization server.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>15. Authorization server returns the credential authorization code</strong></summary>

The authorization server now returns the second code, this time representing successful credential-scoped authorization rather than service discovery. This code is the pivot from wallet approval into actual signature invocation rights.

```http
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://rp.example.eu/callback?code=cred_auth_code_789&state=credential-state-02
```

**Artifact Produced:** Credential authorization code bound to the approved signing transaction.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>16. Driving application exchanges the credential code for a credential access token</strong></summary>

The client redeems the second code at the token endpoint. This exchange turns the wallet-backed approval into the concrete token needed for `signHash` or `signDoc`.

```http
POST /token HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code&
code=cred_auth_code_789&
client_id=rp-signing-client&
code_verifier=pkce-verifier-02
```

**Artifact Produced:** Credential-token request tied to the approved signing transaction.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>17. Authorization server returns the credential access token</strong></summary>

The client now holds the credential-scoped token required to invoke signing. In the stronger profile this token may also be sender-constrained and reflect the approved credential, transaction scope, and authorization lifetime.

```json
{
  "access_token": "cred_at_eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9",
  "token_type": "DPoP",
  "expires_in": 120,
  "scope": "credential"
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Credential access token for signature creation.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>18. Driving application requests signatures from the signature creation service</strong></summary>

With the credential token in hand, the client sends the actual signature-creation request to the remote signing service. Depending on the model, this can be `signHash` for pre-hashed inputs or `signDoc` for document-centric server signing.

```http
POST /signatures/signHash HTTP/1.1
Host: walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev
Authorization: DPoP cred_at_eyJhbGciOi...
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "credentialID": "credential-001",
  "SAD": "credential-scope-sad-or-equivalent",
  "hash": [
    "I8Ck9u/eLZXvbqpxKLX+rFftEzhy6MF61IJCfIUKq02o="
  ],
  "signAlgo": "1.2.840.113549.1.1.11"
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Signature-creation request against the QTSP-side service.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>19. Signature creation service returns the signature result</strong></summary>

The QTSP-side service returns the generated signature material. Depending on the chosen result model, the client may receive detached signature objects or data ready to be assembled into a signed document.

```json
{
  "signatures": [
    "MIIByAYJKoZIhvcNAQcCoIIBuTCCAbUCAQExDzANBglghkgBZQMEAgEFADALBgkqhkiG9w0BBwGgggFQMIIBTAIBADCB..."
  ]
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Remote-signing result returned from the QTSP-side service.

</details>
<details><summary><strong>20. Driving application returns the signed document to the user agent</strong></summary>

The client finishes the end-user flow by assembling or relaying the final signed output back to the RP-facing user-agent surface. In a `documentWithSignature` model this may already be a complete signed PDF; in a detached-signature model the client may first need to embed the CMS result before returning it.

```json
{
  "documentId": "contract-2026-07-001",
  "resultType": "documentWithSignature",
  "signatureFormat": "PAdES",
  "signedDocumentUri": "https://rp.example.eu/signing/session/abc123/result"
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** User-consumable signed document or signed-document locator returned to the RP/user-agent surface.

</details>

##### 35.1.7 Client Security Profile and Registration Signals

`ETSI TS 119 432` clauses `6.4.4` and `6.4.5` describe a high-assurance client profile for a wallet, driving application, or signature creation application. These clauses are **outside** the CIR 2026/1731-selected set; they become deployment requirements only when the provider agreement or adopted service profile selects them.

For an RP-side client that adopts this broader profile, the practical controls are:

- **Authorization Code + PKCE (S256)** for the interactive authorization leg
- **PAR + signed JAR** so the authorization endpoint sees only `client_id` and `request_uri`, while the signed request object carries the sensitive authorization details
- **`private_key_jwt`** at PAR and token endpoints as the default client-auth mechanism
- **sender-constrained tokens** via `DPoP` where the service supports them, with mTLS as an equivalent future-facing alternative
- **dynamic or pre-registered client registration** using `jwks` / `jwks_uri`, plus optional `software_statement` and `client_attestation`

This is also a narrow bridge back to the RP registration work from `ETSI TS 119 475`. `ETSI TS 119 432` clause `6.4.5.2` says a driving application or `SCA` client may register using a public key from its **registration certificate**, and may present that certificate again inside `client_attestation`. Where the service profile accepts an EUDI RP registration certificate for that purpose, client registration can reuse the RP identity established in the national register / WRPRC layer. That mapping is not automatic: the RP must confirm certificate acceptance, subject mapping, lifecycle handling, and authorization semantics with the service.

`ETSI TS 119 432` Annex `C` reinforces the same point at the recommendation level: when the EUDIW or an RP-side signing client acts against the authorization server, the strong reference profile is **FAPI 2.0 + PAR + PKCE + `private_key_jwt` + sender-constrained tokens**. RPs adopting the broader profile should therefore treat “plain OAuth around CSC” as incomplete, while keeping the distinction between a recommended ETSI client profile and the clauses legally selected by Annex VI.

#### 35.2 Document Retrieval Protocol

> ⚠️ **Stability warning**: The Document Retrieval protocol is **not part of the CSC API specification or the CIR 2026/1731-selected Annex A schema**. The current JVM library marks it with: *"This flow may be removed in future versions of the library."* Implement it only when the chosen Wallet/library deployment requires it, and isolate it behind an adapter so it can be replaced.

##### 35.2.1 Purpose and Architecture

The Document Retrieval protocol is a current EUDI library bridge between an RP-initiated document exchange and the downstream remote-signing flow. It solves the deployment question: **how does this library profile tell the Wallet which documents to retrieve, and how does the Wallet return the signed results?** It is not the same object model as ETSI TS 119 432 Annex A `qesRequest` / `qesResponse`.

The protocol uses an **OpenID4VP/JAR-based** request/response wrapper around the RP's document exchange:
1. The RP publishes a `request_uri` (via QR code or deep link)
2. The Wallet resolves the URI to a JAR-signed request object
3. The library-specific request object contains a `documents[]` structure with locations, hashes, and access methods
4. After signing, the Wallet dispatches results back to the RP

This flow should be read as a **multi-surface URL-control problem**, not as a single monolithic “signing callback”. At minimum it exposes distinct control surfaces for the request-object host (`request_uri`), the wallet submission target (`response_uri`), and the document fetch origin (`documents[].uri`). Where a product claims an RP-owned façade or signing edge, those surfaces should be evaluated separately rather than rolled up into one capability. See §26.8 and the vendor treatment in §29.6.1.

##### 35.2.2 Document Retrieval and Signing Sequence

```mermaid
---
config:
  themeVariables:
    noteBkgColor: "transparent"
    noteBorderColor: "transparent"
  sequence:
    messageAlign: left
    noteAlign: left
    actorMargin: 250
---
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant User
    participant Wallet as EUDI Wallet
    participant RP as Relying Party

    rect rgba(148, 163, 184, 0.14)
    Note over RP: Phase 1 — Request
    RP->>User: Present QR code / deep link<br/>(contains request_uri)
    User->>Wallet: Scan QR code
    Wallet->>RP: GET request_uri
    RP->>Wallet: Return JAR-signed request object<br/>(document locations + hashes)
    Wallet->>Wallet: Parse and validate request object
    Note right of RP: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(52, 152, 219, 0.14)
    Note over Wallet: Phase 2 — Document Retrieval
    Wallet->>RP: Download document(s) from locations
    RP->>Wallet: Return document content
    Wallet->>Wallet: Compute document hashes<br/>and verify against request object
    Note right of RP: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(46, 204, 113, 0.14)
    Note over Wallet: Phase 3 — Provider-profiled remote signing
    Note over Wallet: [Selected ETSI profile + companion service flow per §35.1]
    Note right of RP: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(241, 196, 15, 0.14)
    Note over RP: Phase 4 — Dispatch
    Wallet->>RP: Send signed documents<br/>and/or signature objects
    RP->>Wallet: Acknowledge receipt
    Note right of RP: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end
```

<details>
<summary><strong>1. Relying Party Server presents QR code or deep link to User</strong></summary>

The RP generates a QR code (for cross-device flow) or a deep link (for same-device flow) containing a `request_uri` that points to a JAR-signed request object. The current library bridge uses the non-standard `mdoc-openid4vp` scheme shown below; this is not the Annex A `openid4vp://` transport selected by CIR 2026/1731:

```
mdoc-openid4vp://https//walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev/rp
    ?request_uri=https://walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev/rp/wallet/sd/abc123
    &client_id=walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev
```

The RP must pre-compute the document hash and embed it in the request object *before* generating the QR code. The `request_uri` is a one-time URL — it should expire after a short TTL (e.g., 5 minutes) to prevent replay attacks.

**Artifact Produced:** One-time QR code payload containing JAR `request_uri`.


</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>2. User scans QR code into EUDI Wallet</strong></summary>

The User opens their EUDI Wallet and scans the QR code (cross-device) or taps the deep link (same-device). A Wallet that implements this library bridge recognises `mdoc-openid4vp` and extracts the `request_uri` and `client_id` parameters. At this point, no document content has been transferred—the Wallet only has a pointer to the RP's request object.

**Artifact Produced:** Extracted `request_uri` + `client_id` tuple in Wallet memory (User layer).

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>3. EUDI Wallet fetches JAR-signed request object from Relying Party Server</strong></summary>

The Wallet performs an HTTP GET on the `request_uri` to fetch the request object. The RP returns a JAR-signed JWT (RFC 9101) containing the full request parameters:

```http
GET /rp/wallet/sd/abc123 HTTP/1.1
Host: walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev
Accept: application/oauth-authz-req+jwt
```

The RP responds with the signed request object. The Wallet validates the JAR signature against the RP's X.509 certificate (resolved via the `client_id_scheme` — see §35.2.4 for the three supported schemes).

**Artifact Produced:** Raw JAR-signed JWT fetched from `request_uri` (Network layer).

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>4. Relying Party Server returns request object with document locations and hashes</strong></summary>

The bridge request object contains library-specific document metadata—locations, hashes, access methods, and labels:

```json
{
  "iss": "walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev",
  "aud": "https://self-issued.me/v2",
  "client_id": "walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev",
  "client_id_scheme": "x509_san_dns",
  "response_mode": "direct_post",
  "response_uri": "https://walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev/rp/callback",
  "documents": [
    {
      "document_id": "contract-2026-07-001",
      "label": "Service Agreement - Example Corp",
      "uri": "https://contracts.example-bank.de/docs/contract-2026-07-001.pdf",
      "hash": "sha256-kF2Qk8mBNqvXMTb3UvZ4WbYJ9R0cvKHdXsU7oP5wF1M=",
      "hash_algorithm_oid": "2.16.840.1.101.3.4.2.1",
      "access_method": "Public"
    }
  ]
}
```

The `hash` field is critical — it binds the request to a specific document version. The `access_method` tells the Wallet how to authenticate when downloading (see §35.2.3 for the full list of supported methods).

**Artifact Produced:** JAR-signed JWT containing explicit document hashes mapping to unauthenticated URIs.


</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>5. EUDI Wallet parses and validates request object from Relying Party Server</strong></summary>

The Wallet performs structural and cryptographic validation of the request object:

1. **JAR signature verification** — validate the JWT signature against the RP's certificate
2. **Certificate chain validation** — verify the RP's X.509 certificate chains to a trusted root
3. **`client_id` matching** — confirm the `client_id` in the JWT payload matches the SAN in the signing certificate
4. **Document metadata parsing** — extract `documents[]` array with URIs, hashes, and access methods
5. **Supported format check** — confirm the Wallet can handle the requested signing format

If any validation step fails, the Wallet rejects the request and displays an error to the User.

**Failure Path:** If `client_id` does not match the SAN in the X.509 certificate, the Wallet aborts with a `DOCUMENT_REQUEST_INVALID_CLIENT` error and does not proceed to document download.

**Artifact Produced:** Validated request object binding the RP identity, document hashes, and `response_uri` (Cryptographic layer).

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>6. EUDI Wallet downloads documents from Relying Party Server</strong></summary>

The Wallet downloads each document from its `uri` using the specified `access_method`. For the common `Public` method, this is a simple HTTP GET:

```http
GET /docs/contract-2026-07-001.pdf HTTP/1.1
Host: contracts.example-bank.de
Accept: application/pdf
```

For `OAuth2` access, the Wallet uses a bearer token provided in the request object. For `BasicAuth`, it uses credentials from the request. The Wallet stores the downloaded document(s) in its secure local storage.

**Artifact Produced:** Raw document bytes stored in Wallet secure local storage (Device layer).

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>7. EUDI Wallet computes document hashes and verifies integrity against Relying Party Server JAR</strong></summary>

After download, the Wallet computes the cryptographic hash of each document and compares it to the `hash` value from the request object. This is the primary defence against document substitution attacks:

```kotlin
val computedHash = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(documentBytes)
val expectedHash = Base64.getUrlDecoder().decode(requestObject.documents[0].hash)
require(computedHash.contentEquals(expectedHash)) {
    "Document hash mismatch — aborting signing flow"
}
```

If any hash mismatch is detected, the Wallet immediately aborts the flow and alerts the User. This prevents an attacker from modifying the document between when the RP computed the hash and when the Wallet downloads it.

```kotlin
// On success — integrity confirmed
// computed: "kF2Qk8mBNqvXMTb3UvZ4WbYJ9R0cvKHdXsU7oP5wF1M="
// expected: "kF2Qk8mBNqvXMTb3UvZ4WbYJ9R0cvKHdXsU7oP5wF1M="  ✅
```

**Artifact Produced:** Hash-verified document binding proof (Cryptographic layer).

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>8. EUDI Wallet performs full CSC API signing flow against Remote QTSP</strong></summary>

The Wallet executes the selected ETSI TS 119 432 profile plus the provider-agreed companion service flow described in §35.1—for example service authorization, credential discovery, PAdES-specific hash computation, SCAL2 credential authorization, `signHash` or `signDoc`, and document assembly where those broader methods are selected. For the complete deployment example, see the Scenario B walkthrough (§34.2.2, steps 4–10). The bridge itself does not establish which CSC methods or OAuth controls are legally required.

**Artifact Produced:** PKCS#1 signature value returned from Remote QTSP QSCD (Protocol layer).

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>9. EUDI Wallet dispatches signed documents to Relying Party Server</strong></summary>

After signing, the Wallet sends the results back to the RP at the `response_uri` specified in the request object using `direct_post`:

```http
POST /rp/callback HTTP/1.1
Host: walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "document_id": "contract-2026-07-001",
  "documentWithSignature": "&lt;base64-encoded-signed-PDF>",
  "signature_format": "PAdES",
  "conformance_level": "ADES_B_B"
}
```

The RP can request either `documentWithSignature` (complete signed PDF — the Wallet embeds the CMS signature into the PDF) or `signatureObject` (detached CMS signature bytes — the RP assembles the final PDF server-side). See §35.2.5 for the full dispatch specification.

**Artifact Produced:** Signed PAdES document dispatched to Relying Party `response_uri` (Network layer).

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>10. Relying Party Server acknowledges receipt and validates PAdES signature</strong></summary>

The RP validates the received signed document (PAdES signature verification per ETSI EN 319 102-1), stores it, and sends an acknowledgement response to the Wallet:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "status": "received",
  "document_id": "contract-2026-07-001"
}
```

The Wallet displays a confirmation to the User indicating that the signing flow is complete. The RP logs the signing event per §35.6 (transaction logging requirements).

**Failure Path:** If the provided `document_id` does not map to an active signing session managed by the RP, the inbound callback is forcefully terminated with an `HTTP 404` and anomalous behavior metric incremented.

**Audit Telemetry:** `RP_QES_RECEIVED` recorded by the main accounting ledger linking the session reference.


</details>
<br/>

The current library bridge uses this `mdoc-openid4vp` request URI format:

```
mdoc-openid4vp://https//walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev/rp
    ?request_uri=https://walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev/rp/wallet/sd/{sessionId}
    &client_id=walletcentric.signer.eudiw.dev
```

##### 35.2.3 Document Access Methods

The current library bridge models the following document-access methods. These values describe that bridge, not the CIR-selected Annex A `qesRequest` schema:

| Method | Description | Use Case |
|:-------|:-----------|:---------|
| `Public` | Document at a public URL — no authentication needed | Publicly available contracts |
| `BasicAuth` | HTTP Basic authentication | Simple authenticated access |
| `DigestAuth` | HTTP Digest authentication | More secure than Basic |
| `OAuth2` | OAuth 2.0 bearer token | Enterprise document management |
| `OTP` | One-time password provided in the request | Time-limited access |

##### 35.2.4 Client Authentication

The current Document Retrieval bridge uses **JAR (JWT-Secured Authorization Request)** for request integrity and implements the following client ID schemes. They must not be generalized into the selected Annex A profile without a separate conformance mapping:

| Scheme | Mechanism | Verification |
|:-------|:----------|:-------------|
| `x509_san_uri` | X.509 certificate with URI in Subject Alternative Name | Wallet matches client_id against SAN URI |
| `x509_san_dns` | X.509 certificate with DNS name in Subject Alternative Name | Wallet matches client_id against SAN DNS |
| `pre_registered` | Pre-registered client ID (RFC 6749 default) | Wallet has prior knowledge of client |

> **Cross-references**: §10.3 (JAR construction), §11.3.1 (client ID schemes in OpenID4VP). The bridge reuses related JAR and client-identity machinery, but that reuse does not make its `documents[]` payload a standard OpenID4VP presentation request.

##### 35.2.5 Response Dispatch

After signing, the Wallet dispatches results back to the RP. The response can include:

| Field | Content | When Used |
|:------|:--------|:----------|
| `documentWithSignature` | Complete signed PDF documents | RP wants ready-to-store signed documents |
| `signatureObject` | Standalone signature values (detached) | RP wants to assemble the signed document itself |

The selected result shape depends on the signing request and implementation profile. For PAdES—the mandatory **Wallet capability**—`documentWithSignature` is typical because the Wallet or signing stack embeds the signature into the PDF and returns the complete signed file. A detached `signatureObject` still requires an assembly step.

`ETSI TS 119 432` makes this choice more precise than the older article wording. The distinction is not an implementation quirk; it is part of the result model:

- **`signDoc`-oriented flows** naturally align with `documentWithSignature`, because the caller is asking the remote signing service or wallet-side signing stack to return a finished AdES document.
- **`signHash`-oriented flows** naturally align with `signatureObject`, because the immediate output is a detached signature over an already prepared hash set, unless the Wallet or RP performs the final PAdES assembly before dispatch.
- **`responseURI`** is only the transport decision. It controls whether the `qesResponse` comes back inline in the VP Token or is POSTed out of band; it does **not** decide whether the payload is `documentWithSignature` or `signatureObject`.

`ETSI TS 119 432` Annex `B` also defines a bounded secondary approval model here: `qesApprovalRequest` with transaction type `https://cloudsignatureconsortium.org/2025/qes-approval`. That model is useful when the Wallet is approving a signature creation initiated elsewhere by the QTSP / authorization server. It should not be conflated with Annex `A`'s `qesRequest`, which is the stronger RP-facing model when the RP is asking the Wallet to request the QES itself.

#### 35.3 Signature Formats and Conformance

##### 35.3.1 Mandatory Format: PAdES

CIR 2026/1731 replaces the relevant Annex IV entry with **ETSI EN 319 142-1 V1.2.1**. From its application date of **11 August 2026**, the Wallet Provider must ensure that Wallet Units can sign PDF documents using that PAdES baseline. This is the binding Wallet capability floor; it does not mean that every individual SCA or every transaction must output PDF when another supported format is selected.

PAdES is a standard for embedding digital signatures into PDF documents, including:
- The signature value (PKCS#1 or PKCS#7/CMS)
- The signing certificate (X.509)
- An optional qualified timestamp (RFC 3161)
- Optional revocation information (OCSP/CRL responses for long-term validation)

At the API layer, this also explains why `documentWithSignature` is the dominant RP-facing result for PAdES: the signature is embedded into the PDF container before the final artifact is returned. Where the flow instead stops at raw signature values, the result remains a `signatureObject` and an RP-side or Wallet-side assembly step must still convert that detached output into a finished PAdES document.

##### 35.3.2 Optional Formats

ARF v3.0.0 `QES_08` carries the full Wallet format profile. It repeats the PAdES capability as mandatory and defines four additional SHOULD-level format families:

| Format | Standard | CSC Code | Media Type | Use Case |
|:-------|:---------|:---------|:-----------|:---------|
| **PAdES** | ETSI EN 319 142-1 V1.2.1 | `P` | PDF | **Mandatory Wallet capability** — human-readable PDF documents |
| XAdES | ETSI EN 319 132-1 V1.3.1 | `X` | XML | SHOULD — XML documents and B2B data exchange |
| JAdES | ETSI TS 119 182-1 V1.2.1 (2024-07) | `J` | JSON | API payloads, JSON data |
| CAdES | ETSI EN 319 122-1 V1.3.1 (2023-06) | `C` | Binary | Binary data, arbitrary content |
| ASiC | ETSI EN 319 162-1/2 V1.1.1 (2016-04) | — | Container | Multiple files, package signing |

`QES_07` is empty in ARF v3.0.0 and therefore supplies no independent protocol or version requirement. Implementations should not cite it as authority for CSC API v2.0 or any other signing interface.

##### 35.3.3 Conformance Levels

Each signature format supports multiple conformance levels, determining the amount of validation information embedded:

| Level | Code | Content | Long-Term Validity |
|:------|:-----|:--------|:-------------------|
| **Baseline** | `ADES_B_B` | Signature value + signing certificate | ❌ No — depends on real-time revocation |
| **With Timestamp** | `ADES_B_T` | + qualified timestamp | Partial — proves signing time |
| **Long-Term** | `ADES_B_LT` | + revocation data (OCSP/CRL) | ✅ Yes — self-contained validation |
| **Long-Term Archival** | `ADES_B_LTA` | + archive timestamp | ✅ Yes — re-stampable for decades |

The reference implementation defaults to `ADES_B_B` (baseline) but supports all four levels. RPs accepting signed documents should verify at least `ADES_B_B` and SHOULD request `ADES_B_LT` or `ADES_B_LTA` for documents with long retention periods.

The conformance-level choice is therefore separate from the result-shape choice:

- `signHash` vs `signDoc` determines whether the immediate result is closer to a detached signature or a finished signed document
- `documentWithSignature` vs `signatureObject` determines what the RP receives
- `ADES_B_B` / `T` / `LT` / `LTA` determines how much validation evidence is embedded into that result

Those dimensions are also separate from the **qualified-status** decision. A PAdES document at `ADES_B_LT` or `ADES_B_LTA` may carry rich embedded evidence, but the RP still reaches a legally meaningful `QES` / `QSeal` conclusion only after combining technical AdES validation with the trusted-list-based certificate, service, and `QSCD` procedures described by `ETSI TS 119 615`.

##### 35.3.4 Timestamping

Qualified timestamps (per Regulation (EU) No 910/2014, Art. 41–42) provide legally binding proof of the time a signature was created. The EUDI reference implementation uses a qualified TSA (Timestamp Authority):

```
TSA URL: https://timestamp.sectigo.com/qualified
```

For `ADES_B_T`, `ADES_B_LT`, and `ADES_B_LTA` conformance levels, a qualified timestamp is mandatory. The timestamp is obtained via RFC 3161 (Time-Stamp Protocol) and embedded in the PAdES signature.

#### 35.4 RP Obligations for Signing

##### 35.4.1 Topic 16 Responsibility Split

Topic 16 is mostly a Wallet Provider and QTSP requirement set. For RPs, the critical point is to preserve the actor boundary:

| Requirement cluster | Direct actor | RP consequence |
|:--------------------|:-------------|:---------------|
| `QES_01`-`QES_04` | Wallet Provider | Wallets must support qualified certificates bound to local, external, or remote QSCDs, and must provide secure User authentication plus signature/seal invocation. RPs consume the resulting signing capability; they do not inspect the QSCD directly. |
| `QES_05` | Wallet Provider | Wallet Units must support User enrolment to a remote QES Provider unless they use local or external QSCDs. RPs that route Users into remote signing should not assume enrolment has already happened. |
| `QES_06`-`QES_08` | Wallet Provider | Wallets support at least one of the three remote signing patterns. `QES_07` is empty. `QES_08` requires PAdES EN 319 142-1 V1.2.1 capability and recommends XAdES V1.3.1, JAdES V1.2.1, CAdES V1.3.1, and ASiC V1.1.1. |
| `QES_10`-`QES_14` | Wallet Provider / SCA | Where the SCA is in the Wallet Unit, the Wallet presents the document/data representation, computes digest material, supports local or remote signing, logs signing/sealing transactions, and obtains explicit User authorisation. |
| `QES_16`-`QES_17a` | Wallet Provider / external SCA | Wallets should support multiple-signatory scenarios, must show signature-creation confirmation, and external SCAs must return the signature-creation outcome to the Wallet Unit. |
| `QES_19` | Wallet Provider | When the SCA is part of the Wallet Unit and QSCD-managed keys are used, the Wallet-side SCA supports ETSI TS 119 101. This is separate from the RP-side `QES_24a` duty below. |
| `QES_23`-`QES_24` | QTSP | Remote QES components must support ETSI TS 119 431-1, ETSI TS 119 431-2, ETSI TS 119 432, SCAL2, and, where the QTSP provides the SCA, ETSI TS 119 101. |
| `QES_24a` | Relying Party | Only an RP that provides the Signature Creation Application in an RP-centric flow must support ETSI TS 119 101. |

##### 35.4.2 QES_24a: The RP's Core Signing Obligation

QES_24a is the **only High-Level Requirement that directly obligates Relying Parties** in the context of document signing:

> **QES_24a**: "Relying Parties providing the Signature Creation Application in a Relying Party-centric flow SHALL support ETSI TS 119 101."

This means: if an RP operates in **Scenario C** (RP-channelled remote QES, §34.2.3) **and actually provides the SCA**, it must support **ETSI TS 119 101**—the ETSI standard for policy and security requirements for signature creation and signature validation applications. An RP-controlled user journey alone is not enough to assign the SCA role. When that role does apply, the standard covers:

- Security requirements for the SCA implementation
- Policy requirements for signature creation operations
- Audit trail requirements for signing events
- Key management practices for the SCA's cryptographic operations
- User authentication requirements within the SCA

##### 35.4.3 When Is an RP "Providing" an SCA?

Art. 12(1) of CIR 2024/2979 states that SCAs may be "provided by a wallet provider, by a provider of qualified trust services, or by a **wallet-relying party**." An RP is likely "providing" an SCA when the contractual and technical architecture assigns it the signature-creation application controls, including:

1. **Operates the signing application** — selects the QTSP/service profile, manages the remote-signing interaction, and controls the document flow (Scenario C)
2. **Hosts the document and hash computation** — the User's document is on the RP's infrastructure and the RP computes the hash
3. **Channels the authorization** — the RP mediates between the Wallet (for User auth) and the QTSP (for signing)

An RP is **not** providing an SCA merely because it redirects the User to a QTSP portal (Scenario A), supplies a document, hosts a callback, or invokes a Wallet whose own SCA performs the signing work (Scenario B). Record the role allocation in the QTSP/provider contract and system architecture rather than inferring it from a single endpoint.

##### 35.4.4 Free-of-Charge QES

Art. 11(3) of CIR 2024/2979 and `QES_02` require natural persons to have **free-of-charge access through the Wallet Solution** to QES for non-professional purposes. `QES_02` covers qualified signatures or seals over both User-provided and RP-provided data and allows the SCA to be part of the Wallet Solution or external to it. The direct ARF obligation falls on the **Wallet Provider**, not on every ordinary verifier RP.

An RP should therefore avoid presenting its own fee as a charge for the Wallet-provided free QES capability. Whether an RP may charge for a wider service, a professional use, or an added signing-orchestration service depends on its role, contract, and applicable consumer/sector law; `QES_02` alone does not allocate every QTSP cost or establish a universal RP pricing prohibition.

##### 35.4.5 What You See Is What You Sign (WYSIWYS)

QES_10 requires that when the SCA is part of the Wallet Unit, it presents the document representation to the User before signing. For RPs:

- In **Scenario A**: WYSIWYS is the QTSP's responsibility
- In **Scenario B**: WYSIWYS is the Wallet's responsibility — the Wallet displays the document before invoking CSC API
- In **Scenario C**: WYSIWYS is a **shared responsibility** — the RP provides the document and signing context, while the Wallet/SCA presents the User-facing representation. Where the CIR-selected Annex A flow is used, ETSI TS 119 432 Annex A.8 defines the `qesRequest` display/approval interaction and `qesResponse`; Annex B `qesApprovalRequest` is a different, approval-only model. Do not substitute the payment SCA `transaction_data` profile for either QES model.

##### 35.4.6 Signature Creation Confirmation

`QES_17` and `QES_17a` add an outcome loop that is easy to miss in RP-centric designs: after signature creation, the Wallet Unit must inform the User about the outcome, and an external SCA must return the outcome of the signature-creation process to the Wallet Unit after the User authorises private-key use. For RP-channelled signing, this means the RP cannot treat a successful CSC `signHash` response as the only completion event; the wallet-facing path also needs a clear success/failure/cancelled outcome so the Wallet can complete its User confirmation and transaction-log obligations.

#### 35.5 Trust Verification for QESRCs

##### 35.5.1 QTSP Qualification Verification

QES_15 requires that in remote signing scenarios, the Wallet verifies that the QESRC (Qualified Electronic Signature Remote Creation) Provider is part of a **qualified trust service**. This verification uses the same Trusted List infrastructure described in §5.5:

1. The Wallet obtains the RSSP's X.509 certificate from the `/info` or `/credentials/info` endpoint
2. The Wallet traces the certificate chain to a root CA
3. The Wallet authenticates the `LOTL`, authenticates the relevant national Trusted List, and runs trusted-list **service matching** for the certificate and time of interest rather than stopping at a bare CA lookup
4. The Wallet derives the time-specific outcome for the relevant certificate/service tuple — for example whether the certificate maps to a qualified signature or seal service, and whether later `QSCD`-specific checks are needed — before accepting the signing context
5. If the resulting trusted-list outcome is `Not_Qualified` or `Indeterminate`, the signing operation cannot be treated as a qualified-signing path

The important implementation boundary is that **certificate-path success is not enough**. Technical validation proves that the RSSP certificate chains correctly and that the AdES object is structurally sound. `ETSI TS 119 615` is the additional layer that turns that technical result into a trusted-list-backed conclusion about qualified trust-service status, `QSCD` status, and related service roles.

For natural-person signing certificates, the certificate-profile check is also not just "chain valid". Draft ETSI EN 319 412-2 V2.5.0 makes the RP/QTSP validation surface more specific: the certificate should expose the appropriate key usage for content commitment/signing, avoid unsafe mixed key-usage assumptions in uncontrolled environments, carry certificate policies consistent with any EU qualified-certificate QCStatements, and expose CRL/OCSP status pointers unless validity-assured/no-revocation-available semantics apply. These are X.509 certificate-profile checks; they do not change SD-JWT VC or mdoc Status List handling.

##### 35.5.2 CIR 2025/1567: SSASP Conformance

QTSPs managing remote QSCDs must conform to the remote-QES standard stack required by `QES_23`: **ETSI TS 119 431-1**, **ETSI TS 119 431-2**, **ETSI TS 119 432**, and **SCAL2** under CEN EN 419 241-1. CIR 2025/1567 adapts ETSI TS 119 431-1 V1.3.1 for remote QSCD management. Key adaptations include:

| Adaptation | Requirement |
|:-----------|:-----------|
| Cryptographic controls | Aligned with ENISA Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms |
| Personnel controls | Regular training updates (at least every 12 months) on new threats |
| Network security | Quarterly vulnerability scans; firewalls configured to deny-all except required protocols |
| Termination plan | Must comply with implementing acts per Art. 24(5) of eIDAS |
| QSCD certification | Practice statement must reference QSCD certification per Regulation Annex II |

For RPs operating in Scenario C (RP-channelled) that select the QTSP, the RP should verify that the selected QTSP has been assessed and listed per these requirements. This is an operational due diligence obligation, not a protocol-level check.

The conformity packet should also identify the provider's current `ETSI EN 319 401` baseline assessment and the service-specific assessment that refines it. A generic EN 319 401 statement without the applicable remote-signing, qualified-certificate, validation, or other service overlay is insufficient evidence for selecting a particular qualified service.

##### 35.5.3 Multi-QTSP Considerations

QES_18 mandates that Wallet Providers configure at least one **default qualified signing service**. However, Users may have credentials at multiple QTSPs. RPs should be aware of:

- In **Scenario A/B**: The User or Wallet selects the QTSP — the RP has no control
- In **Scenario C**: The RP selects the QTSP — the RP must verify qualification
- No standardized **QTSP discovery protocol** exists — this is tracked as Open Question #23 in §38

#### 35.6 Transaction Logging for Signing

`QES_13` requires Wallet Units to log electronic signing and sealing transactions. `DASH_04` supplies the current minimum event-content floor:

| Field | Required content | Source |
|:------|:-----------------|:------|
| Transaction classification | Electronic signature or electronic seal transaction | `QES_13` |
| Date/time | Date and time of the transaction | `DASH_04` |
| Signed material | The data or document, **if available** to the Wallet Unit | `DASH_04` |
| Failure reason | Reason the transaction failed, **if applicable** | `DASH_04` |

QTSP identity, credential identifier, signature format, document hash/reference, completion state, correlation ID, and validation outcome can be valuable **additional operational telemetry**, but `QES_13` / `DASH_04` do not by themselves make each of those fields part of the mandatory Wallet log floor. Where added, minimize document content and unique credential identifiers, protect the log as sensitive data, and document the retention and User-access policy.

CIR 2024/2979 Art. 9(1) confirms the scope: transactions shall include "electronic signing and sealing."

For RPs, the key implication is that signing requests can be recorded in the User's Wallet transaction log under the Topic 19 / DASH signing-event rules. As noted in Finding #22 (§22), retained, exported, or migrated log entries make over-requesting or unnecessary signature creation attempts discoverable by Users and auditors.

> **Cross-references**: §33 (Monitoring, Observability), §22 (RP Obligations — data deletion and DPA reporting).

#### 35.7 Representative Signing: Mandate and QES

When a representative signs a document on behalf of another entity using QES, the business process requires an authority decision in addition to ordinary signer authentication and signing. The QES proves the natural person's signature; it does not by itself prove representative authority. Any signature-embedded role or authority evidence must follow the selected AdES/QTSP profile rather than RP-invented fields.

**Pre-Signing Scope Check**

Before initiating the QES flow, the responsible RP, QTSP, or signature-attribute collection component verifies that the accepted authority artifact covers the signing operation under its governing profile:

1. **Operation match**: Map the requested signature act to the Rulebook, digital EU PoA template, or EBW mandate profile's exact operation semantics; `"contract_signing"` is only an illustrative local vocabulary
2. **Constraints**: Evaluate any profile-defined value, jurisdiction, document, counterparty, or joint-representation constraints
3. **Temporal validity**: Ensure the authority evidence remains current at the authorization point, applying its authenticated validity fields
4. **Lifecycle evidence**: Apply the profile-selected short-lived, status, or register-backed mechanism; obtain newer evidence only when the earlier result no longer satisfies signed freshness and risk policy

**Signature Metadata**

The selected AdES/QTSP profile determines whether representation metadata can be embedded and how. The following are conceptual needs, not interoperable literal field names:

| Evidence need | Profile-controlled realization |
|:--------------|:-------------------------------|
| **Representative role** | A standards-defined claimed/certified role only where the selected profile supports and constrains it |
| **Commitment semantics** | A registered commitment-type OID only when its published semantics match the act; never a custom reinterpretation |
| **Represented entity** | Signed-document content or a profile-defined signed attribute where legally required and interoperable |
| **Authority evidence link** | A profile-defined reference/hash when supported; otherwise preserve the verified authority package in the RP/QTSP evidence record |

> **RP implementation note**: CSC `signHash` does not create arbitrary interoperable PAdES/XAdES/CAdES attributes merely because an RP adds JSON metadata. In Scenario C, send only parameters supported by the selected QTSP/profile and preserve the RP authority decision separately. In Scenarios A and B, the QTSP or attribute-collection component must support the same profile end to end.

> **ETSI TR 119 462 architecture note**: In representative and other attributed-signature flows, the business RP is not always the only relying party in the signing stack. An external `SCA` can become the effective RP for collecting signature attributes that will be embedded in the signed document, while the business RP remains the `Driving Application`. `ETSI TR 119 462` uses `SIC_EAA` for authenticator- or interaction-side artifacts and `SC_EAA` for certificate-information artifacts in this broader model. This is useful architecture guidance for deciding which component requests mandate-derived attributes and who is responsible for embedding them, but it is not yet a settled interoperability profile for carrying those artifacts end to end.

> **EAA certificate-binding note**: ETSI TR 119 479-1 treats certificate/signature-context binding as a separate EAA binding family from identity binding and wallet binding. For representative QES this means the RP should preserve the mandate/EAA evidence used before signing and, where the selected PAdES/XAdES/CAdES profile supports it, embed or reference the mandate evidence in signed attributes. This is architecture guidance until the future EAA-in-AdES profile settles the exact carriage rules.

**WYSIWYS Display**

The Wallet's What-You-See-Is-What-You-Sign display (§35.4.4) should clearly indicate representative capacity:

- Display: "You are signing as **[representative name]** on behalf of **[legal entity name]**"
- Show the mandate scope restriction that authorises this specific signing operation
- If `max_transaction_value` is set, display the ceiling alongside the document value

**Dual Signature and Joint Representation Scenarios**

Some corporate-governance frameworks require two or more representatives to act jointly (*Gesamtvertretung*). The selected legal/authority profile—not an assumed `joint_representation` claim—must identify the required actors and combination rule:

1. **Sequential signing**: The RP obtains the first signature, then initiates a second QES flow with the joint partner — each partner signs the same document hash
2. **Parallel signing**: Both partners receive the document simultaneously and sign independently — the RP collects both signatures before finalising
3. **Validation**: The business validator verifies every required signature and the governing joint-authority condition using profile-defined evidence. Illustrative `joint_partner_ids` fields are not interoperable until a profile assigns them.

> **Cross-references**: §20.8.5 (mandate verification flow), §20.8.10 (mandate and QES integration overview), §20.6.3 (joint representation orchestration).

---

## Synthesis and Conclusions

This final group synthesises the technical investigation into actionable guidance. It presents evidence-rated findings on the current state of RP integration, prioritised architectural recommendations for implementers, and open questions representing unresolved challenges in the EUDI ecosystem.

---

### 36. Findings

:::important
Treat these findings as the evidence base for architecture, procurement, and compliance planning, not as a narrative recap. They identify where the RP's real delivery risk sits, which gaps are ecosystem-level versus implementation-level, and which assumptions are unsafe to carry into rollout.
:::

The findings are grouped by implementation decision surface rather than by discovery order. The original finding numbers are intentionally preserved so earlier references, review comments, and source notes remain traceable while the final synthesis now follows the baseline-first document structure.

#### 36.1 Baseline, Trust, and Credential Model Findings

1. **The RP integration surface is larger than anticipated.** An RP depends on at least six distinct external capability classes: registration administration, Access-CA and mandatory Registration-Certificate-Provider issuance, LoTE/trusted-list discovery, Wallet Units through OpenID4VP or ISO 18013-5, profile-selected credential/status sources, and sector extensions such as signing or authentic-source services. A Registrar API can support administration and publication, but is not a presentation-time substitute for the carried WRPRC. This creates a significant system-integration burden.
2. **Two parallel credential format stacks create implementation complexity.** Supporting both SD-JWT VC (JSON/JWT-based) and mdoc (CBOR-based) requires two complete verification pipelines, including different selective disclosure models, different device binding verification, and different trust anchor formats.
3. **The trust model has no single point of failure but many points of coordination.** The LoTE hierarchy, the authenticated `LOTL` / national trusted-list path where qualified outputs matter, mandatory access/registration-certificate validation, and profile-selected credential/status verification create a robust but operationally complex trust model. The ARF role, lifecycle, and reference-architecture diagrams make the implementation boundary sharper: RP authentication material, issuer trust/status, and wallet/provider assurance are separate operational planes, not one generic trust store.
17. **ARF 3.0 closes the ordinary-RP WUA ambiguity by making WIA/KA issuance-only.** `CIR 2026/1731` deleted the former `CIR 2024/2982` Article 3(8) RP-request path, while EC TS03 V1.5.2 defines WUA as the WIA+KA umbrella used exclusively by PID/EAA Providers during OID4VCI issuance. Ordinary verification is issuer-mediated; a dual-role organisation needs provider-certificate, WIA/KA, security-level, maintenance-period, and key-binding gates in its issuer pipeline—not a generic presentation WUA verifier. (§5.4, §13.9.2, §17.5, D.2.41)
18. **Device binding is format- and profile-dependent.** ARF v3.0 requires it for PIDs and ISO/IEC 18013-5 attestations, recommends it for SD-JWT VC attestations, and permits non-device-bound attestations. RPs must validate the applicable KB-JWT or mdoc `DeviceAuth` where required, can request cryptographic holder binding through the supported OpenID4VP/DCQL profile, and must produce an explicit accept/step-up/reject result when a permitted credential lacks that evidence; no generic LoA follows from the format alone. (§13.9.3)
20. **Credential churn is a designed privacy feature, not an operational anomaly.** ARF §7.4.3.5 and Annex Topic 10 establish that Wallet Solutions must support once-only and limited-time attestation strategies, may support rotating-batch and per-RP strategies, and use provider `credential_reuse_policy` metadata to steer Wallet behaviour. RPs should expect the same user to present structurally different attestation instances across sessions — with different salts, keys, status indices, and signatures — and should never rely on attestation-level identifiers for session continuity.
21. **Certificate Transparency for WRPACs now has concrete SCT failure semantics, while EU CT operations remain unsettled.** CIR 2025/848 Annex IV §3(j), Topic S, ETSI TS 119 411-8, and ARF Topic 55 make CT logging relevant for Access CAs. If an access-certificate CT log is available, Topic 55 requires Access CAs to include at least one SCT and Wallet Units to treat a missing valid SCT as RP-authentication failure under `RPA_06a`. ETSI TR 119 411-9 sharpens the ecosystem role model around TSP-CAs, log operators, monitors, auditors, and supervisory governance. RPs should ensure their WRPAC issuance setup can satisfy the SCT requirement, monitor for unauthorized certificates, and distinguish rogue issuance from temporary log / `MMD` / inclusion-evidence issues. The unresolved part is EU log admission, lifecycle, governance, and current deployment baseline.
22. **The Wallet's transaction log creates a retention-governed forensic record of RP attribute requests.** Topic 19 / TS10 records identifiers for claims requested versus claims actually presented, not the disclosed attribute values themselves. The log can be exported or migrated under the Wallet's portability rules, and over-requesting remains discoverable by Users, DPAs, and auditors while the relevant entries are retained, exported, or restored.
23. **Embedded Disclosure Policies are Wallet-side decision inputs, not RP-visible authorization codes.** Topic 43 places EDPs by value in issuer metadata for QEAAs, PuB-EAAs, and non-qualified EAAs; Wallets store them locally, evaluate them with RP/intermediary information, show the outcome to the User, and let the User deny or allow presentation. RPs should treat missing or denied attestations neutrally because they cannot tell whether the cause was EDP policy, User refusal, credential absence, or another Wallet-side condition.
35. **The EUDI ecosystem's trust model is X.509-only for the mandatory interoperability core, but permits alternative trust for some non-qualified EAAs.** ARF's Issue #278 clarification and current trust chapters preserve the alternative-framework branch for eligible non-qualified EAAs. The pinned 20 July 2026 EC catalogue contains only PID and mDL Rulebooks and neither mandates a DID method. RPs therefore need no DID resolver for the mandatory PID/QEAA/PuB-EAA/ISO-mdoc core, but must dispatch any future non-qualified EAA through its actual Rulebook rather than assuming the branch can never be used. (§7.2)
36. **Platform-mediated presentation does not itself create a DID requirement.** The browser Digital Credentials API is a mediation surface, not a trust model; the actual protocol and credential profile determine issuer authentication and key resolution. For the documented Apple/Safari and Android/Chrome mdoc paths, verifier trust remains the ISO/EUDI X.509 path. Do not generalise that observation into a timeless claim about every credential type or internal capability of Apple Wallet, Google Wallet, or third-party platform wallets. (§7.4, §7.7, §30.1)
37. **SIOPv2 is not required for EUDI Wallet RP integration.** SIOPv2 (Self-Issued OpenID Provider v2) is a sibling protocol to OpenID4VP within the OID4VC family, enabling user-controlled authentication via self-signed ID Tokens. HAIP 1.0 Final (December 2025) **explicitly removed SIOPv2** from the profile, recommending WebAuthn for pseudonymous login instead. No EUDI regulatory instrument (ARF, CIRs, TS1–TS14) references SIOPv2. While OID4VP 1.0 defines a combined `response_type=vp_token id_token` mode, this is outside HAIP scope. RPs may encounter SIOPv2 in non-qualified EAA/EBSI/DID-based ecosystems but do not need it for PID, QEAA, or PuB-EAA flows. (§10.6)
38. **Organisations acting as both Verifier and Issuer operate under two distinct trust chains.** The Verifier role uses WRPAC/WRPRC evidence for OpenID4VP; the Issuer role uses a Provider access certificate for signed metadata, an applicable Service registration certificate for entitlement/type authorization, Wallet Provider LoTE anchors for WIA/KA, and a separate Attestation Provider signing certificate for the credential. These roles have separate registration, keys, endpoints, status duties, fixtures, and telemetry. Banks already exhibit this duality in SCA flows (§17.4); the pattern generalises to separately registered EAA Providers issuing loyalty cards, student IDs, employee badges, or travel passes (§17.5).
39. **ISO/IEC TS 18013-7 Annex B creates a protocol-version mismatch with EUDI Wallet implementations.** The current 2025 second edition retains the `mdoc://` / older OpenID4VP lineage that diverges from the EUDI HAIP 1.0 use of OpenID4VP 1.0 Final, DCQL, encrypted responses, and URI-prefixed Client IDs. RPs should target the EUDI OpenID4VP profile directly or use the browser-mediated Annex C/DC API branch where applicable. A third-edition Committee Draft exists, but the article does not assume its final contents or publication date. (§10.8)
55. **OID-FED is already embedded in DR-0002 as a data format, but the protocol itself was not previously explained.** The LoTE Entity Statement format uses OID-FED (`application/entity-statement+jwt`, `/.well-known/openid-federation`), but the underlying protocol — trust chain resolution, Entity Configurations, Subordinate Statements, metadata policies, Trust Marks — was not covered. Readers encountering OID-FED references in §5.5 had no protocol context. (§5.5.10)
56. **Italy's IT-Wallet demonstrates a production deployment of full OID-FED trust infrastructure alongside ETSI Trusted Lists.** Italy is the only EUDI LSP using OID-FED as the complete protocol for RP onboarding, trust establishment, and metadata discovery — not merely as a data format. The Italian model includes dual `client_id` scheme support (`openid_federation` vs `x509_hash`) for cross-border interoperability, providing a concrete architectural precedent for other Member States. (§5.5.14)
57. **TS11 permits OID-FED for non-qualified EAA trust, creating an RP obligation to implement three distinct trust verification paths.** RPs accepting non-qualified EAAs must handle OID-FED trust chains, ETSI TS 119 602 LoTEs, and self-signed attestations — a significant increase in verification pipeline complexity compared to PID-only RPs. (§5.5.11, §5.5.19)
59. **Only two attestation Rulebooks appear in the pinned EC catalogue snapshot from 20 July 2026—PID v1.7 and mDL—with different source status.** PID is the operative natural-person source; mDL remains a working document with no legal value. The snapshot contains no healthcare, education, travel, social-security, LPID, or SCA Rulebook. Pilot validation and adjacent consortium specifications such as EWC RFC005 are inputs, not catalogue publication or production authority. (§6.11)
60. **The TS11 Catalogue of Attestations (V1.0.1) provides an RP discovery mechanism, but not an acceptance shortcut.** The `SchemaMeta` model provides machine-readable trust authority references, supported formats, schema URIs, and binding type, enabling RPs to build Rulebook-aware verification pipelines. However, catalogue registration is not mandatory for every attestation type and publication does not itself force RP acceptance or cross-border legal recognition; the Rulebook and applicable law still control acceptance policy. (§6.16)
61. **The education sector uniquely may use LoTE/EBSI-backed trust alongside standard Trusted Lists, creating a bifurcated trust verification pipeline.** DC4EU tested EBSI-backed educational credentials with `did:ebsi` identifiers. If educational credentials use EBSI/DID for trust anchoring, the RP's trust chain resolution differs fundamentally from the Trusted List model — requiring DID resolution, EBSI Trusted Issuer Registry lookup, and public key extraction from DID Documents. This is the only sector where an RP may need to support two distinct trust verification paths for the same credential category. (§6.17.2, §7.3.2)
62. **Hardcoded per-attestation-type verification logic does not scale beyond PID.** Healthcare, education, travel, and social security sectors each impose distinct trust models, format requirements, subject/PID binding obligations, selective-disclosure policies, and revocation models. RPs should implement a pluggable, Rulebook-driven verification architecture that routes trust resolution, schema validation, and obligation enforcement based on the current Rulebook plus `SchemaMeta` fields retrieved from the Catalogue of Attestations. (§6.18)
71. **CIR 2025/1569 Art. 4(5) mandates that QEAA/PuB-EAA providers make revocation status information available to relying parties with integrity and authenticity guarantees — establishing a direct RP-facing obligation that connects to the verification pipeline.** This is distinct from the general revocation check obligation: it places an explicit legal requirement on the provider side to ensure the revocation mechanism is reliable, and on the RP side to use it. The Commission also publishes a machine-readable PuB-EAA provider list (Art. 6) and maintains catalogues of attributes and attestation schemes (Art. 7–8). (§13.13, CIR 2025/1569)
75. **EAA Policy is a distinct trust-policy unit, not just another name for a Rulebook.** ETSI TR 119 479-1 clarifies that a broad ARF/EC Rulebook can coexist with a more specific EAA Policy for a Member State, sector, attestation type, or community. Where the credential, scheme, issuer metadata, or service policy exposes an EAA Policy identifier/version, the RP should capture it and route acceptance logic through it rather than whitelisting only issuer identity or VCT/docType. (§6.11, §6.12, §6.18)
76. **Long-lived EAA decisions need preservation of status evidence, not only runtime status checks.** A verifier can correctly reject revoked credentials at presentation time and still be unable to prove the past decision later if it stores only a boolean outcome. RPs with audit, dispute, regulatory, or signature-validation retention requirements should preserve signed status evidence or timestamped validation reports for the point in time of reliance. (§B.1)
77. **ETSI EN 319 412-1 should be integrated as a certificate-semantics substrate, not as a new wallet credential model.** It defines how common X.509 surfaces such as `serialNumber`, `organizationIdentifier`, semantics identifiers, natural/legal-person prefixes, local registration-authority bindings, and validity-assured short-term certificate extensions are interpreted. RPs should use it to parse WRPAC/WRPRC subjects, bank/PSP `PSD` identifiers, and remote-signing certificate models, while keeping wallet claim semantics, intended-use authorization, Status Lists, and trusted-list qualification checks in their own layers. (§5.1, §5.2, §28.3.1, §34.3)
78. **Draft ETSI EN 319 412-2 turns natural-person certificate handling into a profile-aware parsing problem.** The draft natural-person profile reinforces that `serialNumber` is not self-describing without semantics identifiers, `commonName` is display-oriented rather than formal identity evidence, certificate-subject `pseudonym` is not the Wallet pseudonym model, and natural-person signing certificates need key-usage, QCStatement, CRL/OCSP, and RFC 9608 no-revocation-available checks where applicable. Until V2.5.0 completes ENAP, use it as draft-aware source-watch guidance rather than a final hard baseline. (§5.1, §5.2, §18, §34.3, §35.5)
79. **The refreshed ETSI layer has three different implementation statuses.** `TS 119 478 V1.1.1` and `EN 319 401 V3.2.1` are published baselines; EC TS05/TS01/TS07/TS08/TS09/TS02/TS10/TS11/TS03 are the current published implementation precursors; EN 319 486, EN 319 487, EN 319 482-1 through -6, TS 119 476-2, and TS 119 476-3 remain draft/work-programme source-watch items. RP roadmaps must preserve those status labels instead of treating every ETSI work item as a published mandate. (§2.4, §38.2)
80. **Discovery/publication interfaces are evidence inputs, not acceptance shortcuts.** TS05 registry results, TS11 catalogues, TS02 provider publication, and TS 119 478 authentic-source interfaces improve registration, schema, provider, and upstream issuance evidence. None replaces issuer trust, LoTE/Trusted List authentication, credential status, holder binding, or the RP's own acceptance policy. (§4.4, §5.5, §6.16, §13.13.5)
81. **EN 319 401 is a provider baseline, not an ordinary-RP compliance label.** The standard supplies service-independent policy/security requirements for TSPs, while service-specific certificate, WRPAC, EAA, identity-proofing, validation, and remote-signing standards refine it. An RP's direct action is provider selection, conformity/qualification evidence, and ongoing supply-chain monitoring. (§5.1, §23.6, §35.5)

#### 36.2 Presentation, Verification, and Runtime Findings

6. **The intermediary model solves a real problem but creates reciprocal certificate, UI/log, and forwarding boundaries.** Topic 52 separates the association-specific intermediary WRPAC, the intermediary's unused-for-intermediation own WRPRC, and the single end-RP WRPRC selected for the current Service/intended use. The Wallet authenticates and cross-matches both certificate associations, displays only the end RP and end-RP Service for approval, records the intermediary and its Service in the transaction log, and sends the encrypted response to the intermediary. The intermediary performs the agreed credential checks, forwards only to the named end RP after all agreed checks pass, forwards to no entity on failure, and immediately deletes the PIDs/attestations and their User attributes.
7. **Pseudonym support is non-trivial.** RPs must support the four pseudonym use cases, implement the WebAuthn/passkey route where that is the interoperable Topic 11 profile, keep the architecture open for alternative compliant pseudonym technologies, and ensure they never refuse pseudonyms where identification is not legally required.
8. **User sovereignty is deeply embedded, but approval semantics are not "anything goes."** Wallet flows centre User approval and warning paths, but ARF Topic 6 prefers all-or-none approval for ordinary presentations because partial release can leak data even when the service cannot proceed. RPs should design mandatory requests accordingly, handle denial and warning outcomes cleanly, and accept partial approvals only under an explicit low-risk policy.
12. **SCA attestation type identification relies on profile/rulebook matching, not fixed VCT values.** Annex Topic 20 points payment SUA processing to TS12 and permits future non-TS12 SUA Rulebooks/specifications. RPs must dispatch by the requested SUA attestation type and associated profile rather than hard-coding one VCT or treating TS12 as the universal future profile. ("SUA attestation" is the ARF's generic credential class for strong user authentication with transactional data; "SCA attestation" is TS12's PSD2/payment-specific subtype, identified by `category: urn:eu:europa:ec:eudi:sua:sca` in the VC Type Metadata — see §17.1 for the full hierarchy.)
13. **W2W now has conditional Verifier Wallet proof behavior, but not a settled proof format or registered-RP identity.** In Wallet-to-Wallet flows (§16), the natural-person Verifier has no WRPAC or registration certificate.
