
<details>
<summary><strong>1. RP Server triggers a supplementary remote proofing step-up</strong></summary>

The RP receives a wallet presentation that is valid at the protocol layer but, under the RP's assurance profile (§26.1.2), still requires stronger user-binding evidence before onboarding, recovery, rebinding, or another higher-risk action proceeds. The RP therefore invokes a supplementary remote proofing path — typically selfie video, portrait comparison, or video capture of an identity document.

**Artifact Produced:** Session routed from normal wallet verification into a supplementary remote proofing workflow.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>2. Step-up Capture Channel requests face and optional document capture</strong></summary>

The capture channel opens the RP-controlled step-up ceremony and prompts the presenter for live face capture plus any optional documentary evidence the profile requires. At this point the RP assumes the next capture will come from a genuine person and genuine live artefact.

**Artifact Produced:** Active capture prompt awaiting live face and optional document input.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>3. Attacker presents a biometric or document presentation attack instrument to the capture channel</strong></summary>

Instead of presenting a genuine live face and genuine live document, the attacker uses a presentation attack instrument at the camera boundary: a printed photograph, silicone mask, projected face image, replayed screen video, or a forged / screen-replayed document shown during the capture ceremony.

**Artifact Produced:** Face and/or document capture stream containing non-genuine but camera-visible artefacts.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>4. Step-up Capture Channel uploads spoofed frames to the Proofing Engine</strong></summary>

The capture stack forwards the face frames and any document frames to the proofing engine exactly as if they had come from a genuine live session. Once this handoff happens, the proofing engine is the only control left that can still detect the spoof before the RP upgrades assurance.

**Artifact Produced:** Spoofed capture bundle delivered into the proofing engine evaluation path.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>5. Proofing Engine evaluates PAD and document-liveness checks but misses the spoof</strong></summary>

The proofing engine runs biometric genuineness checks, face comparison, and any basic document-liveness heuristics. If PAD is weak, thresholds are lenient, or the flow relies too heavily on a single face-match score, the attack instrument survives the check.

**Failure Path:** A well-designed step-up path detects the spoof here, emits `STEPUP_PRESENTATION_ATTACK_DETECTED`, and stops the session before any assurance upgrade occurs.

**Artifact Produced:** False-positive internal proofing state — spoofed capture treated as genuine.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>6. Proofing Engine returns a PASS result to the RP Server</strong></summary>

The proofing engine reports the supplementary ceremony as successful. From the RP's point of view, the remote step-up now appears to confirm that the presenter is the rightful user, even though the result was produced from a presentation attack instrument.

**Audit Telemetry:** Remote proofing logs should preserve PAD outcomes, challenge-response traces, decision thresholds, model version, capture metadata, and whether a human reviewer participated.

```json
{
  "signal": "STEPUP_PRESENTATION_ATTACK_DETECTED",
  "severity": "S1",
  "session_id": "stepup_sess_42a7",
  "evidence": {
    "pad_result": "FAIL",
    "attack_class": "PHOTO_OR_SCREEN_REPLAY",
    "face_match_score": 0.93,
    "document_liveness": "FAIL",
    "challenge_response": "INCONSISTENT"
  },
  "action": "BLOCK"
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** PASS decision returned to the RP despite a spoofed input stream.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>7. RP Server upgrades assurance and accepts the session on the false live-person result</strong></summary>

Because the supplementary proofing output is marked PASS, the RP upgrades the session's effective assurance and treats the remote ceremony as successful user binding. The original wallet presentation plus the spoofed proofing result now appear to justify onboarding, recovery, rebinding, or another higher-risk approval.

**Artifact Produced:** Fraudulent session accepted after a failed supplementary proofing control.

</details>
<br/>

**Attack Vector**: The RP adds its own remote live-person step-up on top of a wallet presentation and then over-trusts that step-up result. The attacker does not need to break the wallet protocol or issuer signature. Instead, the attacker defeats the RP's camera-side ceremony with a physical or screen-based presentation attack instrument. This is precisely the attack family highlighted in the ANSSI/BSI remote identity proofing paper: biometric presentation attacks and document presentation attacks are distinct from ordinary face matching and must be evaluated separately.

**Impact**: High — the RP may onboard or re-authenticate the wrong person despite having a valid upstream credential and a superficially "successful" local step-up. In banking or other regulated onboarding flows, this can lead directly to account takeover, mule-account creation, or defective CDD outcomes.

**Responsibility boundary**: Under amended eIDAS ([Regulation (EU) 2024/1183](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?qid=1732470539738&uri=CELEX%3A02014R0910-20241018)), relying parties remain responsible for authenticating and validating the PID / EAA they request from the wallet. By contrast, [Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/798](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2026/798/oj) governs **upstream** remote wallet-user onboarding by providers of person identification data / identity proofing service providers. It does not make the RP's own selfie or portrait step-up trustworthy by default. If the RP processes biometric data in that step-up, GDPR Article 9 special-category constraints and Article 35 DPIA expectations are engaged.

**Mitigation**:

- **Primary**: Do not default to portrait-based or selfie-based step-up where the RP can instead trust upstream user binding, device binding, and issuer proofing. Supplementary proofing should be profile-driven, not automatic.
- **PAD discipline**: If the RP invokes remote proofing, require explicit biometric genuineness / PAD controls resistant to photos, masks, projections, and screen replays. Treat face matching, liveness, and document liveness as distinct controls rather than one blended score.
- **Challenge-response**: Use randomised challenge-response and capture-integrity checks so pre-recorded media cannot satisfy the ceremony passively.
- **Human-review backstop**: Route elevated-risk failures or borderline scores into supervised review rather than silently lowering thresholds to preserve conversion.
- **Portrait optionality**: Because `portrait` is an optional PID attribute under [Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2977](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2024/2977/oj), the absence of `portrait` must not trigger an ad hoc weaker live-person control. If the profile requires stronger evidence, it must define the fallback ceremony explicitly.
- **Portrait lifecycle**: The User's approval to disclose/use the portrait does not authorize durable storage or unrestricted vendor routing. Purge it after the session unless the CIR 2026/1731 retention exception is documented, and block third-country/international-organisation transfer unless Union data-protection law permits it.

##### D.2.43 Remote Live-Person Step-Up: Capture-Pipeline Injection Attack

**Threat Summary**: The RP invokes a remote selfie / video-ident step-up, but the attacker bypasses the physical sensor entirely by injecting a pre-recorded, synthetically generated, or manipulated media stream into the capture pipeline. The RP's proofing engine receives plausible face or document video, yet it no longer has confidence that the stream came from the intended camera path.

**Classification**:

| Property | Value |
|:---------|:------|
| **ARF Reference** | — (supplementary RP-side proofing threat, not separately enumerated in CIR 2024/2981 Annex I) |
| **CWE** | [CWE-345](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/345.html) — Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity |
| **STRIDE** | Spoofing (fake user accepted) · Tampering (capture stream substituted before evaluation) |
| **Severity** | S1 — High |

**Attack Sequence**:

```mermaid
---

  themeVariables:
    noteBkgColor: "transparent"
    noteBorderColor: "transparent"
  sequence:
    messageAlign: left
    noteAlign: left
    actorMargin: 250
---
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant RP as 🏦 RP Server
    participant A as ☠️ Attacker
    participant SDK as 📱 Capture SDK / Browser
    participant ENG as 🧪 Proofing Engine

    rect rgba(148, 163, 184, 0.14)
    RP->>SDK: Trigger remote video-ident /<br/>selfie step-up
    SDK->>A: Open camera / document capture path
    Note right of ENG: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(231, 76, 60, 0.14)
    A->>SDK: Inject deepfake / virtual camera /<br/>altered document stream ⚠️
    SDK->>ENG: Forward injected capture as if<br/>it came from trusted sensor path
    ENG->>ENG: No IAD / tamper detection /<br/>challenge integrity check ⚠️
    ENG->>RP: Step-up marked PASS ⚠️
    Note right of ENG: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(231, 76, 60, 0.14)
    RP->>RP: Accept session as strongly bound<br/>to the user ⚠️
    Note right of ENG: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end
```

<details>
<summary><strong>1. RP Server triggers a remote video-ident or selfie step-up</strong></summary>

The RP starts a remote proofing ceremony assuming that face video and document capture will originate from a genuine camera path controlled by the wallet app, capture SDK, or browser. The entire assurance logic depends on that capture path being trustworthy.

**Artifact Produced:** Remote proofing workflow opened with an expectation of live-sensor input.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>2. Capture SDK or Browser opens the live camera and document path for the Attacker</strong></summary>

The capture client requests camera or document input from the presenter's device and prepares to forward whatever media it receives into the RP's proofing stack. This is the point where the intended trusted sensor path is supposed to begin.

**Artifact Produced:** Active device capture path awaiting live face or document media.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>3. Attacker injects deepfake or substituted media into the capture path</strong></summary>

Instead of presenting a spoof to the camera lens, the attacker inserts media into the pipeline: virtual camera devices, browser media-stream substitution, OS-level hooks, replayed screen capture, or deepfake-generated face video. The proofing engine no longer sees the physical world directly.

**Artifact Produced:** Capture client receives attacker-controlled frames rather than genuine sensor frames.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>4. Capture SDK or Browser forwards the injected stream to the Proofing Engine</strong></summary>

The compromised capture path forwards the injected video or document stream as if it came from the intended trusted camera route. From this point onward, later controls are evaluating already-substituted media rather than trusted raw sensor input.

**Artifact Produced:** Injected media stream delivered into the proofing engine evaluation path.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>5. Proofing Engine evaluates the injected stream without reliable injection detection</strong></summary>

If the RP or vendor capture stack lacks injection-attack detection, tamper detection, challenge integrity checks, or trusted media-path guarantees, the proofing engine accepts the injected stream as normal face or document input. Standard face matching can still succeed because the stream itself was tailored to pass it.

**Failure Path:** A hardened capture path detects virtual camera use, tampered media pipeline state, impossible challenge timing, or stream-manipulation artefacts, emits `STEPUP_CAPTURE_INJECTION_DETECTED`, and blocks the session.

**Artifact Produced:** False-positive internal proofing state based on a substituted capture stream.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>6. Proofing Engine returns a PASS result to the RP Server</strong></summary>

The proofing engine reports the supplementary ceremony as successful. Later review may misleadingly show "face match pass" and "challenge answered" even though the capture path itself was never genuine.

**Audit Telemetry:** Preserve capture-SDK integrity signals, virtual-camera flags, challenge-response timing, tamper-detection outputs, device attestation, and vendor decision metadata.

```json
{
  "signal": "STEPUP_CAPTURE_INJECTION_DETECTED",
  "severity": "S1",
  "session_id": "stepup_sess_b9d1",
  "evidence": {
    "virtual_camera_detected": true,
    "sdk_integrity": "FAILED",
    "challenge_timing_anomaly": true,
    "tamper_score": 0.98
  },
  "action": "BLOCK"
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** PASS decision returned to the RP despite a substituted media stream.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>7. RP Server accepts the session as strongly bound to the user</strong></summary>

The RP upgrades the session's assurance level and behaves as though the live user completed a stronger ceremony, even though the proofing outcome was grounded in an untrusted capture channel. This lets the attacker proceed through onboarding, recovery, or another high-risk flow under a false assumption of strong binding.

**Artifact Produced:** High-assurance decision grounded in a compromised sensor path.

</details>
<br/>

**Attack Vector**: The attacker targets the **capture path**, not just the face or document content. This is the ANSSI/BSI paper's injection-attack class: virtual cameras, deepfake stream insertion, manipulated document video, and other methods that bypass the intended camera or sensor channel. The RP sees a plausible stream, but cannot prove that it came from the expected device sensors.

**Impact**: High — once the capture channel is compromised, downstream biometric and document checks lose much of their value. The RP may incorrectly believe it obtained stronger user binding or stronger onboarding evidence, when in reality it only validated an attacker-controlled media stream.

**Responsibility boundary**: [Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/798](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2026/798/oj) and ETSI TS 119 461 strengthen the **issuer-side** onboarding baseline for PID providers / IPSPs. They do not transfer responsibility for an RP's own supplementary capture ceremony to the issuer. Under eIDAS Article 5b, the RP still owns the correctness of the validation path it operates or outsources. Where the capture path is vendor-operated in a financial-sector deployment, ICT third-party and incident-management obligations under DORA also become relevant.

**Mitigation**:

- **Primary**: Treat injection-attack detection as a first-class control, not a sub-feature of face matching or ordinary liveness.
- **Trusted capture path**: Prefer attested native capture SDKs or similarly hardened paths over generic browser upload flows for any ceremony the RP wants to treat as high assurance.
- **Challenge integrity**: Require randomised challenge-response, stream tamper detection, and timing analysis so injected media cannot simply replay a precomputed answer set.
- **Detection standards**: Test capture-path controls specifically against the injection-threat family described in CEN TS 18099 and referenced by ETSI TS 119 461, not only against ordinary face spoofs.
- **Outsourcing boundary**: If a third-party proofing vendor runs the capture flow, contract for explicit IAD evidence, audit rights, incident handling, and model / rule-change traceability; do not accept a generic "passed KYC" boolean as sufficient assurance.

##### D.2.44 Fallback Document Proofing: OCR and Document Authenticity Failure

**Threat Summary**: The RP asks for an additional physical document during onboarding or step-up because `portrait` is absent, risk is elevated, or the RP wants extra comfort beyond the upstream wallet presentation. The fallback flow then relies on OCR or ordinary image capture, or on a raw NFC chip read without the cryptographic checks that actually preserve document authenticity, allowing forged, altered, screen-replayed, or chip-cloned identity documents to be treated as trustworthy evidence.

**Classification**:

| Property | Value |
|:---------|:------|
| **ARF Reference** | — (supplementary RP-side proofing threat, not separately enumerated in CIR 2024/2981 Annex I) |
| **CWE** | [CWE-345](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/345.html) — Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity |
| **STRIDE** | Spoofing (false identity evidence accepted) · Tampering (altered or replayed document content) |
| **Severity** | S1 — High |

**Attack Sequence**:

```mermaid
---
config:
  themeVariables:
    noteBkgColor: "transparent"
    noteBorderColor: "transparent"
  sequence:
    messageAlign: left
    noteAlign: left
    actorMargin: 250
---
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant RP as 🏦 RP Server
    participant A as ☠️ Attacker
    participant CAP as 📄 Document Capture Flow
    participant ENG as 🧪 OCR / Document Engine

    rect rgba(148, 163, 184, 0.14)
    RP->>CAP: Request extra physical document<br/>for onboarding / step-up
    Note right of ENG: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(231, 76, 60, 0.14)
    A->>CAP: Submit forged / altered /<br/>screen-replayed document ⚠️
    CAP->>ENG: OCR + image extraction only
    ENG->>ENG: Data extraction succeeds but<br/>authenticity not truly verified ⚠️
    ENG->>RP: Document check marked PASS ⚠️
    Note right of ENG: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(231, 76, 60, 0.14)
    RP->>RP: Treat fallback document as strong<br/>identity evidence / user-binding support ⚠️
    Note right of ENG: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end
```

<details>
<summary><strong>1. RP Server requests an extra physical document as fallback evidence</strong></summary>

The RP decides that the session needs extra evidence beyond the wallet presentation. Typical triggers are absence of an optional `portrait`, heightened fraud score, or a policy choice that certain onboarding flows must collect additional documentary evidence.

**Artifact Produced:** Session routed into an additional remote document-capture workflow.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>2. Attacker submits a forged, altered, or screen-replayed document to the Document Capture Flow</strong></summary>

The attacker provides a manipulated document image or video: edited graphics, a photographed counterfeit, or a screen-replayed image shown to the capture flow. The goal is not merely to extract readable text, but to convince the RP that the document itself is genuine and currently possessed.

**Artifact Produced:** Document capture containing attacker-controlled document evidence.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>3. Document Capture Flow forwards OCR and image extraction input to the Document Engine</strong></summary>

The capture flow passes the submitted document images into the OCR or document-checking engine, often without an authenticity-preserving path such as NFC chip reading with cryptographic validation of the chip contents. For ICAO 9303 travel documents and similar eID chips, that means at least verifying the issuer-signed chip data and, where the document and verifier stack support it, enabling the optional anti-cloning checks (for example Active Authentication, Chip Authentication, or PACE-CAM) that prove the chip is genuine rather than merely readable. Without those checks, the engine is still being asked to make an evidential decision from weak inputs.

**Artifact Produced:** OCR and image-extraction payload delivered to the document evaluation engine.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>4. OCR or Document Engine extracts fields but does not truly verify authenticity</strong></summary>

The document engine extracts names, dates, and document numbers successfully. Because OCR or visual parsing appears clean, the RP may treat the fallback as trustworthy even though OCR only proves that text was readable — not that the document was genuine, live, unaltered, or held by the presenter. Even a chip read is only stronger if the verifier actually checks the cryptographic result; merely pulling fields over NFC is still data extraction, not proof that the chip is genuine.

**Failure Path:** A strong document-authenticity control rejects the artefact, prefers chip extraction where available, or marks the result as insufficient for assurance upgrade. Emit `STEPUP_DOCUMENT_AUTH_FAILED`.

**Artifact Produced:** Structured identity data extracted from a document whose authenticity remains unproven.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>5. OCR or Document Engine returns a PASS result to the RP Server</strong></summary>

The document engine reports the fallback check as successful even though it never established real document authenticity or current possession. This creates a false sense that the extra document is strong corroborating evidence.

**Audit Telemetry:** Log whether chip reading was attempted, whether issuer-signed chip data validation passed, whether anti-cloning checks (e.g. Active Authentication / Chip Authentication / PACE-CAM) were available and executed, OCR confidence, replay or screen-detection results, whether law or device capability prevented chip access, and whether the outcome was treated as merely supportive evidence or as a decisive assurance upgrade.

```json
{
  "signal": "STEPUP_DOCUMENT_AUTH_FAILED",
  "severity": "S2",
  "session_id": "stepup_sess_f0a3",
  "evidence": {
    "ocr_extraction": "PASS",
    "chip_read": "NOT_PERFORMED",
    "document_authenticity": "FAIL",
    "screen_replay_detected": true
  },
  "action": "STEP_UP_OR_BLOCK"
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Documentary PASS result returned without an authenticity-grounded evidential basis.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>6. RP Server treats the fallback document as strong identity evidence</strong></summary>

The RP treats the extra document as if it were strong corroborating evidence for the user's identity or for the user-binding question. Operationally, the fallback becomes a substitute for a better-defined ceremony, even though the document channel itself was weak. That lets the attacker complete onboarding or recovery with the benefit of a false documentary pass.

**Artifact Produced:** Wrongful onboarding or recovery decision supported by weak documentary evidence.

</details>
<br/>

**Attack Vector**: The RP relies on OCR or basic image parsing as though it were equivalent to genuine document-authenticity verification. Some implementations also over-credit any NFC read, even when they only extracted chip fields and did not validate the signed chip data or run the available anti-cloning checks. The ANSSI/BSI paper highlights this gap directly: OCR is fragile, easy to manipulate, and distinct from document authenticity. ICAO / BSI document standards likewise distinguish between reading chip data, validating that the data are issuer-authentic, and optionally proving that the chip itself is genuine rather than a clone. Chip reading is therefore materially stronger than OCR, but only if the validation stack actually performs and enforces those checks.

**Impact**: High — the RP may accept false documentary evidence for a higher-risk decision, especially where the fallback is used to compensate for the absence of `portrait` or to strengthen a borderline session. Even if the upstream wallet credential is genuine, the RP's own extra-document decision can still be wrong.

**Responsibility boundary**: [Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/798](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2026/798/oj) places remote onboarding duties on the provider of person identification data / IPSP for wallet issuance, and [Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2977](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2024/2977/oj) treats `portrait` as optional PID data. If the RP nevertheless asks for an extra document, the quality of that extra documentary decision belongs to the RP under eIDAS Article 5b's validation duty. GDPR data-minimisation principles also matter here: collecting extra documents without a clearly defined evidential purpose creates both security and compliance risk.

**Mitigation**:

- **Primary**: Prefer NFC / chip reading with cryptographic document validation, or another authenticity-preserving path, over OCR-only extraction whenever the policy and local law allow it. At minimum, verify issuer-signed chip data; where the document and verifier stack support it, also enable the optional anti-cloning checks (e.g. Active Authentication, Chip Authentication, or PACE-CAM) instead of treating a raw chip read as sufficient.
- **Authenticity ≠ extraction**: Treat OCR success as data extraction only. Likewise, treat a raw NFC chip read as data access, not as proof of genuineness, unless the corresponding cryptographic validation result is checked and enforced. Readable text or readable chip fields do not by themselves prove document genuineness, liveness, or current possession.
- **Profile discipline**: If the assurance profile requires extra documentary evidence, define the exact control set: whether chip access is required, which cryptographic checks must pass, whether screen-replay detection is required, what happens when law or device capability prevents chip access, and when mandatory manual review or a stronger ceremony is required.
- **Weighting discipline**: Where only OCR-heavy capture is available, downgrade the evidential weight. Do not treat OCR-only fallback as equivalent to upstream LoA High onboarding or to a stronger live-person binding ceremony.
- **Minimisation**: Do not request an extra document merely because it is available. Collect it only where the profile can explain why the extra evidence changes the decision and how its authenticity is verified.

##### D.2.45 Security Error Discrepancy Oracle

**Threat Summary**: The RP or a downstream wallet connector returns externally distinguishable failure reasons for security-sensitive ceremonies — for example `nonce_replay_detected`, duplicate `state`, expired session, malformed submission, or a named fraud-rule branch. That turns the error surface into an attacker-feedback oracle: a probing attacker can learn which control fired, whether a live session exists, and how far a crafted request progressed through the RP's pipeline.

**Classification**:

| Property | Value |
|:---------|:------|
| **ARF Reference** | — (supplementary RP-side error-handling threat, not separately enumerated in CIR 2024/2981 Annex I) |
| **CWE** | [CWE-203](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/203.html) — Observable Discrepancy; related: [CWE-209](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/209.html) — Information Exposure Through an Error Message |
| **STRIDE** | Information Disclosure (attacker feedback, control discovery, session-state leakage) |
| **Severity** | S2 — Medium |

**Attack Sequence**:

```mermaid
---
config:
  themeVariables:
    noteBkgColor: "transparent"
    noteBorderColor: "transparent"
  sequence:
    messageAlign: left
    noteAlign: left
    actorMargin: 250
---
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant ATK as ☠️ Attacker
    participant ORCH as 🎛️ RP Orchestrator / Edge
    participant CONN as 🔌 Wallet Connector / Verifier
    participant VSI as 📊 VSI / SIEM

    rect rgba(231, 76, 60, 0.14)
    ATK->>ORCH: Submit replayed / malformed / stale payload
    ORCH->>CONN: Forward for protocol handling
    CONN->>ORCH: Internal result:<br/>nonce replay / duplicate state / expired session
    ORCH->>ATK: Detailed external error ⚠️<br/>409 nonce_replay_detected
    Note over ATK: Learns which control fired<br/>and tunes the next probe ⚠️
    Note right of VSI: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end

    rect rgba(148, 163, 184, 0.14)
    ATK->>ORCH: Repeat with input variations
    Note over ORCH,CONN: Re-evaluate submission internally<br/>and preserve the precise classification
    ORCH->>VSI: Log exact reason, workflow ID,<br/>source IP, UA, timing
    ORCH->>ATK: Generic external failure<br/>with correlation ID only
    Note right of VSI: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
    end
```

<details>
<summary><strong>1. Attacker probes a wallet ceremony with crafted failures</strong></summary>

The attacker sends a replayed wallet submission, reuses an old `state`, submits an expired or malformed payload, or intentionally triggers a high-risk edge case to see how the RP responds. The goal is not only to fail the ceremony, but to observe the exact shape of the failure.

**Artifact Produced:** Crafted wallet-facing probe carrying attacker-selected failure conditions.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>2. RP Orchestrator forwards the submission to the Wallet Connector / Verifier</strong></summary>

The RP-owned edge or orchestrator routes the submission into the connector or verifier that performs protocol parsing, session lookup, replay checks, nonce validation, and connector-internal workflow handling. The connector now has the precise reason for rejection, even if the attacker should not.

**Artifact Produced:** Internal verification result containing an exact rejection reason.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>3. Connector classifies the rejection precisely</strong></summary>

Typical internal outcomes include `nonce_replay_detected`, `duplicate_state`, `session_expired`, `unknown_workflow_id`, malformed JWE / JWS, or a downstream fraud / abuse rule branch. These distinctions are useful inside the RP because they drive fraud scoring, audit records, alert severity, and analyst triage.

**Artifact Produced:** Precise connector-side failure classification tied to the RP workflow.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>4. Vulnerable RP returns the precise reason to the attacker</strong></summary>

If the RP reflects the internal classification back to the caller through distinct HTTP statuses, machine-readable error codes, reason strings, or visibly different UX copy, the attacker learns something about the hidden workflow state. This is the discrepancy-factor problem called out in the [OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html): externally distinct failures become an oracle.

```http
HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "error": "nonce_replay_detected",
  "error_description": "Submission reused nonce n-7f8a3bc1e9d2 for workflow wf_9f3e",
  "state": "sess_4721"
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Externally observable security error that leaks control and session-state detail.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>5. Attacker iterates and maps the RP's hidden control surface</strong></summary>

The attacker varies one dimension at a time: replayed nonce versus duplicate `state`, malformed body versus valid body on an expired session, known versus unknown workflow IDs, or requests from different IPs / devices. Distinct outcomes reveal whether the RP reached session lookup, holder-binding verification, fraud scoring, or a later orchestration stage.

**Artifact Produced:** Control-discovery map of the RP's rejection logic, session states, and defence ordering.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>6. Secure RP logs the precise internal reason into VSI and audit telemetry</strong></summary>

In the hardened pattern, the exact rejection reason remains inside the RP security domain even though the external response is normalised. The RP logs the internal classification, `workflow_id`, source IP, user-agent, timing, and decision stage into VSI, SIEM, and audit records so analysts keep the detail that attackers should not receive.

**Artifact Produced:** Precise internal telemetry tied to the RP workflow and external correlation ID.

</details>
<details>
<summary><strong>7. Secure RP normalises the external response and keeps the detail internal</strong></summary>

A hardened RP returns one generic external failure shape for security-sensitive rejection paths while logging the precise reason into VSI, SIEM, and audit records. Support channels get only a correlation ID; the exact replay / duplicate-state / malformed-submission reason stays inside the RP security domain.

**Audit Telemetry:** Log the exact internal rejection reason, `workflow_id`, source IP, user-agent, TLS / network context, connector decision stage, correlation ID returned externally, and whether the event contributed to fraud score escalation.

```http
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "error": "verification_failed",
  "message": "The wallet interaction could not be completed.",
  "correlation_id": "wf_9f3e"
}
```

**Artifact Produced:** Generic user-facing failure plus precise internal telemetry.

</details>
<br/>

**Attack Vector**: The attacker does not need a protocol break; they need a talkative error surface. Distinct statuses, JSON fields, error descriptions, timing differences, or front-end copy can all disclose whether a session exists, whether a nonce was valid but replayed, whether a fraud rule fired, or whether the request advanced to a later control stage. In OWASP terms, the RP has created a discrepancy factor. In CWE terms, the main weakness is an observable discrepancy, often accompanied by direct error-message information exposure.

**Impact**: Medium — the oracle does not directly forge a credential or bypass holder binding, but it lowers the cost of reconnaissance, replay tuning, abuse automation, and control discovery. It also exposes internal product topology and decision boundaries that should stay inside the RP's own security domain.

**Mitigation**:

- **Primary**: For security-sensitive wallet ceremonies, return a generic external failure rather than the exact internal rejection reason. This is consistent with OWASP guidance for authentication and other adversarial decision points.
- **Internal-only precision**: Preserve the exact cause internally for VSI, fraud scoring, SIEM, case management, and audit. The RP should know whether the event was replay, duplicate `state`, nonce mismatch, session expiry, malformed submission, or a fraud-rule hit even when the caller does not.
- **Response normalisation**: Keep HTTP status, body shape, and user-facing copy stable across replay, duplicate-state, expired-session, and malformed-submission paths unless protocol interoperability strictly requires a distinction. Avoid leaking connector class names, vendor error codes, session IDs, nonces, or workflow states.
- **Timing discipline**: Remove large timing and transport discrepancies where practical. A generic body is not enough if one path returns instantly with `404`, another slowly with `409`, and a third triggers a visibly different redirect.
- **Support boundary**: Expose only a correlation ID externally. Analyst and customer-support tooling should resolve that ID to the detailed internal reason without teaching the attacker what the RP already knows.

#### Signing and Trust Service Standards


- [ETSI EN 319 401 V3.2.1 (2026-01) — General Policy Requirements for Trust Service Providers](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_en/319400_319499/319401/03.02.01_60/en_319401v030201p.pdf) — Published service-independent TSP policy/security baseline refined by service-specific standards (§5.1, §23.6, §35.5)
- [ETSI TS 119 478 V1.1.1 (2026-01) — Interfaces Related to Authentic Sources](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/119400_119499/119478/01.01.01_60/ts_119478v010101p.pdf) — Published DIP/I1 discovery, ASIP/I2 verification, optional I3 retrieval, and the `Match` / `MatchWithVariation` / `NoMatch` / `Unknown` result vocabulary used by CIR 2026/1735 (§6.18.5, §13.13.5, §17.5)
- [ETSI ESI Work Programme — current draft-status source](https://portal.etsi.org/webapp/WorkProgram/Frame_WorkItemList.asp?SearchPage=TRUE&butExpertSearch=Search&includeNonActiveTB=FALSE&includeSubProjectCode=FALSE&optDisplay=ALL&qCLUSTER=17&qCLUSTER_BOOLEAN=OR&qEND_CURRENT_STATUS_CODE=11+WI%3BM58&qETSI_ALL=&qFREQUENCIES_BOOLEAN=OR&qINCLUDE_MOVED_ON=&qINCLUDE_SUB_TB=True&qKEYWORD_BOOLEAN=OR&qREPORT_TYPE=&qSORT=TB&qSTOPPING_OUTDATED=&qSTOP_FLG=N) — Status source checked 2026-07-23 for EN 319 478 V0.0.1, EN 319 486 V0.0.1, TS 119 476-2 V0.0.4, EN 319 487 V0.0.1, EN 319 482-1 through -6, TS 119 476-3 V0.0.9, and EN 319 401 V3.2.2 (§2.4, §38.2)
- [Cloud Signature Consortium API Specification v2.0 (CSC API)](https://cloudsignatureconsortium.org/resources/download-api-specifications/) — Historical remote-signing API baseline named by the pre-amendment Annex IV; retained for transition and legacy-provider analysis, not as the post-11-August-2026 legal floor (§34–§35)
- [Cloud Signature Consortium API Specification v2.2 (CSC API)](https://cloudsignatureconsortium.org/resources/csc-api-v2-2/) — Companion service surface to which ETSI TS 119 432 V1.3.1 is aligned; method support remains subject to the adopted provider/deployment profile beyond the clauses selected by CIR 2026/1731 (§34–§35)
- [ETSI TS 119 432 V1.3.1 (2026-03) — Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures (ESI); Protocols for remote digital signature creation](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/119400_119499/119432/01.03.01_60/ts_119432v010301p.pdf) — CIR 2026/1731 selects clauses `6.4.3` and Annex `A.6`-`A.8`; the broader document covers client security, `qesRequest` / `qesApprovalRequest`, and CSC API 2.2-aligned interaction patterns that require separate profile selection (§34–§35)
- [ETSI TR 119 462 V1.1.1 (2026-03) — Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures (ESI); Wallet interfaces for trust services and signing](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_tr/119400_119499/119462/01.01.01_60/tr_119462v010101p.pdf) — Informative architecture report covering driving-application / SCA / SCDev role splits, signing-request interfaces, certificate-model variants, and standards gaps for wallet-based signing (§34–§35, §38)
- [ETSI TS 119 431-1 — TSP Service Components Operating a Remote QSCD](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/119400_119499/11943101/) — Requirements for Trust Service Providers operating remote QSCDs; referenced by CIR 2025/1567 (§34–§35)
- [ETSI TS 119 431-2 — TSP Service Components Supporting AdES Digital Signature Creation](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/119400_119499/11943102/) — Requirements for TSP components creating AdES digital signatures (§34–§35)
- [ETSI TS 119 101 — Policy and Security Requirements for SCAs](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/119100_119199/119101/) — Policy requirements for signature creation and validation applications; required by QES_24a when the RP actually provides the SCA (§34–§35)
- [CEN EN 419 241-1 — Trustworthy Systems Supporting Server Signing](https://standards.cencenelec.eu/) — Defines Sole Control Assurance Levels (SCAL1/SCAL2) for remote signing; SCAL2 mandated by QES_23 (§34–§35)
- [ETSI EN 319 142-1 V1.2.1 — PAdES Digital Signatures](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_en/319100_319199/31914201/01.02.01_60/en_31914201v010201p.pdf) — Mandatory Wallet PDF-signing capability selected by CIR 2026/1731 from 11 August 2026 (§35.3)
- [ETSI EN 319 132-1 V1.3.1 — XAdES Digital Signatures](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_en/319100_319199/31913201/01.03.01_60/en_31913201v010301p.pdf) — ARF v3 `QES_08` SHOULD-level XML-signature format (§35.3)
- [Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1567 — Remote QSCD Management](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32025R1567) — Standards for managing remote QSCDs as qualified trust services (§34–§35)

#### Standards and Protocols


- [OpenID for Verifiable Presentations 1.0 (OpenID4VP)](https://openid.net/specs/openid-4-verifiable-presentations-1_0.html) — Final Specification (July 2025); extends OAuth 2.0 for Wallet-based credential presentation via `vp_token` and DCQL (§12–§14)
- [High Assurance Interoperability Profile 1.0 (HAIP)](https://openid.net/specs/openid4vc-high-assurance-interoperability-profile-1_0.html) — Final Specification (December 2025); profiles JAR, `x509_hash`, DCQL, and encrypted response handling for EUDI Wallet ecosystem presentation flows (§7)
- [OpenID for Verifiable Credential Issuance 1.0 (OID4VCI)](https://openid.net/specs/openid-4-verifiable-credential-issuance-1_0.html) — Credential issuance protocol used by PID Providers and Attestation Providers to issue credentials to Wallet Units (§16)
- [SD-JWT-based Verifiable Credentials (SD-JWT VC, draft-15)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-sd-jwt-vc/) — IETF draft (draft-ietf-oauth-sd-jwt-vc-15, February 2026); JSON-based selective disclosure credential format with key binding (§6, §10, §12, §A)
- [Selective Disclosure for JSON Web Tokens (SD-JWT, RFC 9901)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9901) — IETF RFC 9901 (November 2025); base selective disclosure primitive for JWTs — `_sd` hash mechanism, Disclosures, and optional Key Binding JWT; SD-JWT VC (above) is an application profile built on this specification (§6.1, §13.3)
- [ISO/IEC 18013-5 — Personal Identification — ISO-Compliant Driving Licence — Part 5](https://www.iso.org/standard/69084.html) — Mobile document (mdoc) data retrieval via BLE/NFC; defines DeviceEngagement, DeviceRequest, DeviceResponse, and SessionTranscript (§6, §14, §15)
- [ISO/IEC 18013-7 — Part 7: Mobile Document Online Presentation](https://www.iso.org/standard/82772.html) — Extends ISO 18013-5 with online presentation of mdoc via OpenID4VP (§11)
- [RFC 9101 — JWT-Secured Authorization Request (JAR)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9101/) — Signed and optionally encrypted authorization request parameters; mandated by HAIP for all RP presentation requests (§7, §10)
- [RFC 6962 — Certificate Transparency](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc6962/) — Baseline Certificate Transparency framework and artefact model still referenced by ETSI CT guidance and ecosystem transition language for WRPAC transparency (§5)
- [RFC 9162 — Certificate Transparency Version 2.0](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9162/) — Public audit log for X.509 certificates; relevant to WRPAC transparency and monitoring (§5)
- [RFC 9608 — No Revocation Available for X.509 Public Key Certificates](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9608) — X.509 extension used by the draft natural-person certificate profile when a validity-assured certificate exposes neither CRL Distribution Points nor OCSP access information (§34–§35)
- [IETF Token Status List — draft-20, CIR-pinned snapshot](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-oauth-status-list-20) — Exact draft selected by CIR 2026/1731 for the EUDI SD-JWT VC Token Status List profile, including ZLIB-wrapped DEFLATE, `sub` URI binding, and `iat` / `exp` / `ttl` processing (§14, §B)
- [IETF Token Status List — current standards record](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-status-list/) — Moving IETF record; draft-21 was the active revision in the RFC Editor queue on 26 July 2026. Track maturity and deltas without silently replacing the CIR-pinned draft-20 profile
- [W3C Digital Credentials API (DC API)](https://wicg.github.io/digital-credentials/) — Browser API for same-device and API-mediated cross-device credential presentation; invokes `navigator.credentials.get()` with OpenID4VP protocol (§10, §A)
- [ETSI TS 119 475 V1.2.1 (2026-03) — Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures (ESI); Relying party attributes supporting EUDI Wallet user's authorization decisions](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/119400_119499/119475/01.02.01_60/ts_119475v010201p.pdf) — Technical specification for RP attributes, WRPAC identity mapping, and WRPRC JWT/CWT structures (§4–§5)
- [ETSI EN 319 412-1 V1.7.1 (2026-05) — Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures (ESI); Certificate Profiles; Part 1: Overview and common data structures](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_en/319400_319499/31941201/01.07.01_60/en_31941201v010701p.pdf) — Common certificate-profile data structures for interpreting `serialNumber`, `organizationIdentifier`, ETSI semantics identifiers, natural/legal person identifier prefixes, eIDAS eID attribute equivalence, and validity-assured short-term certificate extensions (§5, §28, §34)
- [Draft ETSI EN 319 412-2 V2.5.0 (2026-05) — Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures (ESI); Certificate Profiles; Part 2: Certificate profile for certificates issued to natural persons](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_en/319400_319499/31941202/02.05.00_20/en_31941202v020500a.pdf) — Draft natural-person X.509 certificate profile in ENAP public enquiry/vote, covering natural-person subject naming, `serialNumber`, `commonName`, certificate `pseudonym`, key usage, CRL/OCSP, RFC 9608, and QCStatement linkage (§5, §18, §34–§35)
- [ETSI TS 119 472-1 V1.2.1 (2026-02) — Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures (ESI); Profile for implementation of PID and EAA credentials and claims](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/119400_119499/11947201/01.02.01_60/ts_11947201v010201p.pdf) — Supporting semantic baseline for PID/EAA categories, audience, subject identifiers, one-time-use, and status / short-lived semantics used by the RP-facing presentation profile (§12–§21)
- [ETSI TS 119 472-2 V1.2.1 (2026-03) — Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures (ESI); Profile for implementation of PID and EAA presentations to a Relying Party](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/119400_119499/11947202/01.02.01_60/ts_11947202v010201p.pdf) — Primary ETSI presentation profile for RP-facing OpenID4VC-HAIP and ISO/IEC-mdoc request / response construction, including `verifier_info`, `requestInfo`, and API-mediated vs non-API-mediated transport rules (§12–§21)
- [ETSI TS 119 472-3 V1.1.1 (2026-03) — Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures (ESI); Profile for implementation of PID and EAA issuance and disclosure policies](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/119400_119499/11947203/01.01.01_60/ts_11947203v010101p.pdf) — Issuance-side disclosure-policy companion to the 472 series; included as context for RP understanding but not as a primary RP integration target in this document (§2.4)
- [ETSI TR 119 479-1 V1.1.1 (2026-05) — Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures (ESI); Technological Solutions for the EU Digital Identity Framework; Part 1: Foundational EAA Concepts and Architectural Models](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_tr/119400_119499/11947901/01.01.01_60/tr_11947901v010101p.pdf) — Informative conceptual architecture report for EAA Service actors and components, EAA Policy governance, non-wallet delivery/vault boundaries, binding modes, and long-term status/preservation implications (§1, §2, §6, §17, §20, §35, §B)
- [ETSI TS 119 411-8 V1.1.1 (2025-10) — Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures (ESI); Policy and security requirements for Trust Service Providers issuing certificates; Part 8: Access Certificate Policy for EUDI Wallet Relying Parties](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/119400_119499/11941108/01.01.01_60/ts_11941108v010101p.pdf) — Policy and profile requirements for providers issuing WRPACs, including RP-visible status and transparency obligations (§5.2)
- [ETSI TR 119 411-9 V1.1.1 (2026-03) — Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures (ESI); Analysis of Certificate Transparency in the WebPKI and recommendations for use under Regulation (EU) No 910/2014](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_tr/119400_119499/11941109/01.01.01_60/tr_11941109v010101p.pdf) — CT ecosystem, role taxonomy, incident classes, and governance framing used to sharpen WRPAC transparency, monitoring, and response interpretation (§5, §31, §33)
- [ETSI TS 119 461 V2.1.1 (2025-02) — Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures (ESI); Policy and security requirements for trust service components providing identity proofing of trust service subjects](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/119400_119499/119461/02.01.01_60/ts_119461v020101p.pdf) — Identity-proofing and PAD reference standard cited by CIR 2025/1566 for QEAA issuance and by CIR 2026/798 for remote Wallet-user onboarding, and also used in `DR-0002` as the supplementary PAD benchmark for selected RP onboarding flows (§6, §28)
- [ANSSI / BSI — Remote Identity Proofing for EUDI Wallet Onboarding: Strengthening Assurance Against Evolving Threats (July 2025)](https://cyber.gouv.fr/documents/329/ANSSI_BSI_Joint_Paper_remote_identity_proofing_for_EUDI.pdf) — Joint security position paper decomposing remote proofing into biometric genuineness, document authenticity, and face matching; distinguishes presentation vs injection attacks; highlights OCR vs chip-reading trade-offs; and argues for harmonised testing and clearer LoA High mapping around ETSI TS 119 461, CEN TS 18099, and ISO/IEC 19989-3 (§13, §28, §26, §32)
- [ETSI TS 119 495 V1.8.1 (2026-04) — Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures (ESI); Sector Specific Requirements; Certificate Profiles and TSP Policy Requirements for Open Banking](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/119400_119499/119495/01.08.01_60/ts_119495v010801p.pdf) — PSD2/open-banking certificate-profile layer for bank/PSP personas, covering `QWAC` / `QSealC`, open-banking `QCStatement`, `rolesOfPSP`, `organizationIdentifier`, `NCAName` / `NCAId`, register-backed interpretation/revocation, and `VoP` role additions (§23, §28)
- [ETSI TS 119 612 — Trusted Lists](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/119600_119699/119612/) — Specification for EU Trusted Lists of Trust Service Providers; source format authenticated and interpreted via `ETSI TS 119 615` when RPs need trusted-list-backed qualified-status conclusions (§5)
- [ETSI TS 119 615 V1.3.1 (2026-01) — Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures (ESI); Procedures for using EU Trusted Lists to determine qualified status](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/119600_119699/119615/01.03.01_60/ts_119615v010301p.pdf) — Trusted-list interpretation procedure layer for authenticating the `LOTL` / national trusted lists, matching services to certificates, and deriving time-specific qualified / `Indeterminate` outcomes for certificates, `QWAC`s, `QSCD`s, qualified validation services, and `QEAAs` (§5, §13, §14, §35)
- [ETSI TS 119 602 V1.1.1 — Lists of Trusted Entities; Data Model](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/119600_119699/119602/01.01.01_60/) — Abstract data model for LoTEs generalising TS 119 612; defines entity profiles for Wallet Providers, PID Providers, Access CAs, PuB-EAA Providers, and WRPAC Providers; Annex H specifies the JSON serialisation used for non-qualified EAA Provider LoTEs (§5.5, §6.16)
- [European Commission EFDA — EUDI Wallet Lists of Trusted Entities](https://eidas.ec.europa.eu/efda/wallet) — Commission-hosted dashboard publishing the operational LoTEs for Wallet Providers, PID Providers, Access CA Providers, and Registration Certificate Providers; the live instantiation of the Common Trust Infrastructure described in §5.5.1 (§5.5)
- [Google longfellow-zk — Zero-Knowledge Proof Library](https://github.com/google/longfellow-zk) — Experimental proof implementation reviewed locally at snapshot `598816bbff1ac0ee190cc8b908cb15704e057ad8`; its repository does not establish universal proof-size or latency claims (§21)
- [IETF draft-google-cfrg-libzk-01 — A Verifiable Computation Scheme Based on the Sum-Check Protocol](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-google-cfrg-libzk/) — IETF draft specifying the Ligero-based ZKP scheme used for ECDSA anonymous credentials in the EU Age Verification App (§21)
- [ECDSA Anonymous Credentials — Nguyen et al.](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/076) — Cryptographic scheme enabling zero-knowledge proofs over standard ECDSA P-256 signatures without modified issuance; foundation for AV App ZKP path (§21)
- [IRTF draft-irtf-cfrg-bbs-signatures-10 — The BBS Signature Scheme](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-irtf-cfrg-bbs-signatures/) — IRTF CFRG Internet-Draft (Informational, January 2026); BBS multi-message signature scheme on BLS12-381 pairing-friendly curves enabling selective disclosure and unlinkable derived proofs; future candidate for EUDI ZKP credential formats (§13.9, §13.10, §21)
- [OpenID Federation 1.0](https://openid.net/specs/openid-federation-1_0.html) — OIDF specification for hierarchical trust chain resolution via signed Entity Statements and Trust Marks; used by Member States as alternative trust management model alongside X.509-based LoTE (§5.5, §31)
- [RFC 6979 — Deterministic Usage of the Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) and Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6979) — IETF RFC specifying deterministic ECDSA nonce generation to eliminate nonce bias vulnerabilities; recommended for RP-side JAR signing implementations (§31)
- [RFC 9700 — OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) — IETF BCP covering open redirector prevention, exact redirect URI matching, PKCE, and sender-constrained tokens; foundational security baseline for all OAuth 2.0/OID4VP implementations (§31)
- [University of Stuttgart — Formal Security Analysis of OID4VC Protocols](https://sec.ise.uni-stuttgart.de/research/oid4vc/) — Formal analysis of OpenID4VP and OpenID4VCI using the Web Infrastructure Model (WIM); identifies credential injection in Pre-Authorized Code flow, cross-device session confusion, and proves security properties of same-device flows under specified assumptions (§31)

#### Conformance Testing and Interoperability Resources

- [EUDI Functional Conformance Assessment Framework — current rendered documentation](https://conformance.eudi.dev/latest/) — Moving FCAF publication; use for current status while recording an exact release/maturity in evidence (§23.7.6, §29, §30.3)
- [EUDI Functional Conformance Assessment Framework — pinned source snapshot](https://github.com/eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-doc-functional-conformance-assessment/tree/f533bf8e7f72ccdb2a87b3f89842504e815baef0) — Source snapshot inspected locally for SUT/test-class scope, active-development status, `v0.x` partial-coverage boundary, and planned `v1.0.0` full-scope baseline (§23.7.6, §29, §30.3)
- [OIDF Conformance Suite](https://gitlab.com/openid/conformance-suite/) — Open-source conformance testing harness for OpenID4VP 1.0, HAIP 1.0, and OpenID4VCI 1.0; supports automated CI/CD integration via `run-test-plan.py` (§13.8)
- [OpenID Foundation Self-Certification Programme](https://openid.net/certification/) — OIDF-managed certification programme for OpenID4VP/HAIP implementations; launched February 2026; listings published on openid.net (§13.8.1)
- [German EUDI Wallet Sandbox (SPRIND)](https://opencode.de) — December 2025 evidence described an RP-facing PID test environment and Ecosystem Management Portal; current access scope and onboarding route require direct revalidation (§30.3)
- [EUDI Wallets Launchpad 2025 — Technical Report](https://ec.europa.eu/digital-building-blocks/sites/display/EUDIGITALIDENTITYWALLET/EUDI+Wallets+Launchpad) — European Commission interoperability event (Dec 10–12, 2025, Brussels); 570+ tests, 420 successful, 60+ testers from 16 countries (§30.3)
- [EC Relying Party Engagement Programme](https://ec.europa.eu/digital-building-blocks/sites/spaces/EUDIGITALIDENTITYWALLET/pages/978681884/Relying+Party+Engagement+Programme) — Current Commission engagement route for RP sector use cases, implementation scenarios, Member State onboarding, and expressions of interest; first webinar scheduled for 18 September 2026 when checked on 26 July 2026 (§30.3)
- [POTENTIAL LSP — Final Report](https://potential-eudigitalidentity.eu) — Large-Scale Pilot covering banking KYC, eGov, mDL, QES, ePrescription, SIM registration; 19 MS + Ukraine; 1,300+ tests, 1,000+ successful transactions, 249 cross-border; concluded Sep 2025 (§30.3)
- [grnet/eudi-web-wallet-mock](https://github.com/grnet/eudi-web-wallet-mock) — Mock web application simulating EUDI Wallet interactions with credential issuers and verifiers; useful for rapid RP integration testing without mobile apps (§13.8.4)
